### AGRIPPA (HEINRICH CORNELIUS) von Nettesheim, 1486-1535.

**1746. Three Books of Occult Philosophy . . .** <note>original Latin: "De Occulta Philosophia libri tres"</note>
small folio <note>a book format where the paper is folded once, creating large pages</note>, [*Cologne*], (1533).

With portrait on title-page; woodcut initials; figures and tables. Book 3 is followed at leaf F3 verso <note>the back side of the third leaf in the 'F' section of the book</note> by letters of Agrippa and, at leaf F6 verso, by the ‘Criticism or Retraction concerning Magic’ <note>original Latin: "Censura sive Retractatio De magia"</note>, from his ‘Declamation on the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences’ <note>original Latin: "Declamatio de incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum"</note> (Antwerp, 1531).

Book 1 was first printed by itself at Antwerp, by J. Grapheus, in 1531, quarto <note>a book format where paper is folded twice, creating four leaves</note>, and simultaneously by C. Wechelus at Paris. Both editions are exceedingly rare. The 3 books were first printed at Cologne by Johannes Soter in 1533. There are four or five issues of this date, distinguished by typographical differences. (Ferguson; see also Morley, no. 1750, ii, pp. 287 and 310, and Prost, no. 1751, ii, p. 513.)

Some copies lack the portrait. This is a thick-paper copy, the same as the Douce copy in the Bodleian <note>The Bodleian Library at Oxford</note>. Another issue in the Bodleian is on thin paper, but also has the portrait. The Douce copy, an exceptionally fine one, has a note on the flyleaf, “For a copy of this first edition Vogt says an Englishman at Frankfurt offered fifty golden crowns and more, but in vain.”

[William Osler]

<meta>This page serves as the official imperial privilege or copyright grant for the works of Henry Cornelius Agrippa, issued by Emperor Charles V. It establishes the legal protection for Agrippa's most famous writings at the start of the 16th century.</meta>

# CHARLES

By Divine clemency elected Emperor of the Romans, forever August: King of Germany, of Castile, of Leon, of Aragon, of Navarre, of Naples, of Sicily, of Majorca, of Sardinia, of the Indian Islands and of the Ocean Sea; Archduke of Austria; Duke of Burgundy, of Lorraine, of Brabant, of Limburg, of Luxembourg, etc. Count of Flanders, of Artois, of Burgundy Palatine, and of Hainaut, of Holland, of Zeeland, of Ferrette, of Haguenau, of Namur, etc. Prince of Swabia; Marquis of the Holy Empire; Lord of Frisia, of Salins, of Mechelen, of the lands of Utrecht, and ruler <note>original: "dñā teur," likely dominator</note> in Asia and in Africa.

To all those who shall see these present letters, greetings. On behalf of our beloved and faithful judicial counselor and historiographer, Sir Henry Cornelius Agrippa, Doctor of both Laws <note>meaning he held degrees in both Civil and Canon law</note> and Knight, it has been explained to us: That the said petitioner has recently composed and written four books, works, and volumes titled in Latin:

***On Occult Philosophy, Declamation on the Vanity of the Sciences, Commentaries on the Brief Art of Ramon Lull, and the Abbreviated Table. Orations & Epistles*** <note>original Latin titles: "De occulta Philosophia, De Vanitate scientiarum Declamatio, In artem breuem Raimundi Lullij commentaria : Et Tabula abbreuiata. Orationes & Epistolæ"</note> which books and volumes the said petitioner would willingly have printed in our countries and lordships; but he fears that some printers of our said countries, having obtained a copy of each of his volumes, might counterfeit them, which would turn to his great regret and damage, unless we provide him with a grace <note>a formal legal favor or exemption</note>. Humbly beseeching us that, in view of what has been said, it please us to grant and accord him that he may have the said four books and volumes printed by such printer in our said countries as shall seem good to him, without others being able to print them within the term of the next six years; and to this end, to issue our letters patent <note>public legal documents</note> relevant to this. For this reason, having considered these things: And after our beloved and faithful masters George de Themseke, Provost of Cassel, and Herman Suiderhuijsen, counselors and masters of ordinary requests of our household, have by our ordinance thoroughly seen, visited, and signed the said books. Favorably inclining toward the petitioner and his request. We have, by good advice and deliberation of council, granted, consented, and accorded: we do grant, consent, and accord, giving him leave and license of special grace by these presents, that he may and shall be able to have the said four books and volumes printed in such number and quantity and by such printer of our said countries as shall seem good to him. And so that this printer does not lose his pains, costs, and expenses which he must incur and bear for the said new printing and what depends on it, we have forbidden and do forbid by these presents all other printers and others that within the time and term of the next six years, they do not print or cause to be printed the said books nor any of them without the consent of the said printer, upon pain of confiscation of the books and volumes they might have so printed, and beyond this, of being punished and corrected arbitrarily. Thus we command our beloved and faithful chief presidents and people of our Private and Great Councils, the Chancellor and people of our Council in Brabant, the President and people of our Chamber of Council in Flanders, and all our other justices, officers, and subjects whom this may and shall touch, and to each of them in his own place and as it shall pertain to him, that by our present grace, grant, leave, and license during the time and in the manner said, they cause, suffer, and allow the said petitioner together with the said printer to fully and peacefully enjoy and use [this right] without causing or allowing to be caused any disturbance or hindrance to the contrary. For such is our pleasure. In witness of this, we have caused our seal to be placed on these presents. Given in our city of Mechelen <note>Malines</note>, the 12th day of January, the Year of Grace one thousand five hundred and twenty-nine. And of our reigns, namely of the Romans the 11th, and of Castile and others the 14th. Signed on the fold by the Emperor in his council.

->**L. de Soete.**<-

<summary>This document is a royal printing privilege granted by Emperor Charles V to the scholar Henry Cornelius Agrippa in 1529, granting him a six-year monopoly on the publication of his major works, including "On Occult Philosophy." It serves as an early form of copyright protection, threatening rival printers with the confiscation of unauthorized copies.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as the author's preface to the reader. It establishes the defensive tone Agrippa takes regarding the controversial subject of "Magic," distinguishing his scholarly "Occult Philosophy" from common sorcery or heresy.</meta>

->### TO THE READER.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'N' depicting a small figure, possibly a putti or a child, clinging to the framework of the letter.</image-desc>**I DO NOT DOUBT** that the title of our book, *On Occult Philosophy* <note>original: "de Occulta philosophia"</note>, or *On Magic*, will by its rarity attract very many to read it. Among these, some will approach with minds weakened by biased opinions, and many also with malicious intent, ungrateful toward our talent. These people, in their rash ignorance, taking the name of magic in a bad sense, will cry out—barely having seen the title—that we are teaching forbidden arts, sowing the seeds of heresy, and acting as an offense to pious ears and a scandal to noble minds. They will call me a sorcerer, superstitious, and demonic, simply because I am a <term>magus</term> <note>Agrippa uses "magus" here in its original sense of a "wise man" or "priest," though his critics used it to mean "black magician."</note>. To these critics, I would respond that among learned men, the word "magus" does not imply a sorcerer, a superstitious person, or one possessed by demons. Instead, it signifies a wise man, a priest, and a prophet. The **Sibyls** <note>Prophetic women of the ancient world whose oracles were later interpreted by Christians as foretelling the birth of Jesus.</note> were "magae" [female magi], and they prophesied most clearly about Christ. Furthermore, the **Magi** <note>The "Three Wise Men" from the Gospel of Matthew who followed the star to Bethlehem.</note> recognized the birth of Christ, the author of the world, through the world's wonderful secrets, and were the first of all to come and worship Him. The very name of "magic" is accepted by philosophers, praised by theologians, and is not unwelcome even to the **Gospel** itself.

I believe these critics of such stubborn arrogance would sooner forbid themselves from the Sibyls, the holy Magi, and even the Gospel itself than take the name of magic back into their good graces. They are so careful of their own conscience that neither **Apollo**, nor all the **Muses**, nor an angel from heaven could rescue me from their curse. To these people, I now advise that they neither read our writings, nor understand them, nor remember them: for they are harmful, they are poisonous; the gate of **Acheron** <note>original: "Acherontis ostium". Acheron was a river in the Greek underworld; here used to signify the entrance to hell.</note> is in this book. It "speaks stones" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to speak in a harsh, dangerous, or stunning manner.</note>—let them beware lest it knock out their brains.

You, however, who come to read with a fair mind, if you apply as much wise discernment as bees do when gathering honey, then read securely. For I think you will receive no small amount of utility and a great deal of pleasure. But if you find things that do not please you, pass them by and do not use them; for I do not advocate those things to you, but merely report them <note>Agrippa is using a common scholarly defense: he is a "reporter" of ideas rather than a "believer" in every specific detail.</note>. Do not, however, reject the rest for that reason; for even those who look into the volumes of physicians happen to read about poisons alongside antidotes and medicines.

I confess, moreover, that magic itself teaches many superfluous things and curious wonders for the sake of display; leave these aside as vain, yet do not remain ignorant of their causes. But those things which can be done for the utility of humans—to avert bad events, to destroy evil spells <note>original: "maleficia"</note>, to cure diseases, to drive away phantoms, to preserve the well-being of life, honor, and fortune, without offending God or injuring religion—who would not judge those to be as necessary as they are useful?

But because I have warned you that I have written many things by way of reporting rather than asserting—for it seemed necessary to do so lest we omit too few things—moreover, we have followed many of the opinions of the **Platonists** and other pagan philosophers where they suggested an argument for our plan of writing. Therefore, if there is an error anywhere, or if anything is said too freely, forgive my youth; for I composed this work when I was less than a young man, so that I may excuse myself and say—

<sig>aa ii</sig>

<summary>In this preface, Agrippa defends his work against charges of heresy and sorcery by redefining "magic" as a noble, scholarly, and even religious pursuit. He warns hostile readers to stay away while encouraging fair-minded readers to take what is useful and ignore what is reporting or "superfluous."</summary>
<keywords>magic, magus, Sibyls, Magi, Gospel, defense of magic, Platonism, occult philosophy, youth of the author</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's preface to the reader. Having previously defined the "Magus" as a wise man rather than a sorcerer, Agrippa now addresses the history of the manuscript's composition and its previous retraction.</meta>

-># TO THE READER<-

**In truth**, when I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child; but having become a man, I put away childish things <note>Agrippa is quoting the Apostle Paul from 1 Corinthians 13:11, framing his earlier work on magic as a product of youthful curiosity which he later viewed through a more skeptical lens.</note>. Indeed, in my book *On the Vanity and Uncertainty of the Sciences* <note>original: "de Vanitate ac incertitudine Scientiarum"</note>, I retracted a great part of this present book. But here you may perhaps rebuke me again, saying: "Look, you wrote this as a young man and retracted it as an old man; why then have you published it?" I confess that I set out to write these books when I was very young, yet with the hope of eventually sending them out more corrected and enriched. For that reason, I first offered them for correction to **Johannes Trithemius** <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), the Abbot of Sponheim, was a famous scholar, cryptographer, and occultist who served as Agrippa’s mentor.</note>, formerly the Abbot of Sponheim, a man most industrious in secret matters. 

However, it happened afterward that the work was intercepted before I had put the finishing touches upon it. It began to circulate in a truncated and unpolished state through corrupt copies, flying through many hands in Italy, France, and Germany. Already, some—I know not whether through impatience or impudence—wished to subject this unformed work to the printing press. Disturbed by this single misfortune, I decided to publish it myself, thinking there would be less danger if these books came forth from my own hand somewhat more corrected, rather than being spread abroad by the hands of others in confused fragments. Furthermore, I thought it no sin to ensure that the specimen of my youth should not perish. 

We have added several chapters and inserted many things that it seemed careless to omit—which the curious reader will easily detect from the unevenness of the prose itself. For we did not wish to completely renew the work or (as they say) "re-weave the entire web," but only to correct it a little and infuse it with some luster. Therefore, I ask you again, kind reader, do not judge these books based on the present time of their publication, but grant pardon to a curious youth if you find anything in them that perchance does not please you.

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory front matter of Agrippa's work. It transitions from his general address to the reader to a personal dedication letter addressed to his mentor, the renowned Abbot Johannes Trithemius. This letter establishes the intellectual context of the book: a collaborative effort to rescue "Magic" from its reputation as a dark or fraudulent art.</meta>

# TO THE REVEREND FATHER LORD JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF SAINT JAMES in the suburbs of Würzburg, Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim.
-> Sends Greetings <-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'C' depicting a human figure within an architectural or floral frame.</image-desc>
When I stayed with you recently (Reverend Father) in your monastery at Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipolis," the Latin name for Würzburg, Germany</note> for some time, we conferred together on many things concerning chemistry <term>alchemy; the study of transforming matter</term>, many things concerning magic, many things concerning the Kabbalah <term>a form of Jewish mysticism</term>, and other hidden sciences and arts which still lie concealed in secret. A great question arose among other things: why Magic itself—since it once held the highest peak of sublimity by the judgment of all ancient philosophers, and was always held in the greatest veneration by those ancient wise men and priests—was afterwards always hateful and suspect to the holy fathers from the beginning of the nascent Catholic Church, and finally exploded by the theologians, condemned by the sacred canons, and furthermore proscribed by the decrees of all laws. 

Looking for the cause, in my judgment it is none other than this: that through a certain fatal corruption of times and men, many pseudo-philosophers have crept in under the assumed name of Magi. Through various sects of errors and factions of false religions, they have gathered together many truly execrable superstitions and deadly rites, as well as many wicked sacrileges from orthodox religion, for the persecution of nature, the destruction of men, and the insult of God. They have published many books of condemned reading, such as we see circulating today, to which they have attached the most honorable name and title of Magic by theft and robbery. 

Thus, while these men hoped to gain credit for their own execrable trifles with this most holy title of magic, they succeeded in making the name of magic—once most praised—today most hateful to all good and honest men, so that it is considered a capital crime if anyone dares to profess himself a magus in doctrine or works. The only exception is perhaps some crazed old woman living in the country who wishes to be believed as highly skilled and divinely powerful, so that (as Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD), author of *The Golden Ass*, who was himself once accused of using magic to win a wealthy widow.</note> says) she can pull down the sky, hang the earth, harden springs, dissolve mountains, raise the spirits of the dead, weaken the gods, extinguish the stars, and illuminate Hades itself; or as Virgil sings:

> Who promises to release by her charms the minds
> Of whom she wishes, but to cast harsh cares upon others;
> To stop the water in rivers, and turn back the stars,
> And she calls forth the spirits of the night; you will see the earth
> Bellow beneath your feet, and the mountain ash trees descend from the mountains.
<note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book IV, lines 487-491. Agrippa uses these classical literary examples to distinguish "popular" sorcery from the "natural magic" he intends to defend.</note>

Then there are the things Lucan relates of that Thessalian witch <note>The witch Erictho from Lucan’s epic poem *Pharsalia*, known for gruesome necromancy.</note>, and Homer concerning the omnipotence of Circe. I confess that most of these things are the result of such deceptive opinion, such superstitious diligence, and such ruinous labors that, while they cannot fall under an art that is not wicked, they nevertheless presume to clothe themselves in the venerable title of magic. Since things stood thus, I wondered greatly, and felt no less indignation, that until now no one has existed who [would defend] such a sublime and sacred discipline—

<summary>In this dedication to his mentor Johannes Trithemius, Agrippa argues that "True Magic" has been unfairly maligned due to the actions of fraudulent "pseudo-philosophers" and superstitious practitioners. He intends to rescue the term from its association with dark witchcraft and restore its status as a noble, philosophical pursuit.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Trithemius, alchemy, Kabbalah, natural magic vs sorcery, Virgil, Apuleius, corruption of science, defense of magic</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues Agrippa’s dedicatory letter to Johannes Trithemius. It follows a discussion on why Magic has fallen into disrepute. Agrippa here lists previous authors who failed to represent the art correctly and explains his motivation for writing "Three Books of Occult Philosophy" as a way to "purge" the discipline of superstitions after being encouraged by Trithemius during their meeting in Würzburg.</meta>

### E P I S T L E.

...for they would have either vindicated it <note>Magic</note> from the crime of impiety, or handed it down to us purely and sincerely. Indeed, those more recent writers whom I have seen—**Roger Bacon** <note>original: "Rogerium Bachonem," a 13th-century English friar and philosopher</note>, **Robert the Englishman** <note>original: "Robertum Anglicum," a medieval astronomer</note>, **Pietro d'Abano** <note>original: "Petrum Apponum," an Italian physician and astrologer</note>, **Albert the German** <note>original: "Albertum Teutonicum," better known as Albertus Magnus</note>, **Arnald of Villanova**, **Anselm of Parma**, the **Spanish Picatrix** <note>original: "Picatricem Hispanum," a reference to a famous Arabic grimoire of astrological magic</note>, **Cecco d’Ascoli of Florence**, and many other writers of obscure name—when they promise to deliver magic, they have provided nothing but certain delusions backed by no reason, or superstitions unworthy of all honest men. 

Hence my spirit was stirred within me, and because of both admiration and indignation, I too wished to philosophize. I did not think I would be performing an unpraiseworthy work—I who from an early age have always been a curious and intrepid explorer concerning the operations of wonderful effects and those full of mysteries—if I were to restore Magic itself (that ancient discipline of all wise men) ransomed from the errors of impiety, purged and adorned with its own reasoning, and vindicate it from the injury of slanderers. 

Although I have long deliberated this with myself, I never until now dared to descend into this arena. However, after the conversation shared between us at Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipoli"</note> regarding these matters, your surpassing skill and learning, and your burning encouragement, added boldness and spirit to me. Therefore, having selected opinions from philosophers of proven faith, and having purged the introductions of the malicious—those who, lying with feigned knowledge, taught that the traditions of the Magi were to be sought from the very rejected books of darkness as if from the very inner shrines of wonderful operations—having discussed the darkness, I have composed in these recent days three books concerning magic, gathered into a brief compendium. 

I have inscribed them with the less offensive title *On Occult Philosophy*. I now submit these to your examination, you who possess the most complete expertise in these matters, to be corrected, judged, and evaluated. Thus, if anything has been written by me in them which might tend toward an insult to nature, an offense to the heavenly beings, or an injury to religion, you may condemn the error. But if the scandals of impiety are dissolved and purged, you might defend them by the tradition of truth. May you wish to act in this way with these books of ours, and with magic itself: that nothing which might be beneficial be hidden, nor anything approved which can do nothing but harm. By this means, these books, approved by your examination, may at last be worthy to go forth into public one day under happy auspices, and not fear to undergo the judgment of posterity. 

Farewell, and be indulgent of these bold undertakings.

<summary>Agrippa critiques earlier magical writers for their lack of reason and superstition, announcing his intention to "restore" magic as a legitimate discipline in his three-volume work, "On Occult Philosophy," written with the encouragement of Trithemius.</summary>
<keywords>Roger Bacon, Albertus Magnus, Occult Philosophy, Würzburg, Magic, superstition, Johannes Trithemius, restoration of magic</keywords>

<meta>This page serves as a reply to Agrippa’s dedication. Having received the draft of Agrippa's "Three Books of Occult Philosophy," Johannes Trithemius—a renowned scholar, abbot, and rumored master of cryptic arts—writes back to offer his enthusiastic approval and mentorship. He acknowledges the work Agrippa mentioned on the previous page as being of immense value to the learned world.</meta>

# JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF SAINT JAMES AT
## Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipolis"</note>, formerly of Sponheim, to his Henry Cornelius
## Agrippa von Nettesheim, health and
## love.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'O' depicting a scholar or monk's face within a circular frame, surrounded by leafy scrollwork.</image-desc>

**O**ur most distinguished Agrippa, with what great pleasure we received your work entitled *On the More Occult Philosophy*, which you offered for our examination via the bearer of these presents, no mortal tongue can ever express, nor the pen of a writer reveal. We are moved by the greatest admiration for your uncommon learning; though a young man, you have been able to penetrate such secrets and mysteries—hidden even from many most learned men—and bring them forth into the light not only beautifully and truly, but also correctly and elegantly. For this, we first give thanks for your benevolence toward us, and if we are ever able, we shall undoubtedly return the favor according to our strength. We approve your work, which no man, even among the most learned, could sufficiently praise. 

Next, we warn, petition, and request you with what urgency we can, that you proceed with study into higher things as you have begun, and that you do not allow such excellent powers of your genius <note>In this context, "genius" refers to both innate talent and a divine guiding spirit.</note> to grow lukewarm through idleness. Always exercise yourself through your labor toward better things, and demonstrate the light of true wisdom, with which you are so greatly and divinely illuminated, even to the ignorant. Do not let the consideration of any scoundrels <note>original: "nebulonum," literally "men of mist" or worthless people.</note> draw you back from your purpose, of whom it is truly said: *The tired ox plants its foot firmly* <note>original: "Bos lassus fortiter figit pedem." A Latin proverb meaning that those who are dull or set in their ways are often the most stubborn in resisting new ideas.</note>. Since, in the judgment of the wise, no one can be truly learned who has sworn loyalty only to the basics of a single faculty. 

Divinity has gifted you with a broad and sublime genius: therefore, do not imitate the oxen, but the birds. Do not think you must linger around particular details, but confidently turn your mind toward universal things; for a man is considered more learned the fewer things he is ignorant of. Indeed, your intellect, which is fully suited for all things, ought to be rationally occupied not with a few lowly matters, but with many and more sublime ones. 

However, we warn you to keep this one precept: communicate common things to common people, but higher and secret things only to higher and secret friends. *Give hay to the ox, sugar only to the parrot* <note>A metaphor for intellectual discernment: provide basic sustenance to the unrefined, but reserve the "sweets" of higher knowledge for those with the capacity to understand them.</note>; understand my meaning, lest you be subjected to the heels of the oxen, as has happened to many. 

Farewell, happy friend; and if there is anything in our power that can be of use to you, command it and you shall see it done without delay. So that our friendship may gain strength daily, write to us often, and we urgently pray that you send some of your late-night studies <note>original: "lucubrationum," referring to scholarly work produced by lamplight.</note>. Farewell again. From our monastery at Würzburg. The 8th day of April, in the year
->1510.<-

<summary>Johannes Trithemius praises the young Agrippa's brilliance and validates his work on occult philosophy, urging him to continue his studies while warning him to keep his most advanced secrets hidden from the "common" or "unrefined" public.</summary>

# TO THE MOST REVEREND
->FATHER IN CHRIST, AND MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE<-
->Hermann, Count of Wied, by the grace of God Archbishop of the holy church of<-
->Cologne, Prince Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, and Archchancellor<-
->through Italy, Duke of Westphalia <note>A region in northwestern Germany.</note> and Angaria, etc. Legate born <note>original: "Legato nato"; a title for certain Archbishops who held the status of a papal representative by virtue of their office.</note> of the<-

->pontifical matters, Henry Cor-<-
->nelius Agrippa of Nettes-<-
->heim, sends greeting.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter E, depicting four putti or young children in a rural setting with a tree and architectural elements in the background, all within a square border.</image-desc>
**S**UCH IS THE CELEBRITY OF YOUR ILLUSTRIOUS FAME,
most reverend and most illustrious Prince,
such the magnitude of your virtues and the splen-
dor of your learning, the frequent exercise of the
best literature, your grave speech combined with
solid prudence, and your elegant readiness of
speaking; such is your knowledge of many things,
constant religion, and most praised morals, with
which you are endowed far above the common
custom of others. I keep silent regarding the ancient lineages of your eminent nobility, and your treasures of riches both old and new, the breadth of your dominion, and the miters <note>The ceremonial headdress of a bishop, used here to represent his various high ecclesiastical offices.</note> of your sacred dignities, the excellence of which even rivals the decent form and strength of your body. Although all these things are very great, I nevertheless judge you to be far greater for all those heroic and most illustrious virtues of yours. By these you have truly ensured that the more learned and the more loving of virtue a person is, the more they desire to be introduced to your benevolence. For this reason, I too have decided that I must seek that honor of yours, but in the manner of the Parthians <note>original: "Parthorum more"; referring to an ancient custom mentioned by writers like Seneca, where no one was permitted to greet a king or prince without offering a gift.</note>—that is, I say, not without a gift. We see this custom of greeting a Prince derived from the centuries of the ancients down to our own times and observed even to this day. And as I saw all other men, distinguished for their learning, adorning you with the beautiful and great gifts of their teachings, I did not dare to approach your highness with empty hands, lest I alone appear as a deserter of your honor and veneration. While thinking and looking around in my library for what gift I might be able to bestow upon so distinguished a Prince, behold—among the hidden things, there suddenly offered themselves the books on *Occult Philosophy*, or *On Magic*. I had begun to write these as quite a young man, and had for many years set them aside as if forgotten. Soon, out of veneration for your highness, I hurried to complete them, as if to fulfill a vow. Indeed, I persuaded myself that I could give you nothing more pleasing than a new work of the most ancient and most abstruse doctrine—a work, I say, of my curious youth, but the doctrine of antiquity; I might dare to say...

<meta>catchword: re (short for "reddere" or "referre" in the following text)</meta>

<summary>In this formal dedication, Agrippa presents his "Three Books of Occult Philosophy" to Hermann von Wied, the Archbishop-Elector of Cologne. <meta>This page concludes the formal dedication to Archbishop Hermann von Wied. It follows the previous page's praise of the Archbishop’s virtues and titles. Here, Agrippa explains the history of the manuscript—revealing that it is a revised version of a work he began in his youth—and formally asks for the Archbishop's protection as he presents this "restoration" of occult philosophy to the world.</meta>

### EPISTOLA.

[this] matter, which no one until now has attempted to restore. Nevertheless, these works of mine are not dedicated to you because they are worthy of you, but so that they may open a path for me to your goodwill. I ask therefore, if it is not improper, that they might find some favor with you. I shall offer every prayer for your prosperity if these studies of my youth come to public notice under the protection of your greatness; and if—with envy driven away—their memory might endure by right of eternity to the benefit of my own good conscience, since many things in them seem even to my older self to be both highly useful and necessary to be known. 

You have here, therefore, a work not only of my youth, but also of my present age; for I have corrected many errors of that youthful work, inserted many things in various places, and expanded it with many chapters, which can easily be discovered from the unevenness of the prose itself <note>Agrippa is admitting that the writing style is inconsistent because he updated a manuscript written in his early twenties with more sophisticated thoughts from his middle age.</note>,

->and thus you shall know that I will be devoted<-
->to your service for my entire life. Farewell,<-
->most happy Prince of<-
->happy Cologne.<-
->From Mechelen <note>original: "Ex Mechlinia"; a city in the Burgundian Netherlands, modern-day Belgium, where Agrippa was serving as an archivist and historian.</note>.<-
->In the year 1531.<-
->In the month of January.<-

<summary>In this concluding dedication, Agrippa presents his revised work on occult philosophy to the Archbishop of Cologne, acknowledging that while it began as a youthful project, it has been significantly expanded and corrected in his maturity. # THE THREE BOOKS OF THE NOBLE MAN
## HENRY CORNELIUS AGRIPPA, GOLDEN KNIGHT,
### and Doctor of both Laws, Councilor to his Sacred Imperial Majesty and
### judge of the archives, Concerning Occult Philosophy, or Concerning Magic.
#### Three Books.

->Chapter One: How Magi gather virtues from the triple world will<-
->be shown in these three books.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'C' set within a square woodcut border. Inside the letter 'C' is a figure of a scholar or magus sitting at a desk, surrounded by objects including a globe and books.</image-desc>Since there is a TRIPLE WORLD <note>Agrippa refers to the Neoplatonic division of the universe into the physical, the celestial/astrological, and the spiritual/divine</note>—elemental, celestial, and intellectual—and since each lower world is governed by the one above it and receives the influx of its powers, it follows that the Archetype <term>Archetype: the original divine "blueprint" or God himself</term> and supreme Creator, through angels, heavens, stars, elements, animals, plants, metals, and stones, pours out the virtues of his omnipotence into us. For our service he established and created all these things. Therefore, the Magi <note>original: "Magi"; here referring to wise men or practitioners of high natural philosophy</note> do not think it unreasonable that we can ascend through these same degrees, through each individual world, to that very same Archetype, the maker of all things and the First Cause, from whom all things exist and all things proceed. They believe we can not only enjoy these virtues <note>original: "virtutibus"; in this context, "virtue" means an inherent power or medicinal/spiritual quality</note> which already exist in the more noble things, but can also attract new ones from above. Hence, they hunt for the powers of the elemental world through various mixtures of natural things via medicine and natural philosophy; then, they connect celestial virtues to those mixtures by the rays and influences of the celestial world, according to the rules of astrologers and the disciplines of mathematicians; furthermore, they strengthen and confirm all these things by the powers of various Intelligences <note>spiritual beings or angels that govern the spheres</note> through the sacred ceremonies of religions. I will now attempt to pass down the order and process of all these things in these three books: of which the first shall contain Natural Magic, the second Celestial Magic, and the third Ceremonial Magic. But I do not know if I am quite worthy of pardon—being a man of minor talent and learning—for having so freely undertaken such a difficult, arduous, and intricate business in my very youth <note>original: "adolescentia"; Agrippa began this work around age 23</note>. For this reason, regarding whatever has been said by me here and will be said below, I do not wish anyone to agree with me, nor do I agree with myself, any further than they have not been rejected by the Catholic Church and the assembly of the faithful.

From here, it produces its wonderful effects by joining the virtues of things through their application to one another, and to their suitable lower subjects, coupling and marrying the gifts and virtues of the superior things to the inferior ones everywhere. This most perfect and supreme science, this higher and holier philosophy, is finally the absolute completion of all the most noble philosophy. For since all regulated philosophy is divided into physics, mathematics, and theology: physics teaches the nature of those things which are in the world, and investigates and explores their causes, effects, times, places, modes, outcomes, integrities, and parts.

# BOOK ONE.
->a ii<-

<note>original: "Conueniat, quando armatas deducere classes, Aut tempestiua in syluis euertere pinum."</note>
It is fitting to know when to lead forth armed fleets,
Or when to fell the pine tree in the woods at the right season.

Theology, moreover, teaches what God is, what the mind is, what intelligence is, what an angel is, and finally what a demon is; it teaches of the soul, of religion, of sacred institutions, rites, temples, observations, and sacred mysteries. It also instructs concerning faith, miracles, the power of words and figures, the secret operations and mysteries of seals <note>The "seals" or "sigils" refer to symbolic diagrams used to represent spiritual forces</note>, and as Apuleius says, it teaches us to rightly know and be skilled in the laws of ceremonies, the divine law of sacred things, and the justice of religions. But now I shall collect myself. Magic itself embraces, unites, and activates these three most powerful faculties <note>The three faculties are Natural Philosophy (Physics), Mathematics, and Theology</note>. Therefore, it was deservedly held by the ancients as the highest and most holy science. This science is found illustrated by the most serious authors and most famous writers: among whom especially Zamolxis and Zoroaster shone so brightly that they were believed by many to be the inventors of this science. Following in their footsteps were Abbaris the Hyperborean, Charmondas, Damigeron, Eudoxus, and Hermippus; and other more famous priests emerged, such as Hermes Trismegistus <note>literally "Thrice-Greatest Mercury"</note>, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Plotinus, Proclus, Dardanus, Orpheus the Thracian, Gog the Greek, Germa the Babylonian, and Apollonius of Tyana. Osthanes also wrote excellently in this art; his books, dug up from a tomb, were illustrated with commentaries by Democritus of Abdera. Furthermore, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, Plato, and many of the most noble philosophers traveled to learn this art; having returned, they preached it with the highest sanctity and held it among their secrets. Indeed, we have it as a certainty that Pythagoras and Plato, for the sake of learning it, visited the priests of Memphis and traveled through almost all of Syria, Egypt, Judea, and the schools of the Chaldeans, so that the most holy monuments of Magic might not be hidden from them, and they might be imbued with divine things. Whoever, therefore, now desires to study in this faculty, if he is not learned in Physics (in which the qualities of things are declared and in which the hidden properties of every being are found), and if he is not a practitioner of mathematics (and in the aspects and figures of the stars, upon which the sublime power and property of every thing depends), and if he is not learned in theology (where the immaterial substances that dispense and administer all things are manifested), he will not be able to understand the rationality of Magic. For no perfect work exists from Magic itself, nor is there any work truly magical, which does not embrace these three faculties.

### Concerning the four elements, and their qualities, and their mixtures with one another. Chapter III.

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'Q' containing a seated figure, likely a scholar or author, at a desk or lectern, surrounded by foliate flourishes.</image-desc>
There are four elements and primary foundations of all corporal things: fire, earth, water, and air. From these, all "elementated" things <note>Things composed of elements</note> in these lower regions are composed; not by way of a mere heap, but according to transmutation and union; and again, when they decay, they are resolved back into elements. However, none of the sensible elements is pure, but they are mixed more or less and are transmutable into one another: just as earth, becoming muddy and dissolved, becomes water, and that same water, thickened and condensed, becomes earth; through heat...

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of how elements transform into one another and introduces the concept of the "threefold" nature of elements in magical practice.</meta>

<page-num>IIII.</page-num>
<header>ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY</header>

...moreover, when evaporated, [water] passes into air; and air, when overheated, passes into fire. Fire, when extinguished, returns to air; but when cooled from extreme burning, it becomes earth, stone, or sulfur, as is evident from lightning <note>original: "fulmine"</note>. Plato, however, believes that earth is entirely unchangeable, while the other elements are transformed into it and into one another. Thus, earth is divided by the subtler elements—not transformed, but dissolved or mixed into those things which dissolve it—returning again to itself. Each of the elements has two specific qualities, the first of which it retains as its own, while in the second it agrees with the following element as a middle ground. For fire is hot and dry; earth is dry and cold; water is cold and moist; and air is moist and hot. In this way, according to two contrary qualities, the elements are opposed to each other: fire to water, and earth to air. Furthermore, the elements are opposed in another way: for some are heavy, like earth and water, and others are light, like air and fire. For this reason, the Stoics <term>Stoici|Ancient philosophers who viewed the universe as a rational, living organism driven by active and passive principles</term> called the former "passive" and the latter "active." Furthermore, Plato, distinguishing them in another way, assigns three qualities to each: to fire, namely, sharpness, rarity, and motion; but to earth, darkness, density, and rest. According to these qualities, the elements of fire and earth are contraries. The remaining elements change their qualities from these, so that air receives two qualities of fire—rarity and motion—and one from earth, namely darkness. Conversely, water receives two from earth—darkness and density—and one from fire, namely motion. But fire is twice as rare as air, three times as mobile, and four times as sharp. Air is twice as sharp as water, three times as rare, and four times as mobile. Likewise, water is twice as sharp as earth, three times as rare, and four times as mobile. Therefore, as fire is to air, so is air to water, and water to earth. And again, as earth is to water, so is water to air, and air to fire. This is the root and foundation of all bodies, natures, powers, and wonderful works; and whoever knows these qualities of the elements and their mixtures will easily perform marvelous and stupendous works and will be perfected in natural magic <term>Magia naturali|The practice of using the inherent powers of the natural world, rather than calling upon spirits or demons, to achieve results</term>.

-> Concerning the threefold nature of the elements to be considered. Chapter IV. <-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring a cherub or child's face within a circular frame surrounded by foliage.</image-desc> There are, then, four elements which we have mentioned, without the perfect knowledge of which we can produce no effect in Magic. Moreover, each of them is threefold, so that the number four <note>the four elements</note> completes the number twelve <note>often associated with the signs of the Zodiac</note>; and progressing through the seven to the ten, it reaches the supreme unity—from which all power and wonderful operation depend. In the first order, therefore, the elements are pure; they are neither composed nor changed, nor do they undergo mixing, but are incorruptible. It is not *from* them, but *through* them, that the powers of all natural things are brought into effect. Their powers can be explained by no one, because they can do all things in all things. He who is ignorant of these cannot reach the operation of any marvelous effects. The elements of the second order are composed, manifold, varied, and impure; yet they can be reduced by art to pure simplicity; to these then...

returned to their own simplicity, virtue is above all the fulfillment that completes all occult and natural operations: and these are the foundation of all natural Magic. The elements of the third order are not elements primarily in themselves, but are composites <note>original: "decomposita"</note>, varied, manifold, and interchangeable with one another: they are an infallible medium, and therefore are called the "means of nature," or the "soul of nature’s middle ground" <note>original: "anima mediæ naturæ"</note>: there are very few who understand their profound mysteries. In these, through certain numbers, degrees, and orders, is the completion of every effect in any natural, celestial, or super-celestial thing. They are wonderful and full of mysteries that can be worked in Magic, both natural and divine: for through them, the bindings <note>original: "ligationes"</note>, as well as the loosenings and transmutations of all things, the knowledge and prediction of the future—even the driving out of evil demons and the conciliation of good spirits—descends from them. Without these threefold elements and the knowledge of them, let no one trust that they can perform anything in the occult sciences of Magic and nature. However, whoever knows how to reduce these into those—the impure into the pure, the manifold into the simple—and knows how to discern their nature, virtue, and power in number, degrees, and order without dividing the substance: that person shall easily obtain the science and perfect operation of all natural things and celestial secrets.

### On the wonderful natures of fire and earth. Chapter V.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'A' depicting a personified figure, possibly a wind god or celestial being, seated among swirling clouds.</image-desc>

FOR the operation of all wonders, says Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of alchemy and magic</note>, two things suffice: fire and earth; the latter is passive, the former is active. Fire (as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says) comes clearly in all and through all, and is yet removed; it is bright to all, yet simultaneously hidden and unknown; when it is by itself, without the presence of matter in which to manifest its own action, it is boundless and invisible, powerful in its own right for its own action, mobile, yielding itself to all things that approach it in any way, renewing, the guardian of nature, illuminating, ungraspable by virtue of its veiled splendors, clear, distinct, leaping back, tending upward, moving sharply, exalted, not subject to the insult of being diminished, always moving and causing movement, grasping others while remaining ungrasped, not needing another, growing secretly from itself, and manifesting its own greatness to the materials it takes up, active, powerful, present invisibly to all things at once; it does not allow itself to be neglected, but like a kind of vengeance, generally and specifically it suddenly reduces things to reason; it is incomprehensible, impalpable, not diminished, most lavishly distributed in all its own transmissions. Fire is a boundless and unruly portion of things (as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the Roman "Natural History"</note> says), and it is doubtful whether it consumes more or brings forth more. Fire itself is one, and penetrating through all things, as the Pythagoreans <term>Pythagorici|Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed the universe was built on mathematical principles and harmony</term> say, but it is dilated in heaven and shining, yet constricted in hell, dark and tormenting; in the middle world it participates in both. Fire, therefore, is one in itself, but manifold in the recipient, and distributed in different ways according to different things, as Cleanthes <note>A Stoic philosopher whose views were preserved by the Roman orator Cicero</note> testifies in Cicero. There is also this adventitious <note>original: "adinuentitius," meaning artificial or acquired</note> fire which we use: it is in stones, which by the strike of an iron...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter V regarding the wonderful natures of fire and earth. It concludes the description of earth as the "first matter" and begins Chapter VI, which focuses on the properties of water and air.</meta>

<page-num>VI.</page-num>
<header>VI. ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,</header>

struck from steel <note>original: "chalybis excuritur"</note>: it is in the earth, which fumes when it is dug up: it is in the waters, heating springs and wells: it is in the deep sea, which grows warm when agitated by the winds: it is in the air, which we often see glowing with heat: and every animal, all living things, and all plants are nourished by heat: and everything that lives, lives because of the fire enclosed within it. The properties of the **Supernal fire** are a heat that makes all things fruitful, and a light that grants life to all. The properties of the **Infernal fire** are a burning that consumes all things, and a darkness that fills everything with sterility. Therefore, celestial and bright fire puts to flight dark demons: and even our fire made of wood <note>original: "ligneus"; referring to common terrestrial fire</note> puts them to flight, insofar as it possesses an image and is a vehicle of that higher light. Indeed, it is a vehicle of Him who said, *I am the light of the world* <note>original: "Ego sum lux mundi"</note>, who is the true fire, the *father of lights* <note>original: "pater luminum"</note>, from whom every best gift comes, sending out the splendor of his fire and communicating it first to the sun and the other celestial bodies, and through these—as if through intermediate instruments—pouring that light into our own fire. Just as the demons of darkness are more powerful in the darkness itself, so the good demons—who are angels of light—receive an increase of power from light, not only from the divine, solar, and celestial light, but even from the fire that is among us. For this reason, the first and wisest founders of religions and ceremonies decreed that prayers, psalm-singing, and all sacred rites should not be performed except with lamps lit. From this comes that symbol of **Pythagoras**: *Do not speak of God without light.* They also commanded that, to drive away evil demons, lights and fires should be lit near the bodies of the dead, and not be removed until the earth covers them after the sacred rites of expiation are finished. The Almighty himself, in the Old Law <note>A reference to the laws of the Torah or Old Testament</note>, required all his sacrifices to be offered by fire, and that a fire should always burn upon the altar—a tradition which the priests of **Vesta** <note>The Roman goddess of the hearth, whose priestesses maintained a perpetual flame</note> among the Romans also kept and guarded perpetually. 

The basis and foundation of all elements, however, is the **Earth**. For she is the object, the subject, and the receiver of all celestial rays and influences. She contains within herself the seeds <note>original: "feminas," likely a typo for "semina"</note> and feminine virtues of all things. Therefore, she is said to be animal, vegetable, and mineral: fertilized by all the other elements and the heavens, she is the mother of all things generated from herself. She is the receiver of all fertility, and like a first parent, she is the source of all budding growth, the center, the foundation, and the mother of all. If you take from her any amount of her secrets—washed, purified, and refined—and leave them for a time under the open sky, she will soon be fertilized by celestial powers; becoming pregnant, she will produce plants from herself, produce little worms and animals, produce small stones and bright sparks of metals. In her are the greatest secrets, if she is ever purified by the art of fire and reduced to her simplicity by a proper washing. She is the first matter <note>original: "materia"</note> of our creation and the truest medicine for our restoration and preservation.

## On the wonderful natures of water, and air, and the winds. Chapter VI.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial N featuring a figure seated at a desk or table, possibly a scholar or monk engaged in study.</image-desc>

**N**o less powerful are the remaining two elements, namely **Water** and **Air**: nor does nature cease to work wonders in them. For the necessity of Water is so great that without it no animal could live: no herb or plant of any kind could grow without the moistening of water...

<page-num>vii.</page-num>
->### BOOK ONE.<-

...to illuminate. <note>original: "minare"; likely the conclusion of "illuminare" from the previous page.</note> Within water itself is the seminal virtue <term>seminal virtue: the inherent power or "blueprint" within a substance that allows it to generate life</term> of all things: first of animals, whose seed is clearly aqueous; but also the seeds of shrubs and herbs, though they be earthy, must be liquefied by water if they are to be fruitful, whether this happens by the moisture of the earth being absorbed, or by dew, or rain, or by water applied by industry. For only earth and water are described by Moses as producing a living soul. But to water he attributes a double production: namely, of those things swimming in the waters, and of those things flying in the air above the earth. The same scripture <note>Referring to the Book of Genesis.</note> testifies that even earthly productions are partly owed to water, saying that after creation, shrubs and plants had not germinated because God had not yet sent rain upon the earth. Such is the power of this element that even spiritual regeneration <note>original: "spiritualis regeneratio"; referring to the Christian sacrament of Baptism.</note> does not occur without water, as Christ himself testified to Nicodemus. Its power in religion is also greatest, in expiations and purifications, nor is its necessity less than that of fire. Its uses are infinite, and its applications manifold; all things consist of its power, as it possesses the power of generating, nourishing, and increasing. 

Hence ***Thales of Miletus*** <note>An early Greek philosopher who argued that water was the primary substance of the universe.</note> and ***Hesiod*** established water as the principle of all things, and called it the most ancient and powerful of all elements, since it commands all others. For, as ***Pliny*** says, waters devour the lands; they kill flames; they climb on high and claim the sky for themselves by the covering of clouds; these same waters falling become the cause of all things born from the earth. Innumerable are the miracles of waters described by ***Pliny***, ***Solinus***, and many historians, of whose miraculous power ***Ovid*** also makes mention in these verses:

> *At midday, your wave, O horn-bearing Hammon,* <note>original: "Hammon"; referring to the oracle of Jupiter-Ammon in the Libyan desert, whose spring was said to change temperature.</note>
> *Is cold, but at sunrise and sunset it grows warm.*
> *It is told that wood is set on fire by the touch of Athamantis’s waters,*
> *When the moon has retreated into its smallest circles.*
> *The Cicones have a river which, when drunk, turns one's*
> *Entrails to stone, and covers touched objects with marble.*
> *The Crathis and the neighboring Sybaris in your lands*
> *Make hair like amber and gold.*
> *What is more wonderful: there are some waters that can change not only bodies,*
> *But even minds. Who has not heard of the obscene waves of Salmacis?* <note>In mythology, the spring of Salmacis merged the bodies of a nymph and Hermaphroditus.</note>
> *Or the lakes of the Ethiopians? If anyone drinks from these,*
> *He either goes mad or falls into a sleep of strange heaviness.*
> *Whoever quenches his thirst from the Clitorian fount*
> *Shuns wine and, becoming abstinent, delights in pure water.*
> *Opposite in effect flows the Lyncestian river:*
> *Whoever drinks from it with an immoderate throat*
> *Stumbles as if he had drunk pure wine.*
> *There is a lake of Arcadia—the ancients called it Pheneus—*
> *Distrusted for its ambiguous waters, which you should fear at night;*
> *Drunk at night, they are harmful, but by day they are drunk without harm.*

VIII.

-># OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,<-

**Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> also reports the wonderful nature of a certain river between the cities of Arcaea and Raphanea in **Syria**: which, though it flows with a full channel, soon fails through the entire Sabbath as if its springs were stopped, providing a dry crossing of its bed for six whole days. Then, on the seventh day, by unknown causes of nature, it returns to its former abundance of water; for which reason the inhabitants called it the **Sabbatical River**, on account of the seventh day sacred to the **Jews**. The **Gospel** <note>Referring to the Gospel of John 5:2–4.</note> also testifies to us concerning the **Pool of Bethesda** <note>original: "piscina probatica"; literally the "Sheep Pool."</note> into which, after the water was stirred by an angel, whoever descended first was freed from whatever sickness he had. The same force and power is read to have belonged to the spring of the **Ionides Nymphs**, which stood in the territory of the **Eleans** at the village of **Heraclea** near the river **Cytheron**: into which, if one with a diseased body descended, they would depart sound and whole, with every bodily defect driven away. **Pausanias** <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> tells that on **Mount Lycaeus** in **Arcadia** there is a spring called **Agria**, to which, as often as the dryness of the region threatened the destruction of the crops, the priest of **Lycaean Jupiter** <note>original: "Iovis Lycæi"; the local Arcadian form of Zeus.</note> would enter. After sacrificing victims and venerating the sacred waters with holy prayers, holding an oak branch in his hand, he would lower it into the surface of the sacred spring. Then, the waters being stirred, a vapor was carried upward into the air and gathered into clouds; with the mists rushing together, the whole sky was covered in clouds, which shortly after dissolved into rain and healthfully irrigated the entire region. Indeed, concerning the miracles of waters, besides many other authors, **Rufus of Ephesus** <note>A prominent Greek physician and anatomist.</note> wrote many marvelous things which are found in no other author that I know of.

It remains to speak of the **Air**. This is the **vital spirit** <term>vital spirit: a life-force believed to permeate the body and the universe, acting as the bridge between soul and matter</term>, permeating all beings, providing life and consistency to all things, binding, moving, and filling everything. Hence the doctors of the **Hebrews** do not number it among the elements, but regard it as a medium and glue, joining diverse things together, and as it were the resounding spirit of the world's instrument. For it most closely receives the influx of all celestial bodies into itself and communicates them to the other elements, as well as to individual mixed bodies. Not least, it also receives and retains within itself the **species** <term>species: in ancient physics, these are the "forms" or "images" that objects emanate, allowing them to be perceived by the senses</term> of all things, whether natural or artificial, and of whatever speeches, like a certain **divine mirror**. Carrying these with it, and entering through the pores of the bodies of men and animals, it impresses them upon them both in sleep and in waking, providing the material for various wonderful dreams, presages, and omens. Hence also they say it happens that one passing a place where a man has been killed, or where a fresh corpse is hidden, is moved by fear and dread: because the air in that place is full of the **horrible species of homicide**, and while it is inhaled, it affects and disturbs the spirit of the man with similar images; from which it happens that fear follows. For everything that makes a sudden impression astounds nature. Hence many philosophers have thought that the air is the cause of dreams and many other impressions on the soul, through the carrying of **idols** <term>idols: from the Greek "eidolon," meaning phantom images or mental representations that travel from an object to the observer</term>, or likenesses, or species, which fall away from things and speeches multiplied in the air itself, until they reach the senses, and finally the imagination and the soul of the receiver—namely, that soul which is free from cares and not hindered, which...

IX.

### BOOK FIRST.

...expecting something of this kind to meet him, he is informed by them. For the very forms <note>original: "species"; in medieval philosophy, these are the sensible likenesses or "images" that objects emit so they can be perceived by the senses.</note> of things, although by their own nature they are carried to the senses of men and animals, can nevertheless receive some impression from the heavens while they are in the air. By this impression, combined with the aptitude and disposition of the receiver, these forms may be carried more effectively to the senses of one person than to another. And from this it is naturally possible—and far from all superstition, with no other spirit mediating—for a man to be able to announce the conception of his mind to another man at any distance, however great or unknown, in a very short time. Even if the time in which this happens cannot be precisely measured, it must necessarily occur within twenty-four hours. I know how to do this, and have done it often. <term>Abbot Trithemius also knew and did the same thing once.</term> <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a Benedictine abbot and polymath famous for his "Steganographia," which combined cryptography with claims of spirit-assisted long-distance communication.</note>

How also certain images <note>original: "idola"; referring here to optical phantoms or visual emanations rather than religious icons.</note>—not only spiritual but also natural—flow out from things (as if through a certain influence of bodies from other bodies) and gain strength in the air itself, and then show themselves to us through light, motion, sight, and even other senses, sometimes performing wonders within us, is proven and taught by <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who wrote extensively on how the soul and cosmos interact.</note>. And we see how, when the south wind blows, the air is thickened into thin clouds in which images of very distant camps, mountains, horses, men, and other things are reflected as if in a mirror; these vanish as soon as the clouds depart. And in his <term>Meteorology</term>, <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose "Meteorologica" was the standard text on atmospheric phenomena.</note> reveals that the rainbow is formed in a cloud of air through a likeness to a mirror. And <term>Albertus Magnus</term> <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and "Universal Doctor" known for his scientific and occult interests.</note> says that the likenesses of bodies can easily be formed in moist air by the force of nature, in the same way that the images of things exist within the things themselves. 

<term>Aristotle</term> also tells of a man who, because of the weakness of his sight, found that the nearby air became like a mirror for him; his visual ray was reflected back toward him and could not penetrate where it was going, and thus he thought his own image <note>original: "idolum suum"; his double or reflection.</note> was walking before him, face to face. Similarly, by the artifice of certain mirrors, images we desire can be projected into the air, even from a distance, outside of the mirrors themselves. When unlearned men see these, they think they are seeing demons or the shadows of souls, though they are nothing but certain likenesses related to the objects themselves and devoid of all life. 

It is also well known that if someone is in a dark place, devoid of all light except where a sunbeam enters through a very small hole, and a white paper or a flat mirror is placed under it, whatever is being done outside—as long as it is illuminated by the sun—will be seen upon it. <note>This is a description of the "camera obscura," a precursor to the modern camera.</note> And there is another even more wonderful trick <note>original: "praestigium"; a feat of natural magic or optical illusion.</note> where, by painting images or writing letters with a certain skill, one places them against the rays of the full moon on a clear night. Their likenesses are multiplied in the air, caught upward, and reflected back with the rays of the moon; another person, aware of the matter, can see, read, and recognize them at a great distance in the very disk or circle of the moon. This is a most useful artifice for announcing secrets to besieged towns and cities; it was formerly practiced by <term>Pythagoras</term> <note>The famous Greek mathematician and philosopher (c. 570–495 BC).</note>, and today it remains known to some, including myself. All these things, and many more and greater, are founded in the very nature of air, and they have their explanations in mathematics and optics. And just as these likenesses are reflected to the sight, so also are they sometimes reflected to the hearing, which is manifest in the echo. But there are more occult things than these...

From the element of air come also the winds; for they are nothing other than air in motion and agitation. There are four principal winds blowing from the four corners of heaven: namely, Notus from the south, Boreas from the north, Zephyrus from the west, and from the east Apeleotes, also known as Eurus. <note>These are the classical names for the cardinal winds used by Greek and Roman natural philosophers.</note> The poet Pontanus <note>Giovanni Pontano (1429–1503), an Italian humanist and poet.</note> encompassed these in two short verses:

> Boreas blows from the heights, Notus from the depths of Olympus.
> Zephyrus occupies the west, and Eurus comes from the rising sun.
> <note>original: "A summo Boreas, Notus imo spirat olympo. Occasum insedit Zephyrus, uenit Eurus ab ortu."</note>

Notus is the southern wind, cloudy, moist, hot, and sickly, which Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 342–420), the church father known for his Latin translation of the Bible.</note> calls the "cup-bearer of the rains." Ovid <note>The Roman poet Ovid (43 BCE – 17 CE). These lines are from his *Metamorphoses*, describing the Great Flood.</note> describes him thus:

> Notus flies out on soaking wings,
> His terrible face covered in pitch-black gloom;
> His beard is heavy with clouds, water flows from his white hair,
> Mists sit upon his brow, and his feathers and garments drip with dew.
> <note>original: "Madidis Notus euolat alis / Terribilem picea tectus caligine uultum, / Barba grauis nimbis, canis fluit unda capillis, / Fronte sedent nebulæ, rorant pennæq; sinusq;"</note>

Boreas, however, the opposite of Notus, is the northern wind, violent and loud, which, by scattering the clouds, makes the air clear and binds the water with frost. Ovid introduces him speaking of himself in this way:

> Force is natural to me; with it I drive away the dismal clouds,
> And shake the seas, and overturn gnarled oaks,
> I harden the clouds and strike the earth with hail.
> I also, when I have found my brothers in the open sky
> (For that is my field of battle), struggle with such great effort
> That the middle heavens resound with our collisions,
> And fires leap out, squeezed from the hollow clouds.
> I also, when I have entered the winding vents of the earth,
> And fiercely placed my back against the deepest caverns,
> I disturb the spirits of the dead <note>original: "manes"; the ancestral spirits or shades of the underworld.</note> and shake the whole world 
> With tremors.
> <note>original: "Apta mihi uis est, qua tristia nubila pello... Concutio." From Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Book VI.</note>

Zephyrus indeed, who is also called Favonius, is a very gentle wind blowing from the west, breathing peacefully; he is cold and moist, melting the winters and bringing forth buds and flowers. Opposite to him is Eurus, who is also called Subsolanus and Apeleotes, from the east—a watery wind that brings clouds and possesses a rapid voracity. Regarding these, Ovid sings thus:

> Eurus receded toward the dawn and the Nabataean kingdoms,
> And Persia, and the ridges lying under the morning rays.
> The Evening, and the shores which grow warm with the setting sun,
> Are closest to Zephyrus. Shuddering Boreas invaded 
> Scythia and the seven stars of the North: the land opposite
> Grows wet with constant clouds and rain from the rainy South.
> <note>original: "Eurus ad auroram, Nabathæaq; regna recessit... pluuioq; madescit ab Austro." The "seven stars of the North" refers to the constellation Ursa Major.</note>

XI.

<header>BOOK ONE</header>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'P' featuring a landscape scene with foliage and a building in the distance.</image-desc>After the four simple elements, there follow closely the four kinds of perfect compounds formed from them, which are stones, metals, plants, and animals. Although all elements come together in the composition for the generation of each one, nonetheless, each follows and imitates one primary element. For all stones are **earthy**, since they are heavy by nature and sink, and are so solidified by dryness that they cannot be melted. Metals, however, are **watery** and can be liquefied; as the natural philosophers <term>physici; scientists or students of nature</term> admit and the alchemists prove through experience, they are generated from a viscous water, or from watery quicksilver <note>original: "argentum uiuum"</note>. Plants have such an affinity with **air** that they will neither sprout nor grow unless they are in the open. So it is with all animals:

> ->A fiery vigor and a heavenly origin belong to them.<-
> <note>original: "Igneus est ollis uigor & cælestis origo." A quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book VI, line 730.</note>

Fire is so closely related to them that if it is extinguished, all life soon fails. Furthermore, each of these kinds is distinct within itself according to the degrees of the elements. For among stones, those are called primarily **earthy** which are opaque and heavier; those are **watery** which are transparent and have solidified from water, such as crystal, beryl, and pearls in shells. Those are **airy** which float upon water and are spongy, such as sponge-stone, pumice, and tufa <note>A porous rock formed from volcanic ash or limestone.</note>. There are also **fiery** stones, from which fire is extracted and into which they are sometimes resolved, or which are born from fire itself, such as the thunderstone <note>lapis fulminis; prehistoric stone tools once believed to be the physical remains of lightning strikes</note>, the pyrite stone, and asbestos.

Similarly among metals, lead and silver are **earthy**; quicksilver is **watery**; copper and tin are **airy**; but gold and iron are **fiery**. Among plants also, the roots imitate the **earth** because of their density; the leaves imitate **water** because of their sap; the flowers imitate **air** because of their subtlety; and the seeds imitate **fire** because of their generative spirit. Moreover, some are called hot, others cold, some moist, and others dry, borrowing the names of the elements from their qualities.

Among animals as well, some are more **earthy** than others and inhabit the bowels of the earth, such as worms, earthworms, moles, and many reptiles. Others are **watery**, such as fish. Others are **airy**, which cannot live outside of the air. There are also **fiery** ones inhabiting fire, such as salamanders and certain crickets called *pyraustas* <note>original: "pyraustas"; mythical insects believed to live in the fires of copper-smelting furnaces</note>, and those which glow with a certain fiery heat, such as doves, ostriches, lions, and those which the Wise Man <note>Referring to the author of the biblical Book of Wisdom, likely Solomon.</note> calls "beasts breathing out fiery vapor." 

Furthermore, in animals, the bones represent **earth**, the flesh represents **air**, the vital spirit represents **fire**, and the humors represent **water**. These are also divided by the elements: for red choler <note>yellow bile</note> yields to **fire**, blood to **air**, phlegm to **water**, and black bile to **earth**. Finally, in the soul itself, as Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note> testifies, the intellect represents **fire**, reason represents **air**, imagination represents **water**, and the senses represent **earth**. These senses are also distributed among the elements: for sight is **fiery**, since it does not perceive without fire and light; hearing is **airy**, for sound is produced by the striking of air; smell and taste are referred to **water**, without whose moisture there is neither flavor nor scent; finally, touch is entirely **earthy**, taking in the thicker bodies. Even the acts and operations of man are moderated by the elements: for slow and solid movement is marked by the **earth**; fear, sluggishness, and slack work are marked by **water**; cheerfulness and friendly manners by **air**; and impulse...

XII.
<header>ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,</header>

...sharp and irascible, fire. The elements are therefore the first principles of all things; all things consist of them and exist because of them, and they diffuse their powers in all things and through all things.

## How the elements exist in the heavens, in the stars, in demons, in angels, and finally in God himself. Chapter VIII. ##

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a figure, likely a scholar or theologian, seated at a desk or pulpit with books, set within a square frame decorated with architectural and floral patterns.</image-desc>It is the unanimous opinion of all the Platonists that just as all things exist in all others within the <term>archetypal world; the original divine blueprint of the universe</term>, so too in this corporeal world, all things exist in all others, though in different ways according to the nature of those things receiving them. Thus, the elements are not only found in these lower realms, but also in the heavens, in the stars, in demons, in angels, and finally in the very Maker and Archetype of all things. However, in these lower realms, the elements are coarse forms, immersed in matter and acting as material elements. In the heavens, the elements exist through their natures and powers, in a celestial and far more excellent manner than they do below the moon. For the solidity of the celestial **Earth** exists there without the density of water; the agility of **Air** is there, far removed from dissipation; and the heat of **Fire** is there, not burning but shining, giving life to all things through its warmth.

Furthermore, among the stars, Mars and the Sun are **fiery**; Jupiter and Venus are **airy**; Saturn and Mercury are **watery**; and those which inhabit the eighth sphere <note>The "eighth sphere" refers to the firmament or the sphere of the fixed stars in the geocentric model.</note> as well as the Moon are **earthy**. The Moon, however, is thought by many to be watery because, like the earth, it attracts the celestial waters, and being soaked by them, it flows and communicates them to us by its proximity. There are also certain **fiery**, **earthy**, **airy**, and **watery** signs among the <term>Zodiac; the belt of constellations through which the sun and planets move</term>. These govern the elements in the heavens by distributing the beginning, middle, and end of each element into four <term>triplicities; groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</term>. Thus, **Fire** has its beginning in Aries, its progress and increase in Leo, and its end in Sagittarius. **Earth** has its beginning in Taurus, its progress in Virgo, and its extreme in Capricorn. **Air** has its beginning in Gemini, its process in Libra, and its limit in Aquarius. **Water** has its beginning in Cancer, its middle in Scorpio, and its end in Pisces. From the mixtures of these planets and signs, together with the elements, all bodies are composed.

Furthermore, even demons are distinguished from one another by this same logic: some are called **fiery**, others **earthly**, others **airy**, and others **watery**. Hence the four rivers in the underworld: the fiery **Phlegethon**, the airy **Cocytus**, the watery **Styx**, and the earthly **Acheron**. Indeed, we even read in the Gospels of the "fire of Gehenna" and "eternal fire" into which the cursed will be ordered to go; and in the Book of Revelation, we read of a "lake of fire." Isaiah says of the damned: "The Lord shall strike them with corrupt air"; and in the Book of Job: "They shall pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat." In the same book, we read of "a land of darkness, covered by the gloom of death, a land of misery and shadows."

Accordingly, these elements are also placed within the supramundane angels and blessed intelligences. For in them resides a stability of essence, an **earthly** power by which they are the firm seats of God. There is also mercy and piety, a **watery** virtue that cleanses; hence they are called "waters" by the Psalmist where he says of heaven, "You who rule the waters above them." <note>A reference to Psalm 148:4, "Praise him, ye heavens of heavens, and ye waters that be above the heavens."</note> There are also in them a subtle **airy** spirit and the fire of glowing love. Hence they are called in the sacred scriptures "the wings of the winds," and elsewhere the Psalmist says of them: "Who makes your angels spirits, and your ministers a burning fire." <note>A reference to Psalm 104:4.</note>

It classifies the planets, zodiac signs, and even divine attributes according to their elemental nature.</summary>
