XIII.
<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

Among the angelic orders, the **Seraphim**, **Virtues**, and **Powers** are fiery; the **Cherubim** are earthy; the **Thrones** and **Archangels** are watery; and the **Dominations** and **Principalities** are airy. Regarding the <term>Archetype; the original divine blueprint or God</term> himself, the Maker of all things, do we not read: *Let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth a savior* <note>original: "Aperiatur terra, & germinet saluatore"; a reference to Isaiah 45:8</note>? Is it not said of the same: *a fountain of living water, cleansing and regenerating*? Is not the same the *Spirit breathing the breath of life*? And the same, as Moses and Paul bear witness, is a *consuming fire*? Therefore, no one can deny that the elements are found everywhere and in all things in their own way: <margin>Elements are in all things.</margin> first in these lower realms, but drossy and coarse; in the celestial realms, purer and bright; but in the super-celestial realms, living and blessed in every respect. Thus the elements exist: in the Archetype as the ideas of things to be produced; in the <term>Intelligences; the higher angelic minds</term> as distributed powers; in the heavens as virtues; and in the lower realms as coarser forms.

### On the virtues of natural things which depend immediately upon the elements. Chapter IX. ###

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a figure in a landscape, possibly a traveler or scholar holding a staff.</image-desc>
<margin>Various natural virtues of things.</margin>
Certain natural virtues of things are elemental, such as heating, cooling, moistening, and drying; these are called primary operations or qualities, and are active in their effects. For these qualities alone entirely transform the whole substance, which no other qualities do. However, other virtues are present in things because of the elements that compose them, even beyond the primary qualities. These include qualities that are ripening, digesting, dissolving, softening, hardening, <term>styptic; binding or contracting</term>, cleansing, corrosive, caustic, opening, evaporating, comforting, soothing, gluing, obstructing, expelling, retaining, attracting, repelling, numbing, enlarging, lubricating, and many others. For an elemental quality in a mixture has much to do that it cannot perform on its own. These operations are called **secondary qualities**, because they follow the nature and proportion of the mixture of the primary virtues. These are treated at length in the books of physicians. For instance, ripening is the operation of natural heat according to a certain measure in the substance of matter; hardening is the operation of cold; likewise freezing, and other similar effects. And these operations sometimes act upon a specific part of the body, such as those provoking urine, or milk, or menses; these are called **tertiary qualities**, which follow the secondary just as the secondary follow the primary. According to these primary, secondary, and tertiary qualities, many diseases are both caused and cured. <margin>Many admirable artificial things.</margin> Many things are also produced artificially which men greatly marvel at, such as the fire that burns in water, which they call **Greek fire** <note>A famous incendiary weapon of the medieval world whose composition was a state secret</note>. Aristotle teaches several compositions of this in his treatise on this singular subject. In a similar way, a fire is made which is extinguished by oil and ignited by cold water when it is sprinkled upon it; and fire which is ignited by rain, wind, or the sun. There is also a fire called **burning water** <note>original: "aqua ardens"; likely distilled alcohol or "spirits of wine," which was a marvel of early chemistry</note>, the preparation of which is very well known, which consumes nothing except itself. There are also unquenchable fires, incombustible oils, and perpetual lamps which can be extinguished neither by wind, nor water, nor any other means. This would seem utterly incredible, were it not for that most famous lamp which once shone in the temple of Venus, in which burned the stone **asbestos**, which, once truly ignited, is never extinguished. <header>OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,</header>

Furthermore, wood or some other combustible material can be prepared so that it cannot be harmed by fire, and ointments are made so that, once our hands are anointed, we can carry glowing iron, or put a hand into molten metal, or even walk through fire with the whole body without any harm, and other similar wonders. There is also a type of linen which Pliny calls **asbestos** <note>original: "asbestu"</note> and the Greeks call **asbeston** <note>original: "ἄσϐεστον"; literally "unquenchable" or "inextinguishable"</note>, which is not consumed by fire; concerning this, Anaxilaus says that a tree wrapped in it can be felled with "deaf" blows—that is, blows that cannot be heard.

### On the occult virtues of things. Chapter X. ###

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a human figure in a landscape within a square frame.</image-desc>

<margin>Why they are called occult properties, etc.</margin>
In things there are, besides, other virtues that do not belong to any element—such as driving away poison, dispelling <term>anthraces; carbuncles or inflammatory skin boils</term>, attracting iron, or other such effects. This virtue is a consequence of the <term>species; the specific category or essence of a thing</term> and the "form" of this or that object. Because of this, even a tiny quantity can have a significant effect in action, a power not granted to a mere elemental quality. For these virtues, because they are highly **formal** <note>derived from the "substantial form" or spiritual blueprint of the object rather than its physical matter</note>, can do a great deal with very little matter; however, an elemental virtue, because it is material, requires a large amount of matter to act with great force. These are called **occult properties** because their causes are hidden, such that the human intellect cannot fully investigate them; for this reason, philosophers have discovered the greatest part of them through long experience rather than through the investigation of reason. For just as food is digested in the stomach through heat, which we understand, so it is transformed through a certain occult virtue which we do not understand—and certainly not by heat alone, for if it were, food would be transformed better in a hearth by a fire than in the stomach. Thus there are in things, beyond the elemental qualities that we know, certain other innate virtues, created together with nature, which we admire and are often amazed by, being unknown to us or rarely seen—as we read in Ovid concerning the **phoenix**, that unique bird that renews itself:

> There is one bird that restores and reseeds itself;
> The Assyrians call it the phoenix. <note>Ovid, Metamorphoses XV, 392-393</note>

-> And elsewhere: <-

> Egypt gathers at the wonder of such a sight,
> And the cheering crowd greets the rare bird.

Matreas once caused great wonder among both the Greeks and the Romans; he used to say that he nourished a beast that devoured itself. Hence even today <margin>The beast of Matreas.</margin> many still anxiously search for what Matreas's beast might be. Who would not marvel at fish dug up from the earth, of which Aristotle, Theophrastus, and Polybius the historian have written? And the things Pausanias recorded about singing stones—all these are the works of occult virtues. Thus the **ostrich** bird cooks cold and very hard iron and digests it for the nourishment of its body; its stomach is said not to be harmed even by red-hot iron. Thus that little fish, the **echeneis** <note>the remora or suckerfish, believed in antiquity to be able to stop ships</note>, so curbs the force of the winds and tames the fury of the sea that, no matter how much the storms rage, even with infinite sails stretched by the wind, it nevertheless restrains and compels ships to stand still by its touch alone, so that they can in no way be moved. Thus the **salamanders** and the **pyraustae** <note>mythical insects said to live in the fire of copper-smelting furnaces</note>, small beasts, live in the fire; and although they sometimes appear to burn, they are not harmed. It is the same with a certain bitumen with which the weapons of the Amazons are said to have been smeared, which...

xv.
<header>BOOK ONE</header>

It is dissolved neither by iron nor by fire. It is also told in stories that the **Caspian Gates** <note>original: "portæ Caspiæ"; a legendary mountain pass in the Caucasus, often associated with a wall built by Alexander to keep out "uncivilized" nations</note>, crafted from bronze, were coated with it by **Alexander the Great**. We also read that **Noah’s Ark** <note>original: "arcā Noë"</note> was glued together with similar bitumen, and the ark itself still lasts to this day, after so many thousands of years, atop the mountains of Armenia. There are many other wonders of this kind that are scarcely believable, yet they are known through experience itself. Antiquity has handed down such things regarding **Satyrs**, which are animals consisting of half-human and half-beast figures, yet capable of speech and reason. The holy **Jerome** <note>original: "Hieronymus"; the 4th-century scholar and saint</note> himself reports that one of them once spoke to the blessed **Anthony the Hermit**, condemning the pagan error of worshipping animals and begging that the common God be prayed to on their behalf. Jerome also affirms that one of them was once brought out into public while alive and soon afterward sent to the prince **Constantine** <note>the Roman Emperor Constantine the Great</note>.

### How occult virtues are infused into the species of things from the Ideas, through the reasons of the World Soul and the rays of the stars; and which things abound most in this virtue. Chapter XI.

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial P containing a figure within a classical architectural frame, surrounded by scrolling foliage.</image-desc>The **Platonists** <note>followers of Plato's philosophy, specifically Neoplatonists who emphasized the mystical hierarchy of the universe</note> maintain that all lower things are modeled <note>original: "ideata"</note> after higher **Ideas**. They define an "Idea" as a form above bodies, souls, and minds—one, simple, pure, immutable, indivisible, incorporeal, and eternal; and they hold that the nature of all Ideas is the same. They place Ideas first in the Good itself—that is, in God—by way of cause; here, they are distinguished from one another only by certain relative reasons, so that everything in the world is not just a single, undifferentiated thing. Yet, they agree in essence, so that God is not a "multiplex" <note>many-layered or divided</note> substance. 

Secondly, they place Ideas in the "intelligible" itself—that is, in the **World Soul** <note>original: "anima mūdi"; the spiritual force that animates the entire universe</note>—as distinct forms properly speaking, and moreover differing from one another as absolute forms, so that while the Ideas in God are all one single form, in the World Soul they are many. In the minds that follow—whether joined to a body or separated from it—they are placed by a kind of participation, becoming more and more distinct step by step. In **Nature**, they place them as if they were the lowest "seeds" <note>seminal principles</note> of forms infused by the Ideas. Finally, in **matter**, they place them as shadows. 

To this is added the fact that there are as many **seminal reasons** <note>original: "rationes seminales"; the formative blueprints that guide the development of living things</note> in the World Soul as there are Ideas in the Divine Mind. By these reasons, the Soul built for itself figures in the heavens beyond the stars and impressed properties upon all of them. From these stars, figures, and properties, all the virtues and properties of the lower species depend. Thus, every species has a celestial figure matching it, from which it receives a marvelous power in its operation—a gift it receives from its own Idea through the seminal reasons of the World Soul. 

For Ideas are not only the causes of a species' essence, but also the causes of every <term>virtue; an inherent power or specific property</term> inherent in that species. This is what many philosophers mean when they say that by certain virtues—specifically those that have a certain and stable logic, being neither accidental nor by chance, but effective, powerful, and unfailing, doing nothing in vain or fruitlessly—the virtues existing in the nature of things are moved. These virtues are indeed the "operations" of the Ideas, which do not wander or fail except by accident, namely from the impurity of...

XVI.
<header>OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,</header>

...and the inequality of matter; for in this way, even things of the same species are found to be more or less powerful, according to the purity or confusion of their matter. For all celestial influences can be hindered by the confusion and inability of matter. Hence it was a proverb among the **Platonists** <note>philosophers following Plato who believed the physical world is a reflection of a higher, spiritual reality</note> themselves that "celestial virtues are infused according to the merits of the matter." **Virgil** <note>the Roman poet Publius Vergilius Maro</note> mentions this when he sings:

> They have a fiery vigor and a celestial origin
> in their seeds, insofar as harmful bodies do not slow them down. <note>original: "Igneus est ollis uigor, & cælestis origo / Seminibus, quantum non noxia corpora tardant"; from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book VI</note>

Therefore, those things in which the *Idea* <note>the divine "blueprint" or spiritual essence of a thing</note> is less submerged in matter—that is, those which take on a greater likeness to "separate" things <note>entities existing without physical bodies, such as angels or pure spirits</note>—possess powers that are more potent in their operation, similar to the operation of the separate Idea itself. We know, therefore, that the position and figure of the celestial bodies is the cause of every noble virtue found in the lower species.

### How different virtues are influenced in different individuals, even those of the same species. Chapter XII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring a person seated at a desk or table, likely a scholar or philosopher.</image-desc>**Individual** gifts are also present in many individuals, just as wonderful as those found in entire species, arising from the figure of the heavens and the position of the stars. For every individual, when it begins to exist under a specific **horoscope** <note>the configuration of the stars at the exact moment of birth or inception</note> and celestial constellation, contracts along with its existence a certain wonderful power of acting and "suffering" <note>in this context, "suffering" (patiendi) means being receptive to influences or being acted upon</note>. This is a marvelous thing, even beyond what it possesses from its species, arising both through the influence of the heavens and through the obedience of the matter of things that can be generated to the **World Soul** <note>original: "animam mundi"; the spiritual essence that Neoplatonists believed permeated and animated all of nature</note>. Indeed, this obedience is like the obedience of our own bodies to our souls. For we feel within ourselves that toward whatever form we conceive in our minds, our body is moved—whether with delight, or horror, or by fleeing. In the same way, the celestial souls frequently conceive various things, and then matter is moved through obedience to that conception. Thus, many wonders appear in nature from the "imagination" of the higher motions. In this way, not only natural things, but also sometimes artificial things <note>man-made objects</note>, conceive various virtues—and this happens most of all if the soul of the person performing the work is striving toward the same end. Hence **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the influential Persian polymath</note> says that whatever happens here must pre-exist in the motions and conceptions of the stars and the celestial spheres. Thus, various effects, inclinations, and characters are produced in things, not only from matter being variously disposed (as many believe), but from a varied influence and a diverse form—not indeed a diversity of species, but one that is particular and unique to the individual. The degrees of these are variously distributed by the first cause of all things, **God**, who remains the same while distributing to each as He wills. Nevertheless, secondary causes—the **angelic** and **celestial** powers—cooperate with Him, disposing of physical matter and other things committed to them. Therefore, all virtues are infused by God through the World Soul, yet through the particular power of the presiding images and **Intelligences** <note>spiritual beings believed to govern the planets and stars</note>, and through the gathering of the rays and aspects of the stars in a certain unique and **harmonic concord** <note>original: "concentu harmonico"</note>.

XVII.
->### BOOK ONE.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'O' depicting a human figure, possibly a scholar or monk, within a circular frame surrounded by ornamental scrollwork.</image-desc>

**It** is known to all that a certain virtue exists in the **magnet** <note>the loadstone</note>, by which it attracts iron; and that the **diamond** <note>adamas</note> by its presence removes the power of the magnet. In the same way, **amber** <note>electrum</note> and **balagius** <note>a type of pale ruby or spinel</note>, when rubbed and warmed, draw up chaff. The **asbestos** stone, once set on fire, is never or hardly ever extinguished. The **carbuncle** <note>a deep red gemstone, like a garnet or ruby</note> shines in the darkness. The **eagle-stone** <note>aëtites; a hollow stone with another stone rattling inside</note> supports the offspring of women and plants when placed above, and draws them forth when placed below. **Jasper** <note>iaspis</note> restrains blood. The **suckerfish** <note>echineis; the remora, believed to have the power to stop ships</note> halts a ship. **Rhubarb** <note>rabarbarum</note> expels bile. The **chameleon's** liver, if burnt upon the highest roof tiles, stirs up rains and thunders. The **heliotrope** stone <note>the "bloodstone" or "sun-turner"</note> dazzles the sight and renders the wearer invisible. The **lynx-stone** <note>lyncurius; believed to be petrified lynx urine</note> removes illusions from the eyes. The smoke of the **lipparis** stone calls forth all manner of beasts. The **synochitides** stone brings out the shades of the underworld. The **anachitides** makes the images of two people appear. The **ennectis**, when placed under those who are dreaming, gives oracles. 

There is an **Ethiopian herb**, by which they say ponds are dried up and all closed things are opened; and we read of the **latace** herb given to the ambassadors of the Persian kings, so that wherever they went, they might abound in plenty. There is also the **Spartan** or **Scythian herb**, which they say, if tasted or even held in the mouth, allows the Scythians to endure twelve days of hunger and thirst. **Apuleius** <note>Lucius Apuleius, a Roman philosopher and author of 'The Golden Ass'</note> says that he was taught by a divinity that there are many kinds of herbs and stones by which men can even grant themselves perpetual life; but it is not lawful <note>fas; divinely permitted</note> for men to know this science. For since men live for a short time and yet greedily pursue evils and dare any crime, if they were to receive a long extension of time, they would not spare even the gods themselves. 

Truly, from where these virtues come, none of those who have published massive volumes on the properties of things have revealed: not **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, not **Bochus**, not **Aaron**, not **Orpheus**, not **Theophrastus**, not **Thebith** <note>Thabit ibn Qurra</note>, not **Zenothemis**, not **Zoroaster**, not **Euax**, not **Dioscorides**, not **Isaac the Jew**, not **Zacharias of Babylon**, not **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus</note>, nor **Arnoldus** <note>Arnold of Villanova</note>. And yet all these have confessed—as Zacharias writes to Mithridates—that a great power and the fate of humans reside in the virtues of stones and herbs. 

From where, therefore, these things come, a deeper contemplation is required. **Alexander the Peripatetic** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a commentator on Aristotle</note>, not departing from his senses and qualities, thinks these things come from the **elements** and their qualities. This might perhaps be thought true, were it not that those qualities are of the same species, while the operations of stones are many, agreeing neither in species nor in genus. Therefore, the **Academics** <note>followers of Plato</note> with their master **Plato** attribute these virtues to the **Ideas**, the formative blueprints of things. **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina</note> traces them back to the **Intelligences** <note>spiritual beings or angels that govern the heavens</note>, **Hermes** to the stars, and **Albertus** to the **specific forms** <note>the unique essence that makes a thing what it is</note> of things. 

And although these authors seem to oppose one another, none of them, if rightly understood, departs from the truth; for all their sayings agree in many ways toward the same effect. For **God**, who is first of all the end and origin of all virtues, provides the **seal of the Ideas** to His ministers, the **Intelligences**. These Intelligences, like faithful executors, sign each thing committed to them with an ideal virtue, through the heavens and the stars as instruments; meanwhile, matter is being prepared to receive those forms which reside in the Divine Majesty—as Plato says in the *Timaeus*—to be brought down through the stars. And these they give... <note>original: "easq; das" [dant]</note>

XVIII.
### OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

[The Author] of forms <note>This sentence completes a thought from the previous page: "The Author of forms distributes..."</note> distributes through the ministry of **intelligences** <note>spiritual beings or angels that govern specific parts of creation</note>, whom He established over His works as rulers and guardians. To them is entrusted the faculty over the things committed to their care, so that every virtue of stones, herbs, metals, and all other things originates from these presiding intelligences. Thus, form and virtue proceed first from the **Ideas** <note>the eternal blueprints in the mind of God</note>, then from the presiding and ruling intelligences, afterwards from the disposing aspects of the heavens <note>astrological alignments</note>, and further from the disposed complexions of the elements <note>the physical balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> corresponding to the influxes of the heavens, by which the elements themselves are arranged. 

Therefore, these operations exist in these lower things through expressed forms, in the heavens through disposing virtues, in the intelligences through mediating reasons, and in the **archetype** <note>the original model or the divine mind</note> through ideas and exemplary forms. It is necessary that all of these agree in the execution of the effect and virtue of any thing. Therefore, there is virtue and wonderful operation in every herb and stone, but it is greater in a star; beyond this, each thing also acquires much for itself from the presiding intelligences. But most especially, power comes from the **supreme cause** <note>God</note>, to whom all things correspond in a mutual and perfected way, harmonizing in their own harmonic concert, just like certain hymns, always praising that highest Craftsman. This is just as the holy boys in the **Chaldean furnace** <note>referring to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the biblical Book of Daniel</note> invited all things to do while they sang: 

> Bless the Lord, all things that grow on the earth, and all things that move in the waters, all birds of the air, beasts and cattle together with the children of men. <note>original: "Benedicite dominum uniuersa germinantia in terra, & omnia quæ mouentur in aquis, omnes uolucres cæli, bestiæ & pecora simul cum filiis hominum."</note>

There is, therefore, no other cause for the necessity of these effects than the connection of all things with the **first cause** <note>God</note>, and their correspondence to those divine exemplars and eternal ideas. From these, every thing has a determined and particular place in the archetype, from which it lives and draws its origin; and every virtue of herbs, stones, metals, animals, words, and prayers, and all things which are from God, is implanted there. 

Although God works through the intelligences and the heavens in these lower things, He sometimes omits these means or suspends their ministry to do things immediately by Himself. These works are then called **miracles**. For while the secondary causes (which **Plato** and others call "ministers") necessarily act by the command and order of the first cause and necessarily produce their effects, God sometimes frees or suspends them at His own pleasure, so that they completely cease from the necessity of that command and order. These are the greatest miracles of God. 

Thus, the fire in the Chaldean furnace did not burn the boys; thus the sun, at the command of **Joshua**, retreated from its course by the space of one day; thus at **Hezekiah’s** petition, the sun returned backward by ten lines or hours; thus, while **Christ** was suffering <note>during the Crucifixion</note>, the sun underwent an eclipse during the full moon <note>an astronomical impossibility, as eclipses normally only happen during a new moon</note>. The reasons for these operations cannot be investigated or reached by any discourse of reason, no magic, and no science—no matter how occult or profound—but are to be learned and sought out from divine oracles alone.

XIX.
### BOOK THE FIRST. XIX.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap for the letter 'D' featuring a man (possibly a scholar or saint) seated in a chair, framed by Renaissance-style scrollwork and foliage.</image-desc>

Democritus <note>a Greek philosopher often associated with early science and the theory of atoms</note> and Orpheus <note>a legendary Greek hero and musician whose "Orphic hymns" were believed to hold magical power</note>, as well as many followers of Pythagoras, having most diligently investigated the powers of the heavens and the natures of the lower world, declared that "all things are full of gods." This was not said without reason, since no thing is of such outstanding power that it could be satisfied with its own nature if it were deprived of divine help. They called these "gods" the divine virtues <note>spiritual powers or energies</note> diffused throughout all things. Zoroaster <note>an ancient Persian prophet associated with magic and light</note> named them "divine lures," Synesius <note>a 4th-century philosopher-bishop</note> called them "symbolic attractions," while others called them "lives" and still others called them "souls." They said that the virtues of things depend upon these, because it belongs to the soul alone to extend from one matter into other things upon which it acts. This is much like a human being who extends their intellect toward things that can be understood, and their imagination toward things that can be imagined.

This is what they meant when they said that the soul of one being could go out and enter into another, to fascinate <note>original: "fascinare"; in this context, to bind or influence through a spiritual connection</note> it and hinder its operations—just as a diamond hinders a magnet so that it cannot attract iron. Since the soul is the "first mover" and is, as they say, move-able by itself and of its own accord, while the body or matter is by itself ineffective for movement and falls far short of the nature of the soul, they therefore claim there is a need for a more excellent medium. This medium must be, as it were, not quite a body and yet almost a soul, or not quite a soul and yet almost a body; it is the link by which the soul is joined to the body. They imagine such a medium to be the **spirit of the world** <note>original: "spiritum mundi"</note>, which we call the <term>fifth essence <note>also known as the "quintessence," a pure substance distinct from the four classical elements of earth, water, air, and fire</note></term>. It is so named because it is not composed of the four elements, but is a certain fifth thing subsisting above or beyond them.

Such a spirit is therefore necessarily required as a medium so that celestial souls may be present in thicker, material bodies and bestow their miraculous gifts upon them. This spirit is of the same form in the body of the world as our own spirit is in the human body. For just as the powers of our souls are applied to our limbs through our spirit, so the virtue of the **Soul of the World** is spread through all things by the fifth essence. Nothing is found in the entire world that lacks a spark of its virtue. It is, however, infused more—and most greatly—into those things that have drawn in the most of this spirit. It is drawn in through the rays of the stars, insofar as things render themselves conformable to them. 

Through this spirit, therefore, every **occult property** is propagated into herbs, stones, metals, and living creatures—via the sun, the moon, the planets, and the stars positioned even higher than the planets. This spirit can benefit us more if one knows how to separate it from the other elements, or at least how to use those things that abound most in this spirit. Indeed, those things in which the spirit is less submerged in the body and less confined by matter act more powerfully and perfectly, and they generate their own kind more readily, for all generative and "seeding" virtue is contained within it. For this reason, Alchemists strive to separate this spirit from gold and silver. If they have rightly segregated and extracted it, and afterwards apply it to any matter of the same kind (that is, to metals), they may instantly create gold or silver. 

We ourselves know how to do this and have occasionally seen it; yet we were not able to manufacture more gold than the weight of the gold from which we extracted the spirit. For since that spirit is an "extended" rather than an "intense" form, it cannot change an imperfect body into a perfect one beyond its own measure. However, I do not deny that this might be possible through another artifice.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

### Chapter XV. How we ought to investigate and test the virtues of things by following the path of similarity.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter "P" depicting a seated figure in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>

It is clear, therefore, that the **hidden properties** <note>original: "proprietates occultas"</note> in things do not come from their basic physical elements, but are implanted from the heavens. These are hidden from our senses and barely known even to our reason. They proceed from the **life and spirit of the world** <note>the *Anima Mundi*, or "World Soul," which Renaissance philosophers believed connected the spiritual and material realms</note> through the very rays of the stars. We can only discover these through experience and careful observation. 

Therefore, O seeker who wishes to work in this study, you must consider that every single thing moves and turns toward its own **likeness** <note>the Principle of Similarity: the belief that "like attracts like"</note>, and draws things toward itself with all its power—both in its hidden property (its "occult virtue") and its physical quality (its "elemental virtue"). We see this even in the physical substance itself, as with salt: for whatever sits with salt for a long time becomes salt. For every active agent, when it begins to act, does not move toward something lower than itself, but as much as possible toward its own equal and like. We see this clearly in sentient animals, in whom the nutritional power does not turn food into grass or plants, but converts it into sentient flesh. 

Therefore, in whatever things there is an excess of some quality or property—such as heat, cold, boldness, fear, sadness, anger, love, hatred, or any other passion or power—whether it is in them by nature or sometimes by art or chance (such as **boldness in a prostitute**), these things greatly move and provoke one toward that same quality, passion, or power. Thus, fire moves toward fire, water moves toward water, and the bold move others toward boldness. 

It is well known among doctors that the brain helps the brain, and the lung helps the lung. Thus they say that the **right eye of a frog** hung from the neck in a cloth of its natural color heals the right eye, and the left eye heals the left, of **rheum** <note>original: "lippitudines," an inflammation or watering of the eyes</note>. They say the same regarding the eyes of a crab. So also, the feet of a tortoise help those suffering from **gout** <note>original: "podagricis"</note>, when tied on so that foot is to foot and hand to hand—right to right and left to left. 

In this way they say that every sterile animal provokes sterility, especially its testicles, womb, or urine. Thus they say a woman will not conceive if she takes every month some of the urine of a **mule** <note>mules were famously known to be sterile</note>, or something soaked in it. 

Therefore, if we wish to work toward some property or power, let us seek animals or other things in which such a property exists most excellently. From these, let us take the part in which that property or power is most active. For example, if we wish to promote **love**, let us seek an animal that loves greatly, such as the dove, the turtledove, the sparrow, the swallow, or the **wagtail** <note>original: "motacilla," a bird often associated with Aphrodite/Venus in folklore</note>. From these, let us take the members or parts in which the **Venusian appetite** <note>original: "Venereus appetitus," or sexual desire</note> flourishes most: which are the heart, testicles, womb, penis, sperm, or menstrual blood. And let this be done at that time when these animals are most seized by and intent upon such a feeling; for then they strongly provoke and bring about love. 

In a similar way, to increase **boldness**, let us seek a lion or a cock, and from these let us take the heart, or the eyes, or the forehead. This is also how we should understand what **Psellus the Platonist** <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine scholar of the occult</note> says: that dogs, crows, and cocks contribute to wakefulness; also...

<summary>This page explains the magical "Law of Similarity," arguing that objects and animals possess hidden virtues that can be used to influence similar traits in humans, such as using bold animals to increase courage or fertile/sterile animals to affect reproduction.</summary>

...the nightingale, the bat, and the owl, and from these especially the head, the heart, and the eyes. 

For this reason, they say that if someone carries the heart of a crow or a bat upon themselves, they will not sleep until it is put down. The dried head of a bat tied to the right arm of a person who is awake does the same thing; for if it is placed upon a sleeper, it is said they will not be woken until it has been removed. In the same way, the frog and the horned owl <note>original: "bubo," likely referring to the Great Horned Owl or Eagle Owl</note> cause one to become talkative <note>original: "loquacem"</note>, and from these especially the tongue and the heart are used. Thus, the tongue of a water-frog placed under the head makes a person speak in their sleep; and the heart of a horned owl placed upon the left breast of a sleeping woman is said to make her reveal all her secrets. The heart of a night-owl <note>original: "noctua," the Little Owl associated with Minerva</note> and the fat <note>original: "sepum," likely a variant of *sebum* (suet/fat)</note> of a hare placed upon the chest of a sleeper is said to do the same.

In the same way, all long-lived animals contribute to a long life; and whatever things have within themselves a **renewing power** <note>original: "uirtutem renouatiuām"</note> contribute to the renewal of our bodies and the restoration of youth, as doctors have frequently demonstrated they know—as is manifest in the case of the viper and serpents. It is well known that stags renew their youth by eating serpents. In the same way, the phoenix is renewed through the funeral pyre it builds for itself; and a similar power exists in the pelican, whose right foot, if placed under warm dung, is regenerated into a pelican after three months. For this reason, certain doctors, using preparations made from viper and hellebore <note>a medicinal but toxic flowering plant used in antiquity to treat madness and skin diseases</note>, and from the flesh of certain animals of this kind, promise to restore youth—and they do restore it sometimes, even such a youth as **Medea** <note>the sorceress of Greek myth who restored the youth of Aeson and promised the same to Pelias, though she famously tricked Pelias's daughters into killing him</note> restored to the aged Pelias as promised. It is also believed that if the blood of a bear is drunk from a fresh wound with the mouth applied directly, this kind of potion grants increases in bodily strength, because that animal is most robust.

## *How the operations of different virtues are transferred from one thing to another, and are mutually communicated to each other. Chapter XVI.*

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'S' featuring floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
You should know that the power of natural things is so great that they not only affect all things near them with their own virtue, but beyond this, they infuse into them a similar power, through which they themselves may also affect other things with this same virtue—just as we see in the **magnet** <note>original: "magnete," or loadstone</note>. This stone not only attracts iron rings, but also infuses a power into the rings themselves, by which they are able to do this same thing, as **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, who discusses the magnet in *The City of God*</note> and **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and scientist</note> report having seen for themselves. 

In this way, it is said that a public prostitute, in whom there is bold and boundless impudence, affects all things near her with this very property, which then pass it on to others. Therefore they say that if someone wears the garment or shirt of a prostitute, or has with them a mirror in which she has looked at herself daily, they will be rendered bold, fearless, shameless, and lustful. In a similar way, they say a cloth <note>original: "pānū," for *pannum*</note> that has been at a funeral conceives from this a certain property of sadness and a **Saturnine** <note>associated with the planet Saturn, traditionally linked to melancholy, death, and weight</note> quality; and likewise, the noose of a hanged man has some wonderful properties. A similar thing is what **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*</note> recounts: if someone places earth under a blinded green lizard and includes iron or gold rings together with it in a glass vessel, when it appears through the glass that the lizard has recovered its sight, the rings...

### How the Virtues of Things are to be Investigated and Tested through Strife and Friendship. Chapter XVII. ###

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'R' featuring interlaced foliage and vine patterns within a square frame.</image-desc> It remains now to see how all things have friendship and enmity among themselves. Every thing has something to be feared—a horrible, inimical, and destructive enemy. Conversely, every thing has something that causes it to exult, bringing joy and strength. Thus, among the elements, fire is opposed to water, and air to earth, yet they otherwise agree among themselves. Furthermore, among the celestial bodies, the friends of Saturn are Mercury, Jupiter, the Sun, and the Moon; his enemies are Mars and Venus. All the planets are friends to Jupiter except for Mars. Likewise, all hold Mars in hatred except for Venus. Jupiter and Venus love the Sun, while Mars, Mercury, and the Moon are its enemies. All love Venus except for Saturn. The friends of Mercury are Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn; his enemies are the Sun, the Moon, and Mars. Finally, the friends of the Moon are Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn; her enemies are Mars and Mercury. There is another kind of enmity among the stars, namely when they have opposite houses <note>The "houses" or "domiciles" are signs of the Zodiac where a planet's power is greatest; an "opposite house" is the sign 180 degrees across the wheel</note>, such as Saturn to the Luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note>, Jupiter to Mercury, and Mars to Venus. An even stronger enmity exists between those whose exaltations <note>A specific degree of the Zodiac where a planet's influence is most harmoniously amplified</note> are opposite, such as Saturn and the Sun, Jupiter and Mars, or Venus and Mercury. However, the strongest friendship is found between those who agree in nature, quality, substance, and power, such as Mars with the Sun, Venus with the Moon, or Jupiter with Venus. There is also friendship between those whose exaltation is in the house of the other, such as Saturn with Venus, Jupiter with the Moon, Mars with Saturn, the Sun with Mars, Venus with Jupiter, and the Moon with Venus. And just as these friendships and enmities exist among the superior bodies, such are the inclinations of the things subject to them here in these inferior realms. Therefore, these habits of friendship and enmity are nothing other than certain inclinations of things toward one another: desiring a certain thing if it is absent, moving toward it unless hindered, resting once it is attained, and conversely, fleeing from its opposite, dreading its proximity, and finding no rest in it. Led by this opinion, Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for the doctrine that change is central to the universe</note> proclaimed that all things come to pass through strife and friendship. Truly, these inclinations of friendship are found in plants and minerals, such as the attraction the magnet has for iron; the emerald for wealth and favor; jasper for childbirth; and agate for eloquence. In the same way, naphtha <note>A flammable liquid hydrocarbon</note> draws fire to itself and leaps toward it from wherever it is seen. Similarly, the root of the *aproxis* herb <note>A mythical plant described by Pliny the Elder that catches fire from a distance</note> attracts fire from afar, just like naphtha. There is a similar inclination between the male and female palm tree; when the branch of one touches the branch of the other, they wrap themselves in a mutual embrace, and the female bears no fruit without the male. Even a solitary almond tree is less fertile. Vines love the elm and the field maple <note>original: "oppium," likely referring to the Acer campestre, traditionally used as a support for vines</note>, and the olive tree and the myrtle love one another mutually; likewise the olive and the fig. Among animals, there is friendship between the blackbird...

<margin>The friendship of animals with other things.</margin>
Again, there are the little mouse-fish and the whale <note>The "musculus" was believed by ancient naturalists like Pliny to be a small fish that guided the whale, acting as its eyes.</note>. Nor is there friendship only among animals themselves, but also with other things, such as with metals, stones, and vegetables. For instance, the cat <note>original: "feles siue catus"</note> rejoices in the herb catnip <note>original: "nepeta"</note>, by the rubbing of which it is said to conceive and to make up for the absence of a mate. And the mares in Cappadocia expose themselves to the blowing of the wind, and from its breath and inhalation they conceive. So too frogs, toads, snakes, and whatever poisonous reptiles there are, rejoice in the plant called the "parsley of laughter" <note>original: "apium risus," likely the Cursed Buttercup (*Ranunculus sceleratus*), which causes a convulsive facial contraction resembling a grin when eaten</note>; concerning which physicians say that if anyone eats it, they die laughing. Conversely, when the tortoise is hunted by a snake, it eats oregano and is strengthened by it. The stork, when feeding on snakes, seeks its safety in oregano. The weasel, when about to fight against a basilisk <note>original: "regulum," literally "little king," a mythical serpent whose gaze could kill</note>, eats rue; from which we know that oregano and rue possess power against poisons. Thus, in certain animals there is a natural skill and an innate medicinal art. For when a toad is wounded by the bite and venom of another, it is accustomed to go to rue or sage and rub the site of the wound, and so free itself from the danger of the poison.

<margin>What things humans have learned from brute beasts.</margin>
Thus humans have been taught a great many remedies for diseases and the virtues of things by brute beasts. Swallows have shown us celandine <note>original: "chelidoniam"</note> to be a herb healthy for the sight, for they heal the eyes of their young with it. The magpie, when it is sick, puts a laurel leaf into its nest and so recovers its health. Similarly, wood pigeons, jays, partridges, and blackbirds purge their annual sluggishness with laurel leaves; crows also use it to extinguish the poison of the chameleon. If a lion has a fever, it recovers by devouring a monkey. The hoopoe, when harmed by eating grapes, heals itself with maidenhair fern <note>original: "adianto"</note>. In this way, deer taught that the herb dittany is useful for extracting arrows; for if they are struck by a weapon, they eject it by eating this herb. The Cretan goats do the same. But hinds also, shortly before giving birth, purge themselves with a certain herb called seselis. Similarly, those touched by a venomous spider <note>original: "phalangio," referring to the *Phalangium*, a type of poisonous spider or harvestman</note> seek their health by eating crabs. Swine, too, when harmed by snakes, heal themselves with the same food. Crows, when they feel themselves poisoned by Gallic toxin <note>original: "toxico Gallico," likely a lime-based poison or a specific herbal toxin used by the Gauls</note>, seek out oak or, as others say, "crow-herb" <note>original: "coruatiam"</note> for a remedy. Elephants, having swallowed a chameleon, help themselves with wild olive. Bears, harmed by mandrake, escape by devouring ants. Geese, ducks, and other aquatic birds heal themselves with the herb sideritis. Pigeons, turtledoves, and chickens use the herb pellitory <note>original: "helxine"</note>; cranes use the rush. Panthers protect themselves against aconite <note>wolfsbane</note> by using human dung. Wild boars use ivy; hinds use the herb cinnare.

# On the Inclinations of Enmities. Chapter XVIII. #

The inclinations of enmities are the opposite: for such inclinations are like a natural hatred, and just as anger, indignation, and a certain commanding contrariety, so that a thing flees its contrary or repels it, as if they were fleeing from its face.

Similarly, goats so hate basil <note>original: "ocimum"</note> that they consider nothing more pestilential.

<margin>The antipathy and discord of animals.</margin>
Again, among animals, mice and weasels <note>original: "mustelæ"</note> disagree; hence they say that if the brain of a weasel is added to the rennet, mice will not touch the cheese, nor will it be corrupted by age. Scorpions are also enemies with the "stalabores" <note>possibly a type of lizard or spider</note>, asps, and ichneumons <note>the Egyptian mongoose</note>. It is also said that nothing opposes serpents as much as crabs do, and pigs that have been bitten heal themselves with this food. Furthermore, the scorpion and the crocodile kill each other; and if anyone touches a crocodile with an ibis feather, it will be rendered motionless. The bustard bird flies away at the sight of a horse, and the deer flees at the sight of a ram or a viper. The elephant fears the grunting of a pig, and lions are terrified at the sight of a cock. Panthers do not touch those anointed with chicken broth, especially if garlic has been boiled in it. There is also enmity between foxes, swans, bulls, and crows. Likewise, the octopus is so terrified of the lobster that if it sees one nearby, it dies instantly. The conger eels tear at the lobster, and in turn, the octopus tears at the conger. The hyena is said to be such a terror to panthers that the panther does not even try to resist, even if touched by the hyena's skin; and if the pelts of both are hung opposite each other, they say the panther's hair falls out. Similarly, the lamb has an enmity and harmfulness toward the wolf...

against itself, and shudders at it, flees from it, and fears it. And they say that if the tail, skin, or head of a wolf is hung above a manger, the sheep are saddened and will not eat anything due to their excessive fear. Pliny reports <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist whose *Natural History* was a primary source for Agrippa</note> that the merlin <note>original: "esalon," a small bird of prey</note>, a small bird, breaks the eggs of the crow, whose chicks are harassed by foxes; in turn, the bird tears at the fox's cubs and the fox itself. When the crows see this, they come to help, as if against a common enemy. The linnet <note>original: "Acanthis," a small bird often identified as a goldfinch</note>, which lives among thorns, hates donkeys for this reason: they devour the flowers of the thorns. The hedge-sparrow <note>original: "Egithus"</note>, a very small bird, is said to disagree with the donkey to such an extent that it is certain their blood will not mix; furthermore, at the sound of the donkey braying, the eggs and chicks of the hedge-sparrow perish. The olive tree is also said to disagree so much with a prostitute <note>original: "meretrice"</note> that if it is planted by one, it is said either to remain forever barren or to wither away entirely. A lion fears nothing more than burning torches, nor is it believed to be tamed by any other thing but these. A wolf fears neither iron nor spear, but a stone, for if a wound is made by a thrown stone, worms are bred within the wolf. A horse dreads a camel so much that it can neither bear to look at its form nor endure its scent. An elephant, though fierce, becomes gentle upon seeing a ram. A snake fears a naked man, yet pursues one who is clothed. A raging bull's fury is weakened if it is tied to a fig tree. Amber <note>original: "Electrum," here referring to the fossilized resin known for its static properties</note> attracts all things except for basil <note>original: "ocymum"</note> and things smeared with oil, with which it disagrees by a certain natural antipathy.

### Chapter XIX. How the virtues of things are to be investigated and tested, whether they belong to the whole species or are natural gifts to a specific individual.

<margin>Virtues are inherent in things in two ways.</margin>
<gloss>On the customs <note>original: "sup. zoll," likely a reference to "super zollam" or custom/habitual behavior</note></gloss>
Furthermore, you must consider that the virtues <note>Meaning the hidden "powers" or "properties"</note> of things are inherent in some according to their species: such as boldness and courage in the lion and the rooster; timidity in the hare and the lamb; rapacity or greed in the wolf; treachery and craftiness in the fox; fawning in the dog; avarice in the crow and the raven; pride in the horse; anger in the tiger and the wild boar; sadness and melancholy in the cat; lust in the sparrow; and so it is with similar cases. For the greatest part of natural virtues follows the species. Yet certain virtues are inherent in things according to the individual, just as there are some men who vehemently abhor the sight of a cat, so much so that they cannot look at one without a most heavy shuddering; this horror is certainly not inherent in them according to the human species, as is manifest. Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath and physician</note> tells that in his time there lived a man whom all venomous things would flee; every creature that happened to bite him would die, while he remained entirely unharmed. Albertus <note>Albert the Great, a 13th-century philosopher and scientist</note> reports that he saw in Cologne <note>original: "Agrippina Colonia"</note> a girl who hunted spiders for food and was remarkably well-nourished, taking great delight in that kind of meat. Thus there is boldness in a prostitute and timidity in a thief. In this way, philosophers say that a specific individual who has never suffered from sickness bestows health against all sickness; therefore they say that the bone of a dead man who never had a fever, if hung over a patient, frees them from quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where the fever recurs every four days</note>. There are also many singular virtues inherent in individuals infused by the celestial bodies, as we have shown above.

<summary>Agrippa lists various natural antipathies between animals, plants, and objects, then explains that occult "virtues" can belong to an entire species or be unique to a single individual through celestial influence.</summary>

### That natural virtues are present in some things through their whole substance, but in others in certain parts or members. Chapter XX.

**A**gain, you must consider that the virtues of things are present in some according to the whole—that is, according to their entire substance or all its parts. For example, that little fish, the remora <note>original: "echeneis," a suckerfish believed in antiquity to be able to stop large ships simply by clinging to them</note>, which is said to stop a ship by touch alone, does not do this through any particular part, but through its entire substance. Likewise, the hyena possesses through its whole substance the power to make dogs fall silent by the touch of its shadow. Celandine <note>original: "chelidonia," a flowering plant in the poppy family</note> benefits the eyesight not through any one part, but through all its parts—no less by the root than by the leaves and seed—and so it is with similar things. 

However, certain virtues are present in things according to specific parts, such as only in the tongue, or the eyes, or other certain members or sections. Thus, in the eyes of the basilisk <note>A legendary serpent king</note> and the catoblepas <note>A mythical beast from Ethiopia with a heavy head and a lethal gaze</note>, there is a most violent power to kill men as soon as it sees them. A similar power is in the eyes of the hyena: whatever animal it gazes upon remains stuck to its tracks, becomes stunned, and cannot move itself. A similar power exists in the eyes of certain wolves; if they see a man first, he becomes stunned and so hoarse that if he wishes to cry out, he has no use of his voice. Virgil mentions this where he sings:

> ->Even the voice now<-
> ->flees Moeris himself; the wolves saw Moeris first.<-
<note>original: "Vox quoque Mœrim / Iam fugit ipsa, lupi Mœrim uidere priores." From Virgil's Eclogues, 9.54.</note>

<margin>Why sorcerers use eyes and not other parts especially.</margin>
Likewise, there were certain women in Scythia, and among the Illyrians and Triballians, who are said to have killed anyone they looked upon in anger. Similarly, we read of the Telchines, a people of Rhodes, who changed everything for the worse with their gaze, and for that reason were submerged by Jupiter. Therefore, sorcerers of this kind use the eyes of such animals in ointments <note>original: "collyriis," medical or magical eye-washes</note> when they intend to work through fascinations to produce similar effects. 

In a similar way, ants flee from the heart of a hoopoe bird <note>original: "upupæ"</note>, but not from its head, foot, or eyes. Likewise, the bile of a gecko <note>original: "stellionum"</note> rubbed in water is said to gather weasels, but not the tail or the head. The gall of goats enclosed in a bronze vessel in the earth gathers frogs; and a goat’s liver is hostile to all butterflies and moths. Dogs flee from one who carries the heart of a dog; and foxes do not touch chickens that have eaten a fox's liver. Thus, many things have various virtues dispersed in different ways through their various parts, just as they are infused from heaven into them according to the diversity of their capacity to receive them—just as in the human body, the bones receive nothing but life, whereas the eyes receive sight and the ears hearing. 

And there is in the human body a certain very small bone, which the Hebrews call <term>Luz <note>A legendary indestructible bone at the base of the spine or in the skull, said in Jewish tradition to be the "seed" from which the body is rebuilt at the Resurrection.</note></term>, about the size of a cleaned chickpea. It is subject to no corruption, nor is it even overcome by fire, but is always preserved unharmed. From this (as they say), like a plant from a seed, our physical body will sprout again in the resurrection of the dead. And these virtues are not revealed by logic, but by experience.

### Of the virtues of things which are in them during life only, and those which remain in them even after death. Chapter XXI.

<summary>This chapter explains that natural magical powers (virtues) can reside either in an object's entire substance or only within specific parts, such as the eyes or heart. It provides numerous examples from classical lore and introduces the "Luz" bone as an indestructible physical vessel for the soul's resurrection.</summary>

<page-num>XXVII.</page-num>
->BOOK ONE.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' beginning the text. The square frame depicts a classical scene with several figures: on the left, two figures stand engaged in conversation or instruction, while on the right, several other figures are seated or kneeling, suggesting a scholarly or judicial setting.</image-desc>**S**ubsequently, it will be necessary to know that certain properties exist in things only during life, while others remain even after death. Thus, the *remora* <note>original: "echeneis"; a small fish believed in antiquity to be able to stop a great ship by clinging to its hull.</note> stops ships; and the basilisk <note>original: "regulus"; the 'little king' of serpents.</note> and the *catoblepas* <note>A legendary beast whose gaze or breath was thought to be lethal.</note> kill with a look while they are alive. After death, however, they perform no such thing. Likewise, they say that in cases of colic, <note>original: "torminibus"; severe abdominal pain or griping.</note> if a live duck is applied to the belly, the disease passes into the duck and the duck dies. It is similar to what Archytas <note>A Greek philosopher and mathematician of the Pythagorean school.</note> says: if the heart is taken, recently extracted from an animal and still warm and beating, and hung over a patient suffering from a quartan fever, <note>A fever, likely malaria, that recurs every four days.</note> it removes it. Likewise, if anyone swallows the heart of a hoopoe, or a swallow, or a weasel, or a mole, while it is still alive and palpitating, it benefits their memory, recollection, intellect, and divination. 

<margin>Things to be gathered from animals must be removed while they are alive.</margin>From this arose a general precept: that whatever things are to be collected from animals—whether stones, limbs, or excrements such as hair, dung, or hooves—these must be taken from the animals while they are still living, and even, if possible, while they remain alive afterward. Hence they command that when you collect the tongue of a frog, you should return it to the water alive; if you collect the tooth or the eye of a wolf, you should not kill the wolf; and so on with similar things. Thus Democritus <note>A Greek philosopher often associated in the Renaissance with early scientific and alchemical secrets.</note> relates that if someone extracts the tongue from a living sea-frog <note>original: "rana marina"; likely referring to the anglerfish or stargazer fish.</note> with no other part of the body attached, and the frog itself is released back into the sea, and the tongue is placed over the heart-palpitation of a sleeping woman, she will answer truthfully to whatever she is asked. In a similar way, they promise that the eyes of frogs, taken before sunrise and bound to a sick person, so that the frogs are returned to the water blind, will drive away tertian fevers. They also report that these same eyes, bound with the flesh of a nightingale in a deer skin, produce wakefulness and put sleep to flight. Similarly, the spine of a stingray bound to the navel is said to make childbirth easy, if it was taken while the ray was alive and the fish itself was returned to the sea. So they say the right eye of a serpent, bound on, is beneficial against eye inflammations <note>original: "epiphoras"; watery or inflamed eyes.</note> if the serpent is released alive. And there is a certain fish, or rather a very large serpent, named the *myrus*, <note>A species of sea eel mentioned by ancient naturalists.</note> from which if an eye is plucked and bound to the forehead of a patient, it is said to cure eye disease; <note>original: "ophthalmiam".</note> indeed, the eye is said to regrow on the fish. However, it is warned that the one who does not release the fish alive will be seized by blindness in one eye. Likewise, the teeth of all serpents, when taken from the living, are said to cure quartan fever when hung over the patient. Similarly, if a tooth is taken from a living mole and the mole is released, toothaches are cured. Nor do dogs bark at those who carry the tail of a weasel that has been released. And Democritus tells that the tongue of a chameleon, if torn out while alive, is powerful for the outcome of legal trials, and the same is beneficial to women in labor around the house; but one must be careful not to bring it into the house, as that would be most destructive.

<margin>Things which retain their power after death.</margin>There are, furthermore, properties that remain after death. Regarding these, the Platonists say that in things where the Idea <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "Idea" or Form is the eternal, perfect blueprint of a thing; Agrippa suggests that if this essence is strong, it persists even after the physical body dies.</note> of matter is less submerged, that which is immortal does not cease to work wonders even after they are dead and gone. Thus, in herbs and plants, even when plucked and dried, the virtue itself—once infused by the Idea—still flourishes and operates. It is for this reason that, just as the eagle in its life surpasses and conquers all birds, so even when it is dead, its feathers destroy and corrode the feathers and plumes of all other birds. By the same reasoning, the skin of a lion [destroys] all other skins...

<margin>Different effects from drums made of different skins.</margin>...consumes it: and the skin of a hyena destroys the skins of a panther; and the skin of a wolf eats away the skin of a lamb. And these things do not only act through bodily contact, but sometimes even through vocal harmony: thus a drum made from the skin of an *adib* <note>original: "adib"; an Arabic word for wolf.</note>, that is, a wolf, causes a drum made of lambskin to fall silent. In a similar way, a drum made from the skin of a sea urchin <note>original: "Ericius marini"; likely referring here to a specific sea creature believed to have protective properties.</note> puts all reptiles to flight, no matter how great the distance from which the sound is heard. It is also well known that strings made from the intestines of a wolf, if stretched upon a lyre or zither alongside strings made from sheep, can produce no harmony.

## How lower things are subject to celestial bodies, and how the human body, and the very activities and motions of men, are distributed among the stars and signs. Chapter XXII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' depicting figures in a classical setting.</image-desc>It is manifest that all lower things are subject to the higher, and in a certain way (as Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who taught that the universe is a single, interconnected hierarchy.</note> says) they exist within one another: namely, the supreme things in the lowest, and the lowest in the supreme. Thus, there are earthly things in heaven, but after a celestial cause and manner; and there are heavenly things on earth, but in a terrestrial manner—that is, according to their effect. Thus we say there are certain "Solar" beings here and certain "Lunar" ones, in which the Sun and Moon cause something of their own power. Hence, such things receive many operations and properties similar to the operations of the stars and figures to which they are subject. 

In this way, we recognize "Solar" things as relating to the heart and the head, because Leo <note>The Lion.</note> is the house of the Sun, and Aries <note>The Ram.</note> is the Sun’s exaltation. Similarly, "Martial" things <note>Things governed by Mars.</note> contribute to the head and the testicles because of Aries and Scorpio. For this reason, for those whose senses stagger and whose heads ache from being drunk with wine, it is an immediate remedy to plunge the testicles into cold water or wash them with vinegar. 

But regarding these matters, it is necessary to know how the human body is distributed among the planets and signs. Know, therefore, that according to the tradition of the Arabs, the Sun presides over the brain, the heart, the thigh, the marrow, the right eye, and the spirit of life. Mercury, however, rules the tongue and the mouth, and the other instruments or organs of the senses, both internal and external; furthermore, he presides over the hands, feet, legs, nerves, and the power of imagination. Saturn rules the spleen and the fleshier part of the stomach. Jupiter rules the liver and the belly, <margin>Why the image of a navel was in the temple of Jupiter Ammon.</margin>as well as the navel; hence, antiquity records that an image of a navel was placed in the temple of Jupiter Ammon <note>An ancient Egyptian and Libyan deity later identified with the Greek Zeus; his oracle at the Siwa Oasis was world-famous.</note>. There are others who also attribute to him the ribs, the pubic area, the intestines, the blood, the arms and the right hand, the left ear, and the natural power. 

They place Mars in charge of the blood, the veins, the kidneys, the gallbladder, the buttocks, the back, the flow of seed, and the irascible power <note>The "angry" or spirited part of the soul.</note>. Likewise, they attribute the kidneys and testicles, the vulva, the womb, the genital seed, and the concupiscible power <note>The "desiring" part of the soul.</note> to Venus. Furthermore, she is said to rule over the flesh and fat, the belly, the pubic area, the navel, and all such things that serve the work of Venus <note>Meaning sexual acts or reproduction.</note>, such as the sacrum, the spine, and the loins; moreover, she is said to preside over the head and the mouth, where the kiss is given as a pledge of love. The Moon, although she claims the whole body and individual members for herself according to the variety of the signs, nevertheless specifically has the brain, the lung, the spinal marrow, and the stomach ascribed to her.

...and menstrual cycles, and all excrements, as well as the left eye with its power of growth. <margin>The parts of the human body and which planets and zodiac signs they are subject to.</margin> Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origins of alchemy and astrology.</note> himself says there are seven openings in the head of a living creature, distributed among the seven planets: namely, the right ear to Saturn; the left to Jupiter; the right nostril to Mars; the left to Venus; the right eye to the Sun; the left to the Moon; and the mouth to Mercury. In the same way, the individual signs of the zodiac care for their own members: Aries rules the head and face; Taurus, the neck; Gemini, the arms and shoulders; Cancer presides over the breast, lungs, stomach, and upper arms; Leo presides over the heart, the stomach, the liver, and the back; Virgo looks toward the intestines and the base of the stomach; Libra governs the kidneys, the thighs, and the buttocks; Scorpio the genitals, the womb, and the matrix; Sagittarius rules the thighs and the area below the groin; Capricorn rules the knees; Aquarius the legs and shins; Pisces rules the feet. And just as the triplicities <note>Groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note> of these signs correspond and agree with one another in the heavens, so they also agree in the limbs of the body. This is well established by experience, for from the coldness of the feet, the belly and chest ache, as these members respond to the same triplicity. Hence, a remedy applied to one benefits the other; just as when the feet are warmed, the pain in the belly ceases. Therefore, mindful of this order, you should know that things subject to any of the planets have a certain unique aspect or inclination toward the limbs attributed to that same planet, and especially to its houses and exaltations <note>Specific positions in the zodiac where a planet's influence is said to be strongest.</note>; for the other dignities, such as triplicities, terms, and faces, have little power in this matter. For this reason, Peony, citron-leaf, cloves <note>original: "gariophyllon"</note>, citron rinds, marjoram, dorycnium <note>A type of flowering shrub, possibly bindweed.</note>, cinnamon, saffron, aloeswood, frankincense, amber, musk, and partly myrrh, heal the head and the heart because of the Sun, Aries, and Leo. Likewise, the herb plantain <note>original: "arnogloſſa"</note>, a herb of Mars, heals the head and the testicles because of Aries and Scorpio; and so it is for the rest. Furthermore, Saturnine things contribute to sadness and melancholy; Jovial things to joy and dignity; Martial things to boldness, strife, and anger; Solar things to glory, victory, and courage; Venereal things to love, lust, and desire; Mercurial things to eloquence; and Lunar things to common life. <margin>The customs and activities of men are subject to the planets.</margin> Even the very activities and customs of men are distributed according to the planets: for Saturn rules the old, monks, melancholics, hidden treasures, and things acquired through long journeys and difficulty. Jupiter, however, possesses religious men, prelates, kings and dukes, and profits lawfully acquired. Mars has barbers, surgeons, physicians, lictors <note>An officer attending a magistrate, here used to mean a law-enforcer.</note>, executioners, butchers, oven-keepers, bakers, and soldiers, who are everywhere called "men of Mars" <note>original: "Mauortii"; derived from Mavors, an archaic name for Mars.</note>. Similarly, the other stars signify their own activities, just as they are described in the books of the astrologers.

Among metals, gold is solar on account of its splendor; and it possesses from the Sun the property of being a strengthener of the heart. Among stones, indeed, those which with golden drops imitate the solar rays: such as the stone *aetites* <note>Also known as the "eagle-stone," a hollow geode traditionally believed to be found in eagles' nests.</note> with its golden drops. Imitating the Sun, it has power against the falling sickness <note>A historical term for epilepsy.</note> and against poisons. So too the stone called the Eye of the Sun, having a shape similar to the pupil of the eye, from the middle of which a ray flashes out; it strengthens the brain and aids the sight. <margin>The chrysolite stone.</margin> So the carbuncle <note>A term used for red gemstones, typically garnet or ruby, believed in folklore to glow in the dark.</note> shining at night has power against every aerial and vaporous poison. So the chrysolite stone, having a thin and bright greenness in its color, in which a golden star flashes out when it is held against the Sun; it strengthens the spiritual parts and aids asthmatics. And when it is perforated and the hole is filled with donkey hairs and bound to the left arm, it drives away phantasms and melancholic terrors and repels folly. <margin>The Iris stone.</margin> So the Iris stone, similar in color to crystal, which is frequently found as a hexagon; when under a roof part of it is placed against the Sun's rays and the other part is held in the shadow, it collects the solar rays in itself, which it projects by reflection, making a rainbow <note>original: "Irim"</note> appear on the opposite wall. Also the heliotrope stone, green in the manner of jasper or emerald and starred with red drops; it makes one constant, glorious, and of good reputation, and contributes to length of life. And its power is wonderful, which it has over the solar rays, which it is said to convert into blood—that is, to make them appear bloody, as if the Sun were suffering an eclipse—namely when it is anointed with the juice of the herb of the same name and placed in a vessel full of water. And there is another more wonderful power of it over the eyes of men, whose sight it so constricts and so blinds that it does not permit the one wearing it to be seen; which, however, it does not do without the help of the herb of the same name, which is also called heliotrope—that is, the "sun-follower." These powers both Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and polymath known for his work on natural philosophy.</note> and William of Paris <note>William of Auvergne, the Bishop of Paris (c. 1180–1249), who wrote extensively on magic and nature.</note> confirm in their writings. <margin>Virtues of the hyacinth.</margin> The hyacinth <note>In historical texts, this often refers to zircon or blue sapphire rather than the flower.</note> also has power from the Sun against poisons and pestilential vapors; it renders the wearer safe and pleasing, contributes to riches and wit, and strengthens the heart; held in the mouth, it vehemently cheers the spirit. <margin>Pyrophilos.</margin> Also the *pyrophilos* <note>Literally "fire-lover."</note>, a mixed reddish stone; regarding this, with Albert as witness, Aesculapius <note>Referring to legendary Hermetic or medical texts attributed to the god of healing.</note> reports in one of his letters to Octavius Augustus that a certain poison is of such great coldness that it preserves the heart of the person killed by it from burning, so that if it is placed in fire for some time, it is turned into stone; and this is that which is called *pyrophilos* on account of the fire. It has a wonderful power against poisons and renders the wearer glorious and formidable to adversaries. Above all, however, there is a solar stone which Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note> is said to have found, named *pantaura*, which draws other stones to itself just as a magnet draws iron; it is most effective against all poisons, called by others *pantherus* because it resembles the spotted animal the panther; it is also called *Pantochras* because it contains all colors. Aaron <note>Likely referring to a medieval authority on gemstones.</note> calls it *Euanthum*. Furthermore, solar are the topaz, chrysoprase, ruby, and balagius <note>A "balas ruby," actually a type of spinel.</note>. Also solar are orpiment <note>original: "auripigmentum", a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment.</note> and golden colors...
