...and of the greatest light. Among plants and trees, solar things are those that turn toward the Sun, such as the heliotrope <note>The "turnsole" or sunflower family, known for following the sun's path.</note>, and those that fold their leaves as the Sun departs but gradually unfold them as it rises: such as the lotus, which some say is a solar shrub, as the shape of its fruit and leaves testifies. Likewise the Peony, celandine, citron, ginger, gentian, dittany, and also verbena, which is excellent for prophecy and purification, and for driving away evil spirits <note>original: "cacodaemones"</note>. Also the Laurel, sacred to Phoebus <note>A name for Apollo as the sun god.</note>, as well as the cedar, the palm, the ash, the ivy, and the vine; and all those things that repel poisons and lightning, and being evergreen, do not fear the cold of winter. Solar things also include mint, mastic, zedoary <note>A root similar to ginger.</note>, saffron, balsam, amber, musk, yellow honey, aloe wood, cloves, cinnamon, aromatic calamus, pepper, frankincense, marjoram, and *Libanotis* <note>Rosemary or frankincense-herb</note>, which Orpheus calls the incense of the sun. Among animals, solar things are those that are magnanimous, courageous, and eager for victory and glory: such as the lion, the king of beasts; the crocodile; the lynx; the ram; the goat; and the bull, the king of herds, who was consecrated to the sun by the Egyptians at Heliopolis and whom they call the Truthful One <note>original: "ueritem"</note>; and the Apis bull in Memphis, and in Hermonthis a bull by the name of Pathim. The wolf is also sacred to Apollo and Latona. Furthermore, the dog-headed baboon <note>original: "cynocephalus"</note> is solar, for it barks twelve times a day, once every hour, and at the time of the equinox it urinates twelve times every hour; it does the same at night, which is why the Egyptians used to carve its image on water-clocks <note>original: "hydrologiis"</note>. Solar things among birds include the phoenix, the only bird of its kind, and the eagle, the queen of birds; likewise the vulture, the swan, and those birds that applaud the rising sun with a kind of hymn and seem to call out to it, such as the rooster and the raven. The hawk is also numbered among solar things by Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher.</note> because in Egyptian theology it is a symbol of spirit and light. Furthermore, solar things include whatever gathers a likeness of the Sun’s works, such as glow-worms that shine at night, and also the beetle which they call the cat <note>original: "felem"</note> because of its glowing form, and which they also call the *cantharus* <note>The dung beetle or scarab.</note>; it rolls little balls of dung, broods upon them, and generates others. By the interpretation of Apion, it is judged to be solar because it gathers a likeness of the Sun’s works in this very act, and its eyes are observed to change according to the Sun's course; and all things like them. Among small fish, the most solar is the seal <note>original: "uitulus marinus," literally "sea-calf"</note>, which resists lightning; likewise the dactyl <note>A type of bioluminescent mollusk.</note> and the sea-lung <note>A type of jellyfish.</note> which shine at night; and the starfish <note>original: "Stella"</note>, on account of its burning heat, following the king of the spiral-shells; similarly those pearls that have a king among them, which when dried harden into a stone of golden color.

## What things are under the Moon. Chapter XXIV.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial "L" featuring a kneeling figure in prayer or contemplation within an architectural frame.</image-desc>
Lunar things among the elements are the earth, and then water, both of the sea and of rivers, and all moist things: the saps of trees and the fluids of animals, especially those that are white, such as the whites of eggs, fats, sweat, phlegm, and the superfluities of bodies. Among tastes, the salty and the insipid. Among metals, indeed, is silver. Among stones, the crystal belongs to it, as does silver marcasite <note>A metallic mineral, often iron sulfide, with a pale brassy color.</note>, and all white and green stones. Likewise the stone *selenites*—that is, the moon-stone—translucent white with a honey-like glow, imitating the lunar movement and having the shape of the moon within itself, reflecting its daily waxing and waning. Likewise pearls, which are generated from droplets of water in shells; and similarly crystal...

<margin>Lunar trees and plants.</margin>
...and the beryl <note>original: "berillus"</note>. Among lunar plants and trees is the *selenotropion* <note>Literally "moon-turner"; a legendary plant said to follow the moon's path just as the sunflower follows the sun.</note>, which turns toward the moon just as the heliotrope turns toward the sun. The palm tree is also lunar, for it is said to send out a new branch at every rising of the moon. Hyssop is also lunar, as is a species of rosemary; it is the smallest of trees and the greatest of plants, sharing the nature of both. Also lunar are the chaste tree <note>original: "hagnus castus"</note>, or "chaste shrub," and the olive. Similarly, the herb *chinostates* <note>Likely the "moon-herb" or *kinostates*, often identified as a type of peony or mythical plant.</note> is lunar, for it increases and decreases along with the moon—not only in its moisture and potency, but in its very substance and number of leaves. This is a trait that all plants share to some extent, except for Martian onions <note>Onions associated with the planet Mars.</note>, which are the only ones to have the contrary power of growing while the moon wanes and shrinking while it waxes. Just as among birds, the bird of Saturnine origin <note>The owl or raven is often meant here.</note> is most hostile to both the moon and the sun.

<margin>Lunar animals.</margin>
Lunar animals are those that enjoy human company and those that excel in both the various loves and hatreds of nature, such as dogs of every kind. The chameleon is also lunar, for it always takes on a color similar to the object before it, just as the moon changes its nature according to the zodiac sign in which it is found. Likewise, lunar animals include sows, does, she-goats, and any animals that observe and imitate the lunar motion, such as the dog-headed baboon <note>original: "cynocephalus"</note> and the panther. Indeed, it is said that the panther has a spot on its shoulder similar to the moon, which grows into a circle and curves its horns in the same way. Cats are also lunar, for their eyes become larger or smaller according to the phases of the moon. Other things of this kind include menstrual blood, with which magi perform many wonderful and monstrous feats. The hyena is also lunar, as it is said to change its sex and is susceptible to various sorceries. All animals called "amphibious" are lunar, meaning those that live on land and in water together, such as beavers and otters, and those that hunt fish. Furthermore, all monstrous animals are lunar, as are those generated without manifest seeds or through "equivocal generation" <note>The historical belief that life could spontaneously arise from decaying matter rather than from parents.</note>, such as mice born from mating or from the rot of the earth.

<margin>Lunar birds.</margin>
Among birds, the lunar ones are geese, ducks, divers, and all water birds and hunters of fish, such as herons. Also those produced equivocally, such as wasps from the carcasses of horses, bees from the putrefaction of cows, gnats from spoiled wine, and beetles from the flesh of donkeys. Most lunar of all is the two-horned beetle, which they call "bull-formed." Having buried a little ball of dung, it leaves it for twenty-eight days—the time it takes the moon to measure the entire zodiac; on the twenty-ninth day, when it believes the conjunction of the luminaries <note>The meeting of the Sun and Moon, i.e., the New Moon.</note> is about to happen, it opens the ball and casts it into the water, and from it the beetles then emerge.

<margin>Lunar fish.</margin>
Among fish, the lunar ones are the *aelurus* <note>A type of catfish; the name is derived from the Greek word for cat.</note>, whose eyes vary with the phases of the moon, and all those that observe the moon's motion, such as the cramp-fish <note>original: "torpedo"</note>, the remora <note>original: "echeneis"; a fish believed to be able to stop ships by clinging to them.</note>, the crab, the oyster, shellfish, and frogs.

Among birds, the Saturnine ones are those with long necks and heavy voices, such as cranes, ostriches, and peacocks—which are sacred to both Saturn and Juno. Likewise the owl, the screech-owl, the bat, the hoopoe, the raven, and the *origis* <note>original: "origis"; likely referring to a species of plover or a bird mentioned by ancient naturalists as being particularly envious.</note>, a most envious bird. Likewise turtles, oysters, shellfish, sea sponges, and things related to them.

### Things that relate to Mars. Chapter XXVII.

Those things belonging to Mars among the elements are Fire: and in the same way, everything that is burnt or sharp. Among the bodily humors, it rules yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note>. Its tastes are bitter, acrid, stinging to the tongue, and those called "tear-inducing" <note>original: "lachrymosi"</note>. Among metals, it claims iron and red brass, and everything fiery, red, or sulfurous. Among stones, it rules the diamond <note>original: "adamas"</note>, the magnet, the bloodstone, jasper of many kinds, and the amethyst. Among plants and trees, it claims hellebore, garlic, spurge <note>original: "euphorbium"</note>, cartabana, ammoniac, radish, spurge-laurel, monkshood <note>original: "napellus"</note>, scammony, and all things poisonous due to an excess of heat; also those protected by stinging thorns or those that burn, prick, or blister the skin upon contact, such as the thistle, the nettle, and the spearwort <note>original: "flammula"</note>. It also rules those things that sting the eyes to tears, such as onions, shallots, leeks, mustard, and castor. All thorny trees are Martial, and the cornel tree is specifically sacred to Mars. Among animals, those that are warlike, predatory, bold, and of a keen imagination belong to him, such as the horse, the mule, the goat, the kid, the wolf, the leopard, and the wild ass. Also included are serpents and dragons dangerous for their venom, and whatever is troublesome to humans, such as fleas, flies, and the baboon <note>original: "cynocephalus"</note>, because of its ill temper. All birds that are predatory, meat-eating, or "bone-breakers" <note>original: "ossifragæ"</note> belong here, such as the eagle, falcon, hawk, and vulture; also those called dire and funeral birds, like owls, screech-owls, kestrels, and kites; and those that are always hungry and most predatory; and those that swallow and emit a voice as if they were being strangled, such as ravens and crows—and the woodpecker, above all others, is sacred to Mars. Among fish, he possesses the pike, the mullet, the stingray, the sea-ram, the sea-goat, the sea-wolf, and the bluefish <note>original: "Glaucum"</note>, which are at once the most voracious and predatory.

### Which things are of Venus. Chapter XXVIII.

Things belonging to Venus among the elements are air and water. Among the humors, she rules phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note> along with the blood, the spirit, and the genital seed. Among tastes, she possesses the sweet, oily, and delightful. Among metals, she has silver, as well as yellow and red brass. Among stones, the beryl, chrysolite, emerald, sapphire, green jasper, carnelian, eagle-stone <note>original: "lapis aëtites"</note>, lapis lazuli, and coral are suited to her, along with all beautiful, variegated, white, or green stones. Among plants and trees, she rules vervain, the violet, maidenhair fern <note>original: "capillus Veneris"</note>, and the herb "lucia" or Valerian, which in Arabic is called *phu*. Likewise thyme, ladanum, amber, musk, sandalwood, coriander, and all aromatic incenses, and delightful, sweet fruits such as sweet pears, figs, and pomegranates, which poets say were first planted by Venus in Cyprus. Furthermore, the rose of the Morning Star <note>original: "Luciferi rosa"</note> and the myrtle of the Evening Star are dedicated to her. Among animals, she has the lustful, the delicate, and those capable of strong love, such as puppies, rabbits,

### Things that follow Mercury. Chapter XXIX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' depicting a figure holding a caduceus, representing the god Mercury, set against a background of foliage.</image-desc>Mercurial things among the elements include water, although Mercury moves all things without distinction. Similarly, he rules the humors, especially when they are mixed together; but he also regulates the animal spirit <note>original: "spiritum animalem"; in Renaissance physiology, this was the subtle fluid in the nerves that enabled movement and sensation</note>, as well as various foreign and blended tastes. Among metals, his are quicksilver <note>original: "argentum uiuum"</note>, tin, and silver marcasite. Among stones, there is the emerald, agate, porphyry, topaz, and those of many different colors, or those which have various shapes naturally within them, or those made by art, such as glass, and those which mix saffron-yellow with green. Among plants and trees are the hazel, cinquefoil <note>original: "pentaphyllon"</note>, dog's mercury <note>original: "Mercurialis"</note>, fumitory <note>original: "fumus terræ"</note>, burnet, marjoram, parsley, and those that have shorter and smaller leaves, composed of mixed natures and varied colors. His animals are those that are wise, clever, vigorous, of versatile character, swift in running, and who easily live alongside humans, such as dogs, monkeys, foxes, weasels, the deer, and the mule. Also, hermaphroditic animals and those that change their sex by turns, such as the hare, the hyena, and the like. Among birds, those that are by nature clever, singing, musical, and versatile, such as the goldfinch, the fig-eater, the blackbird, the thrush, the lark, the nightingale, the calandra lark, the parrot, the magpie, the ibis, the purple gallinule, and the unicorn beetle <note>original: "scarabeus unicornis"</note>. Among fish, he rules the wheel-fish <note>original: "trochus"</note>, which mates with itself, for which reason they call it "male-female." Likewise, the fraudulent octopus <note>original: "polypus"</note> whose color is versatile, and the stingray because of its skill; similarly, the mullet, which knocks food off a hook with its tail.

### That the whole sublunary world, and those things in it, are distributed among the planets. Chapter XXX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure holding what appears to be a staff or scythe, possibly representing Saturn or a personification of time.</image-desc>Furthermore, whatever is found in the whole world is affected according to the lordships of the planets and receives its power from them. Thus, in fire, the life-giving light is attributed to the Sun and the heat to Mars. On the earth, the varied surfaces belong to the Moon, Mercury, and the starry heavens, but the entire mass belongs to Saturn. In the middle elements, where they rule, the airy humor is subject to Jupiter, the watery humor to the Moon, while the mixed humor obeys Mercury and Venus. By a similar reasoning, in nature, the active causes follow the Sun, while the material follows the Moon. The fertility of active causes follows Jupiter, and the fertility of matter follows Venus. A swift expedition toward an effect follows Mars and Mercury—the former because of his intensity, the latter because of his dexterity and multiform power. The permanent continuation of all things, however, is dedicated to Saturn. Among the number of vegetables, every fruit...

## How Provinces and Kingdoms are Distributed to the Planets. Chapter XXXI.

<note>An ornate woodcut initial letter "I" features intricate floral patterns, marking the beginning of the chapter in the style of early modern typography.</note>

The world itself, through its kingdoms and provinces, is also distributed among the planets and the signs of the Zodiac. For under Saturn, together with Capricorn, are placed Macedonia, Thrace, Illyria, India, Ariane, and Gordiana; many of these regions are in Asia Minor. Under Saturn with Aquarius are the Sauromatic region, Oxiana, Sogdiana, Arabia, Phazania, Media, Ethiopia, and these regions for the most part belong to interior Asia. To Jupiter, with Sagittarius, are subject Tuscany, Celtic Gaul, Spain, and Arabia Felix <note>Literally "Happy Arabia," referring to the fertile southern part of the Arabian Peninsula</note>. With Pisces, he rules Lycia, Lydia, Cilicia, Pamphylia, Paphlagonia, Nasamonia, and Garamantica. Mars rules, with Aries: Britain, Gaul, Germany, Bastarnia, the hollows of Syria <note>original: "concaua Syriae"; referring to Coele-Syria, the valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges</note>, Idumaea, and Judea. With Scorpio, however, he rules Syria, Commagene, Cappadocia, Metagonitis, Mauritania, and Gaetulia. Subject to the Sun with his sign of Leo are Italy, Apulia, Sicily, Phoenicia, Chaldea, and the Orsenii or Orchenii. Venus, with Taurus, holds the Cyclades, the coastal regions of Asia Minor, Cyprus, Parthia, Media, and Persia. With Libra, she commands the Bactrians, the Caspians, Serica <note>The ancient Roman name for Northern China, famed for its silk</note>, Thebaid, Oasis, and the Troglodytes <note>Literally "cave-dwellers," referring to various historical groups along the Red Sea coast</note>. Mercury, with Gemini, holds Hyrcania, Armenia, Mantiana, Cyrenaica, Marmarica, and Lower Egypt. Truly with Virgo, he holds Greece, Achaia, Crete, Babylon, Mesopotamia, Assyria, and Elam—from which the Elamites mentioned in Scripture are named. Following the Moon with Cancer are Bithynia, Phrygia, Colchis, Numidia, Africa, Carthage, and all Carchedonia <note>Another name for the region surrounding Carthage</note>. We have gathered these things from the opinion of Ptolemy; to these, many other things could be added according to the writings of other astrologers. Truly, he who knows how to compare these divisions of provinces and this celestial distribution with the ministries of the presiding Intelligences <note>original: "regentium intelligentiarum"; spiritual beings or angels believed in Hermetic philosophy to govern the movements and influences of the planets</note>, the blessings of the Israelite tribes, the lots of the Apostles, and the symbolic seals of the Sacred Scriptures, will be able to draw out great and even prophetic oracles of the future for every region.

## Things Subject to the Signs, the Fixed Stars, and Their Images. Chapter XXXII.

<summary>This page concludes the list of planetary correspondences for plants and stones and provides an extensive list of geographical regions governed by the seven planets and the zodiac signs according to Ptolemy.</summary>

A similar logic must be maintained in all things concerning the figures of the fixed stars: thus, they hold that the terrestrial ram is subject to the celestial **Aries**, and the terrestrial bull and ox to the celestial **Taurus**. Likewise, crabs are subject to **Cancer**, lions to **Leo**, young women to **Virgo**, scorpions are presided over by **Scorpio**, goats by **Capricorn**, horses by **Sagittarius**, and fish are subject to the sign of **Pisces**. Similarly, the celestial Great Bear <note>original: "Ursa coelestis"</note> presides over bears, the Hydra over snakes, and dogs are subject to the Dog Star <note>original: "cani"; referring to Sirius or the constellation Canis Major</note>; and so it goes for each individual thing. 

Indeed, **Apuleius** <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Apuleius, the author of a highly influential 4th-century herbal manual</note> distributed specific and, as it were, proper herbs to the signs and planets: namely, to **Aries** he gave sage <note>original: "elelisphacon"</note>; to **Taurus**, upright vervain <note>original: "peristereona orthion"</note>; to **Gemini**, supine vervain <note>original: "peristereona hyption"</note>; to **Cancer**, comfrey <note>original: "symphyton"</note>; to **Leo**, cyclamen; to **Virgo**, calamint; to **Libra**, scorpion-tail <note>original: "scorpiuron"; likely a type of heliotrope or caterpillar-weed</note>; to **Scorpio**, mugwort <note>original: "artemisiam"</note>; to **Sagittarius**, pimpernel <note>original: "anagallidem"</note>; to **Capricorn**, sorrel <note>original: "lapathum"</note>; to **Aquarius**, dragonwort <note>original: "dracontem"</note>; and to **Pisces**, birthwort <note>original: "aristolochiam"</note>. 

As for the planets: to **Saturn** he gives houseleek <note>original: "sempervivum"</note>; to **Jupiter**, agrimony <note>original: "eupatorium"</note>; to **Mars**, hog’s fennel <note>original: "peucedanum"</note>; to **the Sun**, heliotrope; to **Venus**, panacea or maidenhair fern <note>original: "callitrichum"</note>; to **Mercury**, mullein <note>original: "phlomum"</note>; and to **the Moon**, peony <note>original: "aglaophotim"</note>. 

However, **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermetic philosophy</note>, followed by **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century polymath</note>, assigns different plants to the planets: to **Saturn** he gives asphodel; to **Jupiter**, henbane <note>original: "hyoscyamum"</note>; to **Mars**, plantain <note>original: "arnoglossam"</note>; to **the Sun**, knotgrass <note>original: "polygoniam"</note>; to **Venus**, vervain <note>original: "verbenam"</note>; to **Mercury**, cinquefoil <note>original: "pentaphylon"</note>; and to **the Moon**, goosefoot <note>original: "chenostacen"</note>. 

Even now we know by experience that asparagus is subject to **Aries**, and basil to **Scorpio**. <margin>The marvelous sowing of asparagus. The production of scorpions.</margin> For if the shavings of a ram’s horn are sown, asparagus grows; and basil, when crushed between two stones, generates scorpions. <note>This reflects the medieval belief in "spontaneous generation," where specific materials were thought to transform into living creatures through celestial influence.</note>

Furthermore, from among the more notable stars, according to the teachings of **Hermes** and **Thebit** <note>Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century astronomer and mathematician</note>, I shall enumerate several here: 

The first is called **Caput Algol** <note>the star Algol in Perseus</note>, and among stones it presides over the diamond; among plants, over black hellebore and mugwort. 

Next follow the **Pleiades**, presiding among stones over crystal and the *diodocus* <note>A legendary gemstone said to be used by magicians</note>; among plants, over the herb *diacedon*, frankincense, and fennel; furthermore, they claim quicksilver among the metals for themselves. 

The third, **Aldebaran**, has under it among stones the carbuncle and ruby; among plants, spurge <note>original: "tithymallum"</note> and woodbine. 

The fourth is called **Hircus** <note>the star Capella</note>; among stones it holds the sapphire; among plants, horehound, mint, mugwort, and mandrake. 

The fifth is **Canis Major** <note>the star Sirius</note>; it has under it among stones the beryl; among plants, savin, mugwort, and dragonwort; among animals, the tongue of a snake. 

The sixth is **Canis Minor** <note>the star Procyon</note>; it has among stones the agate; among plants, heliotrope and pennyroyal. 

The seventh is **Cor Leonis** <note>the star Regulus</note>; it has among stones the garnet; among plants, celandine with mugwort and mastic. 

The eighth is **Cauda Ursae Majoris** <note>the star Alkaid</note>; it has among stones the magnet <note>lodestone</note>; among plants, chicory (whose leaves and flowers turn toward the north), mugwort with the periwinkle flower; among living things, the tooth of a wolf. 

The ninth is called **Ala Corvi** <note>the star Algorab</note>; under it among stones is black onyx; among plants, burdock, *quadrigenum*, henbane, and comfrey; among animals, the tongue of a frog. 

The tenth, **Spica**, has under it among stones the emerald; among plants, sage, clover, periwinkle, mugwort, and mandrake. 

The eleventh is called **Alchamech** <note>the star Arcturus</note>; it presides among stones over jasper; among plants, plantain. 

The twelfth is **Elpheia** <note>the star Alphecca</note>; under it among stones is the topaz; among plants it presides over...

Among animals, even the seal <note>original: "uitulus marinus"; literally "sea-calf"</note> is subject to the Sun and Jupiter. Foxes and apes belong to Saturn and Mercury, and domestic dogs belong to Mercury and the Moon. And we have already taught more concerning these things in the preceding sections.

### On the seals and characters of natural things. Chapter XXXIII.

<margin>
Every thing
has its own
character.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'O' featuring a woodcut illustration of a human head within a circular frame.</image-desc>
All stars have their own proper natures, properties, and conditions, the seals and characters of which they produce through their rays even in these inferior things: in the elements, in stones, in plants, in animals, and in their members. Hence, every single thing—by a harmonic disposition and by its own star shining upon it—obtains some special seal or character impressed upon it, which is significative of that star or harmony, and which contains within itself a special virtue, differing from others either in genus, species, or number, according to the pre-existing matter. Therefore, every thing has its own character impressed upon it by its star for some peculiar effect, especially by that star which holds principal authority over it above all others. These characters contain and retain within themselves these proper natures, virtues, and roots of their stars, and they produce similar operations in other things upon which they are reflected. They provoke and assist the influences of their stars—whether of the planets, the fixed stars, or even the celestial images and signs—provided they are fashioned in the proper material, at the proper time, and with the proper solemnities. Considering this, the ancient sages, who labored greatly to investigate the occult conditions of things, sought out the images, figures, seals, and characters of the stars...

The same is found in the bones and shoulder blades of animals; from this, the practice of spatulamancy

<note>original: "spatularia"; a form of divination performed by inspecting the shoulder blades (scapulae) of animals</note> arose. Since man is the most complete image of the entire universe <note>The concept of the "Microcosm," where the human body reflects the structure and harmony of the whole cosmos</note> and contains within himself every celestial harmony, we undoubtedly find an abundance of the seals

<term>signacula; physical marks or "signatures" indicating a spiritual or planetary influence</term> and characters of all the stars and celestial influences within him. Truly, just as the number of the stars is known to God alone, so too are their effects and signs upon these lower things; therefore, no human intellect can ascend to a full knowledge of them. Thus, very few things have become known, which the ancient philosophers and palmists 
<term>Chiromantici; those who practice chiromancy or palm reading</term> achieved partly through reason and partly through experience, and many things still lie hidden and locked away in the treasuries of nature. These marks are the same and consistent across all nations and languages. Later palmists, both ancient and more recent, have discovered many others; whoever wishes to know them should seek out their volumes. It is enough here to have shown from where the characters of nature derive their origin and in what things they are to be sought.

## How through natural things and their virtues, we can entice and attract the influences and virtues of celestial bodies. Chapter XXXIIII.

Now if you desire to receive the virtue of a star from any part of the world, by applying those things that belong to that star, you undergo its proper influence—just as wood, through the use of sulfur, pitch, and oil, is prepared to receive a flame. Nevertheless, when you properly apply many things to a certain species or individual, which are scattered yet conform to the same idea and star, soon through this matter so opportunely prepared, a singular gift is infused from the "idea" through the reasoning of the World Soul <note>original: "anima mundi"; the vital spirit or "soul" that Renaissance philosophers believed animated the entire universe, connecting the stars to the earth</note>. I say "opportunely prepared," namely under a harmony similar to the harmony that had originally infused a certain virtue into the matter. For although things possess certain virtues, such as those we have mentioned, those virtues are so deeply hidden that a work is rarely completed by them through such virtue alone; <margin>A comparison.</margin> <note>original: "Simile"</note> but just as crushing a mustard seed excites its hidden sharp flavor; and just as the heat of fire brings into view letters written with onion juice or milk that were previously hidden; and as letters inscribed on a stone with goat fat—though entirely hidden—stand out as if carved when the stone is submerged in vinegar; and just as the touch of a broom <note>original: "scopæ"; likely referring to the butcher's broom or a similar shrub used in folk medicine</note> or wild strawberry excites a slumbering madness; so celestial harmony itself brings forth, excites, strengthens, and makes manifest the virtue hidden in matter. It, so to speak, brings it from potentiality into action <term>potentiality into action; "de potentia producit in actum," a philosophical term meaning to take something that is a dormant possibility and make it a physical reality</term>, when things are properly exposed to it under celestial opportunity. For example: if you wish to attract virtue from the Sun, seek out those things which are solar: among vegetables, plants, metals, stones, and animals:

### On the mixtures of natural things with one another, and their utility.
## Chapter XXXV.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a figure, possibly a scholar or a saint, seated in an interior or landscape setting.</image-desc>
We have discovered that in the lower realm of nature, all the gifts of the higher [celestial] bodies are not found contained within a single thing. Instead, many species are dispersed among us, just as there are many "solar" things, yet each one of them does not embrace all the powers of the Sun; rather, one has some properties from the Sun, and another has others. Therefore, it is sometimes necessary in our operations to make mixtures, so that if a hundred or a thousand virtues of the Sun are scattered through as many plants, animals, and similar things, we can fuse these together and reduce them into a single form, in which we will see all the said virtues contained and united. <margin>Double virtue in a mixture.</margin> There is, moreover, a twofold power in such a mixture: one, namely, which was previously inherent in its parts and is celestial; the other, acquired through a specific and skillful mingling of many things confused together according to certain proportions, such as may agree with the heavens when gathered under a specific constellation. This power descends through a certain similarity and relationship of things toward one another and with the higher powers, insofar as the following powers correspond step-by-step to those preceding them, especially where the "passive" material is further accommodated to its "active" celestial agent. 

Thus, by a certain composition of herbs, vapors, and similar things, prepared both physically and astronomically, a certain common form results, endowed with many gifts of the stars. This is like the honey of bees, which, being taken from the juices of innumerable flowers and reduced into one form, contains the power of all, through the nearly divine and admirable skill of the flies <note>original: "muscarum" — Agrippa refers to bees here as "flies," a common archaic classification</note>. It is no less marvelous what Eudoxus of Cnidus <note>A Greek astronomer and mathematician</note> reports about artificial honey, which a certain race of giants in Libya knew how to make from flowers so well that it seemed to differ very little from the honey of bees. 

Every mixture composed of many parts is most perfect when it is so glued together from its parts that it becomes one, consistent in all its parts, and not easily pulled apart. We see this sometimes in stones and different bodies which are glued and united by a certain natural force so that they seem entirely one; such as two trees joined through grafting <note>original: "insitionē"</note>, or oysters joined with stones by a certain hidden power of nature. Animals have even been seen turned into stone and thus united with the substance of the stone, so that they seemed to form one homogeneous body. Likewise, ebony in the genus of trees is at one time wood, and at another, stone. Therefore, when someone fashions a mixture from many materials under celestial influences, the variety of celestial actions on one hand, and the gathered natural powers on the other, produces certain wonders through ointments, eye-salves <note>original: "collyria"</note>, fumigations, and similar preparations. Such things are read in the books of Chiramis, Archytas, Democritus, and Hermes (in the book titled *Alchorat*), and many others.

### On the union of mixed things, and the introduction of a more noble form and of sensible life. Chapter XXXVI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring two figures, likely Adam and Eve, in a landscape with trees.</image-desc>

It should be known, indeed, that the more noble the form of a thing is, the more ready and prone that thing is to receive influence, and also the more powerful it is in action. Thus, incomprehensible wonders of things are produced when, for instance, materials have been mixed and prepared at opportune times; they are set out to be quickened, reconciling to them life from the stars and a sensible soul <note>The "sensible soul" in Renaissance philosophy refers to the level of the soul responsible for perception and movement, shared by humans and animals</note>, as if a more noble form. For there is such great power in prepared materials, which we then see acquire life, when the perfect mixing of qualities is seen to have already broken the previous opposition <note>Agrippa refers to the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—which must be balanced or "tempered" for life to emerge</note>; they have indeed attained a more perfect life, insofar as the temperament is further removed from opposition. The Heaven, indeed—a most powerful cause from the beginning of any thing to be generated—bestows celestial influences and marvelous gifts together with life through the perfect "cooking" and digestion of the matter, insofar as in that life and sensible soul there is a capacity to conceive more noble and sublime virtues. Furthermore, celestial virtue lies dormant elsewhere, like sulfur removed from a flame; but in living bodies, it often blazes up, like ignited sulfur: then it fills everything nearby with its vapor. Thus certain wonderful works are produced, such as are read in the book *Nemith* <note>original: "libro Nemith"</note>, which is also titled *The Laws of Pluto*: because such generations are monstrous and are not produced according to the common laws of nature.

<margin>
The various procreations of different animals.
</margin>
For we know that gnats are generated from worms, wasps from a horse, bees from a calf and an ox; from a crab buried with its legs removed, a scorpion is generated; from a duck roasted until it is ground to powder, when that powder is thrown into water, frogs are generated. If, however, it is cooked in a pastry and cut into pieces and left in a damp and underground place, toads are generated. From the herb basil <note>original: "basilicone"</note> crushed between two stones, scorpions are generated; and from the hair of a menstruating woman placed under dung, serpents are made. Even a hair from a horse's tail thrown into water takes life and turns into a destructive worm. And there is a craft by which, in an egg being sat upon by a hen, a form similar to a human is generated, such as I have seen and I know how to compose, which magi declare effective with marvelous virtues, and they call this the "true mandrake" <note>This refers to the creation of a homunculus, an artificial humanoid creature, which Agrippa here distinguishes from the natural mandrake root</note>. It is necessary, therefore, to know which and what kind of materials—whether begun or perfected by nature or art, or assembled from many—can receive such celestial influences. For the suitability of natural things to celestial ones is sufficient for us to draw influence from them: because since nothing prevents the heavens from diffusing their light to lower things, they permit no matter to be void of their virtue. Therefore, however much of the matter is perfect and pure, it is not unfit for celestial influence.

<margin>
The binding of matter to the soul of the world.
</margin>
For such is the binding and continuity of matter to the soul of the world <term>Anima Mundi: The "World Soul," an animating principle thought by Neoplatonists to connect the physical world to the divine</term>, which daily flows over natural things, and over everything that nature has prepared, so that it is impossible for prepared matter not to be infused with life or some more noble form.

## How, by certain natural and artificial preparations, 
## we draw down celestial and vital gifts from 
## above. Chapter XXXVII.

The Academics <note>Followers of Plato's school of philosophy</note> say, along with Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of Hermeticism and alchemy</note>, and Iarchas the Brahmin <note>A legendary Indian sage and king mentioned in the life of Apollonius of Tyana</note>, and the Kabbalists of the Hebrews <note>original: "Mecubales"</note> admit, that all things which are under the lunar globe in this lower world are subject to birth and decay. They also say that these same things exist in the celestial world, but in a celestial manner; and furthermore in the intellectual world, but with a much higher degree of perfection and a better quality; and finally, they exist most perfectly in the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" refers to the original Divine Mind or the world of ideas from which everything else is modeled</note>. In this sequence, every lower thing corresponds to its superior, and through that to the highest, according to its own kind. From these superiors, they receive their powers: from the heavens, they receive that celestial power which they call the "fifth essence" <note>The quintessence; the pure, transparent element that makes up the stars and planets</note>, or the "spirit of the world," or the "middle nature"; from the intellectual world, they receive a spiritual and living vigor that transcends every physical quality; and finally, from the Archetype, through these intermediaries, they receive the original power of all perfection according to their degree. Hence, from these lower things to the stars, from those to their presiding intelligences, and from there to the Archetype, <margin>Where magic flows from</margin> every single thing can be aptly traced back; it is from this entire sequence that all magic and all more occult philosophy flows. For something natural is drawn daily through art, and something divine is drawn daily through nature; seeing this, the Egyptians called nature a "magician," that is, the magical power itself, in the attraction of likes by likes and of fitting things by fitting things. 

The Greeks called this kind of attraction—the mutual agreement of things with one another, linking the superior with the inferior—**sympathy** <term>συμπάθιαν (sympathian): the invisible bond between things that share the same nature</term>. Thus, earth agrees with water in its coldness, water with air in its moisture, air with fire in its heat, and fire agrees with heaven in its substance. Fire does not mix with water except through the medium of air, nor does air mix with earth except through the medium of water. In the same way, the soul is not joined to the body except through the spirit; nor is the intellect joined to the spirit except through the soul. Thus we see that once nature has shaped the human body in the womb, by this very preparation it immediately draws down the spirit from the universe. This spirit serves as the fuel <note>original: "fomes," meaning tinder or kindling</note> within the spirit and body for the understanding and for attaining the mind by divine means. Just as dryness in wood is a preparation for oil to penetrate it, and the oil soaked into it is the food for the fire, so the fire itself is the vehicle for light. 

By these examples, we see how, through certain natural and artificial preparations, we can receive certain celestial gifts from above. For stones and metals agree with herbs, and herbs with animals, and animals with the heavens, and these with the intelligences, and those with divine properties and attributes—and ultimately with God himself, in whose likeness and image all things were created. The first image of God is the world; the image of the world is man; the image of man is the animal; the image of the animal is the **zoophyte** <term>zoophytum: a creature that is half-animal and half-plant, such as a sea sponge or coral</term>; the image of that is the plant; the image of the plant is metals; and the stones of these represent their likenesses and reflections. Furthermore, in spiritual things, the plant agrees with the brute animal in its power of growth, the animal with man in its senses, man with the demon <note>original: "dæmone," referring here to a guiding spirit or celestial being rather than an evil entity</note> in intellect, and these with God in im-
<meta>catchword: im- (continuity for "immortalitate" / immortality)</meta>

<margin>The wonderful binding together of Nature.</margin>
...joined by mortality: divinity to the mind, the mind to the intellect; this to intention, this to the imagination; that to sensation, sensation to the senses, and these finally to physical things. For such is the binding and continuity of nature, that every superior power flows through each individual inferior thing in a long and continuous series, dispersing its rays down to the very last; and the inferior things reach up to the highest through each of their superiors. For thus the lower things are connected to the upper in turn, so that the influence from their head—the First Cause <note>In this context, the "First Cause" refers to God or the ultimate source of all existence</note>—proceeds like a stretched string down to the lowest parts; if one end of it is touched, the whole suddenly trembles, and such a touch resonates all the way to the other end. If one inferior thing is moved, the superior thing to which it corresponds is also moved, just like the strings in a well-tuned lute <note>original: "cythara"</note>.

### How we can receive gifts from above, not only celestial and vital, but even certain intellectual and divine ones. Chapter XXXVIII

<margin>The Magician attracts hidden things through manifest ones.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring a stylized letter against a background of scrolling vine work and foliage within a square border.</image-desc>The Magicians <note>original: "Magi"; here referring to practitioners of high natural magic or wisdom seekers</note> teach that through lower things that conform to the higher, celestial gifts can be drawn down by the favorable influences of heaven. And thus also through these celestial things, celestial spirits <note>original: "daemones," referring to tutelary spirits or planetary intelligences rather than evil beings</note>, as followers of the stars, can be reconciled and introduced to us. Therefore, when certain materials that possess the natural power of divinity—that is, those which are naturally in harmony with the higher powers—are properly collected, partly through physics <note>natural science</note> and partly through astronomy, and are opportunely joined together from all sides, gifts can be received from above: not only celestial or vital ones, but even certain intellectual, spiritual, and divine ones. Iamblichus, Proclus, and Synesius <note>Prominent Neoplatonist philosophers who explored theurgy and the relationship between the soul and the cosmos</note>, along with the whole school of Platonists, confirm this. And Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus"</note> writes that from specific and certain things fitting for a certain spirit, a statue properly composed is immediately animated by the corresponding spirit. This is also mentioned by Augustine in the eighth book of *The City of God*. For such is the harmony of the world that even super-celestial things are drawn by celestial ones, and supernatural things are joined with and drawn by natural ones. This is because one craftsman-like power <note>original: "virtus opifex"; the creative force of the universe</note> is diffused through all things by participation in its form. This craftsman-like power, just as it produces manifest things from hidden reasons, so the magician assumes manifest things in order to attract hidden ones: for example, through the rays of the stars, through fumigations <note>the burning of ritual incense</note>, through lights, through sounds, and through natural things agreeable to the celestial ones. In these things, beyond their bodily qualities, there are also incorporeal and divine reasons, senses, numbers, and measures. 

Thus we read that the ancients were often accustomed to receive something divine and wonderful through certain natural things. For instance, the stone that is found in the pupil of the hyena's eyes, if held under the tongue, is said to provide the power of divination. The moonstone <note>original: "selenites"</note> is said to do the same. So too they say that by the *anchitis* stone, images of gods are summoned, and by the *synochitis* stone, the shades of the dead <note>original: "umbrae inferorum"</note> are summoned and held. Similar things are done by the herb *aglaoptis*, which is also called *marmoritides* because it grows in the marble of Arabia on the Persian side; Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, author of the encyclopedic "Natural History"</note> narrates that magicians use it when they wish to summon gods, and that there is an herb named *theangelis*, which magicians drink to divine. Furthermore, there are certain herbs by which the dead are recalled to life; regarding this, the historian Xanthus tells of a certain herb named bali,

<margin>Tillo restored to life by an herb.</margin>
...the killed young of a dragon was restored to life by its parent, and in the same way a certain man named Tillo, whom the dragon had killed, was resuscitated. And Juba <note>Juba II, a scholar-king of Numidia known for his writings on natural history</note> reports that in Arabia a certain herb recalled a man to life. But whether such things can truly happen by the power of herbs, or any other natural thing regarding a human being, we shall discuss in the following pages. <margin>Animals can be recalled to life, but man not so easily.</margin> However, it is certain and manifest that this can happen in other living creatures. For instance, drowned flies, if placed in warm ashes, revive; and drowned bees likewise recover their life in the juice of catmint <note>original: "nepetæ"</note>. Eels, dead from a lack of water, if their bodies are still intact and they are placed under dung in vinegar with the addition of vulture's blood, will all recover their life after a few days. They say that if someone cuts a remora <note>original: "Echeneim"; a fish legendary for its ability to stop ships and its magical properties</note> into pieces and throws them into the sea, the parts will shortly come back together and revive. We also know that the pelican recalls its killed young to life with its own blood <note>A common medieval allegory for the sacrifice of Christ, here treated as a natural wonder</note>.

### That by certain materials of the world we can entice worldly deities and the demons who serve them. Chapter XXXIX.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'N' containing a figure seated in a landscape with hills and trees.</image-desc>
<margin>Evil demons are enticed by evil arts.</margin>
No one is ignorant that evil demons can be enticed by evil and profane arts, just as Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, a Byzantine scholar whose work on demons was highly influential in the Renaissance</note> relates that the Gnostic magicians were accustomed to doing. They performed almost execrable and abominable obscenities, such as were once done in the rites of Priapus <note>A Greek god of fertility, often depicted with permanent arousal</note> and in the service of the idol called Panor, to whom they sacrificed with their private parts uncovered. Not unlike these—if indeed it is truth and not a fable—are the things read concerning the detestable heresy of the Templars; and similar things are well known regarding sorceresses, for the madness of old women is often found to go astray in such crimes. By these and similar things, evil spirits are enticed and conspire together, just as the malignant demon said concerning the magician Cynops <note>A sorcerer from the apocryphal Acts of John who challenged the Apostle</note> to John: "All the power of Satan," he said, "dwells there, and enters into a pact with all the principalities; we ourselves are with him, and Cynops obeys us, and we in turn obey him."

<margin>Good angels are won over by good works.</margin>
On the other hand, no one is ignorant that by good works, a pure mind, mystical prayers, devout supplications, and the like, the super-celestial angels are won over to us. Therefore, let no one doubt that in a similar way, by certain materials of the world, worldly deities can also be enticed—or at least the demons who are the ministers or followers of these deities. As Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermetic philosophy</note> says, these are aerial demons, not the super-celestial or even higher ones. Thus we read that the ancient priests made statues and images that predicted the future, and infused the spirits of the stars into them. These spirits were not so much trapped by certain materials as they were delighted by them; for recognizing these materials as being compatible with themselves, they always and willingly dwell in them. Through these objects, they speak and perform wonders, no differently than demons are accustomed to doing when they occupy human bodies.

<margin>Binding is manifold.</margin>

Also the binding of thieves and robbers, so that in a certain place...

...so they cannot steal; the binding of merchants, so they are unable to buy or sell in a particular place; the binding of an army, so it cannot cross a certain boundary; the binding of ships, so that even with the greatest force of the wind and infinite sails stretched to the gale, they are unable to leave the harbor. Likewise, the binding of a mill, so it cannot be turned by any force; the binding of a cistern or spring, so water cannot be drawn from it; the binding of a field, so no crops can be produced in it; the binding of a place, so nothing can be built there; the binding of fire, so it cannot be lit in a certain place, or so that a combustible thing will not burn even when placed in the hottest fire. Also, the binding of lightning and storms, so they cannot cause harm. ### On sorceries, and their power. Chapter XLI.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'V' featuring a seated figure in a classical pose within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>The power of sorceries <note>original: "veneficiis"</note> is said to be so great that it is believed they can overturn all lower things, and make them waste away or change, just as Virgil <note>the Roman poet Publius Vergilius Maro</note> sings:

> These herbs, and these poisons <note>original: "uenena"</note> gathered for me in Pontus,
> Moeris himself gave to me. Many grow in Pontus:
> By these I have often seen Moeris become a wolf and hide in the woods,
> often seen souls come out of deep graves,
> and seen crops moved from one place to another.

Likewise elsewhere, concerning the companions of Ulysses:

> Whom Circe, the cruel goddess, changed from human form
> with powerful herbs, into the faces and backs of wild beasts.

And a little later:

> Picus, the tamer of horses, whom his wife, seized by Desire,
> Circe, struck with her golden wand and changed with poisons
> into a bird, and sprinkled his wings with colors.

There are also types of such sorceries like those recounted by Lucan <note>the Roman poet Marcus Annaeus Lucanus</note> concerning that Thessalian witch <note>Erichtho, a famous literary figure known for her necromancy</note> summoning the spirits of the dead, saying:

> Here everything nature brought forth in a sinister birth
> is mixed: not the foam of dogs who fear the water,
> nor the guts of the lynx, nor the knot of the tough hyena
> was missing, nor the marrow of a stag fed on serpents.
> Nor the remora <note>original: "echeneis"; a legendary fish believed to stop ships by clinging to them</note>, which holds back the ship in the middle of the waters
> though the East wind stretches the ropes; and the eyes of dragons.

XLVII.
->BOOK ONE<-

<margin>
Men turned into beasts of burden.
</margin>
And such are the things that Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century Roman novelist and philosopher; this passage refers to his famous work, *The Golden Ass*.</note> tells of that sorceress <term>Pamphila</term><note>A character in Apuleius's novel who practices dark magic.</note> when she was working for the sake of love: to whom her maidservant Fotis brought goat hairs shorn from inflated skins, instead of the hair of a Boeotian youth. Pamphila, she says: "Now frantic in spirit, she climbs the shingled roof, which—being stripped of its covering and open on one side to the air, and accessible to all eastern and other views—is most suited for these arts of hers, and there she secretly dwells. First, she arranged her deadly workshop with its usual apparatus: every kind of spice, unidentified metal plates inscribed with characters <note>original: "laminis literatis"; likely refers to magical curse tablets or talismans</note>, the surviving nails of ill-fated ships, and many exposed limbs of mourned and even buried corpses. Here were noses and fingers; there, the fleshy nails of hanged men; elsewhere, the preserved blood of those who were slaughtered, and truncated skulls wrenched from the teeth of wild beasts. Then, over the chanting of breathing entrails, she makes an offering with various liquids: now with spring water, now with cow's milk, now with mountain honey and mead. Then, she takes those hairs, entwined and knotted together, and burns them with many perfumes upon living coals. Then immediately, by the inescapable power of the magical discipline and the blind violence of the compelled spirits, those bodies whose sizzling hairs were smoking took on human spirit, and they felt, and heard, and walked, and came to where the scent of their own remains led them, and—longing for entry—they leaped at the doors instead of that Boeotian youth." Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, a Church Father; he discusses such transformations in *The City of God*.</note> also claims that he heard in Italy of certain sorceresses so imbued with these arts that, upon giving a piece of cheese, they would immediately turn men into beasts of burden <note>original: "iumenta"; specifically pack animals like donkeys or horses</note> to carry necessary loads, and when the work was finished, they would restore them to men again.

### On the Admirable Virtues of Certain Sorceries. Chapter 42.

<margin>
The powers of menstrual blood.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' featuring a woodcut illustration of a seated figure, possibly a scholar or authority figure, in a room or landscape.</image-desc>
Now indeed I will relate certain sorceries <note>original: "ueneficia"; here referring to the magical or poisonous properties of substances</note>, and by their example, the way is prepared for this entire consideration. Among these is menstrual blood; let us see what great power it has in sorcery. For as they say, new wine turns sour at its approach; a vine is permanently damaged by its touch; crops become sterile when touched, and grafts die; the buds of gardens are scorched, and the fruits of trees fall off. The brightness of mirrors is dimmed by its very gaze; the edge of steel in barbers' knives and the polish of ivory are dulled; even iron is immediately corrupted by rust. Bronze, when touched, takes on a heavy poison of dreadful odor and verdigris. Dogs are driven into a frenzy if they taste it, and their bite is filled with an incurable poison. Hives of bees die off and flee when the hives are touched; and linen turns black when it is boiled. Mares, if they are pregnant, suffer a miscarriage if touched by it; it also causes an abortion in pregnant women if smeared on them. Female donkeys do not conceive for as many years as the grains of barley they have eaten which were touched by it. Even the ash of menstrual cloths, if one sprinkles it on clothes to be washed, changes purple dyes and takes the color away from flowers. They say that tertian and quartan fevers <note>Types of malaria characterized by paroxysms every three or four days.</note> are driven away by the menstrual fluid kept in the wool of a black ram and enclosed in a silver bracelet. Furthermore, it is said to be most effective for tertian and quartan fevers to smear the soles of the patient's feet with it—and it is much more effective if done by the woman herself, even if the patient is unaware of it. In this way, even the attacks and diseases of the "comitial" sickness <note>original: "comitiales impetus"; an old term for epilepsy.</note> are cured. However, it is agreed among everyone that if

XLVIII.
### OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY, ###

<margin>Remedy for hydrophobia</margin>
If water or drink should be feared due to the bite of a [rabid] dog, it is said that if a scrap of cloth dipped in menstrual blood is merely placed beneath the cup, that fear is immediately dispelled. Furthermore, they report that if women, uncovered during their monthly cycle, walk around the crops, the caterpillars, worms, beetles, Spanish flies <note>original: "cantharides"; these were often used in medicine and as an aphrodisiac, but were considered toxic in large doses.</note>, and all harmful pests fall away. However, one must beware not to do this at sunrise, for the seeds will wither. Similarly, it is said that hailstorms and whirlwinds are driven away by this, and it is effective against lightning; Pliny himself recounts many of these things. You should know that the poison is more potent if it occurs during a waning moon; but its power is greater if it happens during the dark moon; if indeed it occurs during an eclipse of the moon or sun, it becomes incurable. It is of the greatest and most powerful vigor when that purging happens in the first years of puberty and occurs during the first virginity; this also is consistent for her: for if the doorposts of a house are touched by it, every <term>maleficium</term><note>A general term for harmful sorcery or an evil spell.</note> in that house is rendered void. Furthermore, they report that the threads of a garment touched by it cannot even be overcome by fire, and if they are thrown into a blaze, the fire spreads no further. It is also said that if the root of a peony, along with <term>castoreum</term><note>A yellowish secretion from the scent glands of beavers, used historically in medicine.</note> and the scrapings of menstrual cloths, is given to a patient, the <term>falling sickness</term><note>original: "morbum comitialem"; a historical term for epilepsy, so named because Roman public assemblies (comitia) would be cancelled if someone had a seizure.</note> is cured. Furthermore, if you burn or roast the stomach of a stag and add the smoke from menstrual cloths, it is said that <term>ballistae</term><note>Refers here to cross-bows or siege engines; the suggestion is that the ritual ruins the efficacy of hunting weapons.</note> will be of no use for hunting. Also, if the hairs of a menstruating woman are placed under dung, they say serpents are generated; and if they are burned, the serpents are put to flight by the odor—so great is the power of that 
<margin>Hippomanes.</margin>
poisonous substance, that it is a poison even to venomous creatures. There is also the <term>hippomanes</term><note>Literally "horse-madness"; a substance long associated with aphrodisiacs and love magic in antiquity.</note>, a small piece of flesh not at all unknown among sorceries, about the size of a dried fig and black in color, which appears on the forehead of a newborn foal. Unless the mother devours it immediately, she holds her affection completely turned away from her offspring and will not suckle the foal. Because of this, they say its power is greatest for inciting love when it is turned into a powder and drunk in cups mixed with the lover's blood. There is also another poisonous substance which they call by the same name, *hippomanes*, namely that virus which flows from the loins of mares at the time they are said to be in a frenzy of love, of which Virgil <note>Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BCE), the premier Roman poet.</note> makes mention when he sings:

> Hence at last the *hippomanes*, which by its true name
> The shepherds call, a sluggish poison distills from the groin.
> The *hippomanes* which wicked stepmothers have often gathered,
> Mixing herbs with not-unharmful spells. <note>From Virgil's *Georgics*, Book III, lines 280–283.</note>

Regarding this, Juvenal the Satirist <note>Decimus Iunius Iuvenalis (1st–2nd century CE), a Roman poet known for his biting social commentary.</note> also says:

> I shall speak of the *hippomanes*, the incantation, and the brewed poison
> Given to a stepson. <note>From Juvenal's *Satires*, VI, 615–616.</note>

Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Rhodes (3rd century BCE), author of the *Argonautica*.</note> tells in his *Argonautica* of the herb of Prometheus, which he says was born from the gore and blood dripping onto the earth while the vulture tore and fed upon the liver of Prometheus on Mount Caucasus. Its flower, he says, is like a saffron, of a Corycian color <note>A reference to high-quality saffron from Mount Corycus in Cilicia.</note>, with a double stem rising to a cubit's measure; the root beneath the earth is like recently cut flesh, emitting a dark juice like that of a beech tree. If someone, after first performing a ritual to Proserpina <note>The Roman queen of the underworld.</note>, anoints their body with this, he reports that they can be harmed by neither iron nor fire. And Saxo Grammaticus <note>A 12th-century Danish historian.</note> writes that a certain Froto had a garment which, when worn, allowed him to be harmed by no sharp point of any weapon. XLIX.
### BOOK ONE. ###

<margin>The magical properties of the hyena.</margin>
...is infected by magical arts: for, as Pliny reports, if the doorposts are touched with its blood, they say the arts of illusions are infested <note>Meaning the blood acts as a barrier or interference to deceptive magic.</note>, and that the gods can neither be called forth nor spoken with, no matter how they are tempted. Likewise, if the ash from the left ankle-bone of this animal is boiled and smeared on someone along with the blood of a weasel, they say that person will become hated by everyone. They say the same happens if the eye is boiled. Conversely, the furthest part of the intestine is used against the injustices of leaders and those in power, and is effective for the success of petitions, and the outcomes of trials and lawsuits, if one merely carries a small amount of it. Also, if a part of its joint <note>original: "cauerna," likely referring to a joint or hollow of the bone</note> is bound to the left arm and one looks at a woman, it is an aphrodisiac so immediate that she will follow at once; however, the skin of its forehead is said to resist enchantments.

<margin>The basilisk and the magical properties of its blood.</margin>
They also say the blood of the Basilisk, which they call the "Blood of Saturn," has such great power in magic that it grants the one carrying it success in petitions to those in power, and even in prayers to the gods, as well as remedies for diseases and the granting of favors. They also say that a tick, if it is pulled from the left ear of a dog that is nothing but black in color, possesses great power in predicting life; for if a sick person responds to the one who brought it—the questioner standing at the feet and asking about the disease—there is certain hope for life; but the person will die if they do not respond. They also say a stone bitten by a rabid dog has the power to cause discord if placed in a drink. Also, a dog’s tongue placed in a shoe beneath the big toe prevents dogs from barking at you, especially if it is joined with the herb of the same name, namely <term>cynoglossum</term> <note>original: "cynoglossa," also known as Hound’s-tongue.</note>. The same effect is produced by the membrane from a dog's afterbirth; moreover, dogs will flee from someone carrying a dog’s heart. Pliny also relates that there are frogs called "bramble toads" <note>original: "rubetarum"</note> that live only among brambles, which are full of magical properties, and wonderful things are done with them. For a small bone found in the left side, if cast into cold water, causes it to boil immediately; by it, the attacks of dogs are restrained, and love and quarrels are stirred up if it is added to a potion; and if bound to the body, it stimulates lust. On the other hand, with the bone from the right side, boiling water is cooled and will not boil again unless the bone is removed; quartan fevers <note>A form of malaria where the fever returns every four days.</note> and other fevers are cured with it if it is bound in a fresh snakeskin, and love and lust are inhibited. However, the spleen and heart of these frogs are effective aids against the very poisons made from them. Pliny recites these things. It is also said that the iron with which a man was killed has a wonderful power among magical things; for if horse bits and spurs are made from it, they say that with them any horse, even the fiercest, is very easily ruled and overcome. And if horseshoes were made from it, they say the horse becomes the swiftest and never tires from any labor. Furthermore, they maintain that certain characters and names ought to be inscribed upon them. They also say that if someone dips a sword with which men are beheaded into wine, whoever is sick and drinks from it is freed from quartan fever. They even say that a cup fashioned from a bear’s brain, or drunk from its skull, induces a "bear-madness," such that the man who drinks thinks himself transformed into a bear, and judges everything he sees as being in the form of bears, and thus continues in that madness until the power of the cup is dissolved, without any other harm to his temperament being felt from it.

**S**uffumigations <note>The act of burning substances to produce smoke or vapor for medicinal or magical purposes; essentially a ritual incense.</note> adapted to the stars also possess great power, insofar as they vehemently affect the air and the spirit so that one may opportunely grasp celestial gifts under the rays of the stars. For our own spirit is greatly transformed by vapors of this kind, since both are a type of vapor and similar to one another. Furthermore, the air, being very easily affected by the qualities of both lower things and celestial ones through these vapors, penetrates the heart <note>original: "præcordia," referring to the diaphragm or the region around the heart, then considered the seat of the vital spirit.</note> constantly and suddenly, and wonderfully brings us into harmony with similar qualities. For this reason, those about to practice divination are accustomed to use suffumigations to affect the imagination; these, being in harmony with certain divine powers, prepare us to receive divine inspiration. Thus they say that

<margin>Incense leading to prophecy.</margin>
an incense made from flax seed, psyllium seed, violet roots, and celery <note>original: "apii," which could be celery or wild parsley.</note> makes one see future things and contributes to prophecy. Indeed, no one should wonder how much power suffumigations have over the air who realizes, along with Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 234–305 CE) who wrote extensively on the nature of demons and the soul.</note>, that by certain vapors exhaling from their proper suffumigations, aerial spirits <note>original: "dæmones," in the classical sense of intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> are immediately attracted and insinuated, and thunders and lightnings are brought forth, and similar things. Just as it is well known that the liver of a chameleon, if burned on the highest roof-tiles, provokes rain and lightning; similarly, the head and throat, if set on fire with oak wood, produce the clashing of rain and thunder. Suffumigations are also made under the opportune influences of the stars, causing the phantoms of spirits to appear immediately in the air or elsewhere. Thus they say that if a fumigation is made from coriander, celery, or henbane with hemlock, spirits will immediately gather;

<margin>Herbs of the spirits.</margin>
for this reason, they call those the "herbs of the spirits." Similarly, they say that if a mixture is made from the root of the giant fennel <note>original: "cannæ ferulæ."</note> with the juice of hemlock, henbane, *raffi*, mullein <note>original: "barbaffi."</note>, red sandalwood, and black poppy, and then burned as incense, it causes spirits and strange figures to appear; and if celery is added to these, it puts spirits to flight from every place and destroys their illusions. In the same way, incense made from calamint, peony, mint, and the *palma Christi* <note>The Castor Oil plant (*Ricinus communis*).</note> drives away all evil spirits and harmful phantasms. Furthermore, they record that by certain suffumigations certain animals are gathered or put to flight, just as Pliny <note>Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*.</note> reports that by the smoke of the *liparis* <note>Likely referring to a type of fish or stone mentioned by Pliny.</note> all beasts are called forth. Likewise, from the burning of the bones from the upper throat of a deer, serpents are gathered, but they are put to flight by the smoke of a deer’s horn. The feathers of peacocks, when burned, do the same thing. Similarly, when the lung of a donkey is lit, all venomous things flee; if the hoof of a horse is burned in some house, mice are driven away. The same happens with the hoof of a mule. They say flies are also driven away by this if it comes from the left foot. And they say that if a house or some place is fumigated with the gall of a cuttlefish, mixed with frankincense, roses, and aloeswood, and then if some seawater or blood is thrown in that place, the whole house will seem full of water or blood; and if plowed earth is thrown there, the earth will seem to tremble. Moreover, it should not be thought otherwise than that vapors of this kind produce something else in the body, and infuse power into it which persists for a very long time, just as a contagious or poisonous vapor of pestilence, preserved even for more than two years in the wall of a house, infects the inhabitants, and just as the calamity of a plague or leprosy lurking in a garment infects the wearer long afterward. and for rings and similar instruments of magic, as well as for hidden treasures, certain suffumigations <note>The burning of substances to produce ritual smoke.</note> are employed, which Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> testifies are of no small help. Thus they say that if anyone buries gold or silver or any precious thing while the Moon is conjoined to the Sun at the bottom of the sky <note>original: "in imo cœli," referring to the Imum Coeli, the fourth astrological house associated with foundations and hidden things.</note>, and fumes the location with coriander, saffron, henbane, celery, and black poppy—all crushed in equal weights and mixed with the juice of hemlock—that which is thus hidden can never be found or taken away, for demons will always guard it. If anyone tries to take anything from there, he will be infested by them and fall into a frenzy. 

Hermes <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational occult texts were attributed.</note> also says that "spermaceti" <note>original: "spermaceti," likely referring to the waxy substance from sperm whales, highly valued in perfumery and alchemy.</note> has no equal in a suffumigation for alluring demons. Therefore, if a smoke is made from it along with agarwood <note>original: "lignum aloës," a fragrant resinous wood, not the common succulent.</note>, costus, musk, saffron, and incense, mixed with the blood of a hoopoe, it very quickly gathers aerial spirits. If it is fumed around the graves of the dead, it gathers the *manes* <note>The spirits or ancestral shades of the deceased.</note> and shadows of the dead. 

Thus, whenever we direct a work toward the Sun, we use solar suffumigations; if toward the Moon, we use lunar ones, and they did the same for the rest. It must be understood that just as there is opposition and enmity among the stars and spirits, so too is there among their suffumigations. For instance, agarwood and sulfur are contrary to one another, as are frankincense and quicksilver <note>original: "argentum uiuum," meaning mercury.</note>. Spirits brought in by the smoke of agarwood will flee once sulfur is lit. Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> gives the example that a spirit accustomed to appearing in the form of a lion would immediately vanish if a rooster were presented, because the rooster is contrary to the lion; similar things must be considered and practiced.

### The composition of certain suffumigations adapted to the planets. Chapter XLIIII.

<image-desc>A decorative initial "S" showing two scholars or mages in a library, surrounded by books and study materials.</image-desc>

**W**e compose the suffumigation for the **Sun** from saffron, ambergris, musk, agarwood, balsam wood, and laurel fruit, along with cloves, myrrh, and frankincense. All of these are crushed and mixed in a certain proportion—specifically that which yields the sweetest odor—and are incorporated with the brain of an eagle or the blood of a white rooster, formed into the shape of pills or troches <note>Small medicinal or ritual lozenges.</note>.

A **Lunar** suffumigation we compose from the dried head of a frog, the eyes of a bull, and the seed of white poppy, along with frankincense and camphor; these shall be incorporated with menstrual blood or the blood of a goose.

For **Saturn**, one takes the seed of black poppy, the seed of henbane, mandrake root, lodestone <note>original: "lapis magnes," a naturally magnetized mineral.</note>, and myrrh; these are prepared with the brain of a cat or the blood of a bat.

For **Jupiter**, one takes ash tree seed, agarwood, storax, gum benzoin, lapis lazuli, and the tips of peacock feathers; these are incorporated with the blood of a stork or a swallow, or the brain of a deer.

For **Mars**, we take euphorbium, bdellium, gum ammoniac, the roots of both hellebores <note>Both the white (Veratrum album) and black (Helleborus niger) varieties, often used in ritual magic despite their toxicity.</note>, lodestone, and a little sulfur; all these are incorporated with the brain of a raven, human blood, and the blood of a black cat.

For **Venus**, we compose a fume from musk, ambergris, agarwood, red roses, and red coral; these are prepared with the brains of sparrows and the blood of pigeons.
