to elicit presages from properties: thus those which relate to Saturn and Mars are all called dire and deathly birds, such as owls, screech-owls, and the others we recounted above. The horned owl <note>original: "bubo"</note> is also included, because as a bird of Saturn, solitary and nocturnal, it is said to be of the most unpropitious omen, of which the poet says:

> And thus the foul bird, messenger of coming grief,
> The sluggish horned owl, a dire omen to mortals. <note>original: "Fædaq; sic uolucris uenturi nuncia luctus / Ignauus bubo, dirum mortalibus omen." From Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 5.549-550.</note>

The swan, however, a delightful bird sacred to Venus and even to Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>, is said to be of the most happy presage, especially in the auspices of sailors, because it is not submerged by water; hence Ovid sings:

> The swan is always the most joyful bird in auspices. <note>original: "Cygnus in auspiciis semper lætissimus ales."</note>

<margin>Oscine birds.</margin>
There are, furthermore, <term>oscine birds</term> <note>From the Latin "oscines," birds that provide omens through their voices or songs rather than their flight.</note> which provide an auspice by their mouth and song: such as the raven, the woodpecker, and the crow, as Virgil says:

> Often the crow predicted it from the hollow oak on the left. <note>original: "Sæpe sinistra caua prædixit ab ilice cornix." From Virgil, *Eclogues* 9.15.</note>

<margin>What must be considered in the flight of birds.</margin>
Truly, the birds that portend the future by their flight are such as buzzards, ospreys <note>original: "sanqualæ," likely referring to the *sangualis* or bone-breaker bird</note>, eagles, vultures, cranes, swans, and the like. For in their flight, it is considered whether they fly slowly or hurriedly, whether they fly to the right or to the left, and how many fly together at the same time. In this way, when cranes fly hurriedly, they signify a storm; when they fly silently, they signify calm weather. Likewise, when two birds fly together and they are "feral" <note>birds of ill omen associated with death</note>, they are said to portend evil, because two is the number of confusion. In a similar way, you shall investigate the reason concerning other numbers by applying them here. Furthermore, observing similarity in these conjectures is a masterful technique, just as Venus herself, in disguise, teaches her son Aeneas in these verses:

> Unless my vain parents have taught me augury in vain,
> Behold those twelve swans rejoicing in a flock,
> Whom the bird of Jove <note>the eagle</note>, gliding from the ethereal region,
> Was scattering in the open sky; now in a long line they seem
> Either to take the ground, or look down upon the ground already taken.
> As they, returning, play with whistling wings,
> And have encircled the pole in a flock, and given forth their songs:
> Not otherwise do your ships and the youth of your people
> Either hold the harbor, or enter the mouth with full sail. <note>original: "Ni frustra augurium vāni docuere parentes..." From Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.392-400.</note>

The most wonderful kind of augury, however, is that of those who hear and understand the speeches of animals, as it is read that Melampus, Tiresias, and Thales excelled among the ancients, and as Apollonius of Tyana is said to have been eminent, who is reported to have been skilled in the speech of birds. Concerning him, Philostratus and Porphyry relate that when Apollonius once sat in a gathering of friends, looking at sparrows sitting in a tree, one little sparrow came from elsewhere, chirping and making a noise with its voice. When all the others followed it and flew away, he said to his companions that the sparrow had announced to the rest that a donkey loaded with wheat had fallen in an alley near the city, and the wheat was scattered on the ground. At these words, a great many people were moved to go and see, and so it was...

# BOOK ONE.
## PAGE 71.

<margin>
The voices of living creatures are signs of the passions of the soul.
</margin>
They found that things had happened exactly as Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note> had predicted, and they were filled with wonder. Porphyry the Platonist, in the third book of *On Sacrifices*, says it was a swallow. For it is certain that every voice of any animal is a sign of some passion of its soul—whether an affect of joy, or sadness, or anger—and it is not so wonderful that these voices can be understood by men who have practiced in these matters. Indeed, Democritus himself handed down this art, as Pliny says, by naming certain birds from whose mingled blood a serpent is born; whoever eats this serpent will understand the conversations of birds. And Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of Hermeticism.</note> says: "If anyone goes out to hunt on a certain day of the Calends of November and cooks the first bird he catches along with the heart of a fox, all who eat of this will understand the voices of birds and other animals." The Arabs also recorded that those who had eaten the heart or liver of dragons were skilled in understanding the meanings of brute beasts. Proclus the Platonist himself believed and taught that the heart of a mole contributes to foretelling the future. There were also divinations and auspices taken from the entrails and the fibers of sacrifices, the inventor of which was Tages <note>A founding figure of Etruscan religion who was said to have been plowed up from a field as a child with the wisdom of an old man.</note>, of whom Lucan sang:

> "And let there be no faith in the fibers; but rather, let 
> Tages, the founder of the art, have fashioned them." <note>original: "Et fibris sit nulla fides, sed conditor artis / Finxerit illa Tages." From Lucan’s *Pharsalia*.</note>

<margin>
The liver is the chief of the entrails.
</margin>
The religion of the Romans considered the **liver to be the chief of the entrails**. For this reason, the <term>haruspices</term> <note>Etruscan and Roman diviners who interpreted the internal organs of sacrificial animals.</note> searching for the future in the entrails inspected the liver first. Two "heads" <note>lobes</note> were established within it: they called one the "citizen's head" and the other the "enemy's head." By comparing these heads, they pronounced victory for one side or the other, just as we read in Lucan that the entrails signified the slaughter of the Pompeians and the victory of the Caesareans in these verses:

> "Because a wickedness appeared in the entrails that went not unpunished, 
> Behold, he saw a mass grow upon the head of the fibers; 
> Of the other head, a part hangs sickly and withered, 
> While another part glitters, and its wicked pulse moves the veins rapidly." <note>original: "Quodq; nefas nullis impune apparuit extis, / Ecce uidit capiti fibrarum increscere molem, / Alterius capitis pars ægra & marcida pendet, / Pars micat, & celeri uenas mouet improba pulsu." From Lucan’s *Pharsalia*, 1.617-621.</note>

Next, having completed the inspection of the organs, they sought the heart. If the victim was found to be without a heart, or if the "head" on the liver was missing, these were considered pestiferous auspices and were called "expiatory." Similarly, it was a bad omen if the victim fled from the altar, or if it lowed when struck, or if it fell upon a part of its body other than what was proper. Regarding these things, we read that on the day Julius Caesar went forth in purple robes and sat in his golden chair, the heart was missing from the entrails when he sacrificed. And when Gaius Marius was sacrificing at Utica, the liver was missing from the entrails. Similarly, when the Emperor Gaius <note>Caligula</note> and Marcus Marcellus sacrificed, as well as the consuls Gaius Claudius and Lucius Petellius, the liver suddenly wasted away. Not long after, one died of disease and the other fell by the weapons of the Ligurians, just as the entrails had predicted. This is truly thought to happen either by the power of the gods or the work of demons. Hence, it was always held of the greatest importance among the ancients whenever something unusual appeared in the entrails, such as when a likeness of a crown appeared on the head of the liver while Sulla was sacrificing at Laurentum; Posthumius the haruspex interpreted this as portending victory and royal power for him, and therefore advised that Sulla alone should eat of those entrails. Even the color of the entrails has its own significance. Lucan mentions these matters:

### On the divination of lightning and thunder, and how portents and prodigies are to be interpreted. Chapter 56.

<margin>What sort of person the interpreter of prodigies ought to be.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap letter 'A'. Within the letter's frame is a seated figure, likely a scholar or religious figure, looking towards the right.</image-desc>Furthermore, regarding the <term>augury of lightnings and thunderbolts</term><note>Latin: *augurio fulgurum & fulminum*. Agrippa distinguishes between the flash of lightning and the actual strike or thunderbolt.</note>, and signs, and how portents and prodigies are to be interpreted, the Etruscan seers and priests handed down this knowledge. For they established sixteen regions of the sky, with their own deities assigned to each; besides these, they identified eleven types of lightning, and nine gods who would hurl them, providing rules for what they signify from whichever part they appear. Indeed, whenever portents, prodigies, and signs occur, it is certain they always foretell something significant. 

The interpreter of these must be an excellent judge of similarities, as well as a curious investigator of the current affairs of princes and provinces. For the care of the heavens is directed toward princes, peoples, and provinces alone, so that they might be prefigured and warned through the stars, constellations, portents, and prodigies above all others. If in past centuries the same or a similar sign appeared, it will be necessary to consider that very event and what followed from it; according to this, one should predict the same or similar outcomes, because the same signs belong to the same things, and similar signs to similar things. 

Thus, many excellent men and kings were preceded by prodigies at their birth or death. As Cicero relates of the boy Midas, to whom, while he slept, ants carried grains of wheat into his mouth, which was an omen of great wealth. Likewise, when bees settled on the mouth of the infant Plato as he slept in his cradle, it foretold the sweetness of his speech. To Hecuba, about to give birth to Paris, it seemed in a vision that she gave birth to a burning torch that would set Troy and all of Asia on fire. To the mother of Phalaris <note>A cruel tyrant of Acragas in Sicily, known for the "brazen bull" torture device.</note>, it seemed that a statue of Mercury poured blood onto the earth, which flooded the entire house. To the mother of Dionysius, it seemed she gave birth to a small satyr; these prodigious dreams were followed and confirmed by the events themselves. 

The wife of Tarquinius Priscus, seeing a flame lick the head of Servius Tullius, predicted the kingship for him. In a similar way, after the fall of Troy, while Aeneas was discussing flight with his father Anchises, a flame appeared licking the crown of Ascanius's head without causing him any harm; because this portended kingship for Ascanius, it persuaded them all to depart. All notable disasters are preceded by portents and prodigies. Thus we read in Pliny: during the consulship of Marcus Attilius and Gaius Portius, it rained milk and blood, which foretold that a powerful plague would invade Rome the following year. Likewise, in the land of the Lucanians, it rained iron—somewhat resembling sponges—the year before Marcus Crassus was slain among the Parthians...

It is fitting to foretell similar outcomes from similar <term>prognostics</term><note>Signs or indicators of future events.</note>, just as in various past times something was foretold from them. But one must also not neglect the judgments of celestial influences concerning these matters, of which we shall speak more extensively in later parts.

## On Geomancy, Hydromancy, Aeromancy, and Pyromancy: Divinations of the Four Elements. Chapter 57

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial N depicting two figures in a landscape setting, possibly scholars or classical figures, surrounded by ornate foliage.</image-desc>
For even the elements themselves teach us of fated events, from which those four famous types of divination—Geomancy, Hydromancy, Aeromancy, and Pyromancy—received their names. Concerning these, that <term>sorceress</term><note>The witch Erichtho from Lucan’s epic poem "Pharsalia."</note> in Lucan seemed to boast when she said:

> Earth, air, ether, and chaos,
> the seas, and the fields, and the Rhodopeian rocks will speak the truth.
<note>Original: "Ad uerum tellus, aërq́;, ætherq́;, chaosq́; / Equoraq́;, & campi, Rhodopeiaq́; saxa loquentur."</note>

<margin>Geomancy.</margin>
First, therefore, <term>Geomancy</term><note>Divination by means of the earth (from the Greek "geo" for earth and "manteia" for divination).</note> shows future things through earthquakes, noises, swellings, tremors, openings, chasms, exhalations, and its other impressions; the art of which <term>Almadel the Arab</term><note>A reference to the "Ars Almadel," a well-known medieval grimoire or book of magic attributed to an Arabic source.</note> handed down. But there is also another kind of Geomancy, which divines by points inscribed on the earth by some force or by chance; this does not belong to the present speculation, but we shall speak of it among <term>lots</term><note>Divination by casting lots (sortilege) or random markings.</note> in what follows. <term>Hydromancy</term><note>Divination by means of water.</note>, however, provides prophecies through watery impressions, their ebbs and flows, increases and decreases, storms, colors, and the like: to which are also joined visions that occur in water. This is a type of divination discovered by the Persians, such as <term>Varro</term><note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a prolific Roman scholar.</note> reports a boy to have seen in the water—an image of Mercury which foretold the entire outcome of the <term>Mithridatic War</term><note>A long conflict between Rome and King Mithridates VI of Pontus.</note> in a hundred and fifty verses. We also read that <term>Numa Pompilius</term><note>The legendary second king of Rome, often associated with religious and magical origins.</note> practiced hydromancy: for he summoned the images of the gods in water and learned future things from them. <term>Pythagoras</term> also practiced this craft a long time after Numa. There was also once among the Assyrians a type of hydromancy held in great esteem, called
<margin>Lecanomancy, a type of Hydromancy.</margin>
<term>Lecanomancy</term><note>Divination by observing water in a basin (from the Greek "lekane").</note>, named from a basin full of water: into which they placed gold and silver plates and precious stones, inscribed with certain images, names, and characters. To this also can be referred the craft by which, through melted lead or wax cast into water, they express in manifest images the matter we desire to know.

...by marks of images. There were also in ancient times <term>prophetic springs</term><note>Latin: "fontes fatidici." These were natural springs believed to be inhabited by spirits or deities who granted visions of the future.</note>, such as the spring of the Father of Achaia, and what was called the water of Juno at Epidaurus, about which more will be said in the following sections where we speak of oracles. Indeed, one might also refer here to **divination by fish**, such as was practiced of old among the Lycians in a place called Dina, near the sea in the sacred grove of Apollo. This was excavated in dry sand; the one intending to consult about future events would lower roasted meats into it, and suddenly that place would be filled with water, and a great multitude of fish of wondrous shapes unknown to men would appear, from whose forms the seer would predict what was to come. <term>Athenaeus</term><note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian (c. 200 CE) who wrote the "Deipnosophistae," a massive collection of lore.</note> relates these things at length from Polycharmus in his *Histories of the Lycians*. In a similar way, **Aeromancy** provides prognostics by atmospheric impressions, by the blowing of winds, by rainbows, by halos, by mists and clouds, and by images in the clouds and visions in the air. So also **Pyromancy** divines by fiery impressions, by comets, by fiery colors, and by visions and imaginings in the fire. In this way, the wife of **Cicero** predicted that he would be consul the following year because, when she wished to observe something in the ashes after a sacrifice was finished, a flame suddenly leapt out. Of this kind are the things **Pliny** describes: that earthly fires, when pale and murmuring, are perceived as messengers of storms; also rains, if "fungi" <note>This refers to the accumulation of charred carbon or soot on a lamp wick, which looked like a mushroom growth and was thought to signal damp weather.</note> appear in the lamps; if the flame flies in a winding way, a wind is portended; and when lamps cast out flames or are hardly lit; likewise when sparks gather hanging upon them, or when a coal adheres to pots when they are lifted, or when the contained fire shakes off a cinder from itself or emits a spark, or when ash grows thick on the hearth, and when a coal shines intensely. To these is added **Capnomancy**, so called from smoke, because it examines flame and smoke, and their colors, sounds, and motions: whether it extends straight upward, or is carried sideways, or rolls in a circle, just as we read concerning these in <term>Statius</term><note>Publius Papinius Statius, a Roman poet of the 1st century CE; these lines come from his epic, the "Thebaid."</note> in these verses:

> Let piety be overcome; come, maiden, set the altars,
> Let us seek the gods above; she, with keen sight, observes
> The bloody peaks of the flames, and the fire born through the breezes,
> And the bright summits of the central light
> That have arisen; she teaches then how it is rolled in a double-sided whirl
> Into the empty likeness of a serpent, and breaks with a reddish glow.

Furthermore, even in the craters of **Etna** and in the Nymphean fields among the people of Apollonia, auguries were taken from fire and flames—joyful indeed if they consumed what was cast into them, but sorrowful if they rejected them. And we shall speak of these also in later parts among the responses of the oracles.

### On the revival of the dead, on long-lasting sleep and fasting. Ch. LVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative ornamental woodcut initial 'C' depicting a small animal, possibly a dog or rabbit, looking upward toward foliage and branches.</image-desc>
**Arab philosophers** agree that some men can raise themselves above the powers of the body and above the sensory powers, and, having overcome those, receive a divine vigor into themselves through the perfection of the heavens and the intelligences. Since, therefore, the souls of all men are eternal, the **Magi** think that all spirits obey perfected souls; that perfected men, through the powers of their own soul, can command other inferior souls already in some way separated...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous chapter regarding the soul's power and the potential to return life to the body. It shifts from general divination to the specific phenomena of "resurrection" or reanimation through natural, magical, and medical means.</meta>

LXXV
<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

...[they believe they] are able to restore souls to their dying bodies and breathe life back into them, just as a dead **weasel** is called back to life by the breath and voice of its parent, or as **lions** are said to bring life to their stillborn cubs by breathing upon them. Since, as they say, "all like things applied to like produce the nature of like things," and every passive thing that receives the action of an agent is endowed with and made one with the nature of that agent, they believe that certain herbs and magical preparations contribute significantly to this reanimation. These include preparations made from the ashes of a **Phoenix** or the shed skins of serpents—though such things might seem like fables or even impossible to many, were they not proven by historical record.

Indeed, we read of many who had drowned in water, others cast into fires or placed upon funeral pyres, and others killed in war or otherwise rendered breathless, who returned to life even after several days. **Pliny**<note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist, discusses these cases of "apparent death" in his *Natural History*.</note> testifies to this regarding **Aviola** (a man of consular rank), **Lucius Lamia**, **Caelius Tubero**, **Confidius**, **Gabienus**, and many others. Similarly, we read that **Aesop** the storyteller, **Tyndareus**, **Hercules**, and the **Palici** (the sons of Jupiter and Thalia) returned to life after death. Many others were called back to life by magicians and physicians, as history records of **Aesculapius**<note>The Greco-Roman god of medicine, often said to have been killed by Zeus for bringing the dead back to life.</note>, and as we narrated earlier from the accounts of **Juba**, **Xanthus**, and **Philostratus** regarding **Tillo**, a certain **Arab**, and **Apollonius of Tyana**.

We also read of a certain **Glaucus** who died and was restored to life, beyond all expectation, by physicians using a herb they call "the dragon’s herb." Others say he revived after tasting a honeyed medicine, from which the proverb arose: <note>original: "Glaucus poto melle resurrexit."</note> *Glaucus rose again after drinking honey.* **Apuleius**<note>The Roman author of *The Golden Ass*, describing a scene of Egyptian necromancy.</note>, describing the ritual for such revocations, says of the Egyptian prophet **Zachlas**: "The prophet, thus appeased, placed a certain small herb upon the mouth of the body and another upon its chest; then, turning toward the East and silently praying to the rising of the august sun, he drew the attention of the onlookers to so great a miracle. Soon the chest began to swell with breath, the healthy pulse began to throb, the body was filled with spirit, the corpse rose up, and the young man began to speak."

If these accounts are to be believed as true, it must be that dying souls sometimes remain hidden within their bodies, weighed down by intense <term>ecstasies</term><note>Latin: "extasibus." In this context, it refers to a state where the soul is "standing outside" its normal function, making the body appear dead.</note> and released from all bodily action. In such a state, life, sense, and motion desert the entire body, yet the person is not yet truly dead but lies breathless and as if dead, even for a long period. This has been very frequently observed during times of plague: many who were being carried to their graves as dead were found to have revived in their tombs. We read that this has also frequently happened to women suffering from <term>suffocation of the womb</term><note>Latin: "suffocatione matricis." Historically known as "hysterical suffocation," a condition where a patient was thought to stop breathing due to uterine displacement.</note>.

<margin>Wondrous examples of suffocation and ecstasy.</margin>

**Rabbi Moses**<note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher and physician.</note> relates from a book of **Galen** (translated by the Patriarch) an account of a man who suffered a "suffocation" that lasted for six days; he neither ate nor drank, and his arteries became rigid. He says in the same book that a "repletion" can occur in a man which causes the pulse of the whole body to be lost, the heart to stop moving, and the man to lie as if dead. He also says that from a fall from a high place, or from a great shout, or from remaining a long time under water, a <term>syncope</term><note>A medical term for a temporary loss of consciousness or fainting spell.</note> can occur lasting forty-eight hours, during which the man lies as if dead...

LXXVI.
<header>ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,</header>

on whose surface a green dust arises. And he mentions in the same book concerning a man who buried a dead person before seventy-two hours had passed since their death, and thereby killed him; for he had buried the man while he was yet alive. He provides signs there by which it may be known that such people are alive, even though they lie there appearing just like the dead; they will certainly die unless they are assisted, either by bloodletting <term>phlebotomiam: the surgical practice of opening a vein to balance bodily fluids</term> or other medical treatments. These are among those occurrences that happen very rarely. This is also the way by which we understand how magicians and physicians seem to raise the dead—just as those who were once knocked breathless by the bite of a serpent were restored to life by the **Marsi** and the **Psylli** <note>Ancient tribes from Italy and North Africa, respectively, who were legendary for their immunity to snake venom and their ability to heal bites through touch or chanting.</note>. 

Furthermore, we should not think it any less possible for such trances <term>extases: states of suspended animation where the soul seems to stand outside the body</term> to last for a long time without a person being truly dead than it is for **dormice**, **crocodiles**, and many **serpents**. These animals sleep through the whole winter and breathe so faintly in their slumber that they can hardly be revived even by fire. I have often seen a dissected dormouse remain motionless, as if dead, until it was placed over heat to be cooked; only then, in the boiling water, did the dissected limbs first show signs of life.

<margin>Examples of long-lasting sleep.</margin>
Similarly, though it may be difficult to believe, we read in the works of esteemed historians that even certain men have slept a continuous, long-lasting sleep for many years, and when they finally woke, they had not aged at all. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist.</note> testifies to this regarding a certain boy who, exhausted by the heat and his journey, is said to have slept in a cave for fifty-seven years. We also read that **Epimenides of Gnossus** <note>A legendary Greek seer and philosopher-poet from Crete.</note> slept for fifty-seven years in a cavern. From this arose the proverb: *To sleep longer than Epimenides.* 

**Marcus Damascenus** <note>Likely referring to a medieval or Renaissance collector of natural wonders.</note> relates that in his own time, in **Germany**, a weary peasant slept continuously under a heap of hay through the whole of autumn and the following winter; in the summer, as the hay was gradually eaten away by livestock, he was found and awakened. He was found as if half-dead and completely out of his wits. Ecclesiastical history confirms this possibility with the story of the **Seven Sleepers**, who are said to have slept for one hundred and ninety-six years. In **Norway**, beneath a high cliff, there is a cave where—as **Paul the Deacon** and **Methodius the Martyr** write—seven men lay sleeping, numbed for a long time without any decay. They say that people who often entered the cave to harm them were immediately struck with paralysis; finally, the local inhabitants, wary of this immediate punishment, ceased from trying to hurt them. 

Among the philosophers, **Xenocrates** (a man of no small reputation) believed that this long-lasting sleep was a kind of natural punishment, assigned from eternity for certain failings of the soul. Damascenus himself proves with many reasons that this is possible and entirely natural. He does not think it absurd that what is granted to other living creatures—to be able to sleep for many months without food or drink, without excretion, and without wasting away or decay—can also happen to a human. This might occur through a poisonous potion, a sleep-inducing illness, a fearful stupor, or similar causes; it can happen for many days, months, or years, depending on the intensity or relaxation of the powers and passions of the soul. Physicians even speak of certain antidotes of which, if someone eats even a tiny portion, they can then endure a long period without food—just as **Elijah** was once fed with a specific food by an angel...

It argues that such states are natural rather than purely miraculous, often caused by illness, potions, or the state of the soul.</summary>

<margin>Wonderful examples of fasting.</margin>
...he walked and fasted in the strength of that food for forty days <note>A reference to Elijah in 1 Kings 19:8</note>. And Giovanni Boccaccio <note>original: "Ioannes Bocatius"; the famous 14th-century Italian author</note> records that in his own time there was a man in Venice who, every year, would observe a fast for forty days without any food at all. And what is even more wonderful, there was at the same time in Lower Germany a woman who, into her thirtieth year, had never taken any food; this might indeed seem incredible to us, were it not confirmed by a recent miracle of our own century in the person of Brother Nicholas of Flüe <note>original: "Nicolao de Saxo"; the patron saint of Switzerland, known as Bruder Klaus</note>, a Swiss by nationality, who it is well established lived in the wilderness for twenty-two years, until he departed from this life, without any food at all. Also wonderful is that which Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note> reported: that there was a certain Philinus who used no drink or food except for milk. And there are serious authors who describe a certain Spartan herb, by which they say the Scythians <note>Ancient nomadic people of Central Eurasia</note> can endure twelve days without food or drink, once it has been tasted or held in the mouth.

## On divination which occurs through dreams. Chapter 59.

<margin>Dream.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring two figures in a landscape, possibly scholars or classical figures, with floral ornamentation.</image-desc>
THERE is also a species of divination which occurs during sleep, namely that of dreams, proven by the traditions of the philosophers, the authorities of the theologians, the examples of histories, and daily experience. However, I speak here of a "dream" <note>original: "Somnium"</note>, not what is a "phantom" <note>original: "phantasma"</note> or a "nightmare" <note>original: "insomnium"</note>: for these latter are vain and possess nothing of divination. Instead, they arise from the remnants of waking thoughts or from a disturbance of the body; for as often as we are weighed down by the advantages or disadvantages of the body or of fortune, then whatever kind of thought had fatigued the mind while awake, the same thrusts itself upon the sleeper—or sometimes its opposite, deceived by the nightmare. Therefore, I call a "dream" here that which is caused in the <term>imaginative spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritu phantastico"; the faculty of the soul that processes images</note> by the influence of the heavens, when the mind and body are in good condition. The rule for interpreting this is indeed found among the astrologers, in that part written concerning "interrogations," but it is nonetheless insufficient, because dreams of this kind happen to different men in different ways, according to the different quality and disposition of the imaginative spirit. For this reason, the same common rule for interpreting dreams cannot be applied to everyone. Rather, according to the opinion of Synesius <note>A 4th-century philosopher-bishop who wrote "On Dreams"</note>, since the same accidents happen to the same or similar things, so he who falls into the same or a similar vision more often will designate for himself the same or a similar meaning, passion, fortune, action, or finally, event. Just as Aristotle says, memory is confirmed by the senses, and from memory of the same thing frequently obtained, experience is born; from many experiences, art and science are gradually accumulated. By a similar reasoning, one must proceed regarding dreams. Whence Synesius commands that each person observe his own dreams and their outcomes—namely, what visions fell into what outcomes—and to commit such rules (that is, the visions and the accidents) to memory, both of the dreams and of the waking state. By a certain diligent observation, one accumulates many such rules within oneself, from which accumulation a certain art of divination and of interpreting one's own dreams gradually arises, provided nothing slips from the memory. Moreover, dreams are more effective when—

LXXVIII. ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

...when the Moon perverts that sign which was in the ninth house <note>The ninth house in astrology is traditionally associated with travel, religion, and prophecy.</note> of the root of the birth or of the revolution of that year, or in the ninth sign from the sign of the perfection <note>Latin: *profectionis*; a technique in traditional astrology where a point is moved forward by one sign per year.</note>. However, the truest and most certain divination proceeds neither from nature nor human arts, but from purified minds through divine inspiration. We shall now discuss that which pertains to prophecies and oracles.

->On the frenzy and divinations that occur while awake, and on the power of the melancholic humor, by which even demons are sometimes enticed into human bodies.<-

### Chapter LX.

<margin>Frenzy is a type of divination.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a figure of a seated child surrounded by stylized foliage scrollwork.</image-desc>
It happens also, not only to those sleeping but sometimes to those awake, that they divine when the soul is set free and driven by its own impulses. Aristotle calls this divination "frenzy" <note>Latin: *furor*; a technical term in Renaissance philosophy derived from the Greek *mania*, referring to an inspired state of divine madness.</note> and teaches in his treatise on divination that it proceeds from the melancholic humor, saying: "Melancholics, on account of their intensity, guess well from a distance, quickly imagine a habit, and most easily receive the impression of celestial things." And in the *Problems*, he says: "The Sibyls, the Bacchides, Niceratus of Syracuse, and Amon were diviners and poets due to a natural melancholic temperament." Therefore, the cause of frenzy, if there is any within the human body, is the melancholic humor—not indeed that which is called black bile <term>atra bilis: a humor thought to cause depression and madness</term>, which is so wicked and horrible a thing that its force is said by natural philosophers and physicians to entice evil demons to besiege human bodies, beyond the madness it induces. By "humor" here, we mean the melancholic state called natural and white bile. For when this is ignited and burns, it excites the frenzy that leads us to knowledge and divination, especially if it is aided by some celestial influx, particularly that of Saturn. Since Saturn is himself cold and dry—just as the melancholic humor is—he flows into, increases, and preserves it daily. Furthermore, since he is the author of secret contemplation, distant from all public business, and the highest of the planets, he always recalls the soul from external duties to innermost things and makes it ascend from lower things, drawing it to the highest, and bestows knowledge and premonitions of the future. This is what Aristotle intends in the book of *Problems*: "From melancholy," he says, "some have become like divine beings, foretelling future things, and some have become poets."

<margin>Melancholics excel in genius.</margin>
He says, moreover, that almost all men who have been outstanding in any science have been melancholics. Democritus and Plato attest to this, asserting that some melancholics so excel in genius that they seem divine rather than human. Thus, many melancholics who were initially unrefined, unskilled, or insane—such as they say Hesiod, Ion, Tynnichus of Chalcis, Homer, and Lucretius were—are often suddenly seized by frenzy and turn into poets, singing wonderful and divine things which they themselves can scarcely understand. Hence, the divine Plato says in the *Ion*: "Most prophets, after the impulse of frenzy has subsided, do not sufficiently understand what they have written, even though they treated individual arts correctly while in the frenzy, which the skilled practitioners of those arts judge by reading." Furthermore, they say the melancholic...

It cites classical authorities like Aristotle and Plato to link melancholy with genius and divine inspiration.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 60 of Book I regarding the "frenzy" or divine madness caused by the melancholic humor. It specifically moves from the general concept of melancholy to its threefold influence on the human soul—imaginative, rational, and mental—and its role in prophecy.</meta>

LXXIX.
BOOK ONE

<margin>The dominion of the melancholic humor.</margin>...is the dominion of the humor, so that by its own force even celestial demons <note>In this context, "demons" (Latin: *daemones*) refers to intermediary spirits or guiding entities, not necessarily evil beings.</note> are sometimes drawn into human bodies. All of antiquity bears witness that by the presence and prompting of these spirits, men rave like Bacchants and speak many wonderful things. They believe this happens in three different ways, according to the three levels of the soul’s perception: namely the **imaginative**, the **rational**, and the **mental**. They say, therefore, that when the soul is driven by the melancholic humor—with nothing holding it back, having overstepped the reins of the body and the bonds of the limbs—it is transferred entirely into the **imagination**. It suddenly becomes a dwelling place for lower demons, from whom it often receives marvelous insights into the manual arts. Thus we see a very crude man suddenly turn into an excellent painter, or architect, or a master of some other craft. But when demons of this kind portend future events to us, they show those things that pertain to disturbances of the elements and the changes of the seasons, such as future rain, storms, floods, earthquakes, plagues, famines, slaughters, and the like. This is just as we read in Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author of *Attic Nights*.</note> concerning the priest Cornelius, who, at the time when Caesar and Pompey were clashing in Thessaly, was seized by a frenzy in Padua and foretold the time, the order, and the outcome of the battle. 

However, when the soul is turned entirely toward **reason**, it becomes the home of middle demons; from here it obtains knowledge and wisdom regarding natural and human affairs. Thus we see a man suddenly turn into an excellent philosopher, physician, or orator. Concerning the future, such men predict those things which pertain to the changing of kingdoms and the restoration of eras, just as the Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses; the "Sibyl to the Romans" likely refers to the Cumaean Sibyl.</note> did for the Romans. 

But when the soul has flowed entirely into the **mind**, then, having become a receptacle for the sublime demons, it learns from them the secrets of divine things—namely the law of God, the orders of the angels, and those things which pertain to the knowledge of eternal matters and the salvation of souls. Regarding the future, it foresees those things which depend on divine providence, such as future portents or miracles, a future prophet, or a change in religious law. Thus did the Sibyls prophesy concerning Christ long before his coming. Likewise, Virgil—understanding that Christ was soon to be born and remembering the Cumaean Sibyl—sang to Pollio <note>Referring to Virgil’s *Fourth Eclogue*, a poem traditionally interpreted by Christians as a prophecy of the birth of Jesus.</note>:

> Now comes the final age of the Cumaean song,
> <note>original: "Vltima Cumæi iam uenit carminis ætas"</note>
> A great order of ages is born anew.
> <note>original: "Magnus ab integro seclorum nascitur ordo"</note>
> Now the Virgin also returns, and the reign of Saturn returns;
> <note>original: "Iam redit & uirgo, redeunt Saturnia regna"</note>
> Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven.
> <note>original: "Iam noua progenies cœlo demittitur alto"</note>

And a little later, hinting that original sin would be wiped away, he says:

> With you as leader, if any traces of our sin remain, 
> <note>original: "Te duce si qua manent sceleris uestigia nostri"</note>
> They shall be made void, and shall free the lands from perpetual fear.
> <note>original: "Irrita, perpetuo soluent formidine terras"</note>

And he adds:

> He shall receive the life of the gods, and shall see 
> <note>original: "Ille deum uitam accipiet, diuisq́; uidebit"</note>
> Heroes mingled with gods, and he himself shall be seen by them,
> <note>original: "Permixtos heroes, & ipse uidebitur illis"</note>

### Concerning the formation of man, the external and internal senses, and the mind; concerning the threefold appetite of the soul and the passions of the will. Chapter LXI.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'E' featuring a seated classical figure, perhaps a philosopher or deity, in a garden-like setting with architectural elements and foliage.</image-desc>
IT IS the opinion of certain theologians that God himself did not create the body of the first man immediately, but formed and composed it from the elements with the help of celestial beings. This opinion is also supported by Alcinous <note>A 2nd-century Middle Platonist philosopher.</note> based on the teachings of Plato. He believes that the supreme God is the creator of the entire world, the gods, and the demons, and that these are therefore immortal. However, he believes that the "younger gods" <note>In Platonic thought, these are lesser celestial deities or planetary spirits.</note> created the other types of mortal living things at the command of the supreme God. For if God himself had fathered these, they too would have been born immortal. Thus, the gods took certain portions of earth, fire, air, and water—exchanging and binding them together—to fashion one body out of them all. They subjected this body to the service of the soul, assigning specific provinces within it to each of the soul's powers. They assigned the lower seats to the humbler parts: namely, the heart for anger, the belly for desire; but the more noble senses they placed in the head, as if in the citadel of the entire body. Finally, they provided the various organs of speech.

<margin>To which elements the external senses correspond.</margin>
Furthermore, they divide the senses into the external and the internal. The external senses are then partitioned into the five most well-known types, to which five organs or subjects are likewise attributed as foundations. These are arranged so that those placed in the higher parts of the body also hold a higher rank of purity. The eyes, being placed in the highest position, are the purest and are related to the nature of fire and light. Next, the ears, holding the second rank in both location and purity, are compared to the air. The nostrils occupy the third place, containing a middle nature between air and water. Next is the organ of tasting, which is thicker and very similar to a watery nature. Finally, in the last grade is touch, diffused through the whole body and assigned to the thickness of the earth... <meta>catchword: assigned</meta>

LXXXI.

...perceived. The purer senses are those that perceive from a distance without approaching the objects of sense, such as sight and hearing; likewise, smell perceives through the medium of the air from a distance. Taste, however, senses nothing unless it is close by. Touch operates in both ways: for it senses bodies that are near, and just as sight sees through the medium of air, so also touch senses hard, soft, and wet things through a medium such as a rod or a staff. Truly, touch is the only sense common to every animal. Man possesses this sense with the greatest certainty; in this and in taste, he excels all other animals, but in the other three senses he is surpassed by certain creatures. For instance, a dog sees, hears, and smells more keenly than a man; similarly, lynxes and eagles see more sharply than man and many other living things.

<margin>In taste and touch, man excels the other animals.</margin>

As for the internal senses, as **Averroes** <note>A 12th-century philosopher from Islamic Spain whose commentaries on Aristotle were essential to Renaissance thought.</note> maintains, they are divided into four parts. The first is called the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "sensus communis"; not "good judgment," but the faculty that unifies the data from all five external senses into a single experience.</note>, because it is the first to collect and perfect all the images drawn in through the external senses. The second is the **imaginative power**, whose duty is to retain the images received from the primary senses (even when it perceives nothing present) and to offer them to the third, the **sensing nature**. This third power is **phantasy**, the power of estimation and thinking, whose work is to perceive and judge—once the images are received—what or of what kind the object of those images might be. It then commends those things which it has so discerned, joined, perceived, and judged to the fourth power, which we call **memory**, to be preserved. Indeed, within that general category of faculties are discourse, disposition, pursuit and flight, and the impulses to action. But in the intellectual species, these include intellections, virtues, the method of disciplines, counsel, and choice. This [phantasy] is also that which shows us future things through dreams; hence phantasy is sometimes called the **phantastic intellect**. For it is the final trace of the intelligence which—as **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher who explored the relationship between the human soul and the divine through ritual and intellect.</note> says—is born into all the powers of the soul, fashions all figures, likenesses, and species, and transmits the operations and visions (or impressions) of certain powers into others. Those which flash from the senses, it excites into opinion; those which come from the intellect, it offers in the second place to opinion. But from itself, it receives images from all things, and according to its own property, it designates them properly through assimilation; it fashions all actions of the soul, adapts external things to internal ones, and even prints impressions upon the body.

<margin>The organs of the senses are in the head.</margin>

These senses have their organs in the head; for the **common sense** along with the **imagination** occupies the front <term>cells</term> <note>original: "cellulas"; Renaissance anatomy followed the medieval "ventricular theory," which held that different mental functions were located in specific chambers or "cells" of the brain.</note> of the brain, although **Aristotle** placed the organ of the common sense in the heart. The **cognitive power**, however, occupies the highest and middle part of the head, and **memory** the hindmost. Furthermore, the organs of voice and speech are many: the muscles between the ribs of the inner chest, the thorax, the lungs, the trachea, the artery, the throat, and especially the cartilaginous part of these; along with the recurrent nerves, the "pick" <note>original: "plectrum"; Agrippa compares the tongue's action to the pick used to strike the strings of a lyre.</note> of the tongue, and all those small parts and muscles which are the organs of breathing out. But the proper organ of speech is the mouth, in which words and talk are molded, formed, and shaped. The tongue and the throat take the place of the "pick" in that organ, while the palate creates the sound; the teeth and the opening of the mouth represent the strings, as if on a lyre, while the nose...

LXXXII.

...moreover contributing to a good or bad resonance. <note>The context suggests how the physical shape of the body or organs affects the "sound" or expression of the soul's powers.</note>

<margin>The dual nature of the mind.</margin>
Above the sensible soul, which unfolds its powers through the organs of the body, the supreme place is occupied by the **incorporeal mind** itself. This mind possesses a dual nature: One part investigates the causes, properties, and progressions of those things contained within the order of nature, and is content with the contemplation of truth; for this reason, they call it the **contemplative intellect**. The other nature or power of the mind discerns through deliberation what should be done and what should be avoided; it is entirely engaged in deliberation and action, and for this reason, they call it the **active intellect**. Nature has established this order of powers in man so that through the external senses we might know corporeal things; through the internal senses, we might know the likenesses of bodies beyond that; and further, through the mind or intellect, we might know abstract things which are neither bodies nor similar to them.

<margin>The three-fold appetite in the soul.</margin>
And according to this triple order of the soul's powers, three appetites <note>In this context, "appetite" refers to a natural drive or inclination toward something, not just hunger for food.</note> are born in the soul: The first is **natural**, which is a certain inclination of nature toward its own end, such as the downward [tendency] of a stone, which is present in all things. The second is the **animal** [appetite], which follows the senses and is divided into the <term>irascible</term> <note>The "angry" or spirited drive to overcome obstacles or defend oneself.</note> and the <term>concupiscible</term> <note>The "desiring" drive toward pleasure or basic needs.</note>. The third is the **intellectual** [appetite], which is called the **Will** (*voluntas*). This differs from the sensitive appetite in that the latter belongs to things that can be presented to the senses, desiring nothing unless it is perceived in some way. The Will, however, although it is of itself capable of all possible things, is also capable of impossible things because it is free by its very essence—such as it was in the <term>demon</term> <note>A reference to Lucifer or the fallen angels.</note> desiring to be equal to God. Thus, the Will is continually altered and corrupted by pleasure and pain while it gives its assent to the lower powers. From this corrupted appetite, four passions are born within it, which sometimes affect the body in a similar way. The first of these is called **delight** (*oblectatio*), which is a certain softness and compliance of the mind or will, by which it most willingly consents, obeys, and submits to the sweetness offered by the senses; for this reason, they define it as an inclination of the mind toward softening pleasure. The second is called **effusion** (*effusio*), which is a relaxation or dissolving of virtue; namely, when beyond mere delight, the entire power and intention of the mind melts and flows away in the sweetness of a present good, and utterly pours itself out and exerts itself to enjoy it. The third is called **boasting** (*iactantia*), that is, a restless elation, judging that it has attained some greatest good; by the possession of which, lifting itself up quite insolently, it exults and glories in vain. The fourth and last is **malevolence**, a certain pleasure derived from the misfortune of another without any benefit to oneself. It is said "without benefit to oneself" because if someone should rejoice in another’s misfortune for their own utility, this would be out of benevolence toward oneself rather than malevolence toward others. And just as these four passions are generated from the appetite for pleasure, so also does pain itself generate four contrary passions: namely, **horror** [dread], **sadness**, **fear**, and **envy** (which is pain at the good of another without detriment to oneself). Envy is, in fact, sadness at the goods of others, just as **mercy** (*misericordia*) is a certain sadness at the misfortunes of others.

LXXXIII.
<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

The passions of the soul are nothing other than certain movements or inclinations arising from the perception of some thing, regarded as either good or evil, suitable or unsuitable. Moreover, these perceptions are three-fold: namely, sensual, rational, and mental. Accordingly, there are three types of passions in the soul. Sometimes they follow **sensual perception**, and then they regard a temporal good or evil in terms of comfort or discomfort, pleasure or offense; these are called **natural or animal passions**. Sometimes they follow **rational perception**, and thus they regard good or evil in terms of virtue and vice, praise and blame, the useful and the useless, the honorable and the shameful; these are called **rational or voluntary passions**. Sometimes they follow **mental perception**, and they regard good and evil in terms of the just and the unjust, the true and the false; then they are called **intellectual passions**, or <term>synteresis</term> <note>original: *syndæresis*; in medieval philosophy, this refers to the innate spark of conscience that recognizes primary moral truths.</note>. The subject of these passions of the soul is the "desiring power" of the soul itself, which is divided into the <term>concupiscible</term> and the <term>irascible</term>. Each regards good and evil, but in different ways.

The **concupiscible power** <note>The faculty of the soul that is naturally drawn toward what is pleasant and away from what is painful.</note> sometimes regards good and evil absolutely, which causes **love** or **lust**, and conversely, **hatred**. Or, it regards a good as absent, which causes **longing** or **desire**; or an evil as absent but imminent, which causes **horror**, **flight**, and **abomination**. Or, it regards good and evil as present and attained, and from this arises **delight**, **joy**, and **pleasure** on one hand, and **sadness**, **distress**, and **pain** on the other. 

The **irascible power** <note>The faculty of the soul that provides the "spirit" or energy to overcome obstacles or resist threats.</note> regards good and evil in terms of the difficulty of obtaining or achieving it, or of fleeing or repelling it. This happens sometimes with confidence, which causes **hope** on one side and **daring** on the other; and sometimes with lack of confidence, which gives rise to **despair** and **fear** or **dread**. Sometimes the irascible power rises up for vengeance, and this occurs only regarding a past evil, such as an inflicted injury or harm, and it causes **anger**. Thus, we find eleven passions in the soul itself: love, hatred, desire, horror, joy, pain, hope, despair, daring, fear, and anger.

### How the passions of the soul change our own body by altering its physical qualities and moving the spirit. Chapter LXIII.

When the passions of the soul follow sensual perception, the <term>phantasy</term> <note>The "imagination" or the faculty that processes sensory images.</note> or imaginative power holds the ruling force. By its own power, according to the variety of the passions, this faculty first alters and transforms one’s own body in various ways through sensible changes—altering the physical qualities of the body and moving the <term>spirit</term> <note>In the medical theory of the time, "spirits" were subtle, vaporous substances that carried life and sensation through the nerves and blood.</note> upward or downward, outward or inward, and producing different qualities in the limbs. 

Thus, in **joy**, the spirits are expelled outward; in **fear**, they are withdrawn; in **shame**, they are moved toward the brain. In joy, the heart is gradually dilated outward; in **sadness**, it is gradually constricted inward. A similar thing happens in **anger** or fear, but suddenly. Furthermore, anger or the desire for vengeance produces heat, redness, a bitter taste, and a flow of the bowels. Fear induces cold, a [constriction] of the heart...

Even pity, which is a kind of sadness, often affects the body of the one feeling it, so that it seems as if the other person’s body is being affected. It is also well known among lovers that the bond of love is so strong that whatever one suffers, the other suffers as well. Anxiety also brings on dryness and a blackened complexion. Physicians know well how much heat the longing of love excites in the liver and in the pulse; by this sign, they detect the name of the beloved in **heroic passion** <term>heroic passion</term> <note>original: *passione heroica*; This refers to "lovesickness" (amor hereos), a condition recognized by medieval and Renaissance doctors as a literal disease caused by obsessive desire.</note>. This is how Nausistratus <note>Agrippa likely refers here to the famous story of the physician Erasistratus, who diagnosed Prince Antiochus’s secret love for his stepmother Stratonice by watching the prince's pulse.</note> discovered that Antiochus was captured by love for Stratonice.

<margin>
The passions of the soul sometimes bring about death.
</margin>
Furthermore, it is manifest that such passions, when they are most vehement, can bring about death. It is common knowledge among the people that men sometimes die from excessive joy, sadness, love, or hatred, and are often even cured of disease by them. Thus we read that Sophocles and Dionysius, the tyrant of Sicily, both died suddenly upon receiving news of a victory in a tragic poetry contest. Similarly, a mother died suddenly upon seeing her son returning from the Battle of Cannae <note>A major battle in the Second Punic War (216 BCE) where the Romans suffered a massive defeat; the mother had believed her son was dead.</note>. What sadness is capable of is known to everyone. We even know that dogs have often died of excessive grief over the death of their masters. Sometimes long-lasting illnesses follow such passions, and sometimes they are cured by them. For instance, some people looking down from a height tremble with excessive fear, grow dizzy, become ill, and sometimes lose their senses. Thus hiccups, fevers, and **falling sickness** <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: *morbi comitiales*; an old term for epilepsy.</note> sometimes follow, and sometimes indeed they recede. Occasionally, certain wonderful effects occur, as in the case of the son of Croesus; though his mother had given birth to him mute, a powerful fear and longing forced out a voice which nature had long denied him. Thus, by some sudden event, life, sensation, and movement often suddenly leave the limbs, and often return immediately. How much vehement anger joined with great-hearted boldness can do was shown by Alexander the Great himself, who, when surrounded in a battle in India, was seen to pour out light and fire from himself. The father of Theodoric is read to have poured out sparks of fire from his whole body, so that glittering flames leaped out here and there, even with a sound. And things similar to these sometimes even appear in beasts, such as the horse of Tiberius, which is said to have breathed fire from its mouth.

## Chapter LXIIII. How the passions of the soul change the body through imitation and likeness. Also on the transformation and translation of humans, and what powers the imaginative faculty holds not only over the body, but also over the soul.

Thus, one who sees another yawn also yawns, and some, when they hear sour things mentioned, feel their tongue grow sharp with acidity. The distress of some foul spectacle also infects the sense of taste and provokes nausea; some people faint at the sight of human blood; some, when they see another...

when they see food being brought, they feel bitter saliva in the mouth. And William of Paris <note>original: "Gulielmus Parisiensis," a 13th-century bishop and philosopher</note> relates that he saw a woman who was moved to the effects of medicine by the mere sight of it whenever a purging was necessary: even though neither the substance of the medicine, nor its taste or smell, had reached her, but only the perceived likeness of it. By this same reasoning, those dreaming that they are burning, or are in a fire, are sometimes intolerably tortured as if they were truly burning, even though the reality and substance of the fire is not with them, but only the likeness perceived through the imagination. <margin>The wondrous power of imagination.</margin> Not infrequently, even human bodies themselves are transformed, transfigured, and transported—often indeed in dreams, but sometimes even while awake. Thus Cyppus, who was afterwards elected King of Italy, while he meditated with intense admiration upon a battle and victory of bulls, fell asleep that night amidst those cares; in the morning he was found to have grown horns. This occurred from no other source than the vegetative power stimulated by a vehement imagination, which raised "horny" humors to the head and produced horns. For intense thought, while it powerfully moves the "species" <note>In medieval psychology, "species" are the mental images or forms of objects</note>, depicts in them the figure of the thing thought upon; these the imagination impresses upon the blood, and the blood impresses them upon the nourishing limbs—sometimes one's own, and sometimes even another's. Just as the imagination of a pregnant woman impresses the mark of a desired object upon the fetus, and the imagination of one bitten by a rabid dog impresses the images of dogs into the urine. Thus many suddenly turn grey-haired; another, from being a boy, grew into a full-grown man in the dream of a single night. To this phenomenon <margin>The stigmata of Francis.</margin> many also wish to attribute the scars of King Dagobert and the stigmata of Francis <note>St. Francis of Assisi</note>, while the former vehemently feared a blow, and the latter contemplated the wounds of Christ with great intensity. Thus many are also transported from place to place, crossing rivers and fires and inaccessible locations: namely, when the "species" of some vehement desire, fear, or boldness—impressed upon the spirits and mixed with vapors—move the organ of touch at its origin, together with the phantasy <note>The mental faculty that processes sensory images</note>, which is the principle of local motion. Whence the limbs and organs of motion are stirred to movement, and are moved without error to the imagined place, not indeed by sight, but by the internal phantasy. So great is the power of the soul over the body that wherever it imagines and dreams, it simultaneously lifts up and carries the body itself. We read many other examples in which the power of the soul over the body is explained with wonder, such as that which Avicenna writes of a certain man who, when he wished, could afflict his own body with paralysis. He tells of Vibius Gallus, to whom this uniquely happened: that he did not fall into insanity by chance, but arrived there by judgment. For while he imitated the insane, thinking madness to be a mere embellishment of his talent, he turned the insanity he was feigning into the real thing. And Augustine reports certain people who could move their ears at will, and who, without moving their heads, could bring their entire scalp down to the forehead and recall it when they wished; and another who was accustomed to sweat whenever he pleased. It is also known that some weep when they wish and pour out tears abundantly; some have even been found who could bring up various things they had swallowed, one by one like from a bag, whichever they pleased. And today we still see many who so imitate and express the voices of birds, cattle, dogs, and various men that they cannot be distinguished at all. Furthermore, Pliny relates with many examples that women have been changed into males; Pontanus testifies that similar things happened in his own time regarding a certain poor woman of Gaeta.

No one is ignorant of how much the imagination itself can affect the soul: for it is closer to the substance of the soul than the senses are, and therefore it acts upon the soul more powerfully than the senses do. Thus, through strong imaginations, dreams, and suggestions introduced by certain magical arts, women are very often bound in the tightest bonds of love for someone. So they say that Medea, from a dream alone, was inflamed with love for Jason. Yet he later reported that he heard the voices of men, if they shouted loudly, as if from a great distance. Truly, we shall discuss these abstractions more extensively in later sections.

### How the passions of the mind also work outside themselves upon a foreign body. Chapter LXV.

<margin>How white peacocks are produced.</margin>
The passions of the soul which follow the phantasy <note>The "phantasy" or "imagination" was considered a specific faculty of the mind that processed sensory images</note>, when they are most vehement, are not only able to change one's own body, but can even transcend to work upon a foreign body. In this way, certain wonderful impressions may be produced in the elements and external things, and they might even remove or inflict certain diseases of the mind or body. For the passions of the soul are the most powerful cause of the temperament of one's own body. Thus a soul strongly elevated and kindled by a vehement imagination sends forth health or sickness, not only in its own body, but also in the bodies of others. Thus Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the influential Persian physician and philosopher</note> believes that a camel may fall by the imagination of another. Thus, in one who has fallen into rabies after being bitten by a mad dog, the shapes of dogs appear in his urine. Thus the longing of a pregnant woman acts upon a foreign body when she stains the fetus in the womb with the mark of the thing desired. Thus many monstrous births proceed from the monstrous imaginations of pregnant women, such as the one Marcus Damascenus <note>A reference to a historical chronicler</note> relates: at Petra Sancta, a town situated on the borders of Pisa, a girl was presented to Charles, King of Bohemia and Emperor, who was hairy and shaggy over her whole body like a wild beast. Her mother, affected by a certain religious horror while looking at an image of Saint John the Baptist <note>Traditionally depicted wearing a garment of camel hair</note> which was by her bed when she conceived, subsequently brought forth such a child. And we see this happen not only in humans, but also in brute animals. Thus we read that the patriarch Jacob, by throwing rods into the water, changed the color of Laban's sheep <note>A reference to Genesis 30</note>. Thus the imaginative powers of peacocks and other birds while sitting on their eggs imprint color upon their feathers; hence we produce white peacocks by hanging white linens around the places where they sit. And now it is clear from these examples how the affections of the phantasy, when they intend themselves more vehemently, affect not only one's own body, but also the bodies of others. Thus also the desire of sorcerers to do harm fascinates <note>In the sense of "casting a spell" or "evil eye"</note> men most perniciously with fixed gazes. Avicenna, Aristotle, Algazel, and Galen agree with these points. For it is manifest...

Furthermore, the body is no less subject to a foreign mind than to a foreign body. In this way, they say a man acts upon another by his mere affection and habit. Therefore, the philosophers command that the company of evil and unhappy men must be fled far away, for the souls of these people are full of noxious rays and infect those nearby with a calamitous contagion. On the contrary, they command that the company of the good and happy should be sought after, since they benefit us greatly by their proximity. For just as the scent from asafoetida <note>A pungent resin used in medicine and magic</note> or musk leaps out into a neighbor, so does something from the evil man to the evil, and from the good to the good, and it sometimes persists for a long time after being infused. <margin>Reason is more excellent than Imagination <gloss>original: Phantasia</gloss>.</margin> Now indeed, if the aforementioned passions have such great power in the imagination, they certainly have greater power in reason, insofar as reason itself is more excellent than imagination. Finally, they have much greater power in the mind <note>original: mens; here referring to the highest intuitive faculty</note>; for when this is fixed upon the higher powers with the soul's total intention for some benefit, it often affects both its own body and the foreign body toward which it is directed by some divine gift. In this way, we read that miracles were performed by Apollonius, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Philolaus, and many prophets, and even the saints of our religion. Concerning these things, it will be more clearly revealed below, where we shall discuss religion.

## That the passions of the soul are greatly aided by celestial opportunity: and how necessary the constancy of the mind is in every work.
### Chapter LXVI.

The passions of the soul are greatly aided by and do aid the heavens, and they become most powerful insofar as they agree with the heavens, either by a certain natural pact or by voluntary choice and free will. For, as Ptolemy says, he who chooses that which is better seems to differ in no way from him who has this by nature. It is therefore most conducive in any work for receiving the benefits of heaven, if we also present ourselves as harmonious with heaven through our thoughts, affections, imaginations, choices, deliberations, contemplations, and the like. For passions of this kind vehemently stir our spirit into their likeness, and suddenly expose us and our affairs to the higher beings that signify such passions. Then also, because of their dignity and proximity to the higher things, they receive celestial influences much more and more fully than any material things. For our soul, through imagination or reason and a certain imitation, can be so conformed to a star that it is suddenly filled with the gifts of that same star, as if it were the proper receptacle for its influence.

The contemplative mind <note>original: "mens contemplatrix"</note>—insofar as it calls itself away from all sense, imagination, and natural deliberation, and retreats toward separate things—does not fall within the scope of the present investigation, except insofar as it exposes itself to Saturn <note>In Renaissance thought, Saturn was the planet associated with deep contemplation, melancholy, and the highest intellectual pursuits.</note>. For our mind performs many things through faith, which is a firm adherence, a fixed intention, and a vehement application of the worker or the receiver toward any matter, and toward the one cooperating and giving power to the work we intend to do; this happens to such an extent that a kind of "image of the virtue" to be received is formed within us, regarding the thing to be done in us or by us. We must, therefore, in every work and matter, vehemently desire, imagine, hope most firmly, and believe with application; for this will be the greatest assistance. It has been verified among physicians that firm belief <note>original: "credulitas"</note>, undoubting hope, and love toward the physician and the medicine contribute greatly to health, sometimes even more than the medicine itself. For along with that which the virtue and effective power of the medicine performs, the strong spirit <note>original: "animus"</note> of the physician also works, being able to change the qualities in the body of the sick person, especially when the patient, by placing faith in the physician, disposes himself to receive the virtue of the mind and the medicine. Therefore, it is necessary for a practitioner in magic <note>original: "magia"</note> to be of constant belief, confident, and by no means to doubt or hesitate in mind regarding the attainment of the effect. For just as a firm and persistent belief works wonders, even sometimes in false works, so distrust and hesitation dissipate and break the virtue of the worker's mind, which is the medium between both extremes. Thus it happens that the desired influx from the higher powers is frustrated and lost, for it can by no means be joined or united to our things and works without the stable and solid virtue of our mind.

For our mind, when it is carried away into some great excess of any passion or virtue, very often seizes for itself a stronger, better, and more suitable hour or opportunity. <margin>A general rule.</margin>
And there is a general rule in these matters: that every mind which is more excellent in its own desire and affection, makes such things more fit and effective for itself toward that which it craves. Therefore, it is necessary for anyone wishing to work in <term>magic</term> <note>The art of directing natural and celestial influences to produce specific effects.</note> to know and understand the property, virtue, measure, order, and degree of his own soul within the power of the universe itself.

### How our mind can change and bind inferior things to that which it desires. Chapter LXVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' set within a square frame, depicting a winged figure (putto) reaching toward foliage in a landscape.</image-desc>
There is also in the minds of men a certain power of changing, attracting, hindering, and binding things and men to that which he desires; and all things obey him when he is carried into a great excess of some passion or virtue, so much so that he overcomes those whom he binds. For that which is superior binds that which is inferior and turns it toward itself, and the inferior, by the same reasoning, is turned toward the superior, or is otherwise affected or agitated. By this reasoning, things which hold a superior degree of some star bind, attract, or hinder things which hold an inferior degree, according as they agree or disagree among themselves. Hence the cock is feared by the lion, because the presence of the solar virtue suits the cock more than the lion; so the <term>magnet</term> <note>lodestone</note> draws iron because it holds a superior degree in the order of the Celestial Bear <note>The constellation Ursa Major, associated with the North Pole and magnetic alignment.</note>; so the <term>diamond</term> <note>original: "adamas"</note> hinders the magnet because it is superior to it in the order of Mars. In a similar way, a man—exposed at the right time to celestial gifts both through the affections of his mind and through the application of the rites of natural things—if he emerges stronger in solar virtue, he binds and draws the inferior into admiration and obedience; in the lunar order to servitude or infirmity; in the Saturnine to rest or sadness; in the Jovian <note>relating to Jupiter</note> to the showing of veneration; in the Martian to fear or discord; in the Venerean to love or joy; in the Mercurial to persuasion and compliance, and the like.

<margin>The root of binding.</margin>
The root of such binding is the vehement and unrestrained affection of the soul itself, combined with the concurrence of the celestial order. However, the dissolutions or hindrances of such binding are made through a contrary effect, and one that is more excellent and stronger: for just as a greater excess of the mind binds, so also it releases and hinders. Finally, where you fear Venus, oppose Saturn; where you fear Saturn or Mars, oppose Venus or Jupiter; for <term>astrologers</term> <note>Those who study the movements and relative positions of celestial bodies interpreted as having an influence on human affairs.</note> say that these are enemies and greatly contrary to one another. Understand this as causing diverse and contrary affections in these inferior things: for in heaven indeed, where no—
