### On Speech, and the Virtues of Words. Chapter LXIX.

<note>Decorative initial 'O' containing a human face in profile, surrounded by classical foliage and strapwork.</note>
Having now shown that great power resides in the passions of the mind, it must furthermore be understood that no less power exists in words and the names of things, and the greatest power of all in connected speeches and orations. It is by these especially that we differ from the brute beasts and are called "rational." We are not called rational merely because of the reason associated with the soul—which they call the capacity for passions, and which Galen <note>Galen was a prominent Greek physician and philosopher whose views on biology influenced Western medicine for centuries.</note> says even brute animals have in common with us, though some more and others less—but we are called rational from the reason understood through the voice in words and speech. This is called "enunciative reason," the part in which we most excel all other living creatures; for the word <term>Logos</term> <note>original: "λόγος". In Greek, this single word encompasses both "reason" and "speech," a dual meaning central to this argument.</note> signifies to the Greeks both reason and speech, or the word. Moreover, the word is twofold: namely, internal and uttered. The internal word is the concept of the mind and the motion of the soul, which occurs in the presence of thought without a voice; just as in dreams we seem to speak and dispute with ourselves, and even while awake and silent, we often run through an entire oration. The uttered word, however, has a certain expression in the voice and the property of locution; it is brought forth with the breath of man, the opening of the mouth, and the speech of the tongue. In this, nature as a parent has coupled the corporeal voice and speech to the mind and intellect, making the voice the proclaimer and interpreter of the concepts of our intellect to those who hear us; and it is of this we must speak here. Words are, therefore, the most fitting medium between the speaker and the listener, carrying with them not only a concept but also transferring the power of the speaker into the listeners and receivers by a certain energy—often with such great potency that they change not only the listeners but even other bodies and inanimate things. Those words, 
<margin>Which words are of greater efficacy.</margin>
above all others, possess greater efficacy which represent greater things—namely intellectual, celestial, and supernatural things—whether more expressly or more mysteriously. This is also true of words established by a more worthy language and a holier dignity; for these, like certain signs and representations, or sacraments of celestial and supernatural things, obtain power both from the virtue of the things explained (of which they are the vehicles) and from the power implanted in them by the virtue of the one who established and utters them.

### On the Virtue of Proper Names. Chapter LXX.

<note>Decorative initial 'P' featuring a seated mythical creature amidst floral ornaments.</note>
Almost all testify that the proper names of things are highly necessary in magical operations. For since the natural power of things proceeds first from the objects to the senses, then from these to the imagination, and finally from there to the mind (in which it is first conceived), it is then expressed through voices and words. Therefore, the Platonists say that in this very voice, or word, or name—once formed into its distinct parts—there lurks a certain life, as it were, under the form of the thing's significance. It is first conceived by the mind itself as if through the seeds of things, then brought forth through voices or words as if by birth, and finally preserved even in writings. Hence the Magi say that the proper names of things are certain rays of things, always present everywhere, preserving the power of the things, insofar as the essence of the thing signified is in...

<margin>The proper names of things are certain rays.</margin>
[The mind] dominates and discerns them, and recognizes things through those names as if through their own living images. For just as the Supreme Creator produces diverse species and particular things from the influences of the heavens and the elements combined with the virtues of the planets, so too do the proper names of things result from the properties of those same influences. These names were bestowed by Him who "counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names" <note>A reference to Psalm 147:4</note>, of which names Christ says elsewhere: "Your names are written in heaven." <note>Luke 10:20</note> Therefore, the first-formed man <note>original: "protoplastes," referring to Adam</note>, knowing these celestial influences and the properties of individual things, imposed names upon things according to their essences, just as it is written in Genesis: for God brought all things He had created before Adam so that he might name them; and whatever he called a thing, that was its name. Indeed, these names contain within themselves the wonderful powers of the things they signify.

Therefore, every meaningful word signifies first through the influence of celestial harmony, and secondarily through human designation, although it frequently happens differently through one or the other. However, when both significations—those from harmony and those imposed by men—concur in any word or name, then that name is rendered most effective for action by a doubled virtue (namely, the natural and the voluntary). This occurs whenever it is uttered in the proper places and times, with solemnity and exact intention, upon material disposed for it and naturally susceptible to its influence. Thus we read in the writings of Philostratus <note>A 3rd-century Greek scholar</note> that when a certain girl in Rome died on her wedding day and was brought to Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a famous Neopythagorean philosopher and wonder-worker</note>, he touched the maiden and inquired accurately after her name; having learned it, he pronounced something secret, by which the girl returned to life.

There was also an observation among the Romans in their sacred rites that when they besieged a city, they would diligently seek out its proper name and the name of the deity under whose protection that city stood. Once these were known, they would use a certain song <note>original: "carmen," which can mean a poem, song, or ritual incantation</note> to call forth the tutelary gods of that city and devote the city itself and its inhabitants to destruction; thus, with the gods absent, they would finally conquer it, just as Virgil sings:

> All the gods by whom this empire stood
> Have departed, leaving behind their altars and shrines.
> <note>Aeneid, Book II, 351-352</note>

Truly, if anyone wishes to know the song by which the deities were summoned and the enemies devoted to destruction while the city was surrounded by siege, let him seek it in Livy and Macrobius; moreover, Serenus Sammonicus relates more of these matters in his books of hidden things.

### On complex speeches, songs, and the virtues and bindings of incantations. Chapter LXXI.

This virtue of truth is not found in simple words, but in enunciations by which something is affirmed or denied—such as songs, incantations, imprecations, prayers, invocations, protestations, adjurations, exorcisms, and the like. Consider the virtues, effects, and operations that any given star contains within itself, and weave these into songs <note>original: "carminibus"; here referring to incantations or rhythmic verses used in ritual</note> by praising, extolling, amplifying, and adorning those things which a star of this kind is accustomed to bring and influence; while conversely depressing and disparaging those things it is accustomed to destroy and hinder. They then immediately transfer into the thing being enchanted to bind or direct it toward the goal intended by the emotions and words of the enchanter. Indeed, the very instrument of those enchanting is a certain most pure, harmonic spirit—warm, breathing, living, carrying motion, emotion, and meaning with it, composed of its own sections, endowed with sense, and finally conceived by reason. Therefore, through the quality of this spirit and through its celestial likeness, in addition to what has been said, and also from the opportunity of the timing, these songs conceive most excellent virtues from heaven. These are much more sublime and effective than the spirits and vapors exhaling from vegetable life, from herbs, roots, gums, spices, fumigations, and similar things. ## On the Wonderful Power of Incantations. Chapter LXXII.

They say the power of incantations or songs <note>original: "carminum"; in this context, "carmen" refers to a ritual chant, poem, or magical formula</note> is so great that they are believed to be able to subvert almost all of nature, just as Apuleius says: By a magical whispering, swift rivers are turned back, the sluggish sea is bound fast, the harmonious winds are breathed out, the sun is inhibited, the moon is made to foam, the stars are plucked out, the day is taken away, and the night is held back. And Lucan sings of the same:

> The successions of things have ceased, and the day, stretched out,
> Has lingered in a long night; the ether has not obeyed its law.
> The world grew torpid and headlong upon hearing the song. And a little before:
> The song of the Thessalian women flowed into hard hearts,
> For a love not sufficiently induced. And elsewhere:
> A mind polluted by no draught of poisonous gore
> Perishes, enchanted away. Likewise Virgil in *Damon*:
> Songs can even draw down the moon from heaven.
> By songs Circe changed the companions of Ulysses.
> The cold snake in the meadows is burst apart by chanting, and:
> I have seen the sown harvests moved elsewhere.

And Ovid says in *Untitled* <note>referring to the *Amores*</note>:

> By a song, injured Ceres <note>The goddess of grain; here meaning the harvest itself</note> vanishes into sterile grass,
> The waters of a fountain, injured by a song, fail.
> Acorns from the holm-oaks and the chanted grape from the vines
> Fall down, and the fruits drop with no one moving them.

If these things were not true, a penalty would not have been so strictly established and sanctioned by the laws against those who had enchanted away the crops. And Tibullus says of a certain enchantress:

> I have seen her drawing the stars down from heaven,
> She turns the path of a rapid river with a song.
> She cleaves the ground with chanting, and elicits the spirits
> From their sepulchers, and calls down bones from the warm pyre.
> When she pleases, she drives the clouds from the gloomy sky,
> When she pleases, she summons snows in the summer world.

Regarding all of these things, that sorceress <note>original: "uenefica"; literally a poisoner or maker of potions, but used here for a witch or enchantress</note> seems to boast much in Ovid when she says:

> When I have willed it, with the very banks wondering, the rivers
> Return to their own sources; I stay the shaken seas,
> And shake the standing seas with a song; I drive away the clouds,
> And I bring the clouds on; I drive away the winds and call them;
> I burst the viperous jaws with words and song,

Furthermore, all the poets sing of it, and the philosophers do not deny it, that many wonderful things can be accomplished by charms: such as the driving away of crops <note>meaning the magical theft or relocation of harvests</note>, the forcing or commanding of lightning bolts, the curing of diseases, and things of this sort. ### On the virtue of writing, and on the making of imprecations and
### inscriptions. Chapter 73.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'O' depicting a personified face (likely the sun or a moon) within a circular medallion.</image-desc>The duty of words and speech is to announce the inner parts of the mind, to bring forth secrets from the innermost depths of thoughts, and to reveal the will of the speaker. Writing itself, however, is the ultimate expression of the mind; it is the number, collection, state, end, containment, and iteration of speech and voice, creating a lasting habit which is not completed by the act of a single voice. And whatever is in the mind, in the voice, in the word, in the oration, and in speech—all of this, and everything else, is also in writing. And just as nothing that is conceived in the mind is not expressed by the voice, so nothing that is expressed is not also written. And for that reason, the Magi command that in any work, imprecations <note>solemn prayers or invocations</note> and inscriptions must be made, by which the practitioner expresses his intent: as when he gathers a herb or a small stone, he should declare for what use he does it; if he fashions an image, he should say and inscribe for what effect it is made. Indeed, Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century scholar and bishop</note> does not disapprove of these imprecations and inscriptions in his *Speculum*; without them, our works would not be led to their effect, since a disposition does not cause an effect, but rather the act of the disposition. We find also that this same kind of precept was in use among the ancients, as Virgil himself testifies when he sings:

> These three threads first, distinct with triple color,
> I wrap around you, and three times around these altars
> I lead the image.

<margin>and a little after:</margin>
> Tie the three colors in three knots, Amaryllis,
> Tie them now, Amaryllis, and say: "I tie the chains of Venus."

<margin>and in the same place:</margin>
> As this clay hardens, and as this wax melts
> In one and the same fire, so may Daphnis by my love.

# BOOK THREE.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'D' containing a scene of a scholar or saint seated at a desk with an open book, surrounded by architectural and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

God gave to man mind and speech, which (as Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus," the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus and the origin of wisdom</note> says) are considered the reward of the same virtue, power, and immortality. Indeed, Almighty God by his providence divided the speech of men into diverse languages. These languages, according to their diversity, also received their own proper characters of writing, consisting of a certain fixed order, number, and shape—not by chance, nor by accident, nor by the fragile will of men, but disposed and formed by divine intent so that they might harmonize with the celestial and divine bodies and virtues. <margin>The most holy scripture of the Hebrews.</margin> Truly, above all marks of languages, the Hebrew scripture is the most sacred of all in the shapes of its characters, the points of its vowels, and the tips of its accents: existing, as it were, in matter, form, and spirit. In the seat of God, which is heaven, it was first engraved by the position of the stars; according to their shape (as the masters of the Hebrews testify), the letters themselves were formed, being most full of celestial mysteries—both through their shape, form, and meanings, and through the numbers signified in them, as well as through the various harmony of their binding together. Whence the more secret Hebrew Kabbalists <note>original: "Mecubales," a Latinization of the Hebrew 'Mekubbalim,' meaning those who have received the tradition</note> promise to explain all things—how they proceeded from the First Cause and are again reducible to the same—by the shape and character of those letters, the forms and signatures of the same, their simplicity, composition, separation, twisting, direction, defect, abundance, greatness, smallness, crowning, opening, closing, order, transmutation, binding, the revolution of letters, points, and tips, and the calculation of numbers signified through the letters. Furthermore, the Hebrews divide the letters of their alphabet into three parts: namely, into twelve simple, seven double, and three mothers. These they say signify, as characters of things, the twelve signs <note>the Zodiac</note>, the seven planets, and the three elements—namely fire, water, and earth; for they do not consider air an element, but rather the glue and spirit of the elements. With these they also coordinate the points and tips. Therefore, just as all things were and are produced from the aspects of the planets and signs together with the elements by the craftsman spirit and truth, so from these characters of letters and points (signifying those produced things) are constituted the names of all things, like certain sacraments and vehicles of explained things, carrying their essence and powers with them everywhere. The profound meanings and sacraments of these things inhere in those characters and their shapes, numbers, position, order, and revolution, so that Origen <note>original: "Origenes," an early Christian scholar and theologian</note> therefore thinks those names, if translated into another language, retain very little of their proper power: because they do not retain their natural significance. For only the primary names which are rightly imposed, because they signify naturally, have natural activity; it is not so with those which signify by pleasure <note>i.e., by arbitrary human convention</note>, which have no activity as significators but only as certain natural things in themselves. If, however, there is any first and causal language, whose words have natural significance, it is established that this is Hebrew; he who holds its order profoundly and radically, and its letters proportionally—

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

Page 96.

Whoever knows how to revolve these <note>referring to the combinations of letters</note> three times will possess the norm and rule for perfectly discovering any idiom whatsoever. Therefore, there are twenty-two letters which are the foundation of the world and of all creatures that exist and are named within it; every word and every created thing comes from them, and from their revolutions, they receive their name, their being, and their power. It is necessary for the investigator of these things to run through the individual combinations of letters for as long as it takes until the voice of God becomes clear, and the text of the most sacred letters offers itself openly. For this reason, voices and words have efficacy in magical works: because that in which nature first exercises magic is the voice of God. But these matters belong to a higher speculation than should be treated in this book.

Let us return, however, to the partition of the letters. Among the Hebrews, there are three "mothers," namely: א (Aleph), מ (Mem), ש (Shin) <note>In the Sefer Yetzirah, these represent the elements of Air, Water, and Fire</note>. Seven are "double," namely: ב (Bet), ג (Gimel), ד (Dalet), כ (Kaph), פ (Pe), ר (Resh), ת (Tav) <note>So called because they have two pronunciations, hard and soft, and correspond to the seven planets</note>. The remaining twelve, namely: ה (He), ו (Vav), ז (Zayin), ח (Het), ט (Tet), י (Yod), ל (Lamed), נ (Nun), ס (Samekh), ע (Ayin), צ (Tzadi), ק (Qoph), are "simple" <note>Corresponding to the twelve signs of the Zodiac</note>. The same logic applies among the Chaldeans. In imitation of these, the letters of other languages are also distributed among the signs, planets, and elements in their own specific order.

For among the Greeks: Α, Ε, Η, Ι, Ο, Υ, Ω correspond to the seven planets. Β, Γ, Δ, Ζ, Κ, Λ, Μ, Ν, Π, Ρ, Σ, Τ are attributed to the twelve signs of the zodiac. The remaining five—Θ, Ξ, Φ, Χ, Ψ—represent the four elements and the spirit of the world.

Among the Latins, these same things are signified, but in a different order: for the five vowels, A, E, I, O, U, along with the consonants J and V <note>original: "I & V consonantes"</note>, are ascribed to the seven planets. The consonants B, C, D, F, G, L, M, N, P, R, S, T preside over the twelve signs. The others, namely K, Q, X, Z, make up the four elements. The aspiration H represents the spirit of the world. Y, because it is a Greek and not a Latin character and serves only Greek words, follows the nature of its own idiom.

Truly, it must not be ignored that the Hebrew letters have been found by the wise to be the most efficacious of all, because they have the greatest similarity with the celestial things and the world. The letters of other languages do not have such great efficacy because they are more distantly removed from them. The following table will explain their arrangements.

Furthermore, each letter has double numbers of its order: namely, "extended" numbers, which simply express the position of the letters according to their order; and "collected" numbers, which gather together the numbers of all preceding letters. Then there are also "integral" numbers which result from the names of the letters according to various modes of counting <note>This refers to Gematria and other forms of Hebrew numerology</note>. He who knows the powers of these numbers will be able to draw out admirable mysteries in every language through its letters, and likewise gather prophecies of both past and future times. There are, moreover, other mysterious marriages of letters with numbers, but concerning all these, we shall discourse abundantly in the following books; here we place an end to this first book.

# TO THE MOST AMPLE LORD, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE
## HERMANN of Wied, Prince Elector, Duke of Westphalia and Angria, Lord and Arch-prelate of Cologne and Paderborn, his most gracious Lord, Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim sends greetings.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring an ornate scene with a winged putto or angel holding a circular object (possibly a celestial sphere) amidst clouds and foliage, with another figure partially visible in the background landscape.</image-desc>

BEHOLD NOW (most illustrious Prince and most ample Prelate) the remaining books of secret philosophy or magic, which I recently promised to your magnificence I would publish when I gave the first of them to the light. However, the sudden and nearly unexpected death of the Divine Margaret of Austria <note>Margaret of Austria (1480–1530), Governor of the Habsburg Netherlands and Agrippa's patroness.</note>, my princess, occurring at that time, delayed me from that zeal for publishing. Then, the wickedness of certain "beaked" <note>original: "rostratorum" - likely referring to the bird-like masks of doctors or the "beaks" of predatory critics.</note> sycophants and several scholastic sophists stood in the way of their being published. Because of my published declamation *On the Vanity of the Sciences and the Excellence of the Word of God* <note>Agrippa's famous skeptical work which attacked the corruption of the sciences and the church, earning him many enemies.</note>, they have raged against me without intermission, contending against me with a bitter continuation of hatred, envy, malice, and slanders. Some of these men, with raised eyebrows and full cheeks, betrayed me for impiety with declamatory voices in the temples before the common people; others, with corner-whisperings through individual houses, filled the ears of the unskilled throughout the neighborhoods with my infamy; still others, through public and private assemblies, instigated the Popes, the princes, and even the Emperor himself against me. Hence I began to hesitate whether I should publish these remaining books, since I doubted whether by this very act I would expose myself to greater slanders and, as it were, cast myself out of the smoke into the flame. A certain "rustic fear" <note>A Latin idiom for a bashful or unrefined hesitation.</note> invaded me, lest by publishing them I should seem more troublesome than dutiful to you, and also that I might stir up the envy of those "Zoiluses" <note>Zoilus was a Greek grammarian known for bitter criticism; the name became a proverb for a spiteful critic.</note> against your Highness, and likewise expose you to the tongues of detractors. While all these things disturbed me with various despairs, the perspicacity of your intelligence, your exact discretion, the candor of your judgment, your religion without superstition, and your other most well-known virtues—along with an authority and integrity greater than any exception—shook off my fear. These qualities, which could easily restrain and even bridle the tongues of detractors, encouraged me and impelled me to approach again more boldly that which I had almost abandoned out of despair. Receive therefore now (most illustrious Prince) with a good heart this second book of secret philosophy, in which we intimate the mysteries of celestial magic <note>The second book focuses on "Celestial Magic," dealing with mathematics, numbers, and astrology.</note>, with all things revealed and demonstrated which the antiquity of things has produced concerning them, and which have come to our knowledge. Thus, to the studious and those curious about these secrets, after the demonstration of natural powers <note>A reference to Book I, which dealt with "Natural Magic" or the elemental world.</note>, the secrets of celestial magic (hitherto neglected and grasped by posterity with little just knowledge) may now be set forth by us under your auspices. Whoever hereafter shall profit from these or gather any fruit, let him return and ascribe the thanks to you, who were the occasion of this edition, and who provided the means so that, the doors being opened, these things might be released from their chains.

->FAREWELL.<-

# AGRIPPA ON OCCULT PHI-
## losophy, or on Magic.

### On the necessity of Mathematical disciplines, and on the many wonderful
### works which are performed by mathematical arts alone. Chapter I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' depicting two human figures (possibly cherubs or classical deities) amidst elaborate floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>
MATHEMATICAL DISCIPLINES ARE so necessary and related to magic, that he who professes the latter without the former wanders entirely from the path, labors in vain, and will by no means achieve the desired effect. For whatever things exist and are produced in these lower regions by natural virtues, all these are made and governed by number, weight, measure, harmony, motion, and light. All things which we see in these lower realms have their root and foundation in those mathematical principles. Nevertheless, even without natural virtues, works similar to natural ones can be produced by mathematical disciplines alone. As Plato says, these are things not indeed participating in truth and divinity, but certain likenesses related to themselves, such as bodies walking or speaking, which nevertheless lack a vital soul. Such were those which among the ancients were called the statues of Daedalus <note>A mythical Greek inventor and craftsman</note> and *automata* <note>original: "αὐτόματα" - self-moving machines</note>, and those which Aristotle mentions: the tripods of Vulcan and Daedalus moving themselves, which Homer relates came forth to the contest of their own accord; and those which we read moved themselves in the banquet of Iarbas the Gymnosophist <note>A member of a sect of ancient Indian philosophers known for living naked and practicing asceticism</note>, where golden statues performed the work of cupbearers and carvers at the feasts. We also read of the statues of Mercury which spoke, and the wooden dove of Archytas <note>A Greek philosopher and mathematician</note> which flew; and the miracles of Boethius which Cassiodorus relates: a Diomedes trumpeting in brass, a brass serpent hissing, and simulated birds emitting the sweetness of song. Of this kind are whatever miracles of likenesses proceed from Geometry and Optics, of which we made mention in the earlier parts where we spoke of the element of air.

<margin>The wonderful craftsmanship of mirrors.</margin>
Thus mirrors are made—some concave, others columnar—making likenesses of things appear in the air, seen like shadows at distances removed from themselves; of which kind Apollonius and Vitellius <note>Witelo, a 13th-century friar and physicist known for his work on optics</note> taught in their books on Perspective and mirrors. And we read that Pompey the Great brought a certain mirror to Rome among the spoils from the East, in which armies of armed men were perceived. And certain translucent mirrors are made which, being stained with certain juices of herbs and irradiated with artificial light, fill the whole surrounding air with wonderful phantasms. And I myself know how to fashion two reciprocal mirrors in which, when the sun shines, all things whatsoever that are illustrated by its rays are most clearly discerned through remote spaces of many miles. Hence the magician, skilled in natural philosophy and mathematics, knowing the middle sciences <note>The "quadrivium" or intermediate sciences that bridge the physical and the abstract</note> arising from both of these—Arithmetic, Music,

Geometry, Optics, Astronomy, and those sciences which deal with weights, measures, proportions, joints, and unions—and knowing also the mechanical arts resulting from them—it is no wonder if a man, excelling others in art and ingenuity, performs many wonders that even the most prudent and learned greatly admire. Do there not exist to this day traces of ancient works? For instance, the Pillars of Hercules and Alexander; the Caspian Gates cast from bronze and barred with iron beams so that they can be forced by no wit or art; the pyramid of Julius Caesar erected at Rome near the Vatican; and mountains built by art in the middle of the sea; and masses of rocks, the likes of which I have seen in Britain <note>Likely a reference to Stonehenge</note> piled together with scarcely credible skill. And we read in faithful historians that by similar arts, cliffs were once cut away, valleys filled, and mountains leveled; rocks were pierced through, promontories opened to the sea, the bowels of the earth excavated, rivers diverted, seas joined to seas, the oceans restrained, the depths of the sea searched, lakes drained, marshes dried up, and new islands created while others were restored to the mainland. Although all these things seem to fight against Nature herself, we nevertheless read that they were done, and to this day we see their traces. The common people falsely claim such things were the work of demons <note>original: "dæmonum"</note>, since the arts and the craftsmen themselves have perished from memory, and there are none who care to understand or investigate them. Therefore, seeing some wonderful spectacle and being blind in their intellect, they cast every effect upon demons or think them miracles, when they are actually the works of natural or mathematical disciplines. For example, if someone were ignorant of the power of the magnet and saw heavy iron carried upward or suspended in the air—just as it is read that the iron idol of Mercury <note>The Roman messenger god</note> was once suspended by magnet stones in the middle of a temple at Trier—this verse attests to it:

->The iron herald of the gods flies in the midst of the breezes.<-
<note>original: "Ferreus in mediis uolitat caducifer auris."</note>

We read of a similar thing done with the idol of the Sun in the temple of Serapis in Egypt. Would such a person not immediately say it is the work of demons? But if he truly knew the power of the magnet over iron and had experienced it, all his wonder would cease, and no doubt would remain that it is a work of nature. And here it is fitting for you to know that just as we gather natural virtues through natural things, so through abstract, mathematical, and celestial things, we receive celestial virtues—such as motion, life, sense, speech, foreknowledge, and divination—even in matter less disposed to them, such as that which is fashioned not by nature but by art alone. And so it is said that images can be made that speak and predict the future, just as William of Paris <note>William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), Bishop of Paris and philosopher</note> tells of a bronze head cast under the rising of Saturn, which they say spoke with human voices. He who truly knows how to choose a disposed material most ready to receive, and a most powerful agent, will produce undoubtedly more potent effects. For it is the general opinion of the Pythagoreans that just as mathematical things are more formal than physical things, so they are more actual; and as they are less dependent in their being, so also are they in their operation. mathematics; as numbers are more formal <note>In this context, "formal" refers to the "Form" or essential blueprint of a thing in the Platonic sense, rather than just its outward appearance.</note>, so too are they more actualized. To these numbers, not only the pagan philosophers but also the theologians of the Hebrews and Christians attribute power and efficacy for both good and evil.

### On numbers and their power and virtue. Chapter II.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring a leafy design and a small child figure climbing through the vines.</image-desc>
Severinus Boethius <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose works on arithmetic and music were foundational for medieval science.</note> says that all things whatsoever that have been constructed from the primeval nature of things appear to be formed by the ratio of numbers; for this was the principal exemplar in the mind of the Creator. From this, the multitude of the elements was borrowed; from this, the cycles of seasons; from this, the motion of the stars and the turning of the heavens; and the state of all things subsists through the binding together of numbers. Therefore, numbers are powerful with great and sublime virtues. Nor is it a wonder, since there are so many and such great hidden virtues in natural things (even though their operations are manifest), that there should be in numbers themselves virtues much greater, more hidden, more wonderful, and more effective. This is because they are more formal and perfect, implanted in the celestial bodies, mixed with the separate substances <note>A term for angels or purely spiritual beings that exist without physical bodies.</note>, and finally having the greatest and simplest connection with the Ideas in the Divine Mind, from which they receive their own most effective powers. For this reason, they are also very powerful for attaining demonic <note>In the classical sense of "daemonic" or spiritual intermediaries, not necessarily evil spirits.</note> and divine gifts, and they can do more, just as in natural things the elemental qualities are very powerful and capable in transforming something into an elemental state.
<margin>All things consist of certain numbers.</margin>
Again, all things that are and that happen subsist and receive power through certain numbers. For time consists of number, as does all motion and action, and all things whatsoever that are subject to time and motion. Even harmonies and voices have power and consist through numbers and their proportions; and proportions arising from numbers, through lines and points, constitute characters and figures. These are proper to magical works, with a middle ground existing between both, appropriated through a leaning toward the extremes, as in the use of letters. Finally, all species of natural things and those which are above nature are bound by certain numbers. Observing this, Pythagoras said that number is that by which all things consist, and he distributed specific virtues to specific numbers. And Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> says: Number always exists; yet one kind is in the voice, another in their proportion, another in the soul and reason, and another in divine things. Themistius, Boethius, and Averroes the Babylonian <note>The Latin text calls the famous Muslim commentator Averroes "Babylonian," likely a geographical error or a reference to his "Eastern" wisdom.</note> along with Plato, so extol numbers that they think no one can philosophize rightly without them. However, they speak of rational and formal number, not of material, sensible, or vocal number—the number of merchants—about which the Pythagoreans, the Academics, and our Augustine care nothing. Instead, they focus on the proportion resulting from it, which they call natural, formal, and rational number, from which great mysteries <note>original: "sacramenta"</note> emanate, both in natural things and in divine and celestial ones. Through that number, a path is held for investigating and understanding all things that can be known. Through it, there is the closest access to natural prophecy; and Abbot Joachim <note>Joachim of Fiore, a famous 12th-century mystic known for his prophetic theories based on biblical ages.</note> himself, in his prophecies, proceeded by no other way than through formal numbers.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

## How great a power numbers possess in both natural and supernatural things. Chapter III.

<image-desc>A decorative historiated drop cap 'I' featuring floral and leafy scrollwork within a square frame.</image-desc>
That a wonderful efficacy and virtue lies hidden in numbers, as much for good as for evil, is taught not only by the most illustrious philosophers with one voice, but is also confirmed by the Catholic doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church," influential early Christian theologians.</note>. Among these are Jerome, Augustine, Origen, Ambrose, Gregory of Nazianzus, Athanasius, Basil, Hilary, Rabanus, Bede, and many others. Hence Hilary, in his commentaries on the Psalms, testifies that the seventy elders <note>A reference to the translators of the Septuagint.</note> arranged the Psalms in order according to the efficacy of numbers. Rabanus also, a most distinguished doctor, composed a unique book on the virtues of numbers. Furthermore, how much power numbers possess in nature is evident in the herb called *pentaphyllon* <note>original: "pentaphyllon," commonly known as Cinquefoil.</note>, which is to say, "five-leafed."

<margin>The virtues of the Cinquefoil herb.</margin>
For this herb, by the power of the number five, resists poisons, drives away demons, and aids in purification. One of its leaves taken in wine twice daily cures a one-day fever <note>original: "ephemeram," a fever lasting only a day.</note>; three leaves cure a tertian fever <note>A fever that recurs every third day, often associated with malaria.</note>; and four leaves cure a quartan fever <note>A fever that recurs every fourth day.</note>. Similarly, it is said that four grains of heliotrope drunk by women benefit quartan fevers, while three benefit tertian fevers. In a similar way, vervain is said to heal fevers in wine if, for tertian fevers, it is cut at the third joint, and for quartan fevers, at the fourth. If a serpent is struck once with a reed, it dies; if struck a second time, it recovers its strength. These and many similar things are read and testified to among various authors. As to why these things happen, they certainly have a cause, which is the various proportions of different numbers to one another.

<margin>A wonderful experiment of the number seven.</margin>
There is also a wonderful experiment regarding the number seven: that every seventh male child born without a female intervening has the power of curing scrofula <note>A form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes, historically called "the King's Evil."</note> by touch or word alone. Similarly, every seventh daughter born is said to assist in childbirth in a wonderful way. Here, this natural number is observed, but it is the <term>formal reason</term> <note>The essential or spiritual blueprint behind a physical thing.</note> which exists within the number. And let that which we said above be always kept in mind: that these powers are not in the vocal and "merchant" numbers <note>Common numbers used for counting and trade.</note>, but in the rational, formal, and natural numbers; these are the distinct and contained mysteries of God and nature. Whoever knows how to join vocal and natural numbers with divine ones, and to temper them into the same harmony, will be able to work and even understand wonders through numbers. The Pythagoreans also professed to foretell many things by the numbers of names; if some great mystery did not lie hidden in these, John would not have said in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>: "Let him who has understanding calculate the number of the name of the beast, for it is the number of a man." This method of calculation is most celebrated among the Hebrews and Cabalists,

<margin>The significance of numbers.</margin>
as we shall show below. But it must be known that simple numbers signify divine things; tens signify celestial things; hundreds signify earthly things; and thousands signify those things which belong to the future age. ### On Unity and its Scale. Chapter IV.

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'N' featuring a seated man, likely a scholar, in front of an architectural structure.</image-desc>Now let us determine the specifics regarding the numbers themselves: because number is truly nothing other than the repetition of unity, let us first consider unity itself. For Unity penetrates every number in the simplest manner, and is the common measure, fount, and origin of all numbers; it contains every number joined uniquely within itself. It is devoid of all multiplicity, remaining always the same and immutable; hence even when multiplied by itself, it produces nothing but itself. It is indivisible and lacks any parts; but if it were ever imagined to be divided, it is not cut, but rather multiplied—namely, into unities. Yet none of these unities is greater or smaller than the whole unity, in the way that a part is smaller than the whole. It is multiplied,
<margin>Names of Unity.</margin>
therefore, not into parts, but into itself. For this reason, some have called it "Concord," others "Piety," and others "Friendship," because it is so bound together that it cannot be cut into parts. Furthermore, Martianus <note>Martianus Capella, a 5th-century author of an influential encyclopedia on the liberal arts.</note>, following the opinion of Aristotle, asserts it is named "Cupid" <note>original: "Cupidinem"</note>, for the reason that it is one alone, and wishes always to be sought for itself, and has nothing beyond itself; but being devoid of all pride or coupling, it turns its own fires back into itself. One, therefore, is the beginning and end of all things, having itself neither
<margin>The excellence of Unity.</margin>
beginning nor end. Nothing is prior to one, and nothing is posterior to one. One is the principle of all things, and all things exist as far as the one, and beyond it there is nothing; and all things that exist desire that one, because all things proceeded from the one. In order for all things to exist as they are, it is necessary for them to participate in that one. And just as all things proceeded from the one into the many, so it is necessary for all things that strive to return to that one from which they proceeded to strip away their multiplicity. Unity, therefore, is referred to the highest God, who, although he is himself one and innumerable, nevertheless creates innumerable things from himself and contains them within himself. Thus there is one God;
<margin>The "One" in existing things.</margin>
for one God there is one world; for one world, one sun; also one phoenix in the world; one king among the bees; one leader in the flocks; one ruler in the herds; and the cranes follow one leader; and many other living creatures venerate unity. Among the members of the body, there is one principle by which the rest are governed, whether that be the head or (as others prefer) the heart. There is one element that conquers and penetrates all: fire. There is one thing created by God, the subject of every wonder in the heavens and on earth, which is actually animal, vegetable, and mineral; found everywhere, known by very few, expressed by none by its own proper name, but veiled in innumerable figures and enigmas, without which neither Alchemy nor natural magic can reach their complete end. From one man, Adam, all were produced; from that one, all died; from one Jesus Christ, all were again reborn.

## On Duality and its Scale. Chapter V.

<margin>Names of the Binary.</margin>
**The Binary** <note>The number two.</note> is the first number, because it is the first multitude; it can be measured by no number except by unity alone, the common measure of all numbers. It is not composed of numbers, but coordinated from unity alone, one and one. It is not called an "uncomposite" number, but more properly "not composed" <note>In Pythagorean numerology, 2 is the first departure from the 1, but 3 is considered the first true odd/uncomposite number.</note>; however, the Ternary <note>The number three.</note> is called the first uncomposite number. The Binary is the first sprout of unity and the first procreation; hence it is called Genesis, and Juno <note>The Roman goddess of marriage and childbirth.</note>, and the imaginable embodiment, the proof of the first motion, and the first form of parity. It is the number of first equality, of the extremity and the interval, and therefore peculiar to justice, and its proper act, because it rejoices in two things equally weighted. It is called the number of science, and of memory, and of light, and the number of man, who is called the "other" and "lesser" world. It is also called the number of charity and mutual love, of marriage and society, just as it was said by the Lord: "They two shall be in one flesh." And Ecclesiastes <note>original: "Ecclesiasticus," likely referring to Ecclesiastes 4:9-12</note> says: "It is better that two be together than one, for they have the reward of their society; if one falls, he shall be supported by the other. Woe to him who is alone, because when he falls, he has no one to lift him up; and if two sleep together, they shall warm each other; how shall one be warm? And if anyone prevails against one, two shall resist him." And it is called the number of wedlock and sex, for there are two sexes, masculine and feminine; and doves lay two eggs, from the first of which they hatch a male, and from the second a female. And it is called the capable middle, equal in good and evil...

### On the Triad and its scale. Chapter VI.

The number three <note>original: "Ternarius"</note> is the first uncompounded number, a sacred number, a number of perfection, and most powerful: for there are three persons in God, and three theological virtues in religion. Hence it is that this number contributes greatly to the ceremonies of the gods and religion, as it is under its auspices that prayers and libations are repeated three times. Whence Virgil sings:

> God delights in an odd number. <note>Virgil, Eclogues 8.75</note>

And the Pythagoreans used it in sanctifications and purifications; hence in Virgil:

> Three times also he circled his companions with pure water. <note>Virgil, Aeneid 6.229</note>

And it is also most fit for bindings <note>referring to magical ligatures or "binding spells"</note>; hence that passage of Virgil:

> These three threads first, distinct with three colors, 
> I wrap around you, and three times around these altars 
> I lead your image.

And a little after:

> Tie three knots, Amaryllis, in three colors; 
> Tie them, Amaryllis, now, and say, "I tie the chains of Venus."

And we read of Medea,

> And three times she spoke the words that bring placid sleep, 
> Which stop the troubled sea and the stirred-up rivers.

And in Pliny, it was the custom in every medicine to spit three times with a prayer, and by this the effect was aided. For the number three is perfected by a triple increase: length, breadth, and depth, beyond which no progression of dimension is given; hence it is called the first cubic number. Thus it is said that nothing can be added to a three-measured body and a cubic number. Wherefore Aristotle, at the beginning of his discourses *On the Heavens*, calls it a law, as it were, according to which all things are

<margin>The three things in all matters.</margin>
disposed. For both corporal and spiritual things consist of three: beginning, middle, and end. By three (as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus</note> says) the world is perfected: by *Hemarmene* <note>Greek: Destiny/Fate</note>, Necessity, and Order; that is, by the agreement of causes among themselves (which many call Fate), by the execution toward the offspring, and by the due distribution of the offspring. The whole measure of time is concluded in a triad, namely: past, present, and future. All magnitude is contained by three: line, surface, and body. Every body consists of three intervals: length, breadth, and thickness. Harmony contains three symphonies: the octave <note>original: "diapason"</note>, the fifth <note>original: "hemiolion"</note>, and the fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>. There are also three kinds of souls: vegetative, sensitive, and intellectual; and the threefold division of reason, anger, and desire distributes these. And now, even according to the Prophet, the world is disposed by God in three: number, weight, and measure. It is

<margin>The Triad assigned to ideal forms.</margin>
assigned to the ideal forms, just as the number two is assigned to procreating matter, and unity to God the Creator. The Magi also distribute three princes of the world: Oromasis, Mitris, and Araminis—that is, God, Mind, and Spirit. Through the cubic or solid triad, the three groups of nine <note>original: "enneades"</note> of produced things are distributed, namely—

# On the Number Four and its Scale,
## Chapter VII.

<margin>All foundations are square.</margin>
<note>The woodcut initial 'Q' depicts a cherub, symbolizing the divine or innocent origins of numerical truth.</note>The Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the ultimate reality of the universe.</note> call the number four the *Tetractys*, and they prefer it above all the virtues of numbers because it is the foundation and root of all other numbers. For this reason, all foundations—whether in man-made things, in nature, or in divine matters—are square, as we shall show below. It signifies solidity, which is also demonstrated by the square figure. For the number four is the first "flat square" <note>original: "quadratus planus primus"</note>, consisting of two proportions: the first being one to two, and the second being two to four. It is born from a twin progression and proportion—namely, one to one and two to two—beginning from unity and ending in the number four. These proportions differ in that, according to arithmetic, they are unequal to each other, but according to geometry, they are equal. Therefore, the square is ascribed to God the Father; indeed, it even embraces the mystery of the entire Trinity. For by its simple proportion (the first, of one to one), the unity of the Father's substance is signified, from which one Son proceeds, equal to Him. By the other progression, also simple (namely, two to two), the second procession from both is noted as the Holy Spirit, so that the Son is equal to the Father by the first procession, and the Holy Spirit is equal to both by the second. Hence, the most exalted name of God and the divine Trinity is the *Tetragrammaton* <note>The "four-letter" name of God in Hebrew: YHWH.</note>, namely *Yod, He, and Vav, He*. Here, the aspiration of the letter *He* denotes the procession of the Spirit from both; for that same *He* is doubled, ending both syllables and the whole name. It is pronounced *Ioua* <note>An early Latinized attempt at the name Jehovah.</note>, as some wish, from which comes the "Jove" of the Gentiles, whom the ancients used to paint with four ears. Thus, the number four is the fountain and head of all divinity. The Pythagoreans also call it the perpetual fountain of nature.

<margin>The four things found in all matters.</margin>
For there are four degrees in the scale of nature: namely, being, living, feeling, and understanding. There are four motions in nature: ascending, descending, progressing, and circular. There are four cardinal points in the heavens: the rising, the setting, the mid-heaven <note>the zenith</note>, and the bottom of heaven <note>the nadir</note>. There are four elements beneath the heavens: fire, air, water, and earth. According to these, there are four triplicities <note>groups of three zodiac signs</note> in the heavens, and four primary qualities beneath the heavens: cold, heat, dryness, and moisture. From these come the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and melancholy <note>black bile</note>. Likewise, the year is divided into four parts: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Similarly, the air is divided into the East wind, the West wind, the South wind, and the North wind. There are also four rivers of Paradise, and just as many in the underworld. Furthermore, the number four fulfills all knowledge: first, it completes the simple progression of all numbers in four terms—namely, one, two, three, and four—which together constitute the number ten <note>1+2+3+4=10, the "perfect" number</note>. It fulfills every difference of numbers, containing within itself the first even and the first odd. In music, it possesses the *diatessaron* <note>the interval of a fourth</note>, the grace of the voice...

> The fountain of eternal nature and the parent of the soul.

<margin>The name of God is almost everywhere a tetragrammaton <note>a four-letter word</note></margin>
Likewise, there are four rivers of paradise, and four gospels received by as many evangelists throughout the universal church. The Hebrews received the principal name of God written with four letters; similarly the Egyptians, Arabs, Persians, Magi, Mohammedans, Greeks, Tuscans, and Latins write the name of God with only four letters: thus, namely *Theut, Alla, Sire, Orsi, Abgdi, Theos* <note>original: θεὸς</note>, *Esar, Deus*. Hence the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> were accustomed to depict the supreme Jove with four ears. Hence in Orphic theology, it is said that Neptune drives a four-horse chariot. There are also four species of divine frenzy proceeding from individual deities, namely: from the Muses, Dionysus, Apollo, and Venus. Likewise, the prophet Ezekiel saw four animals by the river Chebar, and four Cherubim in four wheels. Likewise in Daniel, four great animals came up from the sea, and the four winds fought. Likewise in the Apocalypse <note>the Book of Revelation</note>, four animals full of eyes before and behind stood around the throne of God, and four angels, to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, stood upon the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds so they would not blow upon the earth, nor upon the sea, nor upon any tree.

-> Concerning the Number Five and its Scale. <-  -> Chapter VIII. <-

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'Q' featuring a putto or cherub seated amidst scrolling foliage and flowers, framed in a square border.</image-desc>

The number five <note>Latin: Quinarius</note> is of no small power; for it consists of the first even and the first odd number, as if from a female and a male: for the odd number is male, but the even is female. Whence mathematicians call the former "father" and the latter "mother." Therefore, the number five is of no small perfection and virtue, which is generated from the mixing of these numbers: and it is, moreover, the most just midpoint of the universal number, namely ten <note>Latin: denarius</note>. For if you take the numbers surrounding five by dividing ten—on this side nine, and on that side one; or here eight, and there two; or seven and three, or six and four—each collection constitutes ten, and five is always its perfect middle and equidistant from them. For this reason, it is called the "number of marriage" by the followers of Pythagoras. It is also called the number of justice, because it cuts the ten in equal balance. There are five senses in man: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. There are five powers in the soul: vegetative, sensitive, concupiscible <note>desiring</note>, irascible <note>spirited/angry</note>, and rational. Five...

### Concerning the number six and its scale. Chapter 9.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial S depicting two figures, likely scholars or biblical figures, in a room with a window or archway in the background.</image-desc>**T**he number six <note>original: "Senarius"</note> is the number of perfection, because it is the most perfect by nature in the entire sequence of numbers from one to ten. It alone is so perfect that the sum of its parts results in itself, neither deficient by any lack nor superfluous by any abundance. For if its parts—namely its half, its third, and its sixth, which are three, two, and one—are gathered together, they perfectly fill the whole body of the six. Other numbers lack this perfection. For this reason, it is asserted by the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the essence of all things.</note> to be entirely suited to births and marriages, and it is called the "seal of the world." For the world was constituted in the number six, neither superfluous with immoderate abundance, nor frustrated and lacking in necessities. This is because on the sixth day the world was perfected and finished by God; for on the sixth day God saw all that He had made, and they were very good. Therefore the heavens and the earth were perfected, and all the host of them. It is also called the number of man, because man was created on the sixth day. It is also called the number of redemption, for on the sixth day Christ suffered for our redemption; hence it also has a great kinship with the Cross. It is also called the number of labor and servitude: hence it was commanded in the Law that work should be done for six days, manna should be gathered for six days, the earth should be sown for six years, and that a Hebrew servant should serve his master for six years. For six days the glory of the Lord rested upon Mount Sinai, covering it with a cloud. There are six wings on the Cherubim, and six circles in the firmament: the Arctic, the Antarctic, the two Tropics, the Equinoctial, and the Ecliptic. There are six wandering planets—Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon—running to and fro across the width of the Zodiac on either side of the ecliptic <note>The author excludes the Sun here because it stays strictly on the ecliptic path, unlike the "wandering" planets.</note>. There are six substantial qualities in the elements, namely: sharpness, thinness, motion, and their opposites: bluntness, density, and rest. There are six differences of position: upwards, downwards, forwards, backwards, to the right, and to the left. There are six natural offices without which nothing can exist, namely: magnitude, color, shape, interval, status, and motion. Even the solid shape of a cube <note>original: "quadrati"</note> has six surfaces. In the harmony of the whole, there are six tones: namely, five tones and two semitones, which together make one tone, which is the sixth.

## Concerning the number seven and its scale. Chapter X.

The number seven <note>original: "Septenarius"</note> is of various and manifold power; for it consists of one and six, or of two and five, or of three and four, and it possesses unity as a link between the twin trinity. Therefore, if we consider its individual members and their connections, we shall undoubtedly admit that it is most full of all majesty, both from the binding together of its parts and from its own fullness separately. The followers of Pythagoras <margin>The naming of the number seven.</margin> call it the vehicle of human life, which it does not borrow so much from its parts as it perfects by the proper right of its totality; for it encompasses both body and soul. For the body consists of the four elements and is affected by four qualities; the number three <note>original: "ternarius"</note> also pertains to the soul because of its triple power, namely the rational, the irascible, and the concupiscible <note>These are the three parts of the soul in Platonic philosophy: reason, spirit/anger, and desire.</note>. <margin>The powers of the number seven in human bodies.</margin> Thus the number seven, because it consists of three and four, joins the soul to the body. The power of this number also pertains to the generation of men, and causes a human being to be conceived, formed, brought forth, nourished, to live, and to consist entirely. For when the genital seed is received in the womb of the woman, if it remains for seven hours without being shed, it is certain that it has taken hold for life. Then, in the first seven days it is curdled and becomes fit to receive the human shape. Next, it produces mature infants who are called "seven-monthlings," that is, those born in the seventh month. After birth, the seventh hour discerns whether the infant is likely to live; for he who has sustained the breath of air beyond this number is understood to be born for life. After seven days, he casts off the remains of the umbilical cord; after twice seven, his sight begins to move toward the light; in the third seven-day period, he now freely turns his eyes and his whole face; after seven months, the teeth appear; after the second seven-month period, he sits without fear of falling; after the third seven-month period, his sound breaks forth into words; after the fourth seven-month period, he stands firmly and walks; after the fifth seven-month period, he begins to shrink from the nurse's milk. After seven years, the first teeth fall out and others are born more fit for solid food, and the integrity of speech is perfected. After the second seven-year period, boys reach puberty and it is the beginning of generation; at the third seven-year period, a man grows in length and shows flowers and downy hair, and his generative power becomes potent and robust. Up to the fourth seven-year period, a man grows in breadth, and the increases of stature are finished. In the fifth, every increase of strength and vigor is completed. The sixth seven-year period preserves the strength of his gathering; in the seventh seven-year period, wisdom is perfected, and it renders the age of men complete. When, however, one arrives at seven decades, where the number seven is led through a complete number <note>i.e., 7 multiplied by 10</note>, then he has the common goal of living, as the Prophet says: "The days of our years are in themselves seventy years" <note>A reference to Psalm 90:10.</note>. And the fourth performs the same functions as the second. It is also assigned to Saturn, who is the seventh of the planets ascending from the lower realms; he signifies rest, and to him the seventh day is ascribed. This indicates the seventh millennium <note>The belief that the world would last 7,000 years, with the final millennium being a time of peace.</note> in which (according to the testimony of <margin>Names of the Septenary.</margin> John) the dragon—the devil, who suggests all evils—having been captured, mortals shall rest, living a tranquil life. Furthermore, the Pythagoreans call the number seven the number of virginity: because it is the first number that is neither generated nor generates <note>In basic numerology (1-10), 7 is not a product of any other numbers multiplied, nor does it produce any other number within the decade when doubled.</note>; for it cannot be divided into two equal parts. Thus, it is not born from any repeated number, nor does it produce any number from itself when doubled that remains within the limits of the number ten, which is established as the first boundary of numbers. For this reason, they made the number seven sacred to Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the virgin goddess of wisdom.</note>. It also possesses the most powerful signs of veneration in religion and is called the number of the oath. Hence, among the Hebrews, "to swear" is said to be "to seven-fold," as if to testify by seven. Thus Abraham, when he made a covenant with Abimelech, set out seven ewe lambs as a witness. It is also called the number of blessedness and rest, whence that saying:

> O thrice and four times blessed, <note>original: "O terque quaterque beati" — a quote from Virgil's Aeneid, where 3+4=7.</note>

Namely, in soul and in body. Also, on the seventh day the Creator rested from his workmanship, for which reason this day is called the Sabbath among Moses' people, that is, the day of rest. Hence, on the seventh day, Christ rested in the tomb. This number also has a great communion with the Cross, as was demonstrated above, and with Christ. For in Christ is all our blessedness, rest, and happiness; and it is, moreover, most fit for purifications. Whence Apuleius says: "And immediately, in my zeal for purification, I gave myself to a sea-bath, and seven times I submerged my head in the waves." And the leper to be cleansed in the Law was sprinkled seven times with the blood of a sparrow; and Elisha the prophet, as it is written in the fourth book of Kings <note>Modern Bibles list this as 2 Kings 5:10.</note>, said to the leper: "Go and wash seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh shall recover its health, and you shall be cleansed." And it follows shortly after: "And he washed himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the prophet, and he was cleansed." It is also the number of penance and remission. Hence a seven-year penance was established for any sin, according to the sentiment of the Wise Man saying: "and sevenfold upon the sinner." Also, in the seventh year, remissions <note>The "Sabbatical Year" where debts were forgiven.</note> were made, and after a square of seven <note>7x7 = 49 years, leading to the Jubilee in the 50th year.</note>, full remission was given, as is read in Leviticus. With seven petitions, Christ completed the prayer of our expiation <note>The Lord's Prayer.</note>; hence it is also called the number of liberty, because in the seventh year the Hebrew slave claimed his freedom. It is also most suited for divine praises. Whence the Prophet says: "Seven times in a day I have spoken praise to you, concerning the judgments of your justice." It is also called the number of vengeance, as the Scripture says: "Vengeance shall be given sevenfold for Cain." And the Psalmist says: "Render to our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom." Hence seven wickednesses are found in Solomon, and seven spirits more wicked are read to be taken up in the Gospel. From all the things mentioned above, it appears that the number seven <note>term: "septenarium" — the septenary or the number seven</note> is deservedly called the most full of all efficacy among other numbers. Furthermore, the septenary has a great conformity with the number twelve: for just as three and four constitute seven, so three times four return twelve, which are the numbers of the celestial planets and signs <note>The zodiac signs</note>, resulting from the same root, and participating through the number three in divinity, and through the number four in the nature of lower things. There is a very great observance of this number in the sacred letters above all others, and its mysteries are great and manifold; many of these we have decided to enumerate here, finding them in the sacred utterances. By these it will easily be established that the septenary signifies a certain fullness of sacred mysteries. 

For we read in Genesis of the seventh day of the Lord's rest; of Enoch, the seventh from Adam, a holy and pious man; and also of another seventh man from Adam, a wicked and twice-married man named Lamech; likewise, in the seventh generation, the sin of Cain was abolished, just as it is written: *Cain shall be punished sevenfold*, and he who kills Cain shall pay seven vengeances. Regarding which, in the same place, the Master of History <note>Peter Comestor, a famous medieval theologian</note> gathers that there were seven sins of Cain. Likewise, seven and seven of all clean animals were introduced into the Ark of Noah, and similarly of the birds; then after seven days the Lord rained upon the earth, and on the seventh day all the fountains of the abyss were broken, and the waters inundated the earth. Likewise, Abraham gave seven ewes to Abimelech; and Jacob served seven years for Leah, and another seven for Rachel; and for seven days the people of Israel mourned the death of Jacob. Furthermore, we read there of seven cows, and seven ears of grain, seven years of fertility and seven of sterility. 

In Exodus, truly, on the seventh day the Sabbath of Sabbaths is commanded, a holy rest to the Lord, because on the seventh day the Lord rested from his work. Likewise, on the seventh day Moses ceased to pray. On the seventh day shall be the solemnity of the Lord; in the seventh year the servant shall go out free; for seven days the ox and the sheep shall be with its mother; in the seventh year the land sown for six years shall be allowed to rest; the seventh day shall be a holy Sabbath and rest; because the seventh day is of the Sabbath, it shall be called holy. In Leviticus also, the seventh day shall be more celebrated and holy, and the first day of the seventh month shall be a memorial Sabbath. # ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

### On the Number Eight and its Scale. Chapter XI.

<margin>
Names for the number eight.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'O' depicting a human face within a circular floral/geometric border.</image-desc>

The followers of Pythagoras call the number eight the number of justice and fullness. Firstly, because it is the first of all numbers to be divided into "even-even" parts <note>original: "pariter pares" — a mathematical term for numbers that can be repeatedly divided by two down to unity</note>, namely into four; and this division itself is woven together by the same ratio into twice two, namely by twice two, twice. Because of this equality in its division, it acquired the name of justice. Secondly, it received the name of fullness because of its connection to physical solidity; for it is the first number to create a solid body <note>In geometry, 8 is the first cube (2x2x2), representing three-dimensional reality</note>. Hence comes the custom of Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek musician and prophet</note> swearing by eight deities whenever he wished to call upon divine justice. 

<margin>
The eight deities by which Orpheus was accustomed to swear.
</margin>

Their names are these: Fire, Water, Earth, Heaven, Moon, Sun, Phanes <note>A primeval deity of procreation and the generation of new life</note>, and Night. There are also exactly eight visible spheres of the heavens. The property of physical nature is signified to us through this number, which Orpheus embraced in his eight maritime hymns. This number is also called the number of the covenant and of circumcision, which was commanded to be performed by the Jews on the eighth day. There were also eight ornaments of the priest under the Old Law: namely the linen breeches, the tunic, the sash, the miter, the long robe, the ephod <note>original: "superhumerale" — a vestment worn over the shoulders</note>, the breastplate, and the golden plate. This number also pertains to eternity and the consummation of the world, because it follows the number seven, which is the symbol of time. For this reason, it is also the number of blessedness, for Christ teaches exactly that many degrees of beatitude in the Gospel of Matthew. It is also called the number of salvation and preservation, for that many souls were made safe in Noah’s ark from the flood of waters. Furthermore, there were eight sons of Jesse, of whom David was the eighth. Likewise, Zechariah, the father of John, received back his speech on the eighth day. They say this number is sacred to Dionysus <note>The Greek god of wine and ecstasy</note>, who was brought into the light in the eighth month. In everlasting testimony of this, the island of Naxos, which was dedicated to him, obtained this privilege: that only Naxian women may give birth healthily in the eighth month and produce living offspring, whereas almost everywhere else in the world, those born at such a time perish, and even the mothers are placed in manifest danger.

# On the Number Nine and its Scale. Chapter XII.

The number nine is sacred to the Muses, and serves as an aid to the order of the celestial spheres and divine spirits. Hence, there are nine moving spheres, and according to them, there are nine Muses: namely, Calliope, Urania, Polyhymnia, Terpsichore, Clio, Melpomene, Erato, Euterpe, and Thalia. Indeed, these nine Muses are assigned to the nine spheres in such a way that the first represents the highest sphere, which they call the *Primum Mobile* <note>The "First Mover," the outermost moving sphere in the Ptolemaic geocentric model</note>, and so descending step by step according to the written order, down to the last, which represents the sphere of the Moon. Thus, Calliope is assigned to the *Primum Mobile*; Urania to the starry sky <note>The Firmament or sphere of fixed stars</note>; Polyhymnia to Saturn; Terpsichore to Jupiter; Clio to Mars; Melpomene to the Sun; Erato to Venus; Euterpe to Mercury; and Thalia to the Moon. There are also nine orders of blessed angels: namely, Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, Dominions, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Archangels, and Angels. Ezekiel represents these through nine stones, which are sapphire, emerald, carbuncle, beryl, onyx, chrysolite, jasper, topaz, and sardius. This number also holds a great and hidden mystery <note>original: "sacramentum"</note> of the cross: for at the ninth hour our Lord Jesus Christ gave up his spirit. Furthermore, the ancients used to bury the dead for nine days, and they say that for just as many years Minos received the laws from Jupiter in a cave. For this reason, this number was especially observed by Homer, such as when laws were to be established, or oracles given, or when a disaster was about to rage. Astrologers also observe "enneatic" years—that is, intervals of nine—in the ages of men, no differently than the "septenary" years <note>intervals of seven</note> which they call "climacterics," as they are marked by notable changes. Sometimes, however, it carries a mark of imperfection and incompleteness, because it does not reach the perfection of the number ten, but being less by one unit, it falls short of it; this is how Augustine interprets the Gospel passage concerning the ten lepers. Nor is the length of nine cubits of Og, the King of Bashan—who is a type <note>A symbolic foreshadowing or representation</note> of the devil—without its own mystery.

CXXVI.
-> ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY <-

### On the Decade and its Scale. Chapter XIII.

The Ten <note>Latin: *Denarius*</note>. This is called the number of all things, or the universal number, and the complete number, denoting the full course of life: for beyond it one does not count except by repetition. It either enfolds all numbers within itself or unfolds them through itself and its own parts by multiplication. For this reason, it is held to possess manifold religious significance and power, and is suited for the purification of souls.
<margin>Ten-day ceremonies were once spoken of.</margin>
Hence the ancients spoke of "ten-day ceremonies," in which those who were to be purified or were about to enter sacred rites had to abstain from certain things for ten continuous days. Thus, among the Egyptians, it was the custom for one who wished to be initiated into the mysteries of Isis to be ordered a ten-day fast, which Apuleius testifies concerning himself, saying: *He clearly commanded in the presence of all witnesses that for those ten continuous days I should restrain the pleasures of food, eat no animal flesh, and drink no wine.* <note>original: "Illud plane cunctis arbitris præcepit, decem illis continuos diebus cibariam uoluptatem coërcerem, & neq; ullū animal essem, & inuinius essem."</note> There are ten parts of a blood-bearing human: the menses, the sperm, the formative spirit, the mass, the humors, the organic body, the vegetative power, the sensitive power, reason, and mind. There are also ten simple integral parts constituting a human: bone, cartilage, nerve, string <note>likely referring to tendons</note>, ligament, artery, vein, membrane, flesh, and skin. There are also ten limbs <note>or internal organs</note> of which the inner man consists: the spirit, the brain, the lungs, the heart, the liver, the gall, the spleen, the kidneys, the genitals, and the womb. Furthermore, there were ten curtains in the Temple, ten strings on the psaltery, and ten musical instruments with which the psalms were sung, the names of which are: *Neza*, in which odes were sung; *Nablum*, the same as an organ; *Mizmor*, in which psalms; *Sir*, in which songs; *Tephila*, in which prayers; *Beracha*, in which blessings; *Halel*, in which praises; *Hodaia*, in which thanksgivings; *Afre*, in which the happiness of someone; *Halleluiah*, in which only the praises of God and contemplations. There are also ten singers of the psalms, namely: Adam, Abraham, Melchizedek, Moses, Asaph, David, Solomon, and the three sons of Korah. There are also ten commandments of the law. And on the tenth day after the ascension of Christ, the Holy Spirit descended. This, finally, is the number in which Jacob, having wrestled with an angel all night, conquered in the struggle; and at the rising of the morning star he was blessed, and his name was called Israel. In this number Joshua conquered thirty-one kings; and David conquered Goliath and the Philistines; and Daniel escaped the dangers of the lions. This number, like the unit <note>the number one</note>, is also circular, because when gathered together it returns to the unity from which it took its beginning; and it is itself the end and fulfillment of all numbers, and the beginning of the decades. Just as the ten flows back into the unity from which it proceeded, so everything that flows returns to that from which it has the beginning of its flow. Thus water runs to the sea, from which it drew its origin; the body returns to the earth, from which it was taken; time returns into eternity, from which it flowed; the mind, made by God, returns to the same; finally, every creature flows into the nothingness from which it was created, and is sustained only by the divine Word, in which all things were established—all things which, with the ten and through the ten, effect a circle, as Proclus says, beginning from God and ending in Him. God also himself, the first Mon— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "Monad."</note>
