These weights of the humors <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> and temperaments are assigned to a healthy and well-composed person: namely, eight parts of blood, four of phlegm, two of yellow bile, and one of black bile. Thus, in each case, there is a double proportion <note>a 2:1 ratio</note> through the series. However, the ratio of the first to the third, and the second to the fourth, is quadruple <note>4:1</note>; and the first to the last is octuple <note>8:1</note>. Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist</note> handed down that the human heart in the first year has a weight of two drachms; in the second, four; and from there, following an equal course until the fiftieth year, it reaches a weight of one hundred drachms. From that point, the decreases are calculated back toward the equilibrium, which, once the circuit is finished, return to the same starting goal. He believed the lifespan does not exceed the decay of that organ; by this reasoning, he circumscribed the life of man to one hundred years. Pliny <note>The Roman naturalist</note> testifies that this was also the doctrine of the Egyptians. Furthermore, the very movements of human limbs correspond to the celestial movements. Every human has within himself the motion of his own heart which, responding to the motion of the sun, is diffused through the arteries into the whole body; it indicates to us years, months, days, hours, and moments by a most certain rule. Moreover, it has been discovered by anatomists that there is a certain nerve near the neck <note>original: "micham," likely referring to the nucha or spinal cord</note> which, when pulled, moves all the limbs of a man in such a way that each is moved by its own proper motions; Aristotle thinks that the members of the world are moved by God in a similar fashion. And there are two veins in the neck which, where they are divided in the throat, go up to the head; if these are gripped firmly from the outside, men soon collapse with their senses taken away, until they are released. Therefore, the eternal Architect of the world himself, being about to send the soul into the body as if into a dwelling, first measures out a lodging worthy of it, and grants a most noble soul even to a beautiful body. Then the soul itself, conscious of its own divinity, fashions and adorns the body for itself according to its own character. Hence the people of the Ethiopians, who were ruled by the wisdom of the Gymnosophists <note>Ancient Indian or African "naked philosophers" known for asceticism</note>—as Aristotle testifies—did not create kings from those who were the strongest or wealthiest, but only those who were the most beautiful and outstanding in form. Indeed, they judged that they could perceive the great dignity of souls through the image of the body. Considering this, many philosophers, both ancient and modern, who have searched out the secrets of hidden causes in the majesty of nature itself, have dared to assert that no defect of the body occurs, and no disproportion exists in the body, which does not also follow a defect and intemperance of the soul; for it is certain that the one grows, coalesces, and works in turn by the function of the other.

### On the composition and harmony of the human soul. Chapter XXVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting two figures, possibly scholars or physicians, in an interior setting.</image-desc>

Just as the harmony of the body consists of the due measure and proportion of the limbs, so the harmony of the soul consists of the due temperament and proportion of its virtues and operations, which are the concupiscible <note>desiring</note>, the irascible <note>spirited/angry</note>, and the rational. These are proportioned thus: for reason has the proportion of an octave <note>original: "diapason"</note> to desire, but a fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note> to anger; and the spirited part has the proportion of a fifth <note>original: "diapente"</note> to the desiring part. Therefore, when a most proportioned soul is joined with a most proportioned body, it is certain that such a person receives a most happy lot in the distribution of gifts, just as the soul agrees with the body in its natural disposition.

agree, which agreement is indeed most hidden, yet has been outlined in other ways by the wise. But hastening toward the harmony of the soul, we must seek it from those intermediaries through which it passes to us—that is, from the bodies and spheres of heaven. Knowing, therefore, which powers of the soul correspond to which of the planets from what has been said above, we shall easily recognize their harmonies among themselves. For the Moon rules the powers of growing and shrinking; the power of imagination <note>original: "phantastica uis"</note> and talent depends on Mercury; the power of desire on Venus; the vital power on the Sun; the impulsive power, which is also called the irascible <note>The part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and spiritedness.</note>, on Mars; the natural power on Jupiter; and all receptive power on Saturn. The will itself is like the "prime mover" <note>The outermost sphere in ancient astronomy that moves all others.</note> and the leader of all those powers according to its pleasure; when joined with the higher intellect, it is always tending toward the good. This intellect shows the paths to the will, just as light does for the eye; yet it does not move the will, for the will remains the mistress of her own operation, which is why it is called free will. And although it always tends toward the good as its proper object, sometimes, blinded by error and driven by animal force, it chooses evil, believing it to be good. Therefore, free will is defined 
<margin>Free will.</margin>
as the faculty of intellect and will by which good is chosen when grace is present, and evil when grace departs. Thus grace itself, which theologians also call charity or infused love, is in the will like the first mover, and when it is absent, the entire harmony falls into dissonance. Furthermore, the soul corresponds to the earth through the senses; to water through imagination; to air through reason; and to heaven through the intellect. The soul enters into their harmony according to how these elements are tempered in this mortal body. Therefore, the ancient sages, recognizing the various harmonic dispositions of bodies and souls according to the different temperaments <note>original: "complexionum," referring to the four humors.</note> of men, used music and songs not in vain, both to preserve the health of the body and restore it when lost, and also to lead minds toward soul-saving morals, until they might attune the human being to celestial harmony and render him entirely heavenly. Moreover, nothing is more effective for repelling evil demons than musical harmony; for having fallen from that celestial harmony, they cannot endure any true concord, as it is hostile to them, and they flee far away—just as David repressed the wicked spirit raging in Saul with his lyre. For this reason, songs and musical sounds were introduced into sacred offices by the ancient prophets and fathers who understood these harmonic mysteries.

I also believe this should by no means be omitted: that you diligently observe Mercury <margin>Mercury must be diligently observed.</margin> in every work. For he is the messenger between both the lower and upper gods; when he joins with the good, he increases their goodness; when with the evil, he flows into their malice. Now, we call a sign or planet unfortunate by the aspect of Saturn or Mars, especially the opposition or the square <note>90 degrees</note>; for these aspects are of enmity. But union, the trine, and the sextile aspect are of friendship. Among these, the conjunction <note>union</note> is the strongest; however, if a planet is already looking through a trine and is also received <note>A technical term where one planet is in a sign ruled by the other.</note>, it is esteemed as if already joined. Indeed, all planets fear conjunction with the Sun, but they rejoice in its aspect, specifically the trine and sextile.

### When the planets are of more powerful influence. Chapter 30.

<margin>When the Moon is powerful.</margin> <image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial P featuring a figure, likely an astronomer or a symbolic representation of a planet, standing in a landscape with hills and a building under a sky with a sun or star.</image-desc> We shall have the planets powerful when they are in their house, or exaltation, or triplicity, or term, or face <note>These are the five "essential dignities" or layers of planetary strength in traditional astrology.</note>, direct <note>moving forward rather than retrograde</note> and outside of combustion <note>original: "combustio"; being too close to the Sun, which "burns up" a planet's power</note>, in their apogee and ruling in the figure of the heaven—namely, when they are in the angles, especially the eastern or the tenth, or in the places immediately following them, or in their joys. Care must be taken, however, that they are not in the borders or under the dominion of Saturn or Mars, nor in dark, pitted, or empty degrees. You shall observe that the angles of the Ascendant, the tenth, and the seventh are fortunate, as well as the lord of the Ascendant, the place of the Sun, the place of the Moon, the place of the Part of Fortune, and its lord, and the lord of the preceding conjunction or prevention <note>The previous New or Full Moon</note>. Let the malevolent planets fall unfortunate, unless by chance they stand as the significators of your work, or can be useful to you in any way; or if they have obtained leadership in your revolution <note>yearly solar return</note> or birth chart, for then they are least to be suppressed. We shall have the Moon powerful if she is in her own house, or exaltation, or triplicity, or face, and in a degree suitable for the desired work, and if she occupies a mansion <note>The 28 Lunar Mansions are segments of the zodiac the Moon passes through daily.</note> out of those twenty-eight that is competent for her and the work. Let her not be in the "combust way" <note>original: "via combusta"; a specific section of the zodiac, usually late Libra to early Scorpio, considered unlucky</note>, nor slow in her course; let her not be in the ecliptic, nor burned by the Sun (unless by chance she is in unity with the Sun <note>Cazimi, or in the heart of the Sun</note>), nor should she descend in southern latitude when she emerges from combustion, nor be opposite the Sun, nor diminished in light, nor hindered by Mars or Saturn. I do not wish to prolong the discourse further here, since these and many other necessary things are sufficiently handed down in the volumes of the Astrologers.

Similarly, in all things, you must hold the same reasoning regarding the fixed stars <note>The "fixed stars" refer to the stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to one another, unlike the "wandering stars" or planets.</note>. Know this: all fixed stars possess the significance and nature of the seven planets. Some are of the nature of a single planet, while others are of two. Hence, whenever a planet is joined with any of the fixed stars of its own nature, the significance of that star is made more powerful, and the nature of the planet is increased. But if it should be a star of two natures, whichever planet is stronger with it, that planet's nature will prevail in significance. For example, if a star is of the nature of Mars and Venus: if Mars is with it, the nature of Mars will prevail; but if Venus is with it, the nature of Venus will overcome. Furthermore, the natures of the fixed stars are discerned from their colors, according to how they match certain planets and are ascribed to them.

The colors of the planets are as follows: **Saturn** is livid or leaden, and with this, glowing white; **Jupiter** is lemon-yellow bordering on pale, and with this, bright; **Mars** is red and fiery; the **Sun** is saffron-colored, and when it rises, burning, and afterwards radiating; **Venus** is white, but glowing as the morning star and reflecting as the evening star; **Mercury** is radiating; the **Moon** is blond <note>original: "blondus," likely referring to a pale golden or silvery-yellow hue</note>. You should also know that the larger and brighter the fixed stars are and appear, the greater and stronger is their significance, such as those stars which are called by Astrologers those of the first and second magnitude.

From these, I shall tell you some of the more powerful ones for this art:
*   **The Navel of Andromeda** <note>original: "Vmbilicus Andromedæ," now known as the star Mirach</note>, in the twenty-second degree of Aries, of the nature of Venus and Mercury; others say it is of Jupiter and Saturn.
*   **The Head of Algol** <note>original: "Caput Algol," the "Demon Star" in Perseus</note>, in the eighteenth degree of Taurus, of the nature of Saturn and Jupiter.
*   **The Pleiades** <note>The Seven Sisters star cluster</note> in the twenty-second degree of the same [Taurus], a constellation lunar by nature and Martian in temperament.
*   Likewise, in the third degree of Gemini, **Aldebaran**, of the nature of Mars and the temperament of Venus; but Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many astrological texts were attributed</note> places this in the twenty-fifth of Aries.
*   In the thirteenth degree of the same Gemini, **The Goat** <note>original: "Hircus," the star Capella</note>, of the nature of Jupiter and Saturn.
*   In the seventh degree of Cancer, the **Greater Dog** <note>original: "Canis maior," the star Sirius</note>, of Venus; in the seventeenth of the same, the **Lesser Dog** <note>original: "Canis minor," the star Procyon</note>, Mercurial by nature and Martian in temperament.
*   In the twenty-first degree of Leo is the royal star called the **Heart of the Lion** <note>original: "Cor leonis," the star Regulus</note>, of the nature of Jupiter and Mars.
*   In the nineteenth degree of Virgo, the **Tail of the Greater Bear** <note>original: "Cauda ursæ maioris," likely referring to Alkaid</note>, of Venus and the Moon.
*   In the seventh degree of Libra, the **Right Wing of the Raven**, and in the thirteenth of the same, the **Left Wing**, both of the nature of Saturn and Mars.
*   In the sixteenth degree of the same [Libra], **Spica**, of Venus and Mercury.
*   In the seventeenth degree of the same, **Alcameth** <note>The star Arcturus</note>, of the nature of Mars and Jupiter; but this one [acts well] when it regards a luminary <note>The Sun or Moon</note> favorably, but otherwise when contrary.
*   In the fourth degree of Scorpio, **Elepheia** <note>The star Alphecca in the Northern Crown</note>, of the nature of Venus and Mars.
*   In the third degree of Sagittarius, the **Heart of the Scorpion** <note>original: "Cor scorpionis," the star Antares</note>, of the nature of Mars and Jupiter.
*   In the 7th degree of Capricorn, the **Falling Vulture** <note>original: "Vultur cadens," the star Vega</note>, a temperate Mercurial and Venusian nature.
*   In the 16th degree of Aquarius, the **Tail of Capricorn** <note>The star Deneb Algedi</note>, of the nature of Saturn and Mercury.
*   In the third of Pisces, the **Shoulder of the Horse** <note>original: "Humerus equi," the star Markab in Pegasus</note>, of the nature of Jupiter and Mars.

And it shall be a general rule for you to hope for specific gifts from each of the stars when it is dominant; but to be hindered when it is unfortunate or positioned in an opposite way, as was shown above. For the celestial bodies, insofar as they themselves [act] happily or unhappily...

affected by fortune, to that extent both we and our works, and those things which we use, are affected either fortunately or calamitously. And although many effects proceed from the fixed stars, they are nevertheless attributed to the planets, both because they are nearer to us and more distinct and known, and because the planets themselves execute whatever the higher stars influence.

### Concerning the Sun and Moon, and their magical reasons. Chapter XXXII.

<margin>The excellence of the Sun.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' featuring a seated cherub-like figure holding an object within the letterform.</image-desc>The Sun and Moon have obtained the administration of the heavens and of all bodies that are under heaven: the Sun is the lord of all elemental virtues <note>virtues here refers to inherent powers or properties</note>, and the Moon, by the virtue of the Sun, is the mistress of generation, increase, and decrease. Hence **Albumasar** <note>An influential 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> says that life is infused into all things through the Sun and Moon, whom **Orpheus** therefore calls the life-giving eyes of heaven. The Sun gives light to all from itself, and bestows it abundantly upon all, not only in the heaven and air, but also in the earth and the innermost depths of the abyss; whatever good we have, as **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says, we have from the Sun, either from it alone, or from it through other things. **Heraclitus** calls the Sun the fountain of celestial light: and many of the **Platonists** placed the soul of the world principally in the Sun, as that which, filling the whole globe of the Sun, pours out its rays everywhere like a spirit through all things, distributing life, sense, and motion to the universe itself. Hence the ancient natural philosophers called the Sun the very heart of heaven: and the **Chaldeans** placed it in the middle of the planets. The **Egyptians** also placed it in the middle of the world, namely between the two "fives" of the world; for they place five planets above the Sun, and below the Sun the Moon and the four elements. The Sun itself among the other stars is the image and statue of the supreme prince of both worlds, the terrestrial and the celestial, the true light, and the most exact likeness of God himself, whose essence represents the Father; its splendor, the Son; and its heat, the Holy Spirit; so much so, that the **Academics** <note>Followers of Plato's Academy</note> have nothing through which they can more expressly show the divine essence. Such a great harmony corresponds to God, that **Plato** calls it the conspicuous son of God: and **Iamblichus** calls it the image of divine intelligence: and our **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note> calls it the clear statue of God. It sits like a king in the center of the other planets, excelling all in light, magnitude, and beauty, illuminating all, and distributing virtue to them for disposing all lower things, and regulating and disposing their steps, so much so, that from there their motions are said to be diurnal or nocturnal, southern or northern, eastern or western, direct or retrograde: and just as it puts to flight the darkness of the night by its light, so also it puts to flight whatever powers of darkness, of which it is read in **Job**: *As soon as the dawn appears, they think of the shadow of death*; and the **Psalmist**, speaking of the lion's cubs seeking permission from God to devour, adds: *The Sun has risen, and they are gathered together, and shall be placed in their dens*; which being put to flight, it follows: *Man shall go forth to his work*. Therefore, since the Sun holds the middle region of the world, and just as the heart itself is to the whole body in living creatures, so the Sun presides over the heaven and the world, having empire over the entire world and those things which are in it, being the author of the seasons, from whom come the day and the year, cold and heat, and the other qualities of the seasons: and, as **Ptolemy** says, when it has come into the place of any star...

it stirs up that power which it holds in the air: so that, with Mars it disposes heat, with Saturn cold, and it disposes the very spirit and mind of man. Hence it is said by Homer, and confirmed by Aristotle, that such motions exist in the mind as the Sun, the prince and moderator of the planets, brings forth each day. The Moon, however, being closest to the earth, is the receptacle of all celestial influences. By the swiftness of her course, she is joined each month to the Sun and the other planets and stars; and having become, as it were, the wife of all the stars, and the most fertile of them, she receives the rays and influences of the Sun and the other planets and stars like an embryo. Then, as if in labor, she brings them forth into the lower world which is near to her. For all stars flow into her as the final recipient, who then communicates the influences of all the superiors to the inferiors and pours them back onto the earth. She disposes these lower things more clearly than the others, and her motion is more sensible <note>meaning "perceptible to the senses"</note> because of the familiarity and proximity she has with us. As a medium between both the higher and lower things, she communicates with all of them. Therefore, her motion is to be observed above all others, as if she were the parent of all conceptions, which she unfolds in various ways to these lower things according to her varied temperament, motion, position, and her diverse aspects toward the planets and other stars. And although she receives powers from all the stars, she is filled with life-giving virtue most especially by the Sun; whenever she is joined to him, she borrows her temperament according to his gaze. For in the first quarter, as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> teach, she is hot and moist; in the second, hot and dry; in the third, cold and dry; and in the fourth, cold and humid. And although she is the lowest of the stars, she nevertheless unfolds all the conceptions of the superiors. For from her begins the series of things in the heavens, which Plato calls the "Golden Chain," by which each thing or cause, connected to another, depends on a superior, until one reaches the supreme cause of all, from whom all things hang. Hence it is that without the Moon acting as an intermediary, we would be entirely unable to attract the power of the superiors. Wherefore Thabit <note>original: "Thebit," referring to the 9th-century astronomer Thabit ibn Qurra</note> commands that to capture the virtue of any star, one must take the stone and herb of that star when the Moon either fortunately enters or fortunately gazes upon <note>an astrological "aspect"</note> that same star.

### On observing the true motion of the celestial bodies in the eighth sphere, and on the method of planetary hours. Chapter XXXIV.

Whoever intends to work toward a celestial opportunity must observe either both or one of two things: namely, the motions of the stars or the times. By motions, I mean when they are in their <term>dignities</term> <note>positions where a planet's influence is strengthened</note> or their debilities, whether essential or accidental. By times, I mean the days and hours distributed under their lordships: concerning all these things, enough is taught in the books of the astrologers. But two things must be especially weighed and observed by us in this place: first, that we observe the motion of the stars, their ascensions, and the <term>cardinal points</term> <note>the four most powerful points in an astrological chart: the East, West, North, and South</note>, as they truly exist in the <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>the sphere of the fixed stars, as opposed to the moving planets</note>; due to negligence of this in the crafting of celestial images, many happen to err and are defrauded of the desired effect. Second, one must observe the times in calculating the planetary hours. For almost all astrologers divide the entire interval of time from sunrise to sunset into twelve equal parts, and they call those the twelve hours of the day. Then, the time that follows from sunset to sunrise, divided by a similar method into twelve equal portions, they call the twelve hours of the night; they then distribute those individual hours to the individual planets according to the order of their succession, always giving the first hour of the day to the lord of that day, and then to each in order until the end of the twenty-four hours. And in this distribution the <term>Magi</term> <note>wise men or practitioners of high magic</note> agree with them, but in the partitioning of the hours some disagree, saying that the interval between sunrise and sunset should not be divided into equal parts, and that those hours are called "unequal" not because the daytime hours are unequal to the nighttime ones, but because the daytime and nighttime hours are each unequal among themselves. Therefore, the partitioning of the unequal or planetary hours has another method of measurement observed by the Magi, which is as follows. Just as in <term>artificial hours</term> <note>standard 60-minute hours</note> which are always equal to one another, the ascensions of fifteen degrees on the equinoctial circle constitute one artificial hour, so also in planetary hours the ascensions of fifteen degrees on the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>the sun's apparent path</note> constitute one planetary or unequal hour, the measure of which must be sought and found from the tables of oblique ascensions for each specific region.

### How artificial things, such as images and seals and the like, obtain some virtue from the celestial bodies. Chapter XXXV.

So great is the magnitude, virtue, and power of the celestial bodies, that not only natural things, but even artificial ones, when they are properly exposed to the higher powers, suddenly experience an influence from a most potent agent and a wonderful life. This often bestows a marvelous celestial virtue upon them, which Saint Thomas Aquinas <note>original: "Diuus Thomas Aquinas"</note>, the holy doctor, confirms in his book *On Fate* <note>De Fato; a work traditionally attributed to Aquinas in the Renaissance, discussing providence and necessity</note>: where he says that even garments, buildings, and any works of art receive a certain quality from the stars. Thus, magicians confirm that not only through the mixing and application of natural things, but also through images, seals, rings, mirrors, and any other instruments—provided they are crafted opportunely under a specific constellation—a certain celestial illumination is captured, and something wonderful can be perceived. For the rays of the celestial bodies are animated, living, and sensory, carrying with them marvelous gifts and a most vehement power; even in a fleeting moment and by a sudden touch, they imprint wonderful forces into images, even in material that is less than suitable. 

However, they bestow more efficacious virtues upon images if they are crafted not from just any material, but from a specific one; namely, one whose natural virtue agrees with the specific purpose of the work, and where the shape of the image is similar to the celestial shape. For such an image—both because of a material naturally congruent to the work and the celestial influx, and because of a shape similar to the celestial shape—is most ready to receive the actions and powers of the celestial bodies and figures. It suddenly conceives the celestial gift within itself, then acts steadily upon another thing, and other matters incline themselves toward it through obedience. Whence Ptolemy says in the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 aphorisms attributed to the astronomer Claudius Ptolemy</note> that inferior things obey the celestial ones—not only the stars themselves, but even their images. Just as earthly scorpions obey the celestial Scorpio, so too do they obey the image of that scorpion which has been fashioned opportunely under its ascent and dominion.

### Concerning the images of the Zodiac, which, when engraved, conceive virtues from their stars. Chapter 36.

Now, the celestial images, in whose likeness images of this kind are fashioned, are very numerous in the heavens: some are visible and conspicuous, others at least imaginable, having been perceived and designated by the Egyptians, Indians, and Chaldeans. Their parts are so arranged that the figures themselves are distinct from one another. By this reasoning, they place twelve universal images in the zodiac circle, according to the number of the signs. Of these, they say that Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius—constituting the fiery and eastern triplicity <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</note>—are beneficial against fevers, paralysis, dropsy, gout, and against all cold and phlegmatic infirmities. They are said to render the wearer pleasing, eloquent, ingenious, and honored, because they are the houses of Mars, the Sun, and Jupiter. 

They also used to make the image of Leo against melancholy phantasms <note>hallucinations or intrusive thoughts associated with "black bile"</note>, dropsy, plague, and fevers, and to expel diseases, during the hour of the Sun when the first degree of the face of Leo was ascending (which face and decan <note>A 10-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign</note> belongs to Jupiter). But against the stone <note>kidney stones</note> and diseases of the kidneys, and against the harm of beasts, they made the same image when the Sun in the Heart of the Lion <note>The star Regulus</note> held the middle of the sky. Again, Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius—because they constitute the airy and western triplicity and are the houses of Mercury, Venus, and Saturn—are said to drive away diseases and lead toward friendship and con-

### On the images of the faces and their virtues, and on those images which are outside the Zodiac. Chapter XXXVII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting two figures, one seated and one standing, seemingly engaged in a scientific or astronomical discussion with a globe positioned between them.</image-desc>

There are, furthermore, thirty-six images in the zodiac, according to the number of the faces, about which (as Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> says) Teucer the Babylonian <note>An ancient astrologer, likely 1st century AD.</note>, a most ancient mathematician, once wrote, after whom the Arabs also wrote concerning them. This image bestows wit, gentleness, joys, and beauty. In the first face of Taurus there rises a naked man, a scout or a plowman, and it is useful for sowing, plowing, building, populating, dividing lands, and for the arts of geometry. In the second face there rises a naked man holding a key in his hand; it bestows power, nobility, and dignity over peoples. In the third face there rises a man in whose hand is a serpent and an arrow; it is an image of necessity and utility, and also of misery and servitude. In the first face of Gemini there rises a man in whose hand is a rod, and he himself is as if serving another; it bestows wisdom and the knowledge of numbers and of arts in which there is no utility. In the first face of **Cancer** ascends the form of a young maiden, adorned with beautiful garments, wearing a crown on her head. And its operation is in justice and the help of the wretched and weak against the wicked and powerful. In the second face ascend two raging and angry men, and a man in ornate clothing sitting in a chair. And their signification is toward indignation against the wicked, and toward the quiet and security of life with an abundance of goods. In the third face ascends a vehement man, holding a bow: and before him a naked man, and another man holding bread in one hand and a cup of wine in the other. Outside the zodiac there are also general figures, which Hyginus and Aratus <note>Ancient authors on astronomy and constellations</note> described for us: and many particular ones, according to the number of faces and degrees existing therein, of all of which it would be too long to speak. From these, however, the more principal ones are held to be: Pegasus, who is effective against the diseases of horses, and preserves knights in war; then there is Andromeda <note>original: "Andromacha," likely referring to the constellation Andromeda</note>, who conciliates love between a man and wife, so much so that she is even said to reconcile adulterers. Hercules bestows victory in war. The Dragon <note>Draco</note> with both Bears <note>Ursa Major and Minor</note> render a man crafty, ingenious, brave, and pleasing to gods and men.

->CONCERNING the images of Saturn.<-
->Chapter 38.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'C' depicting a seated figure in a high-backed chair, possibly a scholar or authority figure, gesturing towards a smaller figure standing before them.</image-desc>
FURTHERMORE, regarding the images they used to attribute to the planets, although the ancient sages have written most ample volumes concerning them—so that there is no need to recount them all here—I shall nevertheless recite a few of them. For they made, among the works of Saturn, while he was ascending, an image upon the stone called a magnet <note>lodestone</note>, depicting a man with the face of a stag and the feet of a camel, sitting upon a chair or a dragon: holding a sickle in his right hand and an arrow in his left. They hoped this image would be profitable for longevity of life. For Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer, 787–886 AD</note> proves in the book *Sadar* that Saturn contributes to the length of life, where he also relates that certain regions of India are subject to Saturn, and the men there are very long-lived, not dying until extreme old age. Likewise, they made another image of Saturn for longevity upon a sapphire, in the hour of Saturn, while he was ascending or fortunately positioned; its figure was an old man sitting upon a high chair, having his hands raised above his head and holding in them a fish or a sickle, and below his feet a bunch of grapes, having his head covered with a black or dark cloth, and all his garments being black or dark. They also made the same image against the stone <note>kidney stones</note> and diseases of the kidneys, specifically in the hour of Saturn, while he was ascending in the third face of Aquarius. They also made, among the works of Saturn, an image for the power of growth, with Saturn ascending in Capricorn; its form was an old man leaning on a staff, having a curved sickle in his hand, clothed in black garments. They also made an image cast from bronze, with Saturn ascending in his rising—that is, in the first degree of Aries—or, what is more true, in the first degree of Capricorn; they assert that this image speaks with a human voice. They also made, from the works of Saturn together with Mercury, an image cast from metal in the form of a beautiful man, which they promised would predict the future; and they made it on the day of Mercury in the third hour (which is the hour of Saturn), with the constellation of Gemini ascending (the house of Mercury, which designates prophets), with Saturn and Mercury joined in Aquarius in the ninth region of heaven, which is also called "God" <note>The 9th House in astrology, associated with divinity and travel</note>. Furthermore, let Saturn look upon the ascendant from a trine aspect, and the Moon likewise, and let the Sun look upon the place of conjunction. Venus, occupying some angle, should be powerful and western; Mars from himself...

### On the images of Jupiter. Chapter XXXIX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'E' depicting two small nude figures standing side-by-side.</image-desc>
From the works of Jupiter, they made an image for longevity in the hour of Jupiter, while he was happily ascending in his exaltation <note>Exaltation refers to the specific zodiac sign where a planet's power is most potent; for Jupiter, this is Cancer</note>, in a clear and white stone. Its figure was a crowned man dressed in saffron-colored garments, riding upon an eagle or a dragon, holding an arrow in his right hand as if about to shoot it into the head of that same eagle or dragon. They also made another image of Jupiter at the same opportune time in a white and clear stone, especially in crystal: and it was a naked man, crowned, with hands raised and joined as if praying, sitting in a four-legged chair <note>or throne</note> carried by four winged boys. They confirm that this image increases happiness, riches, and honor, confers benevolence and prosperity, and frees one from enemies. They also made another image of Jupiter for a religious and glorious life, and for the favor of fortune: its figure was a man having the head of a lion or a ram, and the feet of an eagle, dressed in saffron garments, and he was called the son of Jupiter.

### On the images of Mars. Chapter XL.

From the works of Mars, they made an image in the hour of Mars, while he was ascending in the second face <note>A "face" or decan is a 10-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign</note> of Aries, in a Martial stone, especially in a diamond: its form was an armed man riding upon a lion, holding a naked, upright sword in his right hand, and carrying the head of a man in his left. They say an image of this kind renders a man powerful in both good and evil, so that he will be feared by all: and to him who carries it, they attribute the power of fascination <note>The "evil eye" or a binding gaze</note>, so that he terrifies men with his look when he is angry, and binds them in stupor. They made another image of Mars to confer boldness, courage, and fortune in wars and quarrels: its form was an armed and crowned soldier, girded with a sword, carrying a long spear in his right hand: and they made it in the hour of Mars, in the first face of Scorpio while he was ascending.

### On the images of the Sun. Chapter XLI.

From the works of the Sun, they made an image in the hour of the Sun, in the first face of Leo with the Sun ascending: its form was a crowned king sitting in a chair, having a crow in his lap, and a globe under his feet, dressed in a saffron garment. They say this image renders a man invincible and honored, brings undertakings to a conclusion, and drives away vain dreams; it is also effective against fevers and the plague. They made the same in a balas stone <note>a type of rose-red spinel</note> or a ruby, in the hour of the Sun, when he happily ascends in his exaltation <note>The Sun's exaltation is in Aries</note>. They made another image of the Sun in a diamond stone, in the hour of the Sun, while he was ascending in his exaltation: its figure was a crowned woman with the gesture of one dancing and laughing, standing in a chariot drawn by four horses, having in her right hand a mirror or a shield, and in her left a staff leaning upon her breast,

### Concerning the images of Venus. Chapter 42.

**E**xerting the works of Venus, they used to make an image that was suitable for grace and benevolence, during the hour of Venus, with Venus herself ascending in Pisces: the form of which was the image of a woman having the head of a bird and the feet of an eagle, holding an arrow in her hand. They made another image of Venus for the love of women in a lapis lazuli stone during the hour of Venus, with Venus herself ascending in Taurus: the figure of which was a naked girl with flowing hair, having a mirror in her hand and a chain fastened around her neck, and next to her a beautiful youth holding her by the chain with his left hand, while with his right hand he adjusts her hair; let them both be looking at each other in a friendly manner, and around them let there be a small winged boy <note>a Cupid or Eros figure</note> holding a sword or an arrow. They made another image of Venus in the first face of Taurus, or Libra, or Pisces, with Venus ascending, the figure of which was a girl with flowing hair, dressed in long white garments, holding a laurel, or an apple, or flowers in her right hand, and a comb in her left. It is said to make a man peaceful, pleasant, robust, and cheerful, and to bestow beauty.

### Concerning the images of Mercury. Chapter 43.

From the works of Mercury, they used to make an image during the hour of Mercury, with Mercury itself ascending in Gemini, the form of which was a beautiful youth, bearded, having in his left hand a caduceus—namely, a wand in which a serpent is entwined—carrying an arrow in his right hand, and having winged feet. They say this image bestows knowledge, eloquence, and skill in trade and profit; furthermore, it reconciles peace and concord, and cures fevers. They made another image of Mercury, with Mercury itself ascending in Virgo, for benevolence, genius, and memory, the form of which was a man sitting upon a chair, or riding a peacock, having eagle-like feet, and a crest on his head, and holding a cock or fire in his left hand.

### Concerning the images of the Moon. Chapter 44.

From the works of the Moon, they used to make an image for travelers against weariness, during the hour of the Moon, with the Moon herself ascending in her exaltation <note>the sign of Taurus</note>, the figure of which was a man leaning upon a staff, having a bird on his head and a flowering tree before him. They made another image of the Moon for the increase of things growing from the earth, and against poisons and the infirmities of children, during the hour of the Moon, with the Moon herself ascending in the first face of Cancer: the figure of which was a horned woman riding upon a bull, or a seven-headed dragon, or a crab, and let her have an arrow in her right hand and a mirror in her left, dressed in white or green garments: and having on her head two serpents entwined around her horns, and having one serpent entwined around each arm, and one similarly around each foot. And let these things said concerning the figures of the planets suffice.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

### On the images of the Head and Tail of the Dragon of the Moon. Chapter XLV.

They also used to make an image of the Head and Tail of the Dragon of the Moon <note>The "Dragon" refers to the lunar nodes: the points where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic. The Head (North Node) was considered lucky, the Tail (South Node) unlucky.</note>, specifically the likeness of a serpent between the aerial and fiery circles, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the fashion of the Greek letter *theta* (θ). They made this when Jupiter held the Midheaven <note>The highest point in the sky at the time of the ritual.</note> with the Head. They affirm that this image contributes greatly to the success of petitions, and they intended to signify a good and happy spirit <note>original: "bonum ac felicem dęmonem"</note> through that image. They wished to represent him through the image of a serpent: for the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrate this as a divine animal above all others, and honor its divine nature because a sharper spirit and more abundant fire exists in it than in other animals. This is shown both by its swift movement without any feet or hands or other instruments, and because it repeatedly renews its age with its cast-off skin and becomes young again.

But they made the image of the Tail in a similar way when the Moon was eclipsed in the Tail, or was badly affected by Saturn or Mars. They made it to induce anxiety, infirmity, and misfortune, and they called it an evil spirit <note>original: "malum genium"</note>. A certain Hebrew had enclosed such an image in a golden double-belt which Blanche, daughter of the Duke of Bourbon, gave as a gift to her husband Peter, the first King of Spain of that name <note>Peter of Castile (1334–1369), known as "the Cruel."</note> (whether she was aware of it or ignorant). When he was girded with it, he seemed to himself to be constricted by a serpent; and having later discovered the magic power inserted into the belt, he repudiated his wife for that reason.

### On the images of the Mansions of the Moon. Chapter XLVI.

They also made images in each of the Mansions of the Moon <note>The 28 divisions of the Moon's monthly orbit, used in medieval astrology for timing magical works.</note>. In the first, for the destruction of someone, they made on an iron ring the image of a black man clothed in a hair-shirt and girded, throwing a small lance with his right hand; they sealed it in black wax and fumigated it with liquid storax <note>A fragrant resin used as incense.</note> and made imprecations. In the second, against the wrath of a prince and for reconciliation with him, they sealed in white wax and mastic the image of a crowned king, and fumigated it with aloe-wood. In the third, they made an image on a silver ring, the measure of which was square, and the figure of which was a well-dressed woman sitting in a chair, with her right hand raised over her head; they sealed and fumigated it with musk, camphor, and aromatic claw <note>term: aromatic claw (ungula aromatica) — the operculum of certain sea snails, used in ancient perfumery and incense.</note>. They asserted that this bestowed prosperity of fortune and every good thing. In the fourth, for revenge and separation, enmity and ill-will, they sealed in red wax the image of a soldier sitting on a horse, holding a serpent in his right hand, and fumigated it with red myrrh and storax. In the fifth, for the favor of kings and officials and a good reception, they sealed in silver the head of a man, and fumigated it with sandalwood. In the sixth, to place love between two people, they sealed in white wax two images embracing each other, and fumigated them with aloe-wood and amber. In the seventh, to acquire every good thing, they sealed in silver the image of a well-dressed man, with hands [extended] toward heaven for...

In the twenty-seventh to destroy springs, wells, hot springs, and baths, they made from red earth the image of a winged man, holding an empty and perforated vessel in his hands: and having fired the image, they placed in the vessel asafoetida <note>a pungent, foul-smelling resin</note> and liquid storax: and they submerged or buried it in the well or spring which they wished to destroy. In the twenty-eighth to gather fish, they sealed from copper the image of a fish, and burned incense with the skin of a sea fish, and threw it into the water wherever they wished the fish to gather. Furthermore, together with the aforesaid images, they simultaneously inscribed the names of the spirits and their characters <note>magical symbols or sigils</note>: and they invoked and prayed for that which they intended to obtain.

### On the images of the Behenian fixed stars. Chapter XLVII.

<note>The "Behenian" stars are a selection of fifteen stars considered especially powerful in medieval Arabic and European magic.</note>

Furthermore, now concerning the works of the fixed stars, according to the opinion of Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy and magic</note>, under the head of **Algol** <note>original: "caput Algol", the Demon Star in Perseus</note> they made an image whose figure was the head of a man with a long beard: having a bloody neck. They say it brings about the success of petitions, renders the wearer bold and magnanimous: preserves the limbs of the body unharmed, protects against evil spells, and reflects evil attempts and evil incantations back upon the adversary. Under the constellation of the **Pleiades** they made the image of a young virgin, or the figure of a lamp. It is said to increase the light of the eyes, to gather demons, to summon winds, and to reveal secrets and hidden things. Under **Aldebaran** <note>original: "Aldeboram"</note> they made an image in the likeness of God, or of a flying man: it confers riches and honor. Under the **Goat Star** <note>original: "hirco", referring to Capella</note> they made an image whose figure was like a man wishing to rejoice with musical instruments. It makes the wearer graceful, honored, and exalted before kings and princes, and helps against the pain of teeth. Under the **Greater Dog** <note>original: "cane maiore", referring to Sirius</note> they made the image of a greyhound, or of a young virgin. It confers honor, benevolence, and the favor of men and spirits of the air: and it gives the power of pacifying and reconciling kings, princes, and other men. Under the **Lesser Dog** <note>original: "cane minori", referring to Procyon</note> they made the image of a rooster, or of three young girls. It confers the favor of gods, spirits, and men: it gives power against evil spells and preserves health. Under the **Heart of the Lion** <note>original: "corde leonis", referring to Regulus</note> they made the image of a lion, or a cat, or the figure of an honored man sitting in a chair. It renders a man temperate, takes away anger, and gives favor. Under the **Tail of the Greater Bear** <note>original: "cauda Vrsae maioris", referring to Alkaid</note> they made the image of a pensive man, or a bull, or the figure of a calf. It is effective against incantations and renders the wearer secure in travels. Under the **Wing of the Crow** <note>original: "ala corui", referring to Gienah</note> they made the image of a crow, or a snake, or

### Concerning geomantic figures, which are intermediate between images and characters, and a table of the same.
# Chapter XLVIII.

There are yet certain other figures, fashioned through the numbers and positions of the stars, and assigned both to the elements and to the planets and signs. These are called geomantic <note>from "geomancy," a method of divination using patterns formed by earth or sand</note>, because geomantic diviners reduce the points cast in their lot—through the excess of parity and imparity <note>even and odd numbers</note>—into these figures. These figures also, when engraved or imprinted under the dominion of their planets and signs, conceive the virtue and power of images; and these figures are, as it were, a medium between images and characters. However, he who desires to know exactly the natures, qualities, properties, conditions, significations, and results <note>original: "apotelesmata"; the effects or outcomes of astrological influences</note> of these figures should seek them out in the volumes of the geomancers. ## On images whose form is not according to the likeness of any celestial figure, but according to the likeness of that which the mind of the practitioner desires. Chapter 49.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'E' depicting a scholar or magus seated within the letter frame.</image-desc>There is yet another method of making images, not according to the likeness of celestial figures <note>i.e., the constellations or zodiac signs</note>, but according to the likeness of that which the mind of the practitioner desires, of which they are the effigies and traces. Thus, for love, we fashion images embracing one another; for discord, images striking one another. To bring about calamity, destruction, or an impediment—whether to a person, a house, a city, or any other thing—we construct images that are distorted or broken in their limbs and parts, according to the likeness and figure of that thing which we wish to destroy or hinder. 

The Magi <term>Magi: wise men or practitioners of high magic</term> command that in the casting or carving of images, the name of the desired effect should be inscribed upon them: on the back when the effect is evil, such as "destruction," and on the belly when it is good, such as "love." Furthermore, the name of the species or the individual whom the image designates—or for whom, or against whom, it was fashioned—should be inscribed on the forehead. Again, on the chest, the name of the sign or the <term>face: a ten-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign</term> of the ascendant and its lord should be placed, as well as the characters <note>magical symbols or sigils</note> and the names of their angels. 

They further command that in the fashioning of the image, the incantation of the effect for which it is made must not be kept silent; all of which things even Albertus Magnus <note>A famous 13th-century philosopher and theologian often associated with alchemy and magic</note> affirms in his *Mirror* <note>original: "Speculo"</note>. 

Once the images have been finished according to their various virtues, they are used in different ways. Sometimes they are suspended or bound to the body; sometimes they are buried under the earth or beneath a river; sometimes they are hung in a chimney over smoke, or from a tree to be moved by the wind; sometimes with the head upward, sometimes downward; and sometimes they are cast into boiling water or into fire. For they say that to the extent that the practitioners of images affect the image itself, to that same extent the image brings similar sufferings upon those to whom they are assigned, just as the mind of the practitioner shall dictate. 

In this way, we read that Nectanebus the Magician <note>The legendary last native pharaoh of Egypt, famed in medieval lore as a powerful sorcerer</note> fashioned wax images of ships with such skill that when he submerged the images in water, the ships of his enemies were similarly submerged and endangered at sea. The celestial configurations to be observed for these and similar images are taught to us by that part of astrology which is titled "On Elections" <term>Elections: the branch of astrology used to find the most auspicious time to begin an undertaking</term>.

## On certain celestial observations, and the practice of certain images of the same kind. Chapter 50.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'M' featuring architectural elements within the letter frame.</image-desc>Now I shall relate to you the observations of the celestial bodies which are required for the practice of some images of this kind. Let us further make fortunate the ascendant and the <term>Midheaven: the highest point in the sky at the time of the observation</term>, and their lords. Likewise, the place of the Sun and the place of the Moon; the Part of Fortune, and the lord of the conjunction or prevention <note>the New or Full Moon</note> occurring before his birth, while depressing the malevolent planets. If, however, we wish to fashion an image for calamity, we shall do the opposite: and those things which...

Here we place fortunate things, and in the same way we place unfortunate things by raising up malevolent stars <note>original: "stellas maleuolas"; referring to planets like Saturn or Mars when they are in a position to cause harm</note>. Do in a similar manner for making a certain place, or region, or city, or house fortunate. Likewise, for destroying or hindering any of the aforementioned things, let an image be made under the ascendant <note>The "ascendant" is the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment, believed to govern the physical manifestation of an event.</note> of that thing which you wish to destroy or hinder; and you shall make unfortunate the lord of the house of life, the lord of the ascendant, and the moon, the lord of the house of the moon, and the lord of the house of the lord of the ascendant, and the tenth house, and its lord. 

However, for the improvement of any place, place the fortunate planets in its ascendant: and in the first, tenth, second, and eighth houses; you shall make fortunate the lord of the ascendant and the lord of the house of the moon. 

Indeed, for putting to flight certain animals from certain places, so that they cannot be produced, or dwell, or persist in them, let an image be made under the ascendant of that animal which we wish to drive away, and in the likeness of it: as, if we wish to drive away scorpions from any place, let an image of a scorpion be made, with the sign of Scorpio ascending, with the moon; and you shall make unfortunate the ascendant, and its lord, and the lord of the house of Mars <note>Mars is the planetary ruler of the sign Scorpio.</note>: and you shall make unfortunate the lord of the ascendant in the eighth house: and let them be joined by a malevolent aspect, either opposite or square <note>In astrology, "square" (90°) and "opposite" (180°) aspects are considered tense or conflicting alignments.</note>: and let there be inscribed upon the image the name of the ascendant, and of its lord, and the name of the moon, and the name of the lord of the day, and the name of the lord of the hour: and let a pit be made in the middle of the place from which you wish to expel them: and let there be brought into it some earth taken from the four corners of the same place, and let the image be buried there, with the head downward, while imprecating <note>To imprecate is to utter a ritual curse or command.</note> or pronouncing: *this is the burial of scorpions, so that they may not enter this place*: and so do for similar things. 

Likewise, for profit, let an image be made under the ascendant of a person's birth, or under the ascendant of that place to which you wish to assign the profit; make fortunate the ascendant and its lord: and you should make the lord of the second house (which is the house of substance <note>The "house of substance" or second house in astrology governs wealth and personal possessions.</note>) joined with the lord of the ascendant in a trine or sextile aspect <note>Trine (120°) and sextile (60°) are harmonious, beneficial alignments.</note>: and let there be a "reception" between them; you shall make fortunate the eleventh house, and its lord, and the eighth: and if you are able, place the Part of Fortune <note>A specific calculated point in a birth chart representing well-being and success.</note> in the ascendant or the second house: and let the image be buried in that place, or be carried by the one to whom we wish to assign the profit. 

Likewise, for concord and love, let an image be made on the day of Jupiter, under the ascendant of the birth of the one whom you wish to be loved; make fortunate the ascendant and the tenth house: and hide the evil planets from the ascendant: and have the lords of the tenth and eleventh houses be fortunate planets, joined to the lord of the ascendant by trine or sextile with reception: then make another image, namely for the one whom you wish to incite to love: consider if they be a friend or a companion of the one you wish to be loved: and if so, let the image be made under the ascendant of the eleventh house from the ascendant of the first image. If indeed it be a wife or a husband, let it be under the ascendant of the seventh. If a brother or sister or blood relative, let it be under the ascendant of the third: and so for similar cases: and place the significator <note>The planet representing a specific person in a chart.</note> of the ascendant of the second image joined to the significator of the ascendant of the first image: and let there be reception between them: and let the other things be fortunate, as in the first image; afterward, join both images together in an embrace, or place the face of the second image to the back of the first image: and let them be wrapped in a linen cloth and be carried, or [hidden]. Likewise, for the success of petitions, and for obtaining a thing denied...

# On characters which are fashioned according to the rule 
# and imitation of the celestials, and how they are derived 
# from Geomantic figures, with a table of the same.

## Chapter LI.

Characters also have their own community derived from the rays of the celestials, cast into one another according to a certain number with a particular property. Just as these celestial bodies—in the various strikes of their rays falling upon one another in different ways—conspire toward diverse virtues; so also characters, drawn in different ways according to the various concurrences of such rays, suddenly obtain diverse operations. These are often much more effective than the properties of physical mixtures. But the true characters of the heavens are the very writing of the angels, which among the Hebrews is called the writing of *Malachim* <note>The "Alphabet of the Angels" or "Regal" script used in high magic</note>, through which all things are described and signified in heaven for anyone who knows how to read. But concerning these, more will be said later. Now, however, they also fashion characters from Geomantic figures <note><term>Geomancy: A method of divination using sixteen patterns of points</term></note>, by connecting the points of each in various ways among themselves, and attributing them to those planets and signs according to the logic of the same configurations from which they were formed; the following table explains the construction of these.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

### Concerning characters which are derived from things themselves by a certain likeness. Chapter LII.

<margin>What characters are.</margin>
**W**e have said previously that there is a certain method of images, not made according to the exact likeness of celestial forms, but according to the emulation of that which the mind of the practitioner desires: this must also be understood by the same reasoning regarding certain characters <note>The term "character" here refers to a magical seal or sigil—a simplified graphic shorthand for a complex spiritual force.</note>. For characters of this kind are nothing other than poorly articulated images, yet possessing a certain probable likeness to a celestial image, or to that which the mind of the practitioner desires, whether it be made from the whole image or from some certain mark of it expressing the whole image. Just as we form the characters of Aries and Taurus from their horns, thus: ♈ . ♉ . Of Gemini from an embrace: ♊ . Of Cancer from its forward and backward movement: ♋ . Of Leo, Scorpio, and Capricorn from the tail: ♌ . ♏ . ♑ . Of Virgo from the ear of grain <note>original: "spica"</note>: ♍ . Of Libra from the scales: ♎ . Of Sagittarius from the arrow: ♐ . Of Aquarius from the waves: ♒ . And of Pisces from the fishes: ♓ . By similar reasoning, the character of Saturn is drawn from the scythe: ♄ . Of Jupiter from the scepter: ♃ . Of Mars from the dart: ♂ . Of the Sun from its roundness and golden brightness: ☉ . Of Venus from the mirror: ♀ . Of Mercury from the caduceus <note>The staff entwined with snakes carried by the messenger god.</note>: ☿ . Of the Moon from the horns of her waxing and waning: ☽ . From these, subsequently, according to the mixtures of the signs and stars and their natures, mixed characters are also established, such as for the fiery triplicity <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</note>, the earthy, the airy, and the watery. Similarly, according to the one hundred and twenty conjunctions of the planets, just as many complex or composite characters result in manifold figures: as of Saturn and Jupiter, thus for example: [composite symbol] or thus: [alternate composite]; of Saturn and Mars: [composite symbol] or thus: [alternate composite]; of Jupiter and Mars: [composite symbol] or thus: [alternate composite]; of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars: [composite symbol] or thus: [alternate triple composite]. And just as these have been exemplified regarding two and three, so also they ought to be formed regarding the rest and more; and by the same reasoning, the characters of the other celestial images in any face or degree of the ascending signs are to be drawn as concisely as possible in the likeness of the image, just as in those things which are made according to the way of imitation toward that which the mind of the practitioner desires: as for love, figures mixed together, embracing one another, and obeying one another; but for hatred, on the contrary, turning away from one another, attacking, disparate, and dissolved. Furthermore, I shall not be loath to depict here what characters Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the Hermetic tradition.</note> assigned to the fixed and Behenian stars <note>term: Behenian stars (from Arabic 'bahman', meaning 'root'); fifteen specific stars considered especially powerful in medieval astrology for magical operations.</note>, and they are such:

## That no divination is perfect without astrology.
### Chapter LIII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'L' containing a figure of a winged cherub or angel surrounded by floral scrollwork.</image-desc> We have spoken in the preceding chapters about the various kinds of divination; but it must be observed that all of these require the use and rules of astrology for themselves, as a key most necessary for the knowledge of all secrets. All kinds of divination whatsoever have their roots and foundations in astrology itself, so much so that without it they seem to bring forth little or nothing. Yet astrological dominion itself—insofar as the heavenly bodies are the causes and signs of all those things which are and happen in these lower regions—bestows the most certain demonstrations of whatever is hidden or future, solely from the position and motion of the celestial bodies. This place does not require us to say more on this, since vast volumes have been written on this science by the ancients and are openly available to everyone. Therefore, whether a physiognomist <note>One who judges character or predicts the future from physical features.</note> inspects the body, the face, the forehead, or the hand; or whether an interpreter examines a dream or an omen; if the judgment is to be correct, the figure of the heavens <note>A horoscope or celestial chart.</note> must likewise be examined. From its indications, together with the conjectures of similarities and signs, truthful opinions of the things signified may be born. Even if some prodigy <note>An omen or supernatural event.</note> should appear, a figure of the heavens must be erected. One must also examine what preceded in the revolutions of the years, from the great conjunctions and eclipses; then also the births, origins, enthronements, foundations, revolutions, profections, directions, and what follows from them, of the princes, nations, kingdoms, and cities where these things appeared; and into which house of each celestial figure these fell. Thus, from all these things, we may finally hunt out a reasonable and most probable significance of these matters. They maintain that one must proceed in the same sequence, though with less labor, even in the interpretation of dreams. Furthermore, even those who, alienated by a frenzy <note>Divine madness or prophetic trance.</note>, predict the future, do not do so unless agitated by the stars or their lower instruments; hence their prophecies must also finally be adapted to the heavenly bodies, just as we read in Lucan <note>A Roman poet; the quote is from his epic 'Pharsalia'.</note> regarding the Tuscan Seer <note>Arruns, an Etruscan diviner.</note>:

> Learned in the motions of lightning, and the warm veins
> Of entrails, and the flight of the wing wandering in the air.

After the city was purified, after the victim was sacrificed, and after the entrails were inspected, the judgment was finally brought forth from the dispositions of the heavenly stars. Now indeed, even geomancy <note>Divination by interpreting markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil/rocks.</note> itself—the most accurate of lot-castings, which divines through points inscribed on the earth or another surface, either by chance or by some force—first reduces those points to celestial figures: namely, to those sixteen which we named above. From their properties and reasons, it forms a judgment in the astrological manner. And to this point belong whatever divining-powers of natural lot-castings exist; their force can come from nowhere else than from heaven and from the soul of the operator. For whatever is moved, agitated, and produced by any motion in these lower things, must necessarily imitate the motions and influences of the superior things, to which—

<summary>Agrippa argues that astrology is the essential "key" and foundation for all other forms of divination, including physiognomy, dream interpretation, and geomancy. He asserts that no prophecy is truly accurate unless it is aligned with the positions and movements of the celestial bodies.</summary>

## On Lots, and When and From Where the Power of Divination Befalls Them. Chapter 54.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Q depicting a seated youth or angel figure within a landscape, bordered by an ornamental square frame.</image-desc>Whatever divinations and predictions of human events are made through lots <note>term: "sors" (lot); the practice of cleromancy, or casting objects to determine divine will.</note>, it is necessary that they have some sublime, hidden, and secret cause beyond mere chance. This will certainly not be an "accidental cause," such as Aristotle described fortune to be. Indeed, in the series of causes—since according to the Platonists an accidental cause can never be the primary and sufficient cause—it is necessary for us to look deeper and find a cause that knows and intends the effect itself. This cause must be placed not in corporeal nature, but in immaterial and incorporeal substances which truly administer the lot and dispense it as an indication of truth: such as in human souls, or separate spirits and demons <note>note: "demons" here refers to the Greek "daimones," intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses, not necessarily evil entities.</note>, or in celestial intelligences, or in God himself. 

That there can be sufficient power and virtue in the human soul to direct such lots is evident from this: that there is within our soul a divine power and likeness, and a perception and power over all things. And as we said in the first book, all things have a natural obedience to the soul; they necessarily possess motion and efficacy toward that which the soul desires with a strong longing. All the virtues and operations of natural and artificial things obey the soul when it is carried away into an excess of its own desire. All lots of whatever kind then assist the appetite of such a soul and acquire for themselves wonderful powers of presage—both from the soul itself and from the celestial opportunity at that hour in which the excess of such desire most strongly invades it. 

This same reasoning is also the root of all astrological questions: because the soul, elevated into an excess of some desire, seizes for itself the most convenient and effective hour and opportunity. When a figure of the heavens <note>note: a horoscope or birth chart.</note> is constructed for that moment, the astrologer can then judge and clearly know from it that which the seeker wishes and desires to know. However, because lots are directed not always by the human soul, but also (as we said) by the ministry of other spirits, and because the mind of the seer is not always disposed to that excess of passion we mentioned, it was the custom among the ancients to perform certain sacred rites before the casting of lots, by which they invoked divine intelligences and spirits to direct the lot correctly. Therefore, however much of a presage such lots portend, it must not happen by chance or fortune, but from a spiritual cause, by whose force the imagination is moved, or the hand of the one casting the lot is drawn...

There are many other kinds of lots, including human lots which have nothing of divination in them, observed by the ancients and by us, and even commended by laws for the choosing of magistrates to avoid envy. Cicero made mention of these in his oration against Verres; but those are not part of our current purpose. However, concerning those divine and sacred lots which pertain to oracles and religion, we shall discuss them in the following book. For now, let me advise you: however much of presage, divination, or guidance these lots are found to possess, they do not have it because they are "lots," but through the virtue of some more sublime operation joined to them.

### On the soul of the world and of the celestial bodies, according to the traditions of the poets and philosophers. Chapter LV.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a figure blowing air towards a landscape with buildings and a tree.</image-desc>
Since the heavens and the celestial bodies themselves have power, influence, and manifest operation upon these lower things, it is necessary that they be animated <note>meaning "endowed with a soul" or "living"</note>; for an operation can by no means proceed from a pure body <note>i.e., inert matter</note>. Therefore, all the most noble poets and philosophers affirm that the world itself has a soul, and the celestial bodies likewise, and that this soul is indeed intelligent. Hence Marcus Manilius, in his *Astronomica* dedicated to Augustus, sings:

<margin>Manilius</margin>
> This work constructed of the vast body of the world,
> And the members of nature established in diverse forms,
> Of air and fire, of earth and the lying sea,
> A divine force of soul rules; and by a sacred path
> God breathes in harmony, and governs with silent reason.

->Likewise Lucan:<-

<margin>Lucanus</margin>
> He who sustains the globe balanced in the empty air,
> A great part of the whole of Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note>.

For what else do these verses seem to intend, than that the world not only possesses a spirit and a soul, but is also a participant in the Divine Mind? And that the origin, power, and vigor of all lower things depend upon the Soul of the World itself? This all the Platonists, the Pythagoreans, Orpheus, Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus of mystical knowledge.</note>, Aristotle, Theophrastus, Avicenna, Algazel <note>Al-Ghazali, the influential Persian theologian and philosopher.</note>, and all the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> confess and confirm.

### Chapter LVI.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'H' featuring two figures (one seated, one standing) in a landscape with trees.</image-desc>The world has a soul; the heavens, the stars, and the elements have a soul, with which they cause soul in these lower and mixed things. They also possess a spirit, as we said in the previous book, which is present to the body by means of its soul. For since the whole body of the world is a certain body whose parts are the bodies of living creatures—and as much as the whole is more perfect and noble than its parts, so much more perfect and noble is the body of the world than the body of individual living beings—it would be absurd if every imperfect little body, the particles of the world, and even the vilest little animals like flies and worms were worthy of life, possessed life, and had a soul, while the world itself, being whole, most perfect, total, and the most noble body, neither lived nor had a soul. It is no less absurd that the heavens, stars, and elements, which most generously provide life and soul to individual things, should themselves lack life and soul; or that any plant or tree should be of a more noble condition than the heaven, the stars, and the elements, which are naturally their cause. For who, unless they are devoid of life themselves, would deny that the earth and water live, which of themselves generate, vivify, nourish, and increase innumerable trees, plants, and living creatures? This appears most clearly in those things born spontaneously and in those which lack physical seeds. For the elements could not generate and nourish living things of this kind if they themselves lacked life and soul. Perhaps some will say—
