who [claim] that living things of this kind are produced not by the soul of the earth or water, but from the influences of the celestial souls. To these, the Platonists respond that an accident <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a property that does not exist by itself but only within a substance (like color or heat).</note> cannot generate a substance, unless perhaps it is subjected to a nearby substance as an instrument. They say "nearby substance" because an instrument removed from the craftsman is not moved toward the effect of the art. Thus, even those celestial influences, since they are certain accidents far removed from their vital substances or from life itself, will not generate a vital substance in these lower things. And Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism.</note> in the treatise which he titled *On the Common*, says: "Everything is in the world; it is moved either by increasing or decreasing." Moreover, that which is moved, lives for that reason; and since all things are moved, even the earth—especially by generative and alterative motion—it also lives. If anyone should doubt that the heavens live, says Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle.</note>, he is not considered a philosopher; and he who denies that the heaven is animated, such that its mover is not its form, destroys the foundations of all philosophy. Therefore, the world lives, and has a soul and sense; for indeed it gives life to plants, which are not produced from seed, and provides sense to animals which are not produced through coitus <note>Referring to the historical belief in "spontaneous generation" from the elements.</note>.

## That the Soul of the World and the Celestial Souls are Rational and Participants in the Divine Mind.

### Chapter LVII.

That the souls we have mentioned also possess reason is evident from this: for since all the works of the said souls harmonize with each other in a certain perpetual order, it is necessary that they be governed not by chance but by reason, by which reasons they direct and lead all their operations to certain ends. For it is necessary that the earth possesses the reasons <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning the underlying rational principles or "logoi" of things.</note> of earthly things, and the water of watery things; similarly in the others by which individual things are procreated in their own time, place, and order, and often, when damaged, are restored. Therefore, philosophers do not judge the soul of the earth to be like the soul of some abject body, but rational, and moreover, that it understands and is a goddess. Furthermore, it would be absurd if, while we possess the reasons for our own works, the celestial souls and the soul of the universe itself did not have the reasons for theirs. But if (as Plato says) the world was made as good as possible by the Good itself, it will certainly be a participant not only in life, sense, and reason, but also in intelligence and mind. Since the perfection of a body is the soul, that body is more perfect which has a more perfect soul. It is therefore necessary, since the celestial bodies are most perfect, that they also have the most perfect souls. They are, therefore, participants in intellect and mind; which the Platonists also prove from the perseverance of their order and course: because motion, since it is free by its nature, could easily deviate and wander in turn, unless it were governed by intellect and mind—and indeed a perfect one, foreseeing from the beginning the most chosen path and the best end. This perfect mind, because it is most powerfully present to the soul—such as is the soul of the world, and such as are the souls of the celestial bodies and the elements—undoubtedly [leads] most orderly and perfectly toward...

# SECOND BOOK.

The World Soul governs the work written for itself. Indeed, bodies do not resist the most powerful souls, and a perfect mind does not waver in its counsel. There is, therefore, a World Soul <note>original: "anima mundi"</note>, a certain unique life filling all things, spreading through all things, binding and connecting all things together, so that it renders the entire machine of the world as one. It becomes like a single monochord <note>A one-stringed instrument used to demonstrate musical ratios; here, a metaphor for universal harmony</note>, resounding from three kinds of creatures—the intellectual, the celestial, and the incorruptible—by a single breath alone and a single life.

### Concerning the names of the celestial souls, and their
### dominion over this lower world, namely
### man. Chapter LVIII.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'A' depicting two figures, one seated and one standing, in a rural landscape.</image-desc>The names of the celestial souls are indeed many and diverse, according to their manifold power and virtue over these lower things. From these, they have received various names which the ancients used in their hymns and invocations. Regarding this, it should be noted that every such soul, according to Orphic theology <note>Refers to the mystical teachings attributed to the legendary Greek poet Orpheus</note>, is said to have a double virtue: one placed in knowing, the other situated in giving life to and ruling its body. In this manner, in the celestial spheres, Orpheus calls that former virtue Bacchus <note>The god of wine and ecstasy, here representing divine inspiration</note> and calls the latter a Muse. Hence, no one is intoxicated by any Bacchus who has not been joined to his own Muse. Therefore, nine Bacchuses are designated around nine Muses.

Thus, in the ninth sphere, Orpheus places the Bacchus "Cribronius" and the Muse Calliope. In the starry heaven <note>The Firmament</note>, "Picionius" and Urania. In the heaven of Saturn, "Amphictus" and Polyhymnia. In the heaven of Jupiter, "Sabasius" and Terpsichore. In the heaven of Mars, "Bassarius" and Clio. In the heaven of the Sun, "Trietericus" and Melpomene. In the heaven of Venus, "Lysius" and Erato. In the heaven of Mercury, "Silenus" and Euterpe. In the heaven of the Moon, the Bacchus "Lyaeus" and the Muse Thalia.

Similarly, in the spheres of the elements, he names the souls in this way: In fire, he places the "Shining One" <note>original: "phaneta"</note> and the Dawn. In the air, Jupiter the Thunderer and Juno. In the water, Oceanus and Tethys. In the earth, Pluto and Proserpina. Indeed, the Magi call the Soul of the World, or of the entire universe, the "Worldly Jupiter"; the Mind of the World they call Apollo; and the Nature of the World, Minerva. Furthermore, in fire, Vulcan; in water, Neptune; and they named them by various names.

In the stars of the Zodiac also, the Pythagoreans placed twelve particular gods, or souls, situated in the hearts of such stars, and from there ruling the entire constellation: namely, in the heart of Aries, a particular Pallas <note>Athena</note>; in the heart of Taurus, a particular Venus; of Gemini, a particular Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>; of Cancer, Mercury; of Leo, Jupiter; of Virgo, Ceres; of Libra, Vulcan; of Scorpio, Mars; of Sagittarius, Diana; of Capricorn, Vesta; of Aquarius, a particular Juno; in the heart of Pisces, a particular Neptune. Manilius <note>A Roman poet and astrologer</note> sings of this in these verses:

<margin>Manilius.</margin>
> Pallas protects the Wool-bearer <note>Aries</note>, Venus the Bull,
> Fair Phoebus the Twins, the Cyllenian <note>Mercury</note> the Crab,
> Jupiter himself, with the Mother of the Gods, rules the Lion.
> The Virgin belongs to the spice-bearing Ceres, and the forged Balance <note>Libra</note>...

And the most ancient Orpheus himself, writing to Musaeus, enumerates more extensive divine powers of the heavens than these, assigning to them various names, regards, and duties: and addressing each with their own hymns. Therefore, let no one think that these are the names of evil and deceiving demons: but rather of natural and divine virtues, distributed throughout the world by the true God for the service and utility of the man who knows how to use them. Antiquity itself ascribed individual members of the human body to each of these powers: as, for example, the ear to memory: which Virgil also dedicates to Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>, saying: *Cynthius pulled my ear and warned me.* So the right hand is the seal of fortitude, and that through which an oath is made; Numa Pompilius, as Livy relates, consecrated it to Faith. The fingers are under the protection of Minerva, and the knees are given to Mercy. Hence people bend them when praying for pardon. Some dedicate the Navel to Venus as if it were the seat of luxury. Others, who refer all members to it as if to a center, claim it is consecrated to Jupiter. Hence, in the temple of Jupiter Hammon, the image of a navel was celebrated. The ancients pursue many other things, ascribing even the smallest members and joints to their own deities; if these are rightly understood, and the true powers presiding over them are known, none of these things are foreign to proper piety, since even the sacred scriptures testify that all our members are ruled by supernal virtues, about which we shall say more in the following book. Not only the members, but also whatever human activities there are, have been distributed to their own deities, such as hunting to Diana, wars to Pallas <note>Athena</note>, and agriculture to Ceres; concerning which Apollo says thus in the oracles found in Porphyry:

> The reeds and the drums are the care of the Mother of the Gods <note>Cybele</note>,
> And the feminine choirs; but Pallas loves hard and
> Bristling wars; the groves and glades fit for hunting
> Delight Diana; and the humid air is owed to Juno,
> And the corn-crop to Ceres; the most faithful wife <note>Isis</note>
> Seeks for Osiris on the wide banks of the Nile.

### On the seven governors of the world, the planets, and their various names serving in magical speeches. Chapter LIX.

### That human imprecations naturally impress their powers into external things. And how the human soul ascends through each degree of dependencies into the intelligible world, and becomes like the spirits and higher intelligences. Chapter LX.

<page-num>207.</page-num>
## BOOK THE SECOND.

<image-desc>A decorative historiated initial 'C' featuring two figures within a square frame with leafy patterns. One figure appears to be seated and gesturing towards another standing figure, possibly representing a teacher and pupil or celestial figures.</image-desc>

**C**elestial souls pour their powers into the celestial bodies, which then transmit them to this sensible world: for the powers of the earthly sphere proceed from no other cause than the celestial. Hence the <term>Magus</term> <note>A practitioner of natural magic or a "wise man" who understands the hidden laws of nature.</note>, intending to work through those powers, employs a clever invocation of the higher beings, using mysterious words and a certain ingenious speech, drawing one thing to another. This is done, however, by natural force through a certain mutual correspondence between them, by which things follow of their own accord, or are sometimes drawn against their will. Hence **Aristotle** says in the sixth book of *Mystical Philosophy* <note>original: "Mysticę philosophię." This likely refers to the "Theology of Aristotle," a Neoplatonic text attributed to him in the Middle Ages.</note>: that when someone, by binding or <term>fascination</term> <note>A technical term for a type of natural magic involving the casting of a "spell" or influence through the gaze or voice.</note>, invokes the sun or other stars, praying that they cooperate in the desired work, the sun or other stars do not "hear" that speech, but are moved in some way by a certain natural connection and mutual chain, by which the parts of the world are mutually subordinated to one another. They possess a mutual consent because of their great union. Just as in the human body, one limb is moved by perceiving the movement of another; and as in a lute, when one string is plucked, another is also moved. So when someone moves any part of the world, the others are also moved by perceiving the motion introduced.

Therefore, the knowledge of the dependency of things following one another is the foundation of every miraculous operation, which is necessarily required to exercise the power of attracting superior virtues. Furthermore, the words of men are certain natural things: and because the parts of the world naturally draw one another and act upon each other, the Magus, invoking through words, operates through the fit powers of nature. He leads or draws certain things by the love of one for another because of the sequence of one thing to another; or he repels them, because of the hatred of one for another, arising from the contrariety and difference of things and the multitude of powers. Although these may be contrary or different, they nevertheless complete a single whole. Sometimes he even compels things by a certain mastery through celestial power, since he is not a stranger to heaven.

Therefore, if a man receives the impression of any <term>binding</term> <note>original: "ligatiōis." A magical act intended to restrain or compel a person or spirit.</note> or fascination, he does not receive it according to his rational soul, but according to his sensual soul: and if he suffers in any part of himself, he suffers according to the animal and mundane part. For they cannot draw him by means of his knowing and understanding reason, but only by the sense that conceives that impression and impulse, insofar as the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>The subtle substance in the body believed to mediate between the soul and the physical senses.</note> of a man is affected beyond its original or natural disposition by the influx of the heavens and the cooperation of worldly things. Just as a son moves a father to labors—even against his will—for the sake of serving and nourishing him, even though the father is fatigued; and the appetite for ruling moves one to anger and other labors for the sake of obtaining dominion. And the deficiency of nature, and the fear of poverty, move one to desire riches. And the adornment and beauty of a woman is an incitement to lust for her. And the harmony of a most skillful musician moves the listeners with various passions: some of whom follow the consonance of the art of their own accord, while others even conform themselves with gestures against their will, because their sense is captivated, while the reason does not attend to these things.

But the common people do not wonder at these types of fascinations and bindings, nor do they detest them, because of their familiarity; but they wonder at other physical ones because they are ignorant of them and are not accustomed to them. Hence they fall into errors, thinking that what is from nature and according to it is above nature or against it. It must be known, therefore, that every superior thing moves its nearest inferior, in its own grade and order, not only in bodies but also in spirits. Thus the universal soul moves particular souls: and the rational soul acts upon the sensual, and that upon the vegetable: and every part of the world acts upon another, and each is fit to be moved by another: and every part of the world...

<summary>This page explains the mechanics of natural magic, arguing that "invocations" work not by spirits hearing words, but through the natural, sympathetic resonance between all parts of the universe. It distinguishes between the rational soul, which remains free, and the sensual soul, which can be influenced by celestial and natural forces.</summary>

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

### PAGE CCVIII.

The things of this lower world suffer <note>original: "patitur"; in this context, it means to be acted upon or to receive influence</note> from the heavens according to their own nature and aptitude, just as one part of a living body is acted upon by another. And the superior intellectual world moves all things beneath itself, since it contains all the same beings from the first to the last as the lower worlds. Thus, the celestial bodies move the bodies of the elemental world—composed, generable, and sensible—from the circumference to the center, through superior, perpetual, and spiritual essences hanging from the primary intellect, which is the **active intellect** <note>Latin: "intellectus agens"; a term from Aristotelian and Neoplatonic philosophy referring to the mind that illuminates the human soul</note>. But this is also by a power implanted by God through his **Word** <note>Latin: "verbum"</note>, which Word the Chaldean sages of Babylon call the "Cause of Causes," because from it all beings are produced; even the active intellect itself is made fertile by it. This is due to the union of this Word with the first Author, from whom all existing things are truly produced.

Therefore, that Word is the image of God; the active intellect is the image of the Word; the soul is the image of the intellect; but our word is the image of the soul, through which it acts upon natural things naturally, since nature is truly its work. And each of these perfects its successor just as a father does a son; and no later thing exists without the prior. For they are dependent among themselves by a certain ordered dependency, so that when a later thing is destroyed, it returns to the next prior thing, until it reaches the heavens, then the universal soul, and afterwards the active intellect—by which all other creatures exist, and which exists in the principal Author, which is the creating Word, to which <margin>What must be contemplated by him who wishes to perform a marvelous work.</margin> all things finally return. Therefore, it is necessary for our soul, when wishing to perform any marvelous work in these lower things, to contemplate its own principle, so that it may be strengthened by it, illuminated, and receive the power of acting through each individual step from the first Author himself.

Therefore, effort must be given so that we contemplate the souls of the stars more than their bodies; and the super-celestial intellectual world more than the celestial corporeal world. For the former is more noble, even though the latter exists as a distinguished and preliminary step toward it, and without which medium the influx of that superior world cannot be obtained. For example: the Sun, king of the stars and most full of light, receives that light from the **intelligible world** <note>The realm of pure ideas and spiritual truths</note> above all other stars, because its soul is more capable of that intelligible splendor. For this reason, he who desires to attract the influx of the Sun must contemplate the Sun not only by the observation of the exterior light, but also the interior. And no one can do this unless he returns to the very mind of the Sun and becomes similar to it, grasping its intelligible light with intellectual vision just as he does the sensible light with the corporeal eye. For here he will be filled with its splendor and will receive into himself the light which is the **archetype** <note>original: "hypotypus"; a model or pattern</note> impressed from the higher sphere. Clothed in its illustration, truly equal to it, and aided as if by a lifting force, he will attain that supreme clarity and all its participating forms according to the wish of his intellect. And when he has drawn the light of the supreme grade, then his soul will approach its perfection, will be made like the spirits of the Sun, and will reach the virtues and illustrations of supernatural power, enjoying their authority if he has found faith in the first Author. First of all, therefore, one must implore help and assent from the first Author himself; and this not with the mouth only, but with religious gesture and a suppliant mind, even praying abundantly, incessantly, and with integrity, so that He may illuminate the mind and remove the darkness growing over souls because of the body.

# TO THE MOST NOBLE
### LORD, THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE HERMANN OF
### Wied, Prince-elector, Duke of Westphalia and Angria, Lord
### and Archbishop of Cologne and Paderborn, to his
### most gracious Lord, Henry Cornelius
### Agrippa of Nettesheim.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop-cap initial 'I' depicting a putto or cherub figure intertwined with ornate foliate scrolls and floral motifs, set within a square double-line border.</image-desc>

IT IS A TRULY NOBLE SENTIMENT OF THE ANCIENT MAGI <note>original: "Magorum"; referring here to the wise men and priests of antiquity, particularly the Persian and Hermetic traditions</note> (Most Illustrious Prince) that there is nothing in this life we should labor for more than this: that we do not degenerate from the nobility of the soul, through which we approach closest to God and put on a divine nature. We must ensure the soul never grows sluggish in empty idleness, nor dissolves into the fragility of the earthly body and the vices of the flesh, lest we lose it as if it were cast down through the dark precipices of perverse desires. Therefore, it is fitting for us to so train the soul that, mindful of its own dignity and nobility, it always thinks, performs, and works at something worthy of itself. This is alone and most greatly provided to us by the knowledge of divine science <note>original: "divinae scientię"; here meaning the systematic study of sacred and metaphysical truths</note>, when, occupied always in divine studies by the remembrance of His majesty, we contemplate divine matters through every moment of the hours with keen and ever-vigilant inquiry. By ascending through each level of created things even unto the Archetype <note>The original blueprint or divine mind of God from which all things flow</note> itself, we draw from Him the unerring virtue of all things. Those who neglect this, trusting only in natural and worldly things, are often accustomed to be confounded by various errors and deceptions, and are very frequently deceived by evil demons. However, the understanding of divine things purges the mind of errors and renders it divine; it provides an infallible power to our works and drives far away the frauds and obstacles of all evil demons. At the same time, it subjects them to our command, and even compels the good angels and all the powers of the world into our service—namely, by the power of our works being drawn from the Archetype itself. When we ascend to Him, it is necessary that every creature obey us, and the entire choir of the heavens follows us. For (as Homer says) *No god would dare to remain in his seat when Jove is moved*; and immediately then he rules (as Aristophanes says) through one of the gods, whom it is lawful to take up his commands, and who then, by virtue of his office, may execute our petitions according to our wish. Since, therefore (Most Illustrious Prince), a divine and immortal soul has been given to you—and since the kindness of divine providence, a favorable fate, and the liberality of nature have so endowed you that with sharpness of mind and soundness of senses you are able to behold, scrutinize, contemplate, discern, and judge the pleasant spectacles of natural things, the sublime mansions of the heavens, and the most difficult sanctuaries <note>original: "adytus"; the innermost, most private part of a temple</note> of divine matters—I am bound to you by the necessity of your great virtues, and I am a debtor, even...

<summary>Agrippa dedicates his work to Archbishop Hermann von Wied, arguing that the study of "divine science" allows the human soul to ascend to the Creator and command both natural and supernatural forces. He praises the Prince's intellect and spiritual character as being uniquely suited for such high contemplations.</summary>

# PAGE 208.

## EPISTLE.

For those mysteries of divine and ceremonial magic <note>original: "magiæ"</note> which I have learned without deception, I now communicate through true definitions of thought without envy, and I do not hide the understanding of them. Whatever the ancient priests of the Egyptians (the followers of Isis), the ancient seers of the Babylonian Chaldeans, the divine sages of the Hebrew Kabbalists <note>original: "Cabalistæ"</note>, the profoundest Greek philosophers (the Orphics, Pythagoreans, and Platonists), the Brahmans <note>original: "Bragmani"</note> of the Indians, the Gymnosophists <note>naked philosophers</note> of the Ethiopians, and the pure theologians of our own religion have handed down—and by what power of words, what potency of seals, what songs of blessings and curses, and by what virtue of observations they once performed such stupendous and admirable wonders—all this we reveal to you in this third book of *Occult Philosophy*. We bring to light those things which have until now lain covered in the filth of antiquity and enveloped in the fog of oblivion, as if in Cimmerian darkness <note>A classical reference to a mythical land of perpetual mist and darkness</note>.

We therefore return to you now a full and complete work of *Occult Philosophy* or *Magic* in these three books, which we have perfected with wakeful care and with labor of both mind and body, and with the greatest effort; though the style may be unpolished, the subject matter is clearly most difficult. For this reason, I wish to ask this one indulgence: that you do not look for grace of speech or elegance of language in these books, which we wrote long ago in our youth when our speech was still unrefined and our oratory unformed. Even now, we have revised only the sequence of thoughts rather than the flow of the prose; for we have studied the elegance of speech less, as the richness of the material took its place. I believe I have sufficiently performed my duty if I have provided to the best of my ability those secrets of Magic I promised to report, and have freed my conscience from the debt owed to you.

But since I have no doubt that many nosy sophists <note>original: "sophistas"; here meaning trivial or deceptive philosophers</note> will conspire against me—those who boast that they are the grandsons of God, full of divinity, and who arrogantly claim for themselves the judgment of the Sibyl's leaves <note>original: "Sybillæ foliis"; a reference to the prophetic but easily scattered oracles of the Cumaean Sibyl</note>—they will attempt to judge and condemn these writings of ours with a new fire even before they have read or rightly understood any of them. This is partly because the "lettuce" does not suit their lips and the "marjoram" is unusual to their nostrils <note>Metaphors for things that are distasteful or unfamiliar to the uninitiated</note>, and partly because of the sparks of hatred long ago conceived against me that lie hidden beneath the ashes.

Therefore (most Illustrious Prince and wisest Prelate), this work, dedicated by me to the merits of your virtues and now made your own, we further submit to your censorship and commend to your protection. If wicked and treacherous sophists, in the thick madness of envy and slander, wish to gnaw at it, may you happily protect and defend it by the perspicacity of your discretion and the brilliance of your judgment. Farewell most happily.

# ❧ OF HENRY CORNE-
## LIUS AGRIPPA, CONCERNING OCCULT PHILO-
### sophy, or concerning Magic, Book the third, and last.

### Concerning the necessity, power, and utility of Religion.
### Chapter one.

<note>The historiated initial 'T' depicts a scholar, likely representing Agrippa himself or a classical authority like Hermes, emphasizing the studious nature of divine magic.</note> IT IS NOW TIME FOR US TO TURN toward higher things, and to that portion of Magic which teaches us to be skilled in and to know the laws of religions: and how we ought to attain truth through divine religion: and how we ought rightly to cultivate the soul and the mind, by which alone we are able to comprehend the truth. For it is a common opinion among the Magi <note>term: Magi (wise men or practitioners of high magic)</note> that unless the mind and soul are well, the body cannot be well. A man is truly healthy only when the soul and body are so joined and agree among themselves that the firmness of the mind and soul is not inferior to the strength of the body. Moreover, a firm and robust mind (as Hermes <note>original: "Hermes" referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism</note> says) we can obtain from nowhere else than from integrity of life, from piety, and finally from divine religion. For sacred religion purges the mind and renders it divine: it also aids nature and strengthens natural virtues, just as a physician aids the health of the body, and a farmer aids the strength of the earth. Truly, whoever abandons religion and trusts only in natural things is very often accustomed to be deceived by evil demons. However, from the understanding of religion, there is born a contempt for and a remedy of vices, and a defense against evil demons. Finally, nothing is more pleasing and acceptable to God than a man perfectly pious and truly religious: who excels other men as much as he himself is distant from the immortal gods. We ought, therefore, first to offer and commend ourselves, being purified, to divine piety and religion, and then—with our senses lulled to sleep and with a tranquil mind—to wait for that divine ambrosial nectar (nectar, I say, which the prophet Zechariah calls the wine that brings forth virgins <note>original: "vinum germinans virgines" - a reference to Zechariah 9:17</note>), praising and adoring that super-celestial Bacchus <note>note: Agrippa uses the name of the Greek god Bacchus as a metaphor for divine ecstasy or the Holy Spirit</note>, the highest overseer of gods and priests, the author of regeneration, whom the ancient poets sang of as twice-born, from whom such most divine streams flow into our hearts.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,
### Page CCX.

It is the mark of a [foolish] mind to publish the secrets of many: and the divine Plato commanded that those things which are sacred and hidden in the mysteries should not be made common to the people. Pythagoras also and Porphyry consecrated their followers with a religious silence. Orpheus even demanded an oath of silence, backed by a certain terrible authority of religion, from those whom he initiated into the ceremonies of the sacred rites, lest the secrets of religion be betrayed to profane ears; hence in his poem concerning the sacred word, he sings:

<margin>Orpheus.</margin>
> You who cherish virtue, lend your ears only to my
> Words, and direct your minds toward them.
> On the other hand, you who despise sacred laws, flee
> From here; go far from here, you wretched and profane ones.
> But you, who gaze upon divine things and grasp them with a high
> Mind, embrace the voices of the Muse, and
> Beholding them with sacred eyes, keep them within your breast.
> Having entered upon this path, look up to that one
> Great author of the world, who alone is free from death:
> Whom we teach in our present discourse.

<margin>Virgil <note>Original: "Maro," referring to Publius Vergilius Maro.</note></margin>
In Virgil we also read concerning the Sibyl:
> As the goddess approached, "Far, O far from here be you profane ones,"
> The prophetess cried out: "and withdraw from the entire grove."

For this reason, in the celebration of the sacred rites of the Eleusinian Ceres, only the initiated were admitted, while a herald proclaimed that the profane crowd should stay far away. We read the same precept in Esdras <note>Referring to the apocryphal book of 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra), often cited in Renaissance magic regarding the preservation of secret knowledge.</note>, explained in these words concerning the secret Kabbalists of the Hebrews: "Deliver these books to the wise among the people, whose hearts you know are able to grasp and keep these secrets." Therefore, religious volumes pertaining to the secrets of ceremonies were made from hieratic paper—that is, consecrated paper. In these, they wrote out unrecognizable letters, which they call sacred. Macrobius, Marcellinus, and others record that these are called hieroglyphics; specifically so that writings of this kind could not be understood by the profane. Apuleius also testifies to this in these words: "The sacrifice being completed," he says, "he brings forth from the hidden parts of the sanctuary certain books, marked with unrecognizable letters, partly suggesting the condensed words of a formulated speech through the figures of various animals, and partly protected from the curiosity of the profane by knotted marks, twisted like a wheel and crowded together like vine-tendrils." Therefore, by remaining silent and hiding the secrets of religion, we shall be worthy disciples of this science. <margin>Tertullian.</margin> <margin>Apuleius.</margin> For the faith of silence (as Tertullian says) is owed to religions; those who act otherwise are close to danger. Whence Apuleius says of the secrets of the rites: "I would tell you if it were permitted to speak; you would learn if it were permitted to hear; but both ears and tongues would contract equal guilt for such rash curiosity." Thus we read that the tragic poet Theodotus, when he wished to include certain mysteries of the Jewish scripture in a play, was deprived of his sight. Theopompus also, who had begun to translate certain things from the divine law into the Greek language, was immediately struck by a certain disturbance of mind and spirit; whereupon later...

->PAGE 211.<-
->**BOOK THREE.**<-

...praying earnestly to God to know why this had happened to him, he received an answer through a dream: it was because he had defiled divine matters with lewdness by publishing them to the common people. A certain Numenius <note>A Neopythagorean philosopher of the 2nd century.</note>, who was also overly curious about hidden things, drew upon himself the wrath of the gods because he had made public the secrets of the Eleusinian goddesses <note>Demeter and Persephone, the central figures of the Eleusinian Mysteries.</note> by interpreting them. For he dreamed that the Eleusinian goddesses were standing in the attire of prostitutes before an open brothel; when he marveled at this, they responded angrily that they had been violently dragged from the sanctuary of their modesty by him and prostituted to any passerby. By this he was warned that the ceremonies of the gods must not be made common by their divine power. Therefore, it was always the endeavor of the ancients to wrap the sacraments of God and nature in mystery and to cover them with various enigmas. This law was observed by the Indians, the Brahmans, the Ethiopians, the Persians, and the Egyptians. Hence Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius"</note>, Orpheus, and all the ancient poets and philosophers—Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, Aristoxenus, and Ammonius—kept them with inviolable faith. Hence Plotinus, Origen, and the other disciples of Ammonius, as Porphyry relates in his book *On the Life and Education of Plotinus*, swore not to publish the master's doctrines. And because Plotinus, having violated the oath made to Ammonius, published the secrets, he was consumed—as some claim—by a horrific infestation of lice as punishment for his transgression. Even Christ himself, while he still lived on earth, spoke according to this law and method, so that only his more secret disciples might understand the mystery of the word of God, while the others perceived only parables; commanding furthermore that "what is holy should not be given to dogs, nor pearls cast before swine." Therefore the prophet says:

> I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you. <note>Psalm 119:11</note>

It is not fitting, therefore, to commit to public writings those secrets which are to be communicated by word of mouth alone among a few wise men. For this reason, you will grant me pardon if I have passed over many of the more important and secret sacraments of ceremonial magic in silence. However, I believe I shall have done enough if we report those things which are necessary to know, so that you do not leave the reading of this book entirely empty of those mysteries. But let these things be communicated to you under the same law by which Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> bound Timothy: namely, that the secrets are not to be exposed to the unworthy by those who receive them, but gathered among the wise, they should be guarded with the reverence that is fitting. Furthermore, I wish you to be warned at this beginning that just as the divine powers themselves detest public and profane things and love secrets, so every magical experiment flees the public, seeks to be hidden, is strengthened by silence, but is destroyed by publication; nor does a complete effect follow from it. For all these things suffer loss when they are thrust upon talkative and unbelieving minds. It is necessary, therefore, for a magical practitioner <term>magicum operatorem: one who performs the rites of magic</term>, if he wishes to obtain fruit therefrom, to be secretive, and to disclose to no one his work, nor the place, nor the time, nor his desire, nor his will, except to either his teacher or a co-assistant—or a companion who must also be faithful, believing, silent, and designated by nature or training. Indeed, even the talkativeness, unbelief, and unworthiness of a companion hinders and disturbs the effect in every operation.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' at the beginning of the text, featuring a detailed landscape scene with a circular tower or gazebo beneath clouds.</image-desc>

Near the beginning of the first book of this work, we spoke of what kind of person a <term>magus</term> <note>A practitioner of natural and celestial magic; a wise seeker of hidden truths.</note> ought to be: but now we shall recount a hidden, necessary, and secret matter for everyone who desires to labor in this art, which is the beginning, the completion, and the key of all magical operations: and this is the **dignification** <note>The process of making oneself worthy or spiritually elevated to handle divine powers.</note> of man for such sublime virtue and power. For this faculty requires a marvelous dignification in a man: for the very **intellect** which is within us, the highest mind of the soul, is the sole operator of marvelous works. When it has been submerged too much in the commerce of the flesh, and the soul is occupied with the sensible body, it merits no command over divine substances; and therefore many pursue this art in vain. It is necessary, therefore, for us who strive for such highness, to meditate chiefly on two things: one, namely, by what reason we may desert carnal affections, the fleeting sense, and material passions. The other, by what way and in what manner we may ascend to that pure intellect itself, joined to the powers of the gods, without which we can never happily approach the scrutiny of secret things, nor the power of marvelous operations. For in these consists the whole dignification, which nature, merit, and a certain religious art provide.

**Natural dignity** is the optimal disposition of the body and its organs, obscuring the soul itself with no thickness, nor anticipating it with any tumult or humor <note>Referring to the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were believed to dictate health and temperament.</note>: and this proceeds from the position, motion, light, and influence of the celestial bodies and souls, which are present at the birth of each person: such as those whose **ninth house** <note>In astrology, the house associated with philosophy, religion, and long journeys.</note> is made fortunate by **Saturn, the Sun, and Mercury**. **Mars** also, in the ninth house, commands spirits. But these matters are treated copiously in the books of the stars. He who is not naturally such, must compensate for the defect of nature through education, the best regimen, and the prosperous use of natural things, until he emerges complete in every intrinsic and extrinsic perfection.

Hence such great diligence is cautioned in the **Mosaic Law** <note>The laws of Moses found in the Old Testament.</note> concerning the priest: that he be unpolluted by the dead, by a widowed woman, or by one menstruating: that he be free from leprosy, from a flow of blood, from a hernia: and that he be whole in all his members: not blind, nor lame, nor hunchbacked, nor with a deformed nose. And **Apuleius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman philosopher and author of 'The Golden Ass', who defended himself against charges of magic in his 'Apologia'.</note> in his *Apology* says that a boy to be initiated into divination by a magical song ought to be chosen healthy, unharmed, ingenious, handsome, whole, shrewd in mind, and eloquent of speech, so that the divine power may dwell in him as if in a good house: and that the boy's soul itself, quickly experienced, may be restored to its own divinity.

**Meritorious dignity**, however, is perfected by two things: namely, by **doctrine** and by **work**. The end of doctrine is to know the truth. It is necessary, therefore, as was said near the beginning of the first book, to be learned and experienced in those three faculties <note>Likely referring to the three divisions of magic: Natural, Celestial, and Ceremonial.</note>: then, with impediments removed, to move the soul itself entirely toward contemplation, and to turn it into itself. For the apprehension and power of all things is within ourselves. However, we are prohibited from enjoying these by the passions standing in our way from our birth, by false imaginations, and immoderate appetites: which being expelled, divine knowledge and power are suddenly present. Moreover, **religious operation** obtains no less efficacy, which...

often even by itself it is effective for acquiring for us a deifying virtue. For so great is the power of sacred works rightly performed and presented that even if they are not understood, provided they are observed piously and with integrity and believed with stable faith, they have no less efficacy in adorning us with divine power. But that dignity which is acquired by the art of religion is perfected by certain religious ceremonies, expiations, consecrations, and sacred rites by one whose spirit public religion has consecrated: who has the power of the laying on of hands, and of initiating by <term>sacramental virtue</term> <note>The inherent power believed to reside in a religious rite regardless of the person performing it</note>, from which is impressed a character of divine virtue and power. If, therefore, you are now a man perfected in the sacred mind of religion, who thinks piously and most constantly concerning religion, and believes without hesitation, and if you are such a one to whom the authority of sacred things and of nature have conferred dignity above others, whom the deities by no means despise, you will be able—by praying, consecrating, sacrificing, and invoking—to attract spiritual and heavenly virtues, and to impress them upon whatever things you wish, and to vivify every work of magical science with that very power. However, whoever shall presume to operate anything in magic beyond the authority of his office, without the merit of holiness and learning, and beyond the dignity of nature and education, shall labor without fruit, and will deceive both himself and those believing in him: and he shall incur the indignation of the deities with great danger.

## Concerning the two aids of ceremonial Magic,
## religion and superstition.
### Chapter IV.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' featuring floral or foliate patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

THERE are two things which govern every operation of ceremonial Magic, namely religion and superstition. Religion itself is the constant contemplation of divine things, and a rebinding <note>original: "religatio" — playing on the etymology of 'religio' as a binding back to God</note> with God and the divine deities through pious works, through which, by reverent service, worthy veneration and the sanctification of worship is bestowed upon them, and the ceremonies of divine worship are rightly exercised. Religion is, therefore, a certain discipline of external sacred acts and ceremonies, through which we are admonished of internal and spiritual things as if by certain signs: which is so implanted in us by nature that we are distinguished from other living creatures more by it than by our rationality. Whoever, therefore, neglecting this, trusts only in the powers of natural things (as we said above), is very often accustomed to be deceived by evil demons. For this reason, those who are more religiously and holily instructed do not plant a tree, nor graft a vine, nor undertake any small work without divine invocation, just as the <term>Teacher of the Gentiles</term> <note>A traditional title for St. Paul</note> commands the Colossians, saying: *Whatever you do, in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to him and to God the Father through him.* <note>original: "Quæcunq; feceritis... per ipſum" — quoting Colossians 3:17</note> Therefore, to add the strengths of religion to physical and mathematical virtues is so far from being a fault, that not to join them is an impious crime. Hence in the *Book of Senators* <note>Likely referring to a section of the Talmud or a rabbinical commentary</note> Rabbi Henitia says: Whoever enjoys any of the creatures while omitting a blessing, takes it from God and the church as if by theft and robbery.

is believed to have usurped: concerning which it is written by Solomon: *He who robs anything from his father or mother is the partner of a destroyer.* <note>Proverbs 28:24</note> Now, the Father is God, and the Mother is the Church, just as it is written: *Is he not your father, who possessed you?* <note>Deuteronomy 32:6</note> And elsewhere: *Hear, my son, the discipline of your father, and do not forsake the law of your mother.* <note>Proverbs 1:8</note> Nothing displeases God more than to be neglected or despised; nothing pleases him more than to be venerated and adored. Hence, he permitted no creature of the world to be devoid of religion; all things venerate God, all things pray (as Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who taught that all parts of the universe are linked to the Divine.</note> says) and harmonize with hymns to the leaders of their own order. But some do this in a natural way, others in a sensible way, others in a rational way, and others in an intellectual way: and all things in their own manner, according to the *Song of the Three Children*, bless the Lord. <note>A reference to the "Benedicite" from the Book of Daniel, where all creation is called to praise God.</note> However, the rites and ceremonies of religion are diverse according to the variety of times and regions; and every single religion has something of good in it, which is directed toward God the creator himself. And although God approves of the Christian religion alone, he does not entirely reject other forms of worship undertaken by his grace; and if he does not leave them unrewarded with an eternal prize, he grants them a temporary one, or at least punishes them less. But the impious and the entirely irreligious he hates as enemies, striking them with lightning and exterminating them; for their impiety is greater than that of those who have followed a false and erroneous religion.

<margin>Lactantius</margin> For no religion (as Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian author who argued that even pagan philosophy contained seeds of truth.</note> testifies) is so erroneous that it does not contain some wisdom, by which those who have held to the highest duty of man—if not in reality, then at least in intention—may find mercy. However, man cannot arrive at true religion by himself, nor unless he is taught by God. Therefore, every worship that is foreign to true religion is <term>superstition</term> <note>From the Latin *superstitio*; here used to mean misplaced or excessive religious zeal.</note>; and every veneration that offers more in divine worship than true religion requires is also superstition. Likewise is that which offers divine worship either to whom it ought not, or in a manner in which it ought not. Great care must therefore be taken lest, through some perverse worship of superstition, injury be done to the most high and almighty God and the sacred powers under him; for this would be both wicked and most unworthy of philosophers.

Therefore, although superstition is foreign to true religion, it is not entirely or in every case rejected, since it is tolerated in many things and even observed by the prelates of religion. I call "superstition" especially that which is a certain likeness of religion; which, insofar as it imitates whatever is in religion—from miracles, sacraments, rites, observations, and other such things—obtains no small power therefrom. It also derives no less force from the <term>credulity</term> <note>In this context, "credulity" refers to a focused, unwavering state of belief or expectation that Agrippa argues can trigger magical effects.</note> of the practitioner. For how much constant credulity can achieve was stated in the first book, and is publicly known among the common people. Superstition, therefore, requires credulity just as religion requires faith. Indeed, constant credulity can do so much that it even works miracles in false opinions and operations. For anyone in their own religion, even a false one, provided they most firmly believe it to be true, raises their own spirit by that very reason of credulity until it becomes similar to those spirits who are the leaders and princes of that religion; and they may perform those things which reason and nature do not discern. However, hesitation of credulity and distrust [destroy] every work, not only...

<summary>Agrippa discusses the necessity of religious worship, arguing that while Christianity is the only true path, even "superstitious" or "erroneous" beliefs possess power through the psychological force of firm credulity. He suggests that intense belief allows a practitioner to align their spirit with higher powers to perform seemingly miraculous acts.</summary>

Therefore, wherever you find such things written by us, know that they are related to you from foreign authors, and are handed down to you by me not as truth, but as conjecture which is related to truth, and as an instruction in imitation regarding those things which are true. It is necessary, therefore, for us to gather the truth from their errors: which is indeed a work only of profound intelligence, upright piety, and difficult and laborious diligence; and of wisdom, which knows how to extract good from every evil, and to adapt all crooked things into the right use of those things which it governs, just as Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, influential Christian theologian.</note> gives an example of this regarding a carpenter, for whom crooked and complicated tools are no less necessary and opportune than straight ones.

### On the three leaders of religion, who lead us to the path of truth. Chapter V.

There are three leaders of religion who lead us all the way to the path of truth, and who govern the whole of religion: in whom it entirely consists, namely Love, Hope, and Faith. For Love is the vehicle of the soul, the most excellent of all, descending from the intelligible realms above down to the lower things; it gathers and turns our mind toward divine beauty. It also preserves us in every operation, and grants effects according to our wishes, supplying power to our supplications. Just as is read in Homer, 
<margin>The Iliad</margin>
Apollo heard the supplicating Chryses because he was very dear to him; and it is read of Mary Magdalene in the Gospels: *Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much.* Hope, truly suspended immovably toward those things which it desires, when it is undoubting and undisturbed, nourishes and perfects the soul, establishing all things individually in the good. Faith, however, is a virtue superior to all, insofar as it rests not on human commentaries but entirely upon divine revelation, and surveys all things through the universe. For since it descends from above from the First Light, and stands nearer to it, it is far nobler and more excellent than the sciences, arts, and beliefs that come to our intellect from lower things through a reflection received from the First Light. Finally, through faith, a person is made one with the celestial beings and enjoys the same power. Hence Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> says: Just as faith which is mere belief is below science,
<margin>Proclus.</margin>

Thus faith, which is true faith, exists beyond all substance and above all knowledge and understanding, joining us immediately to God. Thus we read that Daniel escaped the dangers of the lions because he believed in his God; and to the woman with the hemorrhage, Christ said: "Your faith <margin>Iliad, Book 1</margin> has made you whole." <margin>Linus</margin> Therefore the poet Linus <note>A legendary figure in Greek mythology, often cited as a master of song and poetry.</note> sings that all things are to be believed, because all things are easy for God; nothing is impossible for Him, therefore nothing is incredible. Believing, therefore, in those things which pertain to religion, we obtain their power. But where we fail in faith, we shall work nothing worthy of admiration, but only of punishment; just as we read an example of this in Luke, under these words: "Then certain of the surrounding Jewish exorcists attempted to invoke the name of JESUS over those who had evil spirits, saying: 'I adjure you by JESUS whom Paul preaches.' But the wicked spirit answering said to them: 'JESUS I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?' And the man in whom the most evil demon was leaped upon them, and mastering them both, prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded."

### How the human soul, with these guides, climbs into the divine nature, and is made a worker of miracles. Chapter VI.

Our mind, therefore, being pure and divine, burning with religious love, adorned with hope, and directed by faith—positioned at the summit and peak of the human soul—attracts the Truth. It gazes upon all states, reasons, causes, and sciences of things, both mortal and immortal, within that divine Truth itself, as if in a certain mirror of eternity, comprehending them suddenly. From this it follows that we, though established within nature, may know those things which are above nature, and understand all lower things; and we continually receive oracles not only of those things which are and which have been, but even of those which shall soon come to pass, and which are far in the future. Furthermore, such a mind does not only claim divine power for itself in sciences, arts, and oracles, but also receives a miraculous power in transforming any matter by its command. From this it follows that we, established in nature, sometimes dominate above nature; and we perform operations so wonderful, so sudden, and so difficult, that the spirits of the dead obey them, the stars are disturbed, the smallest things are compelled, and the elements serve. Thus men devoted to God, and elevated by these theological virtues, command the elements, drive away mists, summon winds, compel clouds into rain, cure diseases, and raise the dead. The poets sing and historians recount that all these things have been done among various nations; and the most illustrious philosophers, together with the Theologians, confirm that these very things can be done. Thus the prophets, thus the apostles, and thus other men have shone with the greatest powers. It must be known, therefore, that just as through the influence of the first agent...

## That the knowledge of the true God is necessary for the Mage, and what the ancient Mages and philosophers thought concerning God.
### Chapter VII.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a figure in a landscape with a tree and architecture in the background.</note>Since the being and operation of all things depend upon the supreme God, the creator of all, and then also upon the other deities to whom the power of making and creating has been given—not indeed principally, but by way of an instrument in the power of the first creator (for He is the principle of all things, the first cause; and that which is produced by secondary causes is produced even more so by the first cause, which is the producer of the secondary causes themselves, which we therefore call secondary gods)—it is therefore necessary for every Mage to know God himself, the producer of all things and the first cause, and the other gods or deities (whom we call secondary causes). He must not be ignorant of what worship, what veneration, and what sacred rites, conforming to the condition of each, are to be used to honor them individually. For whoever invokes the gods and does not follow them with their proper honor, nor rightly distributes to them what is suitable to each, does not attain their presence or the effects desired from them. Just as in harmony, if one string is broken, the whole suddenly becomes dissonant; sometimes even danger and punishment are incurred, as it is written of the Assyrians whom Shalmaneser <note>original: "Salmanasar"; referring to the King of Assyria mentioned in 2 Kings 17</note> transferred into Samaria: because they were ignorant of the laws of the God of the land, the Lord sent lions among them which killed them, because they did not know the ritual of the God of the land. Now, therefore, let us see what the ancient Mages and philosophers thought in agreement concerning God. For we read that when Nicocreon, the tyrant of the Cypriots, once asked who the supreme God was, the oracle of Serapis answered him that he should be held as the greatest God whose head was the heaven, his belly the seas, his feet the earth, his ears located in the ether itself, and his eyes the light of the shining sun. To which Orpheus sang something not dissimilar in these verses:

> Jupiter himself is the King of the starry house,
> The principle and the source: truly one power and one
> God, and almighty, in whose royal body
> All individual things are placed: earth, wave, fire, and air:
> Night together with day, wisdom, and the first origin.
> And pleasant love, all are in this great body of the King,
> Of high Jupiter: for you shall see his neck,
> Looking up at the great and upright reverence of heaven,

Zoroaster <note>The ancient Persian prophet, often cited by Renaissance scholars as a source of "primeval wisdom" (Prisca Theologia).</note> also defines God in his sacred history of Persian matters as follows:
<margin>What God is.</margin> God is the first among all things that feel no decay or corruption: unbegotten, never to perish, devoid of parts, most like unto himself, the charioteer and author of all good things, the father of all matters, the best and most wise, the sacred light of justice, the most absolute perfection of nature, and its inventor and wisdom. Hence Euripides teaches that the supreme God must be named Jupiter: by whose head Orpheus sang that all things proceeded into the light: but that the other powers must be considered ministers: which are clearly outside of God, and separated from him. Hence these very ministers of God are called "separated intelligences" by the philosophers. Therefore, they say that religious worship is owed to this supreme Jupiter, and to him alone: but to the other deities it is not owed except for his sake.

### What the ancient philosophers felt concerning the divine trinity. Chapter VIII.

<note>Image: Decorative drop cap 'A' with vine and leaf patterns inside a square frame.</note>
Augustine and Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who was often critical of Christianity, yet cited here for his structural similarities.</note> testify that the Platonists placed three persons in God, the first of whom they call the Father of the universe: the second, they call the Son and the First Mind: also so called by Macrobius: the third, the Spirit, or the Soul of the World: which Virgil also, following the opinion of Plato, calls "Spirit" where he sings:

> The Spirit feeds from within, and the Mind, infused 
> through the limbs, moves the whole mass. 
> <note>A famous quote from Virgil's Aeneid, Book VI, often used to show pagan awareness of a divine animating force.</note>

Plotinus and Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who harmonized scripture with Greek philosophy.</note> hand down that the Son of God, the First Mind, namely the divine intellect, flows from God the Father, just as a word from one speaking: or as light from light. Hence he received the names of both Word, and Discourse, and the Splendor of God the Father: for the divine mind, when it understands the Supreme Good by a single and never-interrupted act, without any intermission or change: progenerates within itself an offspring and son, which is full intelligence, a full image of itself, and a full exemplar of the world: which our John <note>Referring to the Gospel of John</note> and Hermes <term>Mercurius</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note> name the Word, or the Discourse; Plato calls him the Son of God the Father; but Orpheus calls him Pallas born from the head of Jupiter, which is to say, Wisdom. This is the highest image of the parent God, yet by a certain relation, or some absolute intrinsic quality, as if begotten distinct from the one generating, who says in Ecclesiasticus: *I came out of the mouth of the most High, the firstborn before every creature.* Moreover, Iamblichus testifies that this Son is one and the same God in essence with the Father, namely naming God the father and son of himself. Hermes Trismegistus also in the *Asclepius* affirms the Son of God in various places. For he says: *My God and Father brought forth another operating Mind for himself.* And elsewhere: *The Monad <note>The "One" or ultimate unity.</note> begets a monad, and reflects its own heat back into itself.* And in the *Pimander* (where he seems to prophesy concerning the future law...

The Father from eternity begot the Son and gave to Him His own substance, yet nonetheless retained it. The Son also, by being born, received the Father's substance; yet He did not assume the Father's own person, nor did the Father transfer His person into the Son. For they are both of one and the same substance, but of distinct persons. This Son also, although He is co-eternal with the Father, begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages, was nonetheless born in time from the substance of a Virgin, and His name was called Jesus: perfect God, perfect man, consisting of a rational soul and human flesh; to whom nothing human was lacking, except for sin. It is necessary, therefore, that we believe that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is God and man: one person, two natures. Before the ages He was begotten as God without a mother; in time He was born as man without a father, from a Virgin, remaining incorrupt both before and after the birth. Having suffered on the cross, He died, but on the cross He restored life and by death He destroyed death. ### Chapter X.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring elaborate foliate scrollwork within a square frame.</image-desc>God himself, although he is of a most united essence in a trinity of persons, we nevertheless do not doubt that there are in him many certain powers, like rays emanating from him. These the philosophers of the nations call gods, the masters of the Hebrews call Numerations <note>Sephiroth</note>, and we call attributes. Such as Wisdom, which Orpheus calls Pallas; Understanding, which he calls Mercury; the production of form, which he calls Saturn; the productive force, which he calls Neptune; the secret nature of things, which he calls Juno; Love, which he calls Venus; the light of life, which he calls the Sun or Apollo; the reason of the entire world, which they call Pan. Truly the soul—as it generates lower things, contemplates higher things, and withdraws into itself—is celebrated by a triple name: Mars, Neptune, and Ocean. And there are many more of this kind, about which he sings elsewhere:

> Jupiter, and Pluto, Phoebus, Dionysius, are one.
> But why do we speak twice? One God stands present in all things.

And concerning the same, Valerius Soranus sang:

> Almighty Jupiter, king of kings, himself both god and goddess,
> The progenitor and the mother of the gods, the one and all-encompassing god.

<margin>Pliny’s opinion concerning God.</margin>Thus those most prudent theologians of the nations worshipped one God under various names and powers, and even under various genders. As Pliny says, "fragile and toilsome mortality has organized him into many parts, mindful of its own weakness, so that each might worship in portions that which he most needed." Thus, those who had need of faith invoked Jupiter; those who needed providence, Apollo; those who needed wisdom, Minerva; and those who needed other things invoked him by other names. Hence that manifold variety of powers, on account of the manifold and varied distribution of graces; yet God is one, from whom all things come. Whence Apuleius says in his book *On the World* to Faustinus: "Since there is one God, and the same divine power, he is indeed called by many names on account of the multitude of appearances, by whose diversity he becomes multiform." And Marcus Varro says in his book *On the Worship of the Gods*: "Just as all souls are led back to one soul..."

It is necessary, therefore, to know how to perfectly intellectualize sensible properties through the path of a more secret analogy. Whoever wishes to truly understand the hymns of Orpheus and the ancient Magi <note>The "Magi" refers to ancient Persian priests or wise men</note> will find that these differ very little from the Kabbalistic secrets and orthodox traditions. For those whom Orpheus calls the *Curetes* <note>Minor Greek deities</note> and the "untainted gods," Dionysius calls *Powers*; the Kabbalists appropriate them to the numeration *Pahad* <note>The Sephirah of Gevurah/Severity</note>, which is to say, "Divine Fear." Thus, what is *En Sof* <note>The Infinite/Boundless</note> in the Kabbalah, Orpheus calls "Night"; the same is *Typhon* in Orpheus as is *Samael* in the Kabbalah. Truly, the Hebrew *Mecubales* <note>term: "Mecubales" (Mekubbalim); those who have received the hidden tradition or Kabbalah</note>, most learned in divine matters, have accepted ten principal divine names as if they were certain deities or members of God. These flow through the ten numerations which they call *Sephiroth* <note>term: "Sephiroth"; the ten emanations or attributes of God in Kabbalah</note>, as if through garments, instruments, or archetypal patterns, into all things that are created, through each superior level down to the lowest in a certain order. For first and most closely, they flow into the nine orders of angels and the choir of blessed souls; and through them into the celestial spheres, the planets, and men; from which individual things then receive force and virtue.

The first of these is the name *Ehieh* <note>I Am</note>, the name of the divine essence. Its numeration is called *Keter* <note>Crown</note>, which is interpreted as "crown" or "diadem." It signifies the most simple being of divinity and is called "that which the eye has not seen." It is attributed to God the Father and flows through the order of the *Seraphim*, or as the Hebrews call them, *Chayot Ha-Kodesh* <note>Holy Living Creatures</note>; and from there through the *Primum Mobile* <note>The "First Moved" sphere in ancient astronomy</note>, it bestows the gift of being upon all things, filling the universe itself through its entire circumference and center. Its particular intelligence is named *Metatron*, that is, the "Prince of Faces," whose office is to introduce others to the face of the Prince, and through him the Lord spoke to Moses.

The second name is *Yod*, or the *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH</note> joined with *Yod*. Its numeration is *Chokhmah* <note>Wisdom</note>, that is, "Wisdom." It signifies the divinity full of ideas and the "first-born." It is attributed to the Son and flows through the order of the *Cherubim*, or what the Hebrews call *Ophanim* <note>Wheels</note>, that is, "forms" or "wheels." From there it flows into the starry heaven, fashioning as many figures there as it contains ideas within itself, distinguishing the chaos of creatures through a particular intelligence named *Raziel*, who was the overseer of Adam.

The third name is called *Tetragrammaton Elohim*. Its numeration is called *Binah* <note>Understanding</note>, that is, "providence" or "intelligence." It signifies remission, rest, jubilee, penitential conversion, the great trumpet, the redemption of the world, and the life of the age to come. It is attributed to the Holy Spirit and flows through the order of *Thrones*, or those whom the Hebrews call *Aralim* <note>The Valiant Ones</note>, that is, "great, strong, and robust angels." From there, through the sphere of Saturn, it administers form to fluid matter. Its particular intelligence is *Zaphkiel*, the overseer of Noah; and another intelligence is *Jophiel*, the overseer of Shem <note>original: "seni"; likely referring to the biblical patriarch Shem</note>. And these are the three highest and supreme numerations, like the seats of the divine persons, by whose command...

# On the Divine Names, and their
# Power and Virtue.
# Chapter XI.

<image-desc>A decorative drop-cap "D" featuring a seated classical figure, possibly a philosopher or deity, holding an object, within an ornate rectangular frame.</image-desc>Although God himself is most unified, he nevertheless receives diverse names—not names that explain different essences or deities, but rather certain properties emanating from him. Through these names, many benefits and diverse gifts distill upon us and upon created things, as if through certain channels. We have described ten of these names above, which Jerome also counts in his letter to Marcella. Dionysius collects forty-five names, both of God the Father and of Christ. The Hebrew *Mecubales* <note>Kabbalists; those who receive the tradition</note> derive seventy-two names of both angels and of God from a certain text in Exodus; this they call the name of seventy-two letters, and the *Schemhamphoras* <note>Hebrew: "The Explicit Name"</note>, which means "the expository." Others, proceeding further, suggest so many divine names from individual passages of Scripture that their number and what they signify are entirely unknown to us.

From these, therefore, besides those we mentioned above, there is the name of the divine essence, *Eheie* <note>Hebrew: "I Will Be"</note>, which Plato translated as *On* <note>Greek: "The Being" or "That which is"</note>. Hence some call God *To On* <note>The Being (neuter)</note>, others *Ho On* <note>The Being (masculine)</note>. There is another name, *Hu* <note>Hebrew: "He"</note>, revealed to Isaiah, suggesting the abyss of divinity; which the Greeks translated as *Tauton* <note>The same</note> and the Latins as *Idemipsum* <note>The very same</note>. There is also another name, *Esch* <note>Hebrew: "Fire"</note>, received from Moses, which sounds like fire; and there is the name of God, *Na* <note>Hebrew: "Now" or "I pray"</note>, to be invoked in disturbances and troubles. There is also the name *Iah*, and the name *Elion* <note>The Most High</note>, the name *Macom* <note>The Place</note>, the name *Caphu*, the name *Innon*, and the name *Emeth*, which is interpreted as Truth—and it is the seal of God. And two other names, *Zur* and *Aben*, both of which signify a solid rock, and one of them expresses the Father with the Son. We have placed many other names in the scales of numbers above. 

Many names of God and angels are extracted from the Holy Scriptures through the Kabbalistic art, the Calculatory art, *Notariaca* <note>A method of shorthand or using initials to form words</note>, and *Gematria* <note>The practice of assigning numerical values to letters to find connections between words</note>: where one name or many phrases are gathered by retracting certain of their letters; or one name, dispersed through its individual letters, signifies or restores several things. They are sometimes gathered from the heads of phrases, just as this name *Agla* is from this verse of Holy Scripture: *Atah Gibor Leolam Adonai* <note>Hebrew: "Thou art mighty forever, O Lord"</note>, which is:

You are strong forever, O Lord. <note>original: "Tu es fortis in æternũ deus." This refers to the prayer *Atah Gibor Le-olam Adonai*, the source of the name AGLA.</note> Similarly, the name *Iaia* <note>Hebrew: יאוא</note> is derived from that verse: *The Lord our God, the Lord is one* <note>Hebrew: יהוה אלהינו יהוה אחד; original Latin: "deus deus noster deus unus." This is the Shema, the central declaration of Jewish faith.</note>. Likewise, the name *Iaua* <note>Hebrew: יאוא</note> comes from that verse: *Let there be light, and there was light* <note>Hebrew: יהי אור ויהי אור; original Latin: "fiat lux & facta est lux."</note>. Similarly, the name *Ararita* <note>Hebrew: אראריתא</note> is from this verse: *One is the beginning of his unity, the beginning of his uniqueness, his permutation is one* <note>Hebrew: אחד ראש אחדותו ראש ייחודו תמורתו אחד</note>. There is also another name, *Hacaba* <note>Hebrew: הקבה</note>, extracted from this verse: *The Holy One, blessed be He* <note>Hebrew: הקדוש ברוך הוא; original Latin: "sanctus benedictus ipse."</note>. Similarly, the name *Iesu* <note>Hebrew: ישו; Note: Agrippa is using a Kabbalistic derivation for the name of Jesus.</note> is found in the heads <note>The first letters of the words.</note> of these two verses, namely: *Until Shiloh comes* <note>Hebrew: יבא שלוחה ולו</note>, and the other: *His name shall endure* <note>Hebrew: ינון שמו ית</note>. Similarly, this name *Amen* <note>Hebrew: אמן</note> is from this verse: *The Lord is a faithful King* <note>Hebrew: אדני מלך נאמן; original Latin: "dominus rex fidelis."</note>. Sometimes these names are extracted from the ends of words, just as the same name *Amen* is from this verse: *Not so the wicked* <note>Hebrew: לא כן הרשעים; original Latin: "non sic impii."</note>, but with the letters transposed. So in the final letters of this verse: *To me, what is his name? What?* <note>Hebrew: לי מה שמו מה</note>, the name of the *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note> is found. In all these cases, a letter is placed for a word, and a letter is extracted from a word, either from the beginning, or from the end, or from anywhere else.

And sometimes these names are extracted from all the letters individually, just as those seventy-two names of God are extracted from those three verses found in Exodus <note>Exodus 14:19-21. Each verse contains 72 letters.</note>, beginning with these three words: *And he moved, and he came, and he stretched out* <note>Hebrew: ויסע ויבא ויט</note>. The first and last verses are written from right to left, but the middle one conversely from left to right, as we shall show in later sections. And thus sometimes a word is extracted from a word, or a name from a name, through the transposition of letters, such as *Messiah* <note>Hebrew: משיה</note> from *Iismah* <note>Hebrew: ישמח; "He shall rejoice."</note>, and *Michael* <note>Hebrew: מיכאל</note> from *Malachi* <note>Hebrew: מלאכי; "My messenger."</note>. Sometimes, however, it is by alphabetical commutation, which the Kabbalists call *Ziruph* <term>Ziruph: A method of swapping letters according to specific cipher alphabets.</term>, just as from the name *Tetragrammaton* <note>יהוה</note> are elicited the names *Mazpaz* <note>מצפץ</note> and *Kuzu* <note>כוזו</note>. Often, names are also exchanged through numerical equality, such as *Metatron* <note>מטטרון</note> for *Sadai* <note>שדי; Shaddai, meaning Almighty.</note>, for both make three hundred and fourteen <note>This is the practice of Gematria, where words with the same numerical value are considered spiritually linked.</note>. By the same reasoning, the name *Iiai* <note>יאוא</note> is equivalent to the name *El* <note>אל; "God"</note> through numerical equality, for both make thirty-one.

And these are hidden secrets about which it is most difficult to offer a judgment or to hand down a complete science; nor can they be understood or taught in any language other than Hebrew. But since the divine names (as Plato says in the *Cratylus*) were held by the "barbarians" <note>In this context, "barbarians" refers to non-Greeks, specifically the Hebrews.</note> who received them from God—without whom no one can in any way grasp true discourses or the true names by which God is called—therefore we can say nothing else of them except what has been revealed to us by God through His kindness. For they are the sacraments and vehicles of divine omnipotence, established not by men, nor even by angels, but by the most high God Himself, in a certain manner, according to the immovable number and figure of their characters with eternal stability, breathing the harmony of divinity, and consecrated by divine assistance. Therefore, those above fear them, those below tremble at them, the angels honor them, the demons dread them, and every creature reveres them, and every religion venerates them: whose religious observation and devotion, with fear and trembling, is invoked...
