invocation, provide us with great virtue, a god-making union, and even a power over supernatural wonders and effects. Therefore, it is never lawful to change those words for any reason. For this reason, Origen <note>A 3rd-century Christian theologian who studied the power of names in prayer.</note> commands that these be preserved incorrupt in their own specific characters; and Zoroaster also forbids that "barbarous" <note>original: "barbara"; in this context, it refers to non-Greek, ancient, or foreign languages like Hebrew, Egyptian, or Chaldean.</note> and ancient words be changed. For as Plato says in the *Cratylus*: All divine words or names were produced either by the gods first, or by antiquity (the beginning of which is not easily known), or by the barbarians. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who defended the use of "meaningless" ritual words.</note> likewise commands that they are not to be translated from their own language into another; for he says that names do not preserve the same meaning when interpreted into another tongue. These divine names, therefore, are the most fit and effective medium for reconciling and uniting man with the gods, just as we read in Exodus: *In every place where there shall be a memorial of my name, I will come to thee, and I will bless thee.* In the book of Numbers the Lord says: *They shall put my name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them.*

<margin>In what manner divine names are to be venerated.</margin>
For this reason, the divine Plato in the *Cratylus* and in the *Philebus* commands that divine names be venerated more than shrines and divine statues; because a more express image and virtue of God is reserved in the duty of the mind—especially when divinely inspired—than in the works of hands. Therefore, sacred words do not have power in magic matters from themselves, insofar as they are words, but from the hidden power of the spirits <note>original: "numinum"</note> working through them in the souls of those who cling to them according to faith. In these people, the hidden virtue of God is transmitted through the words as if through vehicles into those who have ears for hearing, purified through faith and through most pure morals, and who through invocations have been made a dwelling place of God and capable of these divine influences. Whoever, therefore, rightly uses these divine words or names with that purity of mind, in that manner, and by that law by which they were handed down, shall both obtain and effect many wonderful things, just as we read concerning Medea:

> And three times she spoke the words that bring peaceful sleep,
> Which stay the troubled sea and the stirred-up rivers.

<margin>Orpheus.</margin>
The ancient doctors of the Hebrews observed this above all others, who were accustomed to effect many wonders with words. The Pythagoreans also demonstrated this, wonderfully curing diseases of both the soul and the body with certain words. So also we read that Orpheus, when he was one of the Argonauts, turned away a most savage storm with certain words. In a similar way, Philostratus relates that Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a famous 1st-century miracle worker.</note> raised a dead girl in Rome with certain words uttered in secret, and by others evoked the ghost of Achilles. But Pausanias also reports that there were two temples of the goddess whom they called Persian in the Lydian cities of Hierocaesarea and Hypepa; in each of these, when the divine rite was to be performed, a magician placing dry wood upon the altar and singing hymns in his native tongue, then pronounced certain barbarous words from a book which he held in his hand. Once these were uttered, the wood soon seemed to burn of its own accord, with no fire placed beneath it, and to catch a most bright flame. Nor indeed should anyone distrust or marvel that sacred words—by which Almighty God established the heaven and the earth—possess great power when bound <note>The term "alligata" refers to the practice of binding or attaching words to objects or persons as amulets</note>, since it has been found by experiment, as **Rabbi Costa Ben Luca** <note>Qusta ibn Luqa (820–912), a Melkite Christian physician and translator in Baghdad known for his works on physical and spiritual medicine</note> says, that many other non-physical things can do a great deal. For instance, experience has proven that the finger of an aborted fetus hung from a woman's neck prevents conception for as long as it remains attached to her neck. Furthermore, in certain sacred words and divine names, there is a great and divine force, which becomes an operative power of wonderful effect. **Zoroaster**, **Orpheus**, **Iamblichus**, **Synesius**, and **Al-Kindi**, and all the most splendid of the philosophers testify to this; and **Artephius** the mage and philosopher wrote a singular book on the virtues of words and characters. **Origen**, not inferior to any of the most splendid philosophers, asserts against **Celsus** that a wonderful power lies hidden in certain divine words. And in the Book of Judges, the Lord says: "My name, which is *Pele* <note>original: פלא</note>," which is interpreted 

<margin>The true name of God is known to God alone.</margin>
among us as "worker of miracles," or "effecting wonders." But the true name of God is known neither to men nor to angels, but to God alone, nor will it be published (as the sacred scriptures testify) until the disposition of God has been fulfilled. Yet God has, moreover, other names among the angels, and others among men. However, there is no name of God among us (as **Moses the Egyptian** <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher</note> says) that is not taken from His works, signifying Him through participation—except for the name *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter name of God (YHWH), considered too holy to pronounce</note> itself, which is holy, signifying the substance of the Creator in a pure sense, in which nothing else participates with God the Creator. Therefore it is called the "separated name," which is written and not read, nor expressed among us, but merely named; and it signifies according to the celestial idiom, which belongs to God, and perhaps also to the angels. In a similar way, there are also names for the angels—different among themselves and in their own idiom, which **Paul** calls the "tongue of angels," of which very little is held among us. All their other names, however, are derived from their offices and works, which are not of such great efficacy; therefore, magi summon them by their true names, namely those celestial ones contained in the holy letters.

### *On the influence of divine names through individual mediums into these lower things.*
## Chapter XII.

The supreme Creator and First Cause, although He rules and disposes all things, nevertheless distributes the care of execution to various ministers, both beneficial and malevolent, whom **John** in the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note> calls favoring angels and harming angels. Of these, the Prophet sings elsewhere: "The angel of the Lord dwells round about those who fear Him, to deliver them," and elsewhere he describes the sendings through evil angels. Whatever God executes through angels as through ministers, He also does through the heavens and the stars, but as if through instruments, so that in this way all things cooperate in ministry. Just as any portion of the heaven and any star determines a certain region or place of the earth, and time, and species, and individual, so also the angelic [influence] of that portion and star...

<margin>What the garments of God are.</margin>

The "garments" and "ornaments" of God are like certain paths or relations, or emanations or channels, through which He pours Himself out. As often as our mind touches the fringes of these garments, so often does the divine power of some "member" go forth—just as Jesus cried out concerning the woman with the hemorrhage <margin>Luke 8</margin>: "Someone touched me, for I perceived power going out from me." Therefore, these members in God are similar to ours, but they are the *Ideas* <note>In the Platonic sense: the perfect, original patterns of which earthly things are mere shadows.</note> and patterns of our own members. If we rightly conform our members to these, then, being transformed into that same image, we are made true sons of God and like unto God, acting and performing the works of God. # CCXXXVI.

## ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or philosopher, holding a staff or instrument.</image-desc>

Philosophers have posited, as we have shown above, that the heavens and stars are divine living beings, and that their souls are intelligent, participating in the divine mind. They also posited that some separate substances preside over them while others are subject to them, acting as rulers and ministers, which they call intelligences and spirits <note>original: "dæmones" - in this context, referring to guiding spirits or intermediaries rather than evil entities</note>. But even Plato himself asserted that celestial souls are by no means confined by their bodies, as our souls are by our bodies; rather, they are wherever they wish to be, and at the same time they enjoy division, and without any labor or anxiety they rule and move their bodies, and by moving these they easily govern the lower things. For this reason, they used to call such souls gods, and they established divine honors for them, dedicated prayers and sacrifices to them, and worshipped them with various rites. And these are the gods to whom all nations are assigned, concerning whom Moses commanded in Deuteronomy, saying: Lest perhaps, lifting up your eyes to heaven, you see the sun, and the moon, and all the stars of heaven, and being deceived you adore and worship them, to which all the nations under the whole heaven are assigned; but the Lord <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often considered too sacred to pronounce</note> took you and brought you out of the iron furnace of Egypt, that he might have a people of inheritance for himself. And in the same volume, in the seventeenth chapter, he calls the sun and moon and stars gods. And the teachers of the Hebrews, regarding what is read in Genesis—that Abraham bestowed gifts upon the sons of his concubines, namely *Shemoth steltonia* <note>original: "Shemoth steltonia" - likely a corruption of Hebrew 'Shemot hatumeah' meaning 'names of impurity' or magical names</note>, that is, foreign names; but to Isaac he left the inheritance of all that he possessed—they say that the sons of the concubines were not assigned to the God Tetragrammaton and the supreme creator in the blessing of Abraham, but to foreign gods and powers. Isaac, however, and his seed were assigned to the almighty God Tetragrammaton himself, and in no part assigned to foreign powers. Whence they are reproached in Deuteronomy because they served foreign gods and adored those whom they did not know, and to whom they had not been assigned. Furthermore, Joshua <note>original: "Iesus Naue" - Joshua, son of Nun</note>, after leading the people into the promised land, and overcoming the enemies, and distributing the lots of the possessions of Israel, gave the people an option that they might choose which power they would worship, saying: The choice is given to you to choose today what pleases you, whom you ought especially to serve, whether the gods whom your fathers served in Mesopotamia, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But when the people answered, "We will serve the Lord Tetragrammaton, and he shall be our God," Joshua said to them: "You will not be able, because the Lord God Tetragrammaton is holy and strong and jealous." But as the people persevered in wanting to serve the Tetragrammaton, he said to them: "You are witnesses that you yourselves have chosen the Lord for yourselves to serve him; therefore take away the foreign gods from your midst, and incline your hearts to the Lord God of Israel." And he set up a very large stone, saying: "This stone shall be a witness to you, lest perhaps afterward you wish to deny and lie to the Lord your God." There were, therefore, gods to whom the other nations were assigned: the sun and moon, the twelve signs <note>The signs of the Zodiac</note>, and the other celestial bodies and divine works; yet not according to their bodies, but insofar as a soul dwells in them, and the whole host of heaven, and that which Jeremiah calls the Queen of Heaven—that is, the power by which the heaven is ruled, namely the <term>Soul of the World</term> <note>Anima Mundi - the concept of an intrinsic connection between all living things on the planet</note>, of which Jeremiah says: The children gather wood,

On Mount Eryx in Sicily, and in Calydonia, Cyrene, and Samos: and (according to the testimony of Aristotle) it is read that no power of the ancient gods was worshipped with greater ceremonies or in more frequent places. The Gauls worshipped Mercury most of all, calling him *Teutates* <note>A Celtic deity often identified by Roman writers with Mercury due to his role as a protector of travelers and trade.</note>: furthermore, he was worshipped by the Arcadians and the people of Hermopolis, the Egyptians, and the people of Memphis. The Moon was worshipped under the name of Diana by the Taurians of Scythia, and she had a most celebrated temple in Ephesus; and in Mycenae, after the killing of Thoas the king of Taurica, her image was carried away by Iphigenia and Orestes, and she was worshipped near Aricia after the rite of the sacrifices was changed. She was also worshipped by the Magnesians, a people of Thessaly, and in the city of Pisa in Achaia, and in Tibur, and on the Aventine Hill in Rome, and in the town of Perga in Pamphylia, and in the region of Agrae in Attica; and it is read that the people of Caria worshipped the Moon under the masculine sex <note>Referring to the lunar god Men, common in Asia Minor.</note>. There were also sacred sites for the remaining deities, such as Athens, which was sacred to Pallas (who is also Minerva), as were the mountains of Pyreus and Aracynthus, the river Triton, the town of Alalcomenae in Boeotia, and Neo, one of the Cyclades islands. The sacred places of Ceres are Eleusis in Attica, and Enna and Catana, cities of Sicily, and Mount Etna. Vulcan was chiefly worshipped on the island of Lemnos, and on the island of Imbros in Thrace; the island of Therasia was also sacred to Vulcan, as was Sicily. Vesta was the goddess of the Trojans, whom the refugee Aeneas carried into Italy; to her are also attributed the Phrygians, and the mountains of Ida and Dindymus in Phrygia, and the town of Rieti in Umbria. Likewise Mount Berecynthus and the town of Pessinus in Phrygia. Carthage and Prosenna, the cities of Argos and Mycenae, the island of Samos, and the Faliscan people worshipped Juno. To Neptune was sacred the city of Onchestus in Boeotia, and Taenarum, a promontory of Laconia; the people of Troezen and their city were also under the protection of Neptune. Such, therefore, were the gods of the nations who presided over and ruled them, whom Moses himself in his book of Deuteronomy calls the "gods of the earth" to whom all peoples are assigned, signifying none other than the celestial stars and their souls.

->What our Theologians think concerning<-
->celestial souls. Chapter XV.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure (likely a saint or scholar) seated within a stone architectural niche or interior.</image-desc>That the heavens and celestial bodies are therefore animated by certain divine souls is not only the opinion of poets and philosophers, but also the assertion of the Sacred Scriptures and of Catholic writers. For Ecclesiastes describes the soul of the heaven <note>original: "animam caeli"</note>; and Jerome, commenting on the same, expressly confesses this. Similarly, Origen, in his book *On First Principles*, writes that he believes the celestial bodies are entirely animated, since they are said to receive commands from God, which is consistent only with a rational nature; for it is written: *I have given a command to all the stars.* <note>A reference to Isaiah 45:12.</note> Furthermore, it is noted that Job agreed that the stars are not entirely separated from the stain of sin, for it is read: *The stars also are not pure in his sight* <note>Job 25:5</note>, which certainly cannot refer to the brightness of the physical body. Moreover, Eusebius Pamphilus in his *Theological Solutions*, and Augustine in his *Enchiridion*, also believe that the celestial bodies are animated. Among more recent writers, however, Albertus...

# BOOK THREE.

Albertus Magnus <note>original: "Albertus Magnus"</note>, in his book on the four coevals, and Thomas Aquinas in his books on spiritual creatures, and John Duns Scotus on the second book of the Sentences, are joined by the most learned man, Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa. But even Aureolus <note>Petrus Aureolus, a 14th-century Franciscan theologian</note> proves these things with vigorous disputation; he does not even think it foreign to worship the celestial bodies with the veneration of *Dulia* <note>A theological term for the honor given to saints/angels, distinct from *Latria*, which is worship reserved for God alone</note>, and to implore their intercession and aid. Even Thomas himself agreed to this, were it not that the risk of idolatry hindered the rite. Furthermore, Plotinus asserts that they know our prayers and even hear them. But if anyone wishes to oppose these men entirely and hold these as sacrilegious dogmas, let him hear Augustine in the *Enchiridion* <margin>Enchiridion & Retractions</margin> and in the book of *Retractions*, and Thomas in the second book *Against the Gentiles* <margin>Against the Gentiles, book 2</margin> and in the *Quodlibets*, and Scotus on the *Sentences* <margin>Sentences, book 2, distinction 1</margin>, and William of Paris in his *Summa on the Universe*, all responding unanimously: that whether one says the celestial bodies are animate or inanimate matters nothing to the Catholic faith. Therefore, although it may seem ridiculous to many that souls are placed in the spheres and stars, and that like the gods of the nations each presides over his own regions, cities, tribes, peoples, nations, and languages, yet it will not seem strange to those who understand rightly.

### Concerning intelligences and demons, and their threefold kind, and
### their various names, and concerning hellish and subterranean demons.
### Chapter XVI.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'N' containing a woodcut illustration of a scholar or monk seated at a desk, writing in a book, with shelves and a window in the background.</image-desc>
Now, consequently, we must discuss intelligences, spirits, and demons. <margin>What an intelligence is.</margin> An intelligence is an intelligible substance, free from all bulk of a gross and perishable body, immortal, insensible, assisting all things, and flowing into all things. And the nature of all intelligences, spirits, and demons is the same. <margin>Who the demons are here, and how many kinds there are.</margin> I do not call "demons" here those whom we call devils, but spirits so named from the property of the word, as if they were "knowing," "understanding," and "wise" <note>The author derives "demon" from the Greek *daimon*, implying knowledge rather than inherent evil</note>. Truly, according to the tradition of the Magi, there are three kinds of these: the first they call supercelestial, being minds entirely separated from the body and like intellectual spheres, worshipping the one God as their most firm and stable unity or center. For this reason, they are even now called "gods" because of a certain participation in divinity, for they are always full of God and drunk on divine nectar. These are occupied only around the one God; they do not preside over the bodies of the world, nor are they adapted to the ministry of lower things, but they flow the light received from God into the lower orders and distribute specific duties to each. These are followed closely in the second order by the celestial intelligences, whom they call "worldly demons," namely those who, beyond divine worship, are accommodated to the spheres of the world, presiding over each of the heavens and stars. Hence they distribute them into as many orders as there are heavens in the world and as there are stars in the heavens. They called some "Saturnine," who preside over the heaven of Saturn and Saturn itself; others "Jovian," who preside over the heaven of Jupiter and Jupiter itself; and similarly for the others...

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

[Page] CCXL.

They name various demons <note>original: "dæmones"; in this context, the author refers to "daemons" in the classical sense—mediating spirits or guiding intelligences—rather than purely evil beings</note> according to both the name and the virtue of the stars. And because the ancient astronomers claimed there were fifty-five motions, they devised just as many intelligences, or demons, for them. They also placed demons in the starry sky to preside over the signs, the triplicities <note>groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</note>, the decans <note>ten-degree subdivisions of the zodiac</note>, the quinaries <note>five-degree subdivisions</note>, the degrees, and the stars. For although the entire school of philosophers, including the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle</note>, assigns only one single intelligence to each orb of the stars, nevertheless, since every star and particle of heaven has its own proper and different power and influence, it is necessary that they also have their own presiding intelligence 

<margin>The number and offices of demons.</margin>

which confers and enacts that power. Thus, they established twelve princes of demons who preside over the twelve signs of the zodiac, and thirty-six who preside over as many decans, and seventy-two who preside over as many quinaries of heaven and over the languages and nations of men, and four who preside over the triplicities and the elements, and seven governors of the whole world according to the seven planets. They assigned names and seals to all of them, which they call characters, and they used these in their invocations, incantations, and carvings, inscribing them upon the instruments of their operations—images, plates, mirrors, rings, papers, waxen figures, and the like. For instance, if they were working in relation to the Sun, they invoked by the names of the Sun and by the names of the solar demons, and so on for the rest. Thirdly, they place demons as ministers to arrange those things which are in the lower worlds, whom Origen <note>an early Christian theologian</note> calls certain invisible powers to whom the arrangement of things upon the earth is entrusted. For often, visible to no one, they direct our journeys and whatever our business may be; often they are even present in battles and, through secret aid, provide desired successes to their friends; indeed, they are said to be able to reconcile 

<margin>The distinction of demons.</margin>

prosperous things or inflict adversity at their pleasure. They distribute these in a similar way into several orders: some are of fire, others of water, others of air, and others of earth. These four species of demons are accounted for according to the four powers of the celestial souls: namely, Mind, Reason, Imagination, and the life-giving and moving Nature. Hence, the fiery ones follow the Mind of the celestial souls, whereby they join together for the contemplation of sublime things. The aerial ones, following Reason, favor the rational power, separating it in a way from the sensual and vegetative; they therefore serve the active life, just as the fiery ones serve the contemplative. The watery ones, following imagination and sense, serve the voluptuous life. The earthly ones, following Nature, favor the vegetative nature. Furthermore, they also distinguish this genus of demons into Saturnine and Jovial <note>pertaining to Jupiter</note>, according to the names of the stars and heavens. Moreover, some are of the East, others of the West, others of the South, and others of the North. Finally, no part of the world is destitute of the proper assistance of these demons—not because they are only there, but because they reign there most greatly; for they are everywhere, although some work and influence most powerfully in one place rather than another. Nor should these things be understood as if they were subject to the influences of the stars, but rather that they correspond to the supramundane heaven, by which all things are chiefly directed and to which all things must conform; hence, just as they are assigned to various stars, so also to various places, and...

# BOOK THREE.
### PAGE 241.

These demons are assigned to specific times: not because they are restricted by time or place, any more than they are by the bodies over which they are appointed to preside, but because the order of Wisdom has so decreed. Therefore, they favor and protect those bodies, places, times, and stars more specifically. Thus, some have called them diurnal <note>active by day</note>, others nocturnal <note>active by night</note>, and others meridian <note>active at noon</note>. In a similar way, some are called forest-dwellers, some mountain-dwellers, some of the fields, and others domestic. From this come the **Sylvans, Fauns, Satyrs, Pans, Nymphs, Naiads, Nereids, Dryads, Pierides, Hamadryads, Potamides, Hinnides, Agaptae, Pales, Parcades, Dodonae, Feniliae, Lavernae, Pareae, Muses, Aonides, Castalides, Heliconides, Pegasides, Meonides, Phebiades, Camoenae, Graces, Genii, Lemures**, and the like: whom some call the "common folk of the gods," and others call demigods or goddesses. Some of these are so close and familiar to humans that they are even affected by human disturbances; Plato believes that by their instruction, men often perform wonderful feats of magic, just as by the instruction of men, certain beasts closer to us—such as apes, dogs, and elephants—often perform wonders beyond their own species. And those who have written the histories of the Danes and Norwegians testify that demons of various kinds in those regions are subject to the service of men. Furthermore, they say that some of these are corporeal and mortal, whose bodies are born and perish, though they are long-lived. This is the opinion of the Egyptians and the Platonists, especially approved by **Proclus**; **Plutarch** also, and the philosopher **Demetrius**, and the rhetorician **Aemylianus**, affirm the same. For they testify, from many wonders of their time, that the great demon **Pan**, and many others, first lived and then later died. Of these demons of the third kind, as is the opinion of the Platonists, they say there are as many legions as there are stars in heaven; and that in every legion there are as many demons as the heaven itself contains stars. Truly, regarding the number of good demons (as <margin>Athanasius relates</margin>) there are those who estimate them at ninety-nine parts <margin>compared to the number of men,</margin> according to the parable of the hundred sheep; others think there are only nine parts, <margin>according to the parable</margin> of the ten drachmas <note>coins</note>; others judge the number of angels to be equal to that of men, because it is written: *He set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God.* And concerning their number, many <margin>have written much:</margin> but more recent theologians, following the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard</note>, <margin>Augustine, and Gregory,</margin> easily resolve the matter, saying that the number of good angels <margin>surpasses all human</margin> understanding. Opposed to these are innumerable unclean spirits, as many existing in the lower world as there are world-spirits in the upper world, as some theologians assert they have received from oracles. Beneath these they place a class of subterranean or shadowy demons, whom the Platonists call "deserter angels," the punishers of crimes and impiety according to the decree of divine justice. They call them evil demons and wicked spirits because they often hurt and harm of their own accord. They count many legions of these as well, distinguishing them in a similar way according to the names of the stars and elements and parts of the world, and they assign to them kings and princes...

### Concerning the same according to the opinions of the theologians. Chapter XVII.

<margin>A threefold distinction of Angels.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, within a landscape featuring distant buildings.</image-desc>Our theologians, however, following Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian theologian who wrote "The Celestial Hierarchy"</note>, similarly posit threefold distinctions of angels: each of these they divide into three orders, so that there are clearly three distinctions and nine orders. These they call hierarchies, and those they call choirs, which Proclus also distinguishes by the number nine. They place, therefore, in the superior hierarchy the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones, as super-celestial spirits contemplating the order of divine providence: the first in the goodness of God; the second in the essence of God as form; the third in wisdom. In the middle hierarchy, they place Dominations, Virtues, and Powers, as worldly spirits concurring in the government of the world: the first of these command what the rest execute; the second administer the heavens and sometimes join together to perform miracles; the third restrain those things which seem able to disturb the divine law. In the lower hierarchy, they place Principalities, Archangels, and Angels, whom Iamblichus also counts: these, as ministering spirits, descend to care for lower things. The first of these care for public affairs, princes and magistrates, provinces and kingdoms, each assigned to each. Whence it is read in Daniel: "But the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me twenty-one days," and Jesus son of Sirach <note>The author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus</note> testifies that a ruling angel is set over every nation; which Moses also seems to indicate in the Song of Deuteronomy, saying: "When the Most High divided the nations, he set their bounds according to the number of the angels of God." The second are present at sacred rites, directing divine worship around individual men, and offer the prayers and sacrifices of men before the gods. The third arrange all smaller matters, and are present as guardians to each individual. There are also among them those who supply virtue to the smallest herbs and stones, and to all lower things, who have many things in common with God and many with men, and are mediating ministers.

<margin>Athanasius's opinion on angels.</margin>
But Athanasius, besides the Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim who are closest to God, magnifying Him with unceasing hymns and restless praise and praying for our salvation, names seven other orders, which he calls by the common name "the host of heaven." The first of these is the Doctrinal order, from which came he who spoke to Daniel, saying: "I have come to teach you what is to come to your people..."

In the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> he is called the accuser of our brothers, accusing them before the sight of our God day and night.
<margin>Revelation 12.</margin>
Furthermore, the last place is held by the tempters or waylayers, who are present individually with every human being; these we therefore call "evil geniuses" <note>The "genius" was a personal spirit in Roman belief; here adapted to mean a personal tempting demon</note>, and their prince is Mammon, which is interpreted as "greed." However, all evil spirits are commonly called "devils," concerning whom Augustine says in the first book of *On the Incarnation of the Word to Januarius*: "Regarding the devil and his angels, the ecclesiastical preaching has taught that these opposing powers indeed exist; but what they are, or how they are, has not been explained with sufficient clarity." Yet among many, the opinion is held that this devil was an angel who, having become an apostate, persuaded a great many angels to fall away with him, who even until now are called his angels. Nevertheless, Greece <note>Referring to Greek theologians or Neoplatonists</note> does not think all of these are damned, nor that all are evil by purpose, but that from the beginning of time the distribution of things was established by such a reason that the execution of sinful souls was delegated to them. Other theologians say that no demons were created evil, but were cast out and thrown down from the orders of the good angels because of their transgression. Not only our theologians and those of the Hebrews teach of their fall, but also the Assyrians, Arabs, Egyptians, and Greeks confirm it in their doctrines. Pherecydes of Syros <note>A 6th-century BCE Greek thinker</note> describes the fall of the demons, and names *Ophis*—that is, the demonic serpent—as the head of the rebelling army. Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary founder of Hermeticism</note> in the *Pimander* sings of this same fall, as does Homer under the name of *Ate* in his poems; and Plutarch, in his discourse on usury, indicates that Empedocles knew of such a lapse of the demons. The demons themselves have also confessed their fall many times. Thus, having been cast down into this valley of misery, some wander near us in this dark air; others inhabit lakes, rivers, and seas; others terrify the lands and earthly things, and attack those who dig wells and mines; they provoke chasms in the earth, shake the foundations of mountains, and vex not only men but also animals. Some, content with mere laughter and illusion, strive to weary people rather than harm them. Others, raising themselves up with giant bodies beyond normal height, and then shrinking themselves down to the smallness of pygmies and turning themselves into various shapes, disturb men with empty terror. Others devote themselves to lies and blasphemies, such as the one we read of in the third book of Kings <note>1 Kings 22 in modern Bibles</note>, saying: "I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all the prophets of Ahab."
<margin>The various pursuits of demons.</margin>

Now indeed, Scripture commemorates nocturnal, diurnal, and midday demons; and describes other spirits of wickedness by various names, such as those we read of in Isaiah: Onocentaurs <note>half-man, half-donkey</note>, hedgehogs, hairy ones <note>satyrs</note>, sirens, lamias <note>vampiric spirits</note>, owls, and ostriches...

<margin>The opinion of Origen regarding demons.</margin>
The opinion of Origen <note>An early Christian theologian known for the controversial theory of "apocatastasis" or universal restoration</note> regarding demons is this: That demons who, by their own will, withdrew from the service of God with their prince the devil, if they begin to repent even a little, are clothed in human flesh, so that through this subsequent penance, after the resurrection, they may return by the same path by which they came into the flesh to their original state <note>original: "postliminio" — a legal term for returning to one's previous status or country</note>, being then liberated even from ethereal and aerial bodies. And then every knee shall bow to God—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—so that God may be all in all. Furthermore, Saint Irenaeus approves the opinion of Justin Martyr, who said: That Satan never dared to speak blasphemy against God before the Lord had arrived on earth, because he did not yet know his own damnation. Moreover, many think that there are many among the fallen demons who hope for their future salvation, as learned from the history of Paul the Hermit written by Jerome and venerated by the Church in the canonical hours, and from the legend of Saint Brendan <note>A reference to the "Navigatio Sancti Brendani," a famous medieval voyage tale</note>. They even bring this argument that their prayers are to be heard: because it is read in the Gospels that Christ heard the prayers of the demons and granted them permission to enter the herd of swine. This is also supported by the seventy-first Psalm according to our numbering (but the seventy-second according to the Hebrew numbering), where we read: "The Ethiopians shall fall down before him, and his enemies shall lick the earth." There, according to the Hebrew truth <note>original: "Hebraicam veritatem" — a common Renaissance term for the original Hebrew text of the Bible</note>, it is read: "Before him shall bow the knees of those inhabiting the desert," that is, the spirits of the air shall adore him, as the Cabalists <note>term: Cabalists — practitioners of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) often cited by Renaissance occultists</note> assert; "and his enemies shall lick the dust," which they explain regarding Azazel <note>original: "Zazele"</note> and his army, of whom it is read in Genesis: "Dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life," and elsewhere the prophet says: "Because the dust of the earth is his bread."

# BOOK THREE.

<page-num>247.</page-num>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a scholar or monk seated at a desk within a study, surrounded by books and architectural or floral motifs.</image-desc> Concerning the bodies of demons, there is a great disagreement between modern theologians and the philosophers. For Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and theologian.</note> affirms that all angels are incorporeal <note>Without physical bodies.</note>, and likewise the evil demons; however, they sometimes assume bodies, which they soon cast off. Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian philosopher whose works were foundational to medieval angelology.</note> also constantly affirms in *The Divine Names* that angels are incorporeal. Augustine, however, in his commentary on Genesis, reveals this: "Demons are called aerial and fiery animals, because they thrive by the nature of aerial bodies, nor are they dissolved by death, since the element more suited for acting than for suffering prevails in them." <note>original: "Dæmones aërea atq; ignea dicuntur animalia..."</note> He seems to assert the same: that all angels from the beginning of their creation had aerial bodies, formed from the purer and higher part of the air, suitable for acting but not for suffering. These bodies were preserved for the good angels after their confirmation, but for the evil ones, they were changed during their fall into the quality of thicker air, so that they might even be tormented by fire. Furthermore, Basil the Great attributes bodies not only to demons, but even to pure angels, as if they were certain thin, aerial, and pure spirits. Gregory Nazianzen also agrees with these views. Apuleius does not think all demons have bodies; indeed, in his book *On the God of Socrates*, he says: "There is another more august <note>Dignified or high-ranking.</note> class of demons, who, always free from corporeal shackles and bonds, are managed by certain prayers."

But Psellus, both a Platonist and a Christian, does not think the nature of demons is without a body. However, he does not think the angelic and demonic body are the same, for the former is devoid of all matter. The demonic body, truly, is in some way material like the bodies of shadows, and subject to passion <note>In this context, "passion" means the capacity to be acted upon or to feel pain.</note>, so that it even feels pain when struck, and may be burned by fire into visible ashes—which is recorded to have happened once in Tuscany. And although it is a spiritual body, it is nevertheless highly sensible and sensitive to touch; and although it may be cut, it joins back together and is restored, just like air and water, yet in the meantime it suffers greatly. For this reason, they fear the edge of a blade, and missiles, and swords. Hence, in Virgil, the Sibyl says to Aeneas:

> "Advance on your way, and unsheathe your sword from its scabbard." <note>original: "Tuq; inuade uiam, uaginaq; eripere ferrum." From the Aeneid, Book VI.</note>

<margin>Various kinds of demonic bodies</margin>
Regarding this, Servius says that Aeneas wished to have a consecrated sword. Orpheus also describes the types of demonic bodies. There is indeed one body which consists only of fire, but it does not allow itself to be seen; these Orpheus calls fiery and celestial demons. Another is tempered by a mixture of fire and air, whence they are called ethereal and aerial. If something watery is added to this, a third kind arises, whence they are called watery, who are sometimes perceived by sight. If something earthy is added to these, but not so thick, they are called earthly demons, and these are now more conspicuous and encounter our senses. However, the bodies of the more sublime demons—the angels—are joined together from the purest ethereal element, visible to no man rashly, unless they offer their appearance by divine will. They are woven from threads so splendid and so thin that, by their rarity, they transmit all the rays of our sight, and by their splendor they beat them back, and by their subtlety they frustrate them. Concerning these, Chalcidius says: "Ethereal and aerial demons, because their bodies have neither so much fire as to be transparent, nor so..."

Yet, not every kind of spirit can achieve all figures at will; rather, this faculty is easily available to the fiery and airy ones to transform themselves into everything that their imagination conceives. But the subterranean and dark spirits, because their imaginative power is confined within the narrowness of a thick and sluggish body, cannot produce that diversity of figures that the others can. Those of the water, and those who inhabit the moist surface of the earth, mostly resemble women due to the softness of the element; of this kind are the Naiads and Dryads <note>water and tree nymphs</note>. Those who dwell in watery and arid places exhibit themselves as males with drier bodies, either as Satyrs, or *Onoscelos* with donkey legs, Fauns, Sylvans, and *incubi*. Regarding these, Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note> relates that many have learned through the mastery of experience that these have often been wicked toward women, desiring and performing coitus with them; and certain spirits, whom the Gauls call *Dusii*, constantly attempt this lust.

## On the infestation of evil spirits, and the protection
## provided to us by good spirits. Chapter XX.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring a classical scene with two figures and architectural elements.</image-desc>

IT IS the common opinion of theologians that all evil spirits are of such a nature that they hate both gods and men equally. Therefore, divine providence has placed over us purer spirits as neighbors, to whom we are commended as if to shepherds or rulers, so that they may help us daily and ward off, restrain, and banish evil spirits, lest they harm us as much as they wish. This is just as we read in the Book of Tobit, that Raphael seized the spirit named Asmodeus and banished him to the desert of upper Egypt. Of these, Hesiod says: "There are thirty thousand living on the earth, guardians of mortal men by the will of immortal Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, who indeed observe justice and wretched deeds, clothed in air, going everywhere over the earth." For no prince, no nobleman would remain safe, no woman would remain uncorrupted, and no man in this valley of ignorance would reach the end appointed for him by God, if good spirits did not stand by us for protection, or if evil spirits were permitted to satisfy the evil wills of men. Therefore, just as a specific guardian is assigned to each person from the good spirits, strengthening the spirit of man toward the good, so from the evil ones some enemy is sent down, presiding over the flesh and its itching; and the good guardian fights for us on behalf of the spirit, against the enemy and the flesh.

Man, however, stands in the middle between these contending forces, and is left in the hand of his own counsel <note>A reference to Sirach 15:14: "God made man from the beginning, and left him in the hand of his own counsel."</note>, granting victory to whichever side he wills. We cannot, therefore, accuse the angels if they do not lead the nations 
<margin>The malice of the nations is not to be imputed to the angels.</margin>
entrusted to them to the knowledge of the true God, to true piety and religion, and instead allow them to slide into errors and perverse worship. Rather, it must be imputed to those who have turned aside from the right path of their own accord, clinging to spirits of error and giving victory to the devil. For it is in the hand of man to choose whom he wishes to cling to and whom he wishes to conquer. If the enemy, the demon <term>demon: here used in the classical sense of a spirit or supernatural power, though the author clearly distinguishes between good and evil types</term>, is once overcome by a man, that man is made his master; once defeated, the demon cannot further attack another, just like a wasp that has lost its sting. This opinion is also supported by Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 185–253 AD)</note> in his book *On First Principles* <note>original: "Periarchon"</note>, concluding that the saints, by fighting against evil demons and conquering them, diminish their army, so that it is no longer permitted for one who has been defeated by someone to molest another thereafter. Just as a good spirit is given to every man, so also an evil, diabolical spirit is given; both of these seek union with our spirit, striving to draw it to themselves and to mix with it, like wine with water. The good spirit, through good works conforming to itself, transforms us by uniting us into angels, just as it is written of John the Baptist in Malachi: 
<margin>Malachi 3</margin>
"Behold, I send my angel <note>original: "angelum"; usually translated as 'messenger' in this context, but the author emphasizes the angelic transformation</note> before your face." Concerning this transformation and union, it is written elsewhere: "He who clings to God is made one spirit with Him." The evil demon also strives to render us conformed and united to himself through evil works, just as Christ said of Judas: 
<margin>John 6</margin>
"Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?" And this is what Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus</note> says: when a demon flows into a human soul, he sows the seeds of his own notion, whence such a soul, sprinkled with these seeds and pregnant with madness, brings forth wonders and whatever the duties of demons are. For when a good demon flows into a holy soul, he raises it to the light of wisdom; but an evil demon, poured into a depraved soul, incites it to thefts, murders, lusts, and whatever the duties of evil demons are. Good demons (as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD)</note> says) most perfectly purify souls; moreover, they provide various things to us—being present themselves, they give health to the body, virtue to the soul, and security to the mind; they erase what is death-bearing in us, cherish our heat, and make us more effective for life, always infusing light into the mind through an intelligible harmony. Whether there are many guardians of a man, or only one, theologians contend among themselves; we think there are several, as the Prophet says: 
<margin>Psalm 90</margin>
"He has given His angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways." Which, according to the testimony of Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the scholar and Bible translator (c. 347–420 AD)</note>, has its place not only in Christ, but in every human being. Therefore, all men are ruled by the ministry of various spirits and are led to whatever degree of virtue, merit, and dignity they have shown themselves worthy of. Those who show themselves unworthy are cast down and thrust away by evil demons, as well as by good spirits, even to the extreme degree of misery, according as their evil merits require. Furthermore, whoever is assigned to the more sublime angels is preferred even over other men; for the angels having care of them exalt them, and subject others to them...

Therefore, we must strive so that, having been purified by acting rightly and following sublime things, and also by choosing opportune times and places, we may be committed to the rank of the more sublime and powerful angels, who, taking care of us, may deservedly prefer us over others.

->On obeying one's own Genius, and investigating its nature.<-

### Chapter XXI.

<note>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a historiated scene of two figures in a landscape, possibly representing a guardian angel and a protégé or a philosopher in contemplation.</note>

Just as every region in the heavens obtains a certain star and celestial image flowing into it more than others; so also in the super-celestial realms, it obtains a certain Intelligence <note>A high-ranking spiritual being or angel governing a sphere.</note>, presiding and protecting, with infinite other ministering spirits or demons of its order, who are all called by the common name "sons of Elohim Sabaoth" <note>original: בני אלהים צבאות</note>, that is, the sons of the God of Hosts. Hence, as often as the Most High deliberates on war, or slaughter, or the desolation of some kingdom and the subjection of a people in these lower regions, then, just as these things are to come to pass on earth, a conflict of those spirits in the higher realms precedes them, just as it is written in Isaiah: *The Lord of hosts shall visit upon the host of the high ones on high, and upon the kings of the earth on the earth.* Regarding this conflict of spirits and presidents, we also read in 

<margin>Daniel 10.</margin>

Daniel, namely concerning the Prince of the kingdom of the Persians, the Prince of the Greeks, and the Prince of the people of Israel, and their conflict with one another. Concerning which Homer also once seems to have sensed, when he sang:

> Such a great rumor spread through the celestial hall,
> When the gods rushed into savage battles by turns:
> Against Neptune, Phoebus Apollo waged war,
> Against Mars, Pallas Athena contended,
> And Diana of the quiver stood against Juno in war.

# PAGE 251.
## BOOK THREE.

->The swift-winged Mercury <note>original: "Cyllenius," an epithet for Mercury/Hermes born on Mt. Cyllene</note> pursues Latona <note>Mother of Apollo and Diana</note> with his arrows.<-

<margin>The guiding spirit changes as the location changes.</margin>
Nevertheless, although spirits and demons <note>In this Renaissance context, "demon" refers to a mediating spirit or "daimon," not necessarily an evil entity.</note> of every kind exist in every individual region, those who belong to the same order as the presiding ruler of that region are more powerful there than others. Thus, in a solar region, solar spirits flourish above the rest; in a lunar region, lunar spirits; and so on for the others. From this it follows, and we find, that as we change locations and provinces, various outcomes of our affairs and businesses present themselves and follow us—some more fortunate in one place than another. This occurs where our <term>genius</term> <note>A personal guardian spirit assigned at birth</note> has obtained greater power, or where we have acquired a more powerful spirit of that same order. Thus, solar people, if they migrate to a solar region or province, will be rendered far more fortunate there; for they will have more powerful and favorable leaders or spirits there, by whose excellent protection in that place all their affairs are often led to happy conclusions, even beyond expectation and the measure of their own strength. Hence it is that the choice of place, region, and time—where one may exercise, dwell, and frequent according to the nature and instinct of one's own spirit—contributes greatly to the happiness of life.

<margin>A change of name is sometimes beneficial.</margin>
A change of name is also sometimes beneficial; for since the properties of names are indicators of the things themselves, declaring the conditions of their forms as if from a mirror, it follows that when names are changed, the reality often happens to change as well. For this reason, Holy Scripture—not without cause—introduces God changing the names of Abram and Jacob when He was about to bless them, calling the former Abraham and the latter Israel.

<margin>From where the nature of the guiding spirit can be discerned.</margin>
The ancient sages teach that the nature of each person's spirit can be known from the stars, their influence, and their aspects as they appear in each person's <term>Genesis</term> <note>Here meaning a birth chart or nativity</note>. However, they do so with such diverse and conflicting systems that it is extremely difficult to snatch these heavenly secrets from their hands. For Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> seeks the spirit from the star that rules the birth; but Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a Roman astrologer</note> seeks it either from there, or from the planets that hold the most dignities there, or from that house which the Moon is about to enter after the one holding the person at birth. The Chaldeans, however, seek the spirit only from either the Sun or the Moon. Others, including many of the Hebrews, seek it from one of the angles of the heavens, or from the eleventh house (which they therefore call the "Good Spirit"), while they seek the evil spirit from the sixth house (which they call the "Evil Spirit"). Since the investigation of these matters is laborious and most occult, we shall much more easily seek out the nature of our spirit from within ourselves. We should attend to those things suggested by the soul and dictated by natural instinct—and toward which heaven inclines us—when the mind is undistracted by the contagions of early age, or when it is purged of empty cares and sinister affections, and impediments are removed. These are, without doubt, the persuasions of the spirit given to each person from the beginning of their birth, leading and persuading us toward that which its star inclines us.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,
## CCLII.

# That every man has a threefold guardian, and from what sources each
## proceeds. Chapter XXII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar, within a floral border.</image-desc>
<margin>The sacred spirit</margin>
Every man has a threefold good spirit <note>original: "dæmon" — in this context, it refers to a guiding spirit or divine mediator, not an evil entity</note> as his own proper guardian: one is sacred, the second is of the birth, and the third is of the profession. The sacred spirit, according to the doctrine of the Egyptians, is assigned to the rational soul as it descends—not from the stars or planets, but from a supernal cause, from God himself, the president of spirits. This spirit is universal and above nature. It directs the life of the soul and always presents good thoughts to the mind, acting constantly within us by illuminating us, although we do not always notice it. But when we are purified and live tranquilly, then it is perceived by us; then it speaks as if with us and communicates its voice to us, having previously been present in silence, and it strives continually to lead us to sacred perfection. By the help of this spirit, we are also able to avoid the malice of fate. The Platonists believe that if this spirit is religiously honored by us with integrity and holiness—which we know Socrates did—we are marvelously helped by it, both through dreams and signs, by turning away evils and anxiously preserving what is good. For this reason, the Pythagoreans, in harmony with this, were accustomed to pray to Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> that he might either lead them away from evils himself or show them by which of the spirits such a thing could be provided.

<margin>The spirit of the birth, the genius.</margin>
The spirit of the birth, which is also called the *genius* <note>term: genius — a personal tutelary spirit allotted to a person at birth to determine their character and fortune</note>, descends from the disposition of the world and the circuits of the stars which are active during generation. There are those who believe that the soul, just as it is about to descend into the body, naturally sets apart a guardian for itself from the choir of spirits; and that the soul does not so much choose this leader for itself as it is, in turn, chosen by the spirit for protection. This spirit is the executor of life and its guardian; it joins the soul to the body and cares for it once communicated to the body, helping the man in that very office for which the celestial powers designated him at birth. Therefore, whoever receives a fortunate genius is rendered virtuous, effective, strong, and prosperous in their works; for this reason, they are called "well-fortuned" or "well-born" by the Philosophers.

<margin>The spirit of the profession.</margin>
The spirit of the profession is given by the stars to which the particular profession or sect that a man has professed is subject; the soul secretly desires this spirit when it begins to use choice within this body and takes on specific habits. This spirit changes when the profession is changed; according to the dignity of the profession, worthier and even more sublime spirits of profession are present with us. These spirits care for a man successively, as he acquires one guardian of profession after another day by day, just as he ascends from virtue to virtue. Therefore, when our profession is in agreement—similar to us and in harmony with our genius—the spirit of the profession is present, and life is rendered more tranquil, happy, and prosperous. But when we undertake a profession dissimilar or contrary to our genius, our life is rendered laborious and disturbed by disagreeing patrons. Thus it happens that someone may profit in a certain science, art, or ministry with little time and labor, while another labors in vain with much sweat and study. And although no science, no art, and no virtue is to be despised, nevertheless, so that you may live prosperously and act happily, first know your genius...

<summary>Agrippa explains the three types of guardian spirits that guide a human being: the sacred spirit (divine), the genius (astrological/birth), and the professional spirit (chosen path). He argues that success in life depends on aligning one's chosen profession with their innate spiritual nature.</summary>

# BOOK THREE. PAGE 253.

...your own good, and your nature, and what the celestial arrangement—and God, the distributor of all these things, who distributes to each as He wills—promises you as good. Follow these beginnings, profess these things, and occupy yourself in that virtue to which the Supreme Distributor raises and leads you. He made Abraham excel in justice and mercy, Isaac in fear <note>original: "timore," likely referring to the "Fear of God" or awe</note>, Jacob in strength, Moses in gentleness and miracles, Joshua in war, Phinehas in zeal, David in religion and victory, Solomon in knowledge and proclamation, Peter in faith, John in charity, James in devotion, Thomas in prudence, Magdalene in contemplation, and Martha in service. Therefore, in whichever virtue you feel yourself more easily making progress, take care to climb to its summit, so that you may excel in one thing, since you cannot excel in all. Nevertheless, do not despise making as much progress as you are able in the others. For if you have the guardians of your nature and your profession <note>meaning one's calling or religious life</note> in harmony, you will feel a double progress and increase of both nature and profession. But if they should be at odds, follow the better one; for sometimes you will receive better nourishment from an excellent profession than from your birth.

## On the language of angels, and their conversations both among themselves and with us. Chapter XXIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial D containing a woodcut illustration of a seated scholar or saint in a study, pointing towards an open book.</image-desc> We might doubt whether angels or demons, since they are pure spirits, use any vocal speech or language among themselves or toward us, were it not that Paul says somewhere: *If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels.* <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:1</note> But what that speech of theirs is, or what language, is still a matter of doubt among many. <margin>What the speech of angels is.</margin> For most people think that if they use any idiom, it is Hebrew, because this was the first of all, it flowed down from heaven, and it existed before the confusion of languages arose in Babylon. In this language the Law was given by God the Father, the Gospel was preached by Christ the Son, and so many oracles were given through the Holy Spirit in the prophets. And while all languages have undergone and continually undergo various changes and corruptions, this one alone always remains inviolate. Furthermore, an evident sign of this opinion is that while demons and individual Intelligences <note>term: Intelligences; in Renaissance philosophy, these are the spiritual beings that move the celestial spheres</note> practice the speech of the individual nations with whom they dwell, yet to those who know the Hebrew tongue, they never speak in another idiom, but in that one alone. However, the way in which angels speak is hidden <margin>The speech of angels is hidden from us.</margin> from us, just as they themselves are. For us to speak, a tongue is necessary along with the other instruments, which are the jaws, the palate, the lips, the teeth, the throat, the lungs, the windpipe, and the pectoral muscles, which receive the beginning of its motion from the soul. Truly, if someone speaks to another from a distance, he requires a louder shout; thus one nearby whispers into the listener's ear. And if he could be joined to the listener by a tighter spirit, his speech would require no sound at all, but would glide into the listener without noise, like an image into the eye or a mirror. Thus souls departed from the body, thus angels, and thus demons speak. And what man does with a perceptible voice, they do by impressing the concept of the speech upon those to whom they speak, in a better way than if it were expressed through an audible voice. Thus the Platonists say that Socrates perceived his own "daemon" <note>original: "daemonem," here referring to a personal guiding spirit rather than an evil entity</note> by a sense—not indeed of this body, but by the sense of the ethereal body hidden within this one; by which...

## ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

Likewise, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and philosophy were highly influential in the Latin West.</note> believes that by reason, angels are accustomed to be seen and heard by the prophets. That instrument—whatever that power may be through which a spirit makes itself known to another spirit, or to a man, regarding the things that bubble up in the mind—is called the "tongue of angels" by the Apostle Paul. Yet very often they also emit a sensible voice <note>A voice that can be perceived by the physical senses.</note>,
<margin>Acts 1.</margin>
as when they cried out at the ascension of the Lord: "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?" <note>original: "viri Galilaei, quid statis spectantes in coelum"</note> and in the Old Law they spoke with a sensible voice to many of the fathers. But this occurs only in assumed bodies. Truly, by what senses the spirits and demons themselves hear our invocations and prayers, and see our ceremonies, we are utterly ignorant. For the body of demons is spiritual, by nature sensible <note>capable of sensation</note> in great part everywhere and on all sides, so that it touches, sees, and hears without an intermediary, and nothing can be an impediment to them. Yet they do not perceive by that reason by which we do through discrete organs, but perhaps just as sponges soak up water, so they drink in all sensible things with their whole body, or in some other way unknown to us. For not all living creatures that we see are furnished with the same sensory organs; for we know many lack ears, yet we know sound is perceived by them, but by what means, we do not know.

### Chapter XXIV.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring two human figures (putti) among scrolling foliage and floral patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

The names of spirits, both good and evil, are manifold and diverse. However, their proper and true names, just like those of the stars, are known to God alone, who alone counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names. None of these can be known by us except by divine revelation, and very few are expressed for us in the sacred scriptures. But the masters of the Hebrews think that names were imposed upon the spirits themselves by Adam, according to that which is written: "God brought all things which he had made to Adam so that he might name them; and whatever he called a thing, that is its name." Hence the *Mecubales* <note>Kabbalists; practitioners of Jewish mysticism.</note> of the Hebrews, together

But this is only for that man who has already been dignified and sublimated to this virtue by some divine gift or sacred power. Because truly no name can be composed by any human voice that can express the nature of divinity and the all-encompassing virtue of the angelic essence,

From whence names are imposed upon spirits.

I myself have seen and known a certain man writing on virgin parchment the name and seal of a certain spirit in the hour of the Moon; when he had afterwards given this to be swallowed by a river frog, and had murmured a certain charm, once the frog was released into the water, rains and storms immediately arose. <margin>Angels presiding over the planets.</margin>
Thus we have received from the ancient fathers of the Hebrews the names of the angels presiding over the planets and signs: for Saturn, Zapkiel; for Jupiter, Zadkiel; for Mars, Camael; for the Sun, Raphael; for Venus, Haniel; for Mercury, Michael; and for the Moon, Gabriel. These are those seven spirits who always stand before the face of God, to whom is entrusted the management of the entire celestial and terrestrial kingdom which is beneath the orbit of the moon. For these (as the more secret theologians say) rule all things by a certain succession of hours, days, and years, just as the Astrologers teach concerning the planets over which they preside. For this reason, Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of alchemy and magic.</note> calls them the seven governors of the world, who, through the heavens as if through instruments, distribute the gathered influences of all the stars and signs into these lower realms. There are, however, those who assign them to the stars with slightly different names, saying that the intelligence named Oriphiel presides over Saturn; Zachariel over Jupiter; Samael over Mars; Michael over the Sun; Anael over Venus; Raphael over Mercury; and Gabriel over the Moon. Each of these governs the world for three hundred and fifty-four years and four months. This reign begins with the intelligence of Saturn; after which the intelligences of Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, the Moon, and the Sun rule in order; and then the government returns again to the spirit of Saturn.

<margin>The Treatise of Abbot Trithemius.</margin>

### Chapter XXV.

There are also other sacred names of both good and evil spirits deputed to individual offices, much more powerful than those mentioned before, which are extracted from the holy scriptures according to the art handed down by the <term>Mecubales</term> of the Hebrews, just as certain <margin>General rule.</margin> names of God are elicited from specific places. The general rule for these is that wherever in the holy scriptures something of the divine essence is expressed, a divine name can be rightly gathered from that place. But wherever a divine name is found expressed in the holy scriptures, there consider the ministry that lies beneath that name. Therefore, wherever the scripture speaks of the ministry or work of any spirit, whether good or evil, the name of that same spirit—whether good or evil—can be <margin>Canon for extraction.</margin> extracted from that place, observing this unchangeable canon: that from good things, the names of good spirits are drawn, and from evil things, the names of evil...

TABLES OF NUMERICAL TRANSPOSITIONS.

<note>These tables illustrate a system known as "Aiq Beker" or the "The Nine Chambers." It is a method of Kabbalistic numerology where letters are grouped by their numerical values (units, tens, and hundreds). By transposing letters of equal value, practitioners believed they could uncover hidden meanings within names or sacred texts.</note>

CCLXVI.
->ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,<-

## On finding the names of spirits and geniuses from the disposition of the celestial bodies. Chapter XXVI.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut drop cap 'T' showing a scholar seated at a desk in a study with books and a landscape visible through an architectural frame.</image-desc>

The ancient Magi <note>original: "Magi"; refers to the wise men or priestly caste of ancient Persia, often associated with astrology and magic</note> handed down the art of finding the name of a spirit for any desired effect, drawing it out from the disposition of the heavens. For example, if a certain celestial harmony is proposed to you for the purpose of crafting an image or a ring, or any other work to be performed under a specific constellation, and you wish to find the spirit who governs that work: having erected a figure of the heavens <note>a horoscope or astrological chart</note>, project the letters in their number and order starting from the degree of the ascendant <note>the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>, following the succession of the signs through each individual degree until the entire circle of heaven is completed. Then, those letters which fall into the locations of the stars whose protection you are using—noted down in number and order according to the power and strength of those same stars—constitute the name of a spirit, specifically a good one. If, however, you do this from the beginning of the western degree <note>the descendant</note> against the progress of the signs, the resulting spirit will be of the class of evil ones.

By this artifice, several masters of the Hebrews and Chaldeans <note>ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia famous for astrology</note> teach how to seek out the nature and name of the genius <note>a guardian spirit or guiding soul</note> of any man. Namely, once the degree of the ascendant of someone's birth is known, along with the other three corners of the sky <note>the "cardinal points": Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli</note>, then whichever planet has the most dignities <note>astrological "points" or strengths</note> in those four corners—which the Arabs call the *Almutez* <term>Almuten: the planet with the most essential dignity over a specific point in a chart</term>—that planet is noted first among the others. In the second place, the one closest to it in the number of dignities is noted, and so on in order for the rest of those who hold any dignity in the aforementioned corners. Having established this order, you must know their true place and degree in the heavens; then, beginning from the degree of the ascendant, project the twenty-two Hebrew letters through each degree according to the order of the signs. Then, the letters that fall into the places of the aforementioned stars—noted and arranged according to the order previously found among the stars, and properly combined according to the rules of the Hebrew language—constitute the name of the genius. To this name, according to custom, some monosyllabic name of divine omnipotence is added, such as *El* or *Iah* <note>Hebrew names for God</note>.

But if the projection of letters is made from the western angle and against the succession of the signs, and the letters which fall into the *Nadir* (that is, the opposite point) of the aforementioned stars are joined in the order we have described, they will constitute the name of an evil genius. However, the Chaldeans proceed by another way; for they do not take the *Almutez* of the corners, but the *Almutez* of the eleventh house <note>traditionally the house of "Good Fortune" and friends</note>, and they do in all things as has been said. They seek the evil genius from the *Almutez* of the angle of the twelfth house <note>traditionally the house of "Evil Spirit" and hidden enemies</note>, which they call the "evil demon," projecting from the western degree against the progress of the signs. There are also many Arabs and some Hebrews who seek the name of the genius from the five places of the *hylegians* <term>Hyleg: the "giver of life," a specific point in a birth chart used to determine longevity</term>, always making the projection from the beginning of Aries. The letters found according to the order of the *hylegians* known among astrologers are reduced into order and joined to constitute the name of the good genius. They elicit the name of the evil genius from the places opposite the *hylegians*, making the projection from the last degree of Pisces against the order of the signs. Others, however, do not take the places of the *hylegians*, but the places of the *Almutez* over the five *hylegians*, making the projection from the horoscope <note>the ascendant</note>, as was said in the previous methods; and these names, thus distributed according to proportionate numbers by starry calculation...

<meta>catchword: distributed</meta>

<summary>This page describes complex astrological methods for deriving the names of good and evil spirits or personal geniuses by mapping letters of the alphabet onto the degrees of a horoscope. It cites various traditions, including Hebrew, Chaldean, and Arabic practices, focusing on the "Almuten" and "Hyleg" points of a birth chart.</summary>

->On the calculatory art of such names from the tradition<-
->of the Cabalists. Chapter XXVII.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter E featuring two cherubic figures in a landscape setting; one is seated and the other appears to be leaning or reaching towards them.</image-desc>

THERE is yet another artifice for names of this kind which they call the "calculatory art" <note>The "Ars Calculatoria" refers to Gematria or other combinatorial methods used in the Kabbalah to derive new names from existing ones.</note>, and it is performed through the following tables. One enters with a certain sacred name—whether divine or angelic—into the descending column of letters, taking those letters which you find in the common angles beneath their stars and signs. When these are arranged in order, they constitute the name of a good spirit according to the nature of that star or sign under which you entered. But if you enter in the ascending column, taking the common angles above the stars and signs marked in the bottom line, it constitutes the name of an evil spirit. And these are the names of spirits from any order or heaven that serve, both good and evil, which according to this method you can multiply into nine names for as many orders; thus, by entering with one name, you can elicit another spirit of a higher order from it, whether good or evil. 

However, the principle of this calculation depends upon the names of God: for every voice has power in Magic insofar as it depends upon and is formed from the voice of God. Therefore, we must know that every angelic name ought to proceed from some primary name of God; for this reason, angels are said to "bear the name of God," according to that which is written: *for my name is in him* <note>A reference to Exodus 23:21.</note>. Thus, so that the names of good angels may be distinguished from the names of the evil ones, a name of divine omnipotence is often subjoined to them, such as *El*, or *On*, or *Iah*, or *Iod* <note>Hebrew divine names or suffixes: El (God/Might), Iah/Iod (shortened forms of the Tetragrammaton)</note>, and pronounced together with it. And since *Iah* is a name of beneficence, and *Iod* a name of deity, these two names are only attached to the names of angels. But the name *El*, which carries force and virtue, is therefore added not only to good spirits but sometimes even to evil spirits; for even evil spirits cannot exist or act anything without the power of God. 

Furthermore, it should be known that the common angles of the same star and sign must be taken, unless one has entered with a "mixed name," such as the names of genii <note>In this context, "genii" refers to personal guardian spirits or tutelary deities.</note> and those discussed in the preceding chapter, which are composed from the dispositions of heaven according to the harmony of various stars. For with these, whenever the table is to be entered, the common angle must be taken under the star or sign of the entering letter. There are, moreover, those who extend these tables so far as to think that even if one enters with the name of a star, or an office, or some desired effect, a daemon <note>The term "daemon" here is used in the classical sense of a spirit or intermediary, not necessarily an evil entity.</note> may be elicited, both good and evil, serving that office or effect. By a similar reasoning, entering with the proper name of any person <gloss>person</gloss>, the names of genii...
