# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

### Page 268

They trust that they can extract these names for themselves under that star which is seen to preside over such a person, according as they have recognized him to be either of Mars, of Saturn, of the Sun, or of the nature of another star, whether by <term>Physiognomy</term><note>The practice of judging character or predicting the future from facial features or body structure.</note>, or by the passions and inclination of the mind, or by his profession and fortune. And although primary names of this kind have little or no power from their own literal meaning, nevertheless, names extracted in this manner and derived from them are of the greatest efficacy—just as the solar rays collected in a hollow mirror burn most strongly, even when the sun itself is scarcely providing moderate heat. 

Furthermore, the order of letters in these tables under the stars and signs is almost identical to the order of <term>decans</term><note>Subdivisions of zodiac signs into ten-degree segments, each ruled by a different planet.</note>, ninths, and twelfths used by astrologers. Alfonso the Cypriot <note>Likely a reference to a medieval astrological authority or a specific manuscript tradition attributed to a "Cyprian."</note> once wrote about this calculating artifice, and someone else (I know not who) adapted it for Latin characters. Truly, because the letters of every language—as we showed in the first book—possess a celestial and divine origin in their number, order, and figure, I would easily concede that this calculation of the names of spirits can be performed not only through Hebrew letters, but also through Chaldean, Arabic, Egyptian, Greek, Latin, and any others, provided the tables are duly fashioned from them in imitation of the presiding powers. 

But here an objection is raised by many: it often happens in these tables that several men of different nature and fortune, on account of having the same name, happen to obtain the same <term>genius</term><note>A guardian spirit or guiding entity assigned to a person at birth.</note> or a spirit of the same name. It must be understood, therefore, that it is not considered absurd for the same spirit to be discerned by many souls, and for the same spirit to be able to preside over many. Furthermore, just as different men often use the same name, so also spirits of different offices and natures can be noted by one name and one and the same seal or character, yet with respect to different contexts. For just as the serpent at one time represents a type of Christ and at another the devil, so the same names and the same seals are equated now to some order of evil spirits, and now to some order of good angels. Finally, the ardent intention of the one invoking—through which our intellect is joined to the separate intelligences—ensures that we have now this spirit, now another, obedient to us, even if invoked under the same name.

# BOOK THREE.

### How the names of spirits are sometimes derived from the very things over which they are set. Chapter XXVIII.

<margin>Spirits of the planets.</margin>
<margin>Spirits of the signs.</margin>
<margin>4 Esdras 4</margin>
I find yet another kind of names imposed upon spirits from the very things over which they preside, as if borrowing a name from the stars, or men, or places, or times, or similar things, with a divine name added as a suffix <note>The suffix "-el" or "-iah" signifies a connection to the Divine/God</note>, in this manner: The spirit of Saturn is called Sabathiel; the spirit of Jupiter, Zedekiel; the spirit of Mars, Madimiel; the spirit of the Sun, Semeliel or Semeschiah; the spirit of Venus, Nogahel; the spirit of Mercury, Cochabiah or Cochabiel; the spirit of the Moon, Jareahel or Levanael. By a similar reasoning, they also name the spirits who preside over the signs <note>The signs of the Zodiac</note>, namely from the names of the signs themselves in order: from Aries, Teletiel; Suriel, Tomimiel, Sartamiel, Ariel, Betuliel, Masniel, Acrabiel, Chesetiel, Gediel, Deliel, Dagymiel. It is as if we were to say from Latin words: Ariel <note>from Aries, the Ram</note>, Tauriel <note>from Taurus, the Bull</note>, Geminiel, Cancriel, Leoniel, Virginiel, Libriel, Scorpiel, Sagittariel, Capriel, Aquariel, Pisciel; and from the planets: Saturniel, Joviel, Martiel, Soliah, Veneriel, Mercuriel, Lunael or Lunaiah.

Because truly (as we have also said above) all spirits, both good and evil, seek union with man—which they not infrequently attain in a certain way, whence we read in the sacred scriptures of some men being called gods, and angels, and devils—so also the names of those who, endowed with some singular excellence of virtue, or obstinate in persistent or incurable malice, have departed from this world, have allotted a place among the names of good or evil demons <note>The author uses "demon" in the classical sense of a spirit, not necessarily an evil one</note>, and are numbered with them, whether we consider the souls of those men or their good or evil geniuses <note>guiding spirits</note> to be signified. Thus we read in Esdras the name of the archangel Jeremiel, from Jeremiah the prophet; so Zachariel, from Zachariah; and Uriel, from Uriah the prophet whom Joachim killed. Similarly Samuel, Ezekiel, and Daniel are names of prophets and angels alike. Phaniel is the name of both an angel and the place in which Jacob wrestled throughout the night. Ariel is the name of an angel and is translated as "Lion of God"; sometimes it is also the name of an evil demon, and of the city which was called Ariopolis from it, where the idol Ariel was worshipped.

We also find many names of evil demons in the sacred scriptures to have taken their origin from the worst of men or the habitations of the worst of men, such as the name Astaroth, which is the name of an evil demon, and was formerly the name of the city of Og, King of Bashan, in which giants dwelt; similarly Astaroth, formerly a city of the Amorites; the valley of Rephaim; and Jeramiel, a region of the foreigners <note>original: "Allophylorum," often referring to the Philistines</note>. There are also names of idols and evil demons, such as Remma, the image of a Damascene idol; Chemosh, the idol of Moab; Milcom, the idol of the Ammonites; Bel, the idol of the Babylonians; Adramelech, the idol of the Assyrians; Dagon, the idol of the foreigners. And Philo relates that there were seven golden images among the Amorites, which they called the holy nymphs, which when invoked showed the Amorites their works hour by hour; and their names were the names of women, who were the wives of seven sinful men, who consecrated them after the flood, namely:

Canaan, Phut, Selath, Nimrod, Abirion, Elath, Defuat: and placed over them were precious stones, engraved and consecrated, in one of which was the power to restore light to the blind. Fire could not consume these stones, and sacred books were kept with the stones which likewise could not be burned by fire, nor cut by iron, nor erased by water, until the angel of the Lord took them away and buried them in the depths of the sea. Now indeed we also know that Nimrod, Chedorlaomer, Balak, and Amalek are names of kings adopted into the order of evil spirits <note>original: "cacodaemonum"</note>. Similarly, the giants are called by the common name of demons, *Enakim* <gloss>Anakim; Hebrew: ענקים, meaning "giants"</gloss>, because they did not participate in the image of God—that is, they did not receive the splendor of spiritual intellect. Instead, their reason multiplied evil forms of fraud and sin. Therefore, they are not numbered among the species of men (as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides, the famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher</note> says) but among the species of beasts and demons, except for the fact that they possess a human shape. And such, he says, were the sons of Adam who preceded Seth after Abel, of whom the Hebrew sages said that Adam fathered *Tochot* <gloss>Tokhot; Hebrew: תוכות, often interpreted here as "spirits" or "specters"</gloss>, that is, devils. But after he found grace in the eyes of the Lord, he fathered Seth in his own image and likeness—that is, one who attained human perfection according to the image of God. He who does not possess this is not numbered among the species of men, because of the depravities which are the cause of all evil and harm. There is also (according to the testimony of
<margin>Souls becoming demons.</margin>
Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>) a teaching of the Magi that wicked souls are converted into the nature of demons and become as destructive as they are. This is also attested by that word of Christ concerning Judas Iscariot, saying: "Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?" For this reason, they call them "adventitious demons," because they are recruited into the ranks of demons from human souls. Hence, the names of the worst men and of demons are the same, whether we call their souls by these names or their evil geniuses, who have put on the names of evil men like masks. Now indeed, even Behemoth and Leviathan signify both beasts and demons. By these examples, therefore, the diligent seeker can easily find and recognize the names of both good and evil spirits.

### On the Characters and Seals of Spirits. Chapter XXIX

<note>The decorative 'D' marks the start of a new technical discussion on magical symbols.</note>
We must now speak concerning the characters and seals of spirits. Characters are nothing other than certain unknown letters and writings, guarding the sacred names of gods and spirits from the use and reading of the profane. The ancients called these letters "hieroglyphic" or "sacred," because they were devoted solely to the sacred rites of the gods. Indeed, they considered it a sin to commit the sacred mysteries of the gods to those characters with which anything profane or shameful might be written by the common people. Whence Porphyry says that the ancients, wishing to hide God and divine virtues through sensible figures—signifying invisible things through those which are visible—handed down great mysteries as if in sacred letters, and explained them with certain symbolic figures. Thus, they dedicated a ball and all round things to the World, the Sun, the Moon, Hope, and Fortune; the circle to Heaven; parts of the circle to the Moon; pyramids and obelisks to Fire and the Olympian gods; the cylinder to the Sun and the Earth; the phallus <note>original: "penem"</note> to generation and to Juno, to whom they also gave a triangular figure because of the female sex. Therefore, this kind of character has another root...

# Another method of making characters, handed down by the Kabbalists.
## Chapter XXX.

Among the Hebrews, I find several methods of characters, one of which is the most ancient: namely, the ancient writing used by Moses and the prophets, the form of which must not be revealed to anyone rashly. For the letters they use today were established by Ezra <note>Referring to the transition from Paleo-Hebrew to the square Aramaic script</note>. There is also among them a writing which they call "Celestial," because they show it placed and formed among the stars, just as other astrologers derive the images of the signs from the outlines of the stars. There is yet another method among the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, a Jewish mystical tradition often adapted by Renaissance scholars into "Christian Cabala."</note>, formerly held in great veneration, but today become so common that it has almost found a place among profane things. It is as follows: Let the twenty-seven Hebrew characters be divided into three classes, each of which contains nine letters. The first class consists of Aleph, Beth, Gimel, Daleth, He, Vau, Zain, Cheth, Teth (א ב ג ד ה ו ז ח ט), which are the signs of the simple numbers <note>The units 1 through 9.</note> and of intellectual things, distributed among the nine orders of angels. The second class holds Iod, Caph, Lamed, Mem, Nun, Samech, Ain, Pe, Zade (י כ ל מ נ ס ע פ צ), the signs of the tens <note>The numbers 10 through 90.</note> and of celestial things within the nine orbs of the heavens. The third class truly holds the four remaining letters along with the five final forms in order, namely: Kuph, Res, Shin, Tau, and the final forms of Caph, Mem, Nun, Pe, and Zade (ק ר ש ת ך ם ן ף ץ). These are the signs of the hundreds <note>The numbers 100 through 900.</note> and of inferior things, namely the four simple elements and the five kinds of perfectly composed bodies. These three classes they then distribute into nine "chambers," of which the first is for the three units—namely the intellectual, the celestial, and the elemental. The second is for the twos, the third for the threes, and so on for the rest. And this method is most accepted among the Arabs, nor is there any script which may be so promptly and elegantly connected as the Arabic. However, it is necessary to know that angelic spirits, since they are pure intellects and entirely incorporeal, are not compelled by seals, characters, paintable figures, or other human gestures. But we, being ignorant of their essence and quality, devote and consecrate characters, figures, and seals to them based on their names, or their works, or otherwise according to our own affections. These are not things by which we can compel them to us in any way, but by which we rise up to them; insofar as through such unknowable characters and figures, we first direct our senses—both internal and external—toward them. Then, by a certain wonder of our reason, we are led into a religious veneration of them, and from there we are snatched away with our whole mind into ecstatic adoration. It is there, with miraculous faith, infallible hope, and life-giving love, invoking them in spirit and in truth with their true names and characters, that we obtain the power requested from them.

### Yet another method of characters, and concerning the seals of spirits which are received by revelation alone. Chapter XXXI.

There is another kind of character, received by revelation alone, which can be investigated by no other reason. The power of these characters is from the revealing deity itself, of whom they are certain hidden seals, breathing the harmony of some divinity; or they are like certain covenants or pacts of an initiated treaty between us and them. Of this kind is the seal shown to Constantine <note>The Roman Emperor Constantine the Great (r. 306–337 AD).</note>, which most called a cross, inscribed with Latin letters: IN THIS CONQUER <note>original: "IN HOC VINCE"</note>. And another was revealed to Antiochus, surnamed Soter <note>Antiochus I Soter (r. 281–261 BC), a Seleucid king.</note>, in the figure of a pentagon, which proclaims health; for when resolved into letters, it speaks the word *Hygeia* <note>original: "υγίεια"</note>, that is, HEALTH. In the confidence and power of these signs, both kings reported a distinguished victory against their enemies. So Judas, who for that reason was afterwards surnamed Maccabeus, when about to fight with the Jews against Antiochus Eupator, received that noble seal *MCBI* <note>original: "מכבי"</note> from an angel. By its power, they first laid low fourteen thousand men with a huge number of elephants, and then again thirty-five thousand of the enemy. For this seal is representative of the four-letter name <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH.</note>, and is a memorable symbol of the name of seventy-two letters by equality of number; and its explanation is: WHO IS LIKE UNTO THEE AMONG THE GODS, O LORD? <note>original: "מי כמוך באלים יהוה" (Mi Camoka Baelim Yehovah). The first letters of these Hebrew words form the name 'Maccabee'.</note>

Furthermore, Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote extensively on magic and theurgy.</note> speaks of these seals and characters in his book *On Oracles*, saying that the gods themselves indicated the things in which they delighted, by which they were summoned, and what ought to be offered to them. He says they also showed the very shapes their images should take, as well as the characters and figures, and that he learned these things from the oracle of Proserpina <note>The Roman name for Persephone, queen of the Underworld.</note>. He says, moreover, that Hecate <note>The goddess of magic, crossroads, and the night.</note> commanded how images should be set up for her: that they should be surrounded with wormwood; that domestic mice should be painted, which were her most beautiful ornaments and most pleasing to her soul; and that as many mice should be taken as she has forms. Then blood, myrrh, storax <note>A fragrant resin used in incense.</note>, and certain other things were to be burned. If these things were done, she would appear in a dream and answer the one performing these rites. But we shall subjoin the oracle of Hecate herself, for she speaks thus:

<margin>The Oracle of Hecate.</margin>
> Pay heed, I shall teach you what kind of image you should make for me:
> Take plants born in a wild place, and place wormwood
> Around it; then carve the whole and paint mice
> Such as are wont to dwell in houses; let these be
> Most beautiful ornaments and most pleasing to our soul.
> Then grind together myrrh, frankincense, storax, and the blood
> Of the mice themselves; then over the sacrifice
> Sing sacred words, and employ and set out as many mice
> As you see forms that I possess; then take laurel,
> And from its trunk prepare a sheath; then pour out
> Pious prayers to the image, and pay your owed
> Vows; if you do these things, you shall see me in your sleep.

Such were formerly the secret mysteries of the pagan gods and demons, by which they persuaded men that they could be compelled, detained, and bound. Hence Iamblichus <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who defended the use of ritual magic.</note> and Porphyry teach that one invoking sacred spirits <note>original: "dæmones" - in this context, referring to intermediary spirits or 'daemons' rather than modern 'demons'.</note> must honor each with their own proper respect, and distribute to each what is fitting—whether by favors, offerings, gifts, sacrifices, words, or characters—agreeable to their condition and as similar to them as possible. Otherwise, one will by no means attain the presence of the divinities or spirits, nor the desired effect; indeed, those invoked will attempt to do harm, especially to those who conduct themselves negligently in this matter.

### How good spirits are attracted by us, and how evil spirits are overcome by us.

### Chapter XXXII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting two winged putti or cherubs in a landscape, one appearing to hold a musical instrument or object, framed within a square border.</image-desc>

The effective presence of religion gains the influence of spirits <note>original: "dæmonum"; in this context, the author refers to "daemons" in the classical sense of intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense</note>, for no work of any wonderful efficacy can be performed in religion unless some good spirit is present there as the director and fulfiller of the work. Good spirits, however, although they are attracted by us in various ways, can be bound by no chains—or at least only with great difficulty—but are rather to be entreated with certain sacred oaths. As we read in Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius, a 2nd-century Roman philosopher and author of 'The Golden Ass'</note>, they are called upon by 
<margin>How it is necessary to entreat spirits.</margin>
the celestial stars, by the powers of the underworld, by the natural elements, by the silence of the night, by the "conceived fruits" <note>original: "adepta conceptitia"; likely referring to ritual offerings or symbolic seeds</note>, by the "increments of the Nile" <note>the rising waters of the Nile river</note>, by the secrets of Memphis, and the rattles <term>sistra: ancient Egyptian percussion instruments used in the worship of Isis</term> of Pharos. And elsewhere in Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>: "You who emerged from the linen, who sit in the place, who sail in the ship, who change form every hour, and are changed in every sign of the zodiac." By these and similar symbolic prayers and hymns, because they are signs of divine virtues, spirits sometimes accommodate themselves to human uses—not because they are compelled by any necessity, but they approach more easily of their own accord and by a certain habit, overcome by the prayers of those who invoke them. Hence, in Porphyry’s *Book of Responses*, Hecate <note>The Greek goddess of magic and crossroads</note> says:

> Entreated by your words, I have come hither.

And in the same book elsewhere it says:

> Overcome by the prayers of men, the celestial powers
> Are forced to seek the earth, and reveal future events.

<margin>The reason for the assistance of spirits.</margin>
But also the fellowship of divinity with the human mind brings it about that the good spirits themselves willingly assist us and communicate their power and virtue to us. They help us daily with illuminations, inspirations, oracles, prophecies, dreams, miracles, wonders, divinations, and auguries, working and acting upon our souls as their fellow images, shaping them by their influences and making them most like themselves—to such an extent that our soul often performs wonders almost as marvelous as those the celestial spirits are accustomed to do. Evil spirits, however, are overcome by us with the help of the good ones, especially when the petitioner excels in holiness toward God and chants sacred words and a "terrible speech" <note>meaning a speech that inspires awe or dread in the spirits</note>—namely, by conjuring through divine power, through the venerable names and seals <term>signacula: mystical symbols or characters used in ritual magic</term> of supernatural virtues, through miracles, through sacraments, through sacred mysteries and the like. Indeed, evil spirits fear these conjurations or exorcisms insofar as they are performed in the name of religion and divine power. Hence, even profane men often bind or cast out evil spirits with such sacred conjurations, for the spirits cannot endure them. Thus Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian, a 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note> says in his book *That Idols are Not Gods*: "That spirits, when adjured by the true God, immediately yield to us and confess, and are forced to depart from possessed bodies; they either leap out instantly or vanish gradually, according as the faith of the sufferer helps, or the grace of the one swearing inspires." And Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius, a 4th-century theologian and defender of orthodoxy</note> in his book on...

# BOOK THREE.

In various inquiries, he says that there does not exist a word more terrible or more destructive to the power of demons than the beginning of the sixty-seventh Psalm: *Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered* <note>Psalm 68:1 in modern numbering; original: "Exurgat deus, & dissipentur inimici eius"</note>: for as soon as the word is spoken, the devil immediately wailing vanishes and disappears. And Origen <note>A prominent early Christian scholar (c. 185–253 AD)</note> in his work *Against Celsus* says that the naming of the name of Jesus has been seen many times to cast out innumerable demons both from the souls and bodies of men, and has exercised the greatest power in those from whom the demons had been driven out. But Apollonius, recognizing at once what it was, rebuked it with heavy and insulting words, and urged his companions to do the same: for he knew this was the best remedy against such invasions. When the companions had obeyed his words, the shrieking phantom fled quickly like a ghost: for this genus of demons is so fearful that they are moved, tremble, and are driven away even by feigned terror and false or impossible threats. Whence Chaeremon the sacred scribe <note>An Egyptian Stoic philosopher and priest</note> says these are the things by which demons are most greatly compelled.

There is, moreover, as was said above, a certain genus of demons not so harmful, but even close to men, so that they are even affected by human passions; and many of these rejoice in the conversation of men and gladly dwell with them. Some are desperately in love with women, others with boys; others delight in the company of various domestic or wild animals. Some inhabit the woods and groves, others dwell around springs and meadows. Thus Fauns and Lemures <note>spirits of the dead</note> inhabit the fields; Naiads, the springs; Potamides, the rivers; Nymphs, the pools and waters; Oreades, the mountains; Humedes, the meadows; Dryads and Hamadryads, the woods, which are also inhabited by Satyrs and Sylvans; and these same delight in trees and turf, just as the Naptae and Agaptae delight in flowers; the Dodonae in acorns; and the Paleae and Feniliae in fodder and the countryside. Therefore, whoever wishes to invoke these can easily do so in the places where they dwell, by alluring them with fragrant fumigations, with sweeter sounds on lutes and musical instruments which have been fashioned from the intestines and appropriate woods of certain animals; having also applied <note>original: "adhibitis"</note> songs, poems, and incantations suitable for this purpose: and that which...

### On the bonds of spirits, and their adjurations and expulsions. Chapter XXXIII.

<insert>V</insert>incula <note>The bonds</note>—The bonds by which spirits are bound, entreated, or expelled are threefold. Some of them are taken from the elemental world, such as when we adjure a spirit by lower and natural things related or adverse to it, insofar as we wish to invoke or expel it—such as by flowers, herbs, animals, snow, ice, the depths of the earth <note>original: "tartara"</note>, fire, and such things, just as these are also often inserted into divine praises, blessings, and consecrations. This is evident in the *Song of the Three Children* <note>A biblical hymn from the Book of Daniel</note>, and in that psalm: *Praise the Lord from the heavens*, and in the consecration and blessing of the Paschal candle. Indeed, this bond works upon spirits through the power of perception by reason of love or hatred, insofar as the spirits themselves preside over or favor some natural thing (or even something beyond nature) and abhor another—just as these things are also in mutual love or hatred among themselves. Hence that saying of Proclus: "Just as a lion fears a cock, especially a white one, so a spirit appearing in the form of a lion suddenly vanished when a cock was presented." The second bond is taken from the celestial world, namely when we adjure by the heaven, the stars, and by their motions, rays, light, grace, brightness, nobility, strength, influence, wonders, and such things. And this bond works upon spirits by way of a certain admonition...

### On the order of souls and on heroes. Chapter XXXIV.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' containing an illustration of a seated figure, likely a scholar or cleric, at a desk.</image-desc> After the choirs of blessed spirits, the next is the order of souls <term>animasticus: relating to the "Anima Mundi" or World Soul</term>, which the Hebrew theologians call the *Issim* <note>original: "Issim," meaning "Strong Men" or "Individuals"</note>, that is, strong and robust men. They perpetually provide for mortals with the same virtues and benefits they once did in this life. Or perhaps they were procreated from the secret seed of those above, whom they believe were born from the mingling of gods or demons with humans; and therefore they were allotted a certain middle nature, being neither angels nor men. This is an opinion which Lactantius also follows. And there are even today those who have commerce and conjugal mingling with demons; and it is now believed by all that Merlin the British seer was the son of a demon and born of a virgin. # ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<note>The author is discussing the origins of the Huns, citing a legend that they descended from "filthy" women and spirits.</note> It is said that women of remarkable appearance and wit, having departed from the camps of Filimirus or (as others say) Idanthresus, King of the Goths, migrated into the wilderness of Asiatic Scythia beyond the Maeotian marshes. There, they were embraced by Fauns and Satyrs, and gave birth to the first Huns. Furthermore, according to the author Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, a 11th-century Byzantine philosopher known for his writings on demonology</note>, demons sometimes cast forth seed from which certain small creatures arise. Therefore, the power of these heroes in arranging and ruling these lower realms is no less than the power of gods and demons; they have their own distributed duties and protections. For this reason, temples, images, altars, sacrifices, vows, and other mysteries of religion were dedicated to them just as to the gods themselves. Their invoked names were believed to possess divine and magical virtues for performing certain miracles, which Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Christian historian</note> relates many experienced regarding the invoked name of Apollonius of Tyana. We read of many such things concerning Hercules, Atlas, Aesculapius, and other heroes of the nations among the ancient poets, historians, and philosophers; but these are the ravings of the heathens.

Regarding our own holy heroes <note>The author refers to Christian Saints as "heroes" in the classical sense of divinized humans</note>, we believe they prevail through divine power. Indeed, the soul of the Messiah <note>original: "anima Meschihæ"</note> rules over all of them; he is Jesus Christ himself, who through his various saints—as if through members adapted for this purpose—administers and distributes the various gifts of his grace in these lower realms. Each saint is allotted a peculiar duty of cooperation. Hence, when we implore them through various prayers and invocations according to the manifold distribution of graces, each most willingly imparts to us their own gifts, benefits, and favors. They do so much more promptly and even more abundantly than the angelic powers, because they are closer to us and more related to our nature, as they themselves were once humans and suffered human affections and infirmities; their names, ranks, and offices are better known to us.

### Concerning mortal and earthly gods. Chapter XXXV.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure surrounded by foliage and decorative scrollwork.</image-desc>After those, the next are the mortal gods, whom we likewise call heroes, and earthly gods, or companions of the supernal gods; namely the kings, and princes, and pontiffs <note>high-ranking religious or civil leaders</note> by whom this world is ruled, and by whose laws it is disposed. We look up to, worship, and venerate these men as gods for this reason: because God himself allowed his own name to be shared with them, and confirmed it to them by his own naming, calling them gods, just as he said to Moses, saying: *I have made you a god to Pharaoh* <note>Exodus 7:1</note>. And elsewhere he commanded concerning them, saying: *You shall not disparage the gods* <note>Exodus 22:28</note>. And again: *If the theft be hidden, the master of the house shall be brought to the gods* <note>Exodus 22:8; often translated as "judges" in modern bibles</note>. And the Psalmist says: *The princes of the peoples are gathered together with the God of Abraham, for the strong gods of the earth are greatly exalted* <note>Psalm 47:9</note>. And elsewhere: *God stood in the council of gods, but in the midst he judges the gods* <note>Psalm 82:1</note>. And a little after: *I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High* <note>Psalm 82:6</note>. Furthermore, he even commanded that they be worshipped and venerated, decreeing tithes and first-fruits for them, and granting them the right of the sword, and forbidding that they be cursed, and commanding that obedience be shown to them even if they are difficult. Hence all antiquity called its princes "gods," and worshipped them as divine powers, just as Janus testifies in Ovid, saying in the first book of the *Fasti*:

> Then I was reigning, when the earth was full of gods,
> And divine powers were mingled with human places.

And the divine Plato, in the third book of the *Republic*, established that princes, both living and dead, should be celebrated with divine honors: which institution has been received among all nations and from the earliest age—namely, to deify Princes with divine honors and consecrate them with eternal memory. Hence they bestowed upon cities, and provinces, and mountains, and rivers, and waters, and islands, and the sea, names of those men that would never fail. Then they dedicated pyramids, colossi, triumphal arches, trophies, statues, shrines, games, and festivals to them with great pomp; they who also called the heavens, and stars, and days, and months by their names. Hence January is from Janus, July from Julius, August from Augustus: so the day of Mercury <note>Wednesday</note> is from Mercury Trismegistus, the day of Jove <note>Thursday</note> from Jove <note>Jupiter</note>; which custom we read was observed not only by the Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans, but even by the furthest barbarians, the Goths, Danes, and Teutons. Hence, as Saxo Grammaticus <note>A medieval Danish historian</note> testifies, what those people call the day of Mercury, these call the day of Odin <note>original: "Othinus"</note>; what those call from Jove, these call Thor, from Odin and Thor, formerly kings of the Goths and Danes. Nor were the Goths named for any other reason than that they [called] their highest god...

### How Man Was Created in the Image of God. Chapter XXXVI.

<margin>Mercury Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure who originated the Hermetic tradition of philosophy and magic.</note></margin>
The most transcendent God (as Trismegistus says) fashioned two images similar to himself: namely, the world and man. In one of these, he might play with certain wondrous operations, while in the other, he might enjoy delights. Since he himself is one, he created one world; since he himself is infinite, he created the world round; since he himself is eternal, he created the world incorruptible and everlasting; since he himself is immense, he created the world the greatest of all things; since he himself is the highest goodness, he adorned the world with vital seeds, bringing forth all things from itself. And since he himself is omnipotent, by his will alone—not by any necessity of nature—he created the world not from pre-existing matter, but from nothing. And since he is the highest goodness, embracing his Word (which is the first <term>Idea</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, an "Idea" is the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing.</note> of all things) with his best will and essential love, he fabricated this external world according to the pattern of the internal, ideal world. Yet, he sent nothing out from the essence of the Idea, but created from nothing that which he held from eternity through the Idea. God also created man in his own image:

<margin>The image of God is the world; the image of the world is man.</margin> for just as the world is the image of God, so man is the image of the world. For this reason, some think it was said that man was not created simply as the image of God, but *according to* the image, as if he were the image of an image. Therefore, he is called the <term>microcosm</term> <note>From the Greek for "little world."</note>, that is, the lesser world. The world is a rational, immortal living being; man is likewise a rational living being, but mortal—that is, dissoluble. For (as Hermes says), since the world itself is immortal, it is impossible for any part of it...

to perish: therefore the name of death is empty. And just as a vacuum exists nowhere, so it is with dying. Therefore we say that a person, when the soul and body are separated, does not perish, nor is any part of them turned into nothingness. Nevertheless, the true image of God is His Word <note>original: "verbum suum"</note>, wisdom, life, light, and truth, existing through itself; of which image the human soul is a reflection. It is because of this that we are said to be made in the image of God, not in the image of the world or of created things. For just as God can neither be touched, nor perceived by the ears, nor beheld by the eyes, so the soul of man can neither be seen, nor heard, nor touched. And just as God Himself is infinite and can be compelled by no one, so too the human soul is free, and can neither be forced nor measured. Furthermore, as God governs this whole world and whatever is in it by mind alone, so the human soul encompasses that world in thought; and—what is unique to it alone along with God—just as God moves and governs the whole world by a mere nod, so the human soul drives and rules its own body by a mere nod. It was necessary, therefore, for the human soul, thus sealed by the word of God, to also bring the corporeal man into the most perfect pattern of the world. Thus, man is called "another world" <note>The concept of the Microcosm, or "little world."</note> and another image of God, because he has within himself everything contained in the greater world, so that nothing is left out which is not also truly and realistically found within the human being. And all these things within him perform the same functions as they do in the greater world. There are in him the elements, through the truest properties of their nature. There is in him an ethereal little body, the vehicle of the soul, corresponding in proportion to the heavens. There is in him the vegetative life of plants, the senses of animals, the celestial spirit, angelic reason, and the divine mind; and the true union and divine possession of all these things flowing together into one. Hence, in the Sacred Scriptures, man is called "every creature." Not only is man made another world, embracing all its parts within himself, but he even conceives and contains God Himself. Hence Xystus the Pythagorean <note>Likely referring to the "Sentences of Sextus," a collection of moral aphorisms popular in the Renaissance.</note> says that the mind of man is the temple of God, which Paul expressed much more clearly, saying: "You are the temple of God" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 3:16.</note>; and the Holy Scripture testifies to this same thing in many
<margin>
Man, the temple of God.
</margin>
places. Man is, therefore, the most expressive likeness of God, since man contains in himself all things that are in God. But God contains all things through a certain eminence, by His own power and in simplicity, as the cause and principle of all things; whereas He gave to man the power to similarly contain all things, but in actuality and through a certain composition, as the connection, bond, and knot of all things. Thus man, and man alone, enjoys this honor: that he has a shared symbol <note>term: "symbolum" — here meaning a shared essence or connecting link</note> with all things, an operation with all things, and a conversation with all things. He shares a

## Concerning the human soul, and by what means it is joined to the body.
### Chapter XXXVII.

<margin>What the human soul is.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial "A" featuring a seated figure surrounded by ornate vine and leaf patterns.</image-desc>
The human soul is a certain divine light, created according to the image of the Word—the cause of causes and the first exemplar—and it is a substance of God, shaped by the seal whose character is the eternal Word. Likewise, the human soul is a certain divine substance, indivisible, and present in its entirety to every part of the body, produced by an incorporeal Author in such a way that it depends solely on the power of the agent, not on the lap of matter. The soul is a substantial number <note>A Pythagorean and Platonic concept where "number" refers to an essential, organizing principle rather than a mere quantity.</note>, uniform, self-turning, and rational, surpassing all bodies and material things by a vast interval; its division is not according to matter, nor does it proceed from lower and thicker things, but from the efficient cause. For it is not a quantitative number, but is removed from all corporeal laws; hence it is neither divided nor multiplied by parts. The soul is therefore a certain divine substance, emanating from divine fountains, bringing with it a number: not indeed that divine number by which the Craftsman <note>original: "opifex," referring to the Demiurge or Creator.</note> arranged all things, but a rational number, by which, having proportion with all things, it is able to understand all things.

Such then is the human soul, according to the opinion of the Platonists, proceeding immediately from God; it is joined to this thicker body through suitable intermediaries. Whence, first indeed in its very descent, it is wrapped in a celestial and airy little body, which they call the ethereal vehicle of the soul <note>original: "æthereum animæ uehiculū," a Neoplatonic concept of a "spirit-body" that bridges the gap between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh.</note>; others call it the chariot of the soul. By this medium, at the command of God, who is the center of the world, it is first poured into the middle point of the heart, which is the center of the human body, and from there it is diffused through all the parts and members of its body. This happens when it joins its "chariot" to the natural heat; through that heat to the spirit generated from the heart; through this spirit it immerses itself in the humors <note>The bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, etc.) believed to govern health.</note>; and through those it adheres to the limbs. Thus it becomes equally close to all of these, even though it is poured from one into another: just as the heat of a fire adheres most closely to air and water, even though it is carried through the air to the water. Thus it is clear how the immortal soul, through an immortal little body—namely, the ethereal vehicle—is enclosed by a thicker and mortal body. But when these intermediaries are dissolved or fail through disease or evil, then the soul itself recollects its being through each medium and flows back into the heart, which was the first receptacle of the soul. When the spirit of the heart fails and the heat is extinguished, the soul leaves it and the man dies; the soul flies away with this ethereal vehicle, and as it departs, the guardian spirits <note>original: "genii custodes dæmones"</note>...

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;What divine gifts man receives from above from the individual orders of the heavens and the intelligences.

### Chapter XXXVIII.

<margin>What man receives from the planets</margin>
Through the seven planets, as if through instruments from the highest source of all good, all virtues are poured into men: through **Saturn** <note>The planet associated with time, melancholy, and deep thought</note> comes sublime contemplation, profound intelligence, gravity of judgment, firm speculation, stability, and an immovable purpose; through **Jupiter** comes unshakable prudence, temperance, benevolence, piety, modesty, justice, faith, grace, religion, equity, clemency, and royalty; through **Mars** comes undaunted truth, constant strength and fortitude, the fire of courage and the power of action and practice, and an unchangeable vehemence of mind; through the **Sun** comes nobility of soul, clarity of imagination, the nature of knowing and opining, maturity, counsel, zeal, the light of justice, reason and judgment separating right from wrong, purging light from the darkness of ignorance, the glory of discovered truth, and charity—the queen of all virtues; through **Venus** comes fervent love, sweetest hope, the movement of desire, order, longing, beauty, sweetness, the desire for increase, and the propagation of oneself; through **Mercury** comes penetrating faith and belief, clear reasoning, the vigor of interpreting and pronouncing, gravity of speech, sharpness of wit, the discourse of reason, and a swift mobility of the senses; through the **Moon** comes peaceful harmony, fecundity, the power of generating and increasing, of waxing and waning, and moderate temperance, and a faith which, moving in things both open and hidden, provides leadership to all, yet moves toward earthly things for the sake of cultivating life and granting growth to oneself and others. These influences are drawn principally from those seven intelligences <note>The angelic beings or "presiding spirits" of the planets</note> who stand before the face of God, who arrange the soul as the seat of those virtues. The planets, however, only arrange the body, rendering the temperament <note>original: "complexionem," referring to the balance of bodily humors</note> manageable, and proportioned and tempered for all good things; they are like the instruments of the intelligences. But God, as the primary cause, provides both the influx and the increase with all things. Therefore, those who have scrutinized the virtues and various dispositions of souls judge that they obtain various natures according to the diversity of the mediums through which they pass to us, and that these are joined with the bodies themselves only through the proportioned stars. Thus, in a body guided by a Jovial <note>Jupiter-like</note> temperament, they believe a soul is infused that is tempered by the deity and intelligence of Jupiter, and so on for the rest. According to which disposition, if the soul works well in this body, being purged and expiated, it returns to the deity and the mansion from which it descended.
<margin>What man receives from the angelic orders.</margin>
And now, man is also strengthened with wondrous virtues by the angelic orders: for instance, by the **Angels**, that he may be a messenger of the divine will and an interpreter of the divine mind; by the **Archangels**, that he may rule over all things over which they are given presidency—the beasts of the earth, the fish of the sea, and the birds of the heaven; by the **Principalities**, that all things may be subject to him, and he himself [ruler] of all...

## How celestial influences, though they are good by nature,
## are corrupted in these lower things, and become causes of evil.
### Chapter XXXIX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a cherub or putto holding a circular frame or shield.</image-desc>Since all virtue and power is from above—from God, from the Intelligences, and the stars, who can neither err nor do evil—it is necessary that all evils, and whatever is found discordant and dissonant in these lower things, proceed not from the malice of the influence, but from the bad disposition of the receiver, just as **Chrysippus** <note>A Stoic philosopher known for his works on fate and ethics.</note> rightly sang:

> How falsely mortals accuse the gods, and foolishly complain:
> For we ourselves are the cause of our own evils,
> And his own folly harms each man.

Hence **Jupiter**, remembering the fate of **Aegisthus** who was slain by **Orestes**, says in the council of the gods in **Homer**:

> O what a crime, the mortal race first blames us deities,
> And thinks us the cause and fountain of the evils
> Which come: but they perish by their own wicked deeds,
> When beyond fate they seek troubles for themselves by their own will.

### Page 292

Therefore, when the perversity of a subject <note>The "subject" refers to the person or material thing receiving the influence.</note> receives influences perversely, or when its weakness cannot endure the power of the higher realms, then from the influx of the celestial bodies—received thus into matter full of discord—there results something dissonant, deformed, and evil. Meanwhile, the celestial powers themselves always remain good. While they exist in themselves and flow from the Giver of Lights <note>A reference to God, derived from James 1:17.</note> through the holy Intelligences <note>Angels or spiritual administrators of the spheres.</note> and the heavens until they reach the Moon, their influence is good, as if in the first degree. 

But afterward, when it is received in a baser subject, the influence itself becomes base. For then, because of the diverse nature of the receiver, it is received in diverse ways; and with the qualities within that same subject disagreeing among themselves, the influence is varied and suffers along with the suffering subject. Thus, from everything finally contained within the subject, something results other than what the higher powers poured in. 

Therefore, a harmful quality in these lower things is far removed from the influx of the celestial beings. Just as the affliction of a bleary-eyed person should not be blamed on the light, nor a fire on the heat, nor wounds on the iron, nor chains and prisons on the judge—but rather on those who are ill-disposed or who act wickedly—so too must the blame for evils not be cast upon the celestial influxes. 

Thus, in those of us who are well-disposed, the influx of the higher powers "works all things together for good" <note>original: "omnia cooperantur in bonum"; a citation of Romans 8:28.</note>; but for those ill-disposed, and in whom that divine spark within us has withdrawn because of our sins, all things turn to evil. Therefore, the cause of all our evils is sin, which is the disorder and distemper of our soul. When the soul is thus ruling poorly, or is prostrate and declining from what the celestial influxes require, all things rebel and are disordered to our destruction. 

Then, in the human body—otherwise most temperate and composed of the most consonant harmony—there arises a distemper of the elements. Evil humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note> surge up, and even good ones become disordered and separated from one another, and by a certain turn of events, they vex and torment the body. Then a most violent dissonance is felt, either from excess, or from lack, or from an internal accident, or from excessive food, from which superfluous humors are birthed. From this same cause, infirmities arise; even the animal spirits <note>The subtle substances in the body believed to act as the interface between soul and flesh.</note>, having lost their restraint, clash in battle. 

Then the celestial influxes, otherwise good in themselves, are rendered harmful to them, just as the light of the Sun is to ill-disposed eyes. 

<margin>What the higher powers pour into the wicked.</margin>

Then **Saturn** influences anxiety, weariness, melancholy, delusions, sadness, stubbornness, rigidity, blasphemy, despair, lies, the masks of ghosts, the terrors of sepulchers, the dread of burial mounds, and the provocations of demons. 

**Jupiter**, however, then influences greed, wicked opportunities for wealth, and tyranny. 

**Mars** influences impetuous anger, profane arrogance, the recklessness of audacity, and fierce stubbornness. 

The **Sun** influences imperious pride and insatiable ambition. 

**Venus** influences the deceptions of concupiscence, wanton loves, and shameful lusts. 

**Mercury** influences frauds, deceits, lies, the machinations of evil men, and a readiness for sinning. 

The **Moon** influences the unstable progress of all things, and whatever is contrary to human nature. 

And in this way, man himself, because of his dissimilarity with the celestial beings, receives harm where he ought to have reported a benefit. Because of this same dissonance with the celestial beings (as **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy and the soul.</note> says), they are even subjected...

...then men [are handed over] to evil demons, who prepare themselves like the gods' executioners <note>original: "lictores," Roman officers who carried out sentences</note> to torment them. ->That a divine character is impressed upon every man, by the power of which he can reach the point of performing wonders.<-

### Chapter XL.

<margin>Why fierce beasts fear fragile man.</margin>
It has been proven by no small experience that there is a certain power of dominating and binding implanted in man by nature. For as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> testifies, the elephant is said to show the way with mercy and gentleness to a man wandering lost in the wilderness. The same author says that the elephant, noticing the tracks of a man before seeing the man himself, is said to tremble with fear of an ambush, to stop, look around, and be terrified. In the same way, the tiger—more ferocious than all other wild beasts—is said to move its cubs immediately upon seeing a man. We read many similar things in various authors who have written great volumes about animals. But from where do these animals recognize that man is to be feared, whom they have never seen? And if they have seen and known him often, why do they fear him, when they so greatly surpass him in size, strength, and speed? What this nature of man is that strikes this fear into wild beasts, all the historians of animals inquire and hint at, but they have left it to others to teach and prove.

Regarding this, Apollonius of Tyana <note>A famous Neopythagorean philosopher and miracle-worker</note> (as read in Philostratus), upon seeing a boy leading a massive elephant and being asked by Damis where this great obedience of such a vast animal toward a small child came from, replied: it is from a certain "active terror" implanted in man by the Creator. Sensing this, the lower creatures and all animals fear and revere man himself, who is like a terrifying "character" <note>A spiritual seal or mark</note> and the signet of God impressed upon man. By this, all things are subjected to him and acknowledge him as superior, whether it be a servant or an animal; for otherwise, a boy could not rule herds and elephants, nor a king terrify a people, nor a judge the accused.

Therefore, this character is impressed upon men by the Divine Idea, which the Cabalists of the Hebrews call *Pahad* <note>original: פחד; meaning "Fear" or "Awe," the fifth Sephirah on the Tree of Life</note>, and the "Left Hand" and "Sword of God." Nor does man only have a sign by which he is feared, but also one by which he is loved; the Idea of this in the divine numerations <note>The Sephirot or divine emanations</note> is called *Hesed* <note>original: חסד; meaning "Mercy" or "Loving-kindness"</note>, which signifies clemency, and the "Right Hand" and "Scepter of God." From these divine numerations, through the Intelligences and the stars, signs and characters are impressed upon us, each according to his capacity and purity. These signs the first "protoplast" <note>The first-formed man, Adam</note> undoubtedly possessed in all integrity and fullness, when—attracted by calm gentleness and subjected by terror—all living creatures came to him as to a lord, so that he might give them names. But after the sin of transgression, he fell from that dignity along with all his descendants; yet not entirely...

that divine mark <note>original: "character"; referring to the 'Seal of God' or the divine image imprinted on the human soul</note> is extinguished within us; but the more one is weighed down by sin, the further he stands from these divine marks and the less he receives of them. Where he ought to receive kindness and reverence, he instead falls into the service and fear of others—both of animals and of men and demons. Sensing this, Cain was afraid, saying to God: *Everyone who finds me will kill me* <note>Genesis 4:14</note>. Indeed, he feared beasts and demons, not so much men, who were very few. In ancient times, however, many men who lived in innocence, leading the best of lives, still enjoyed that obedience and power, such as Samson, David, and Daniel over lions, Elisha over bears, Paul over the viper; and many anchorites <note>hermits or religious recluses</note> lived in the deserts, in the dens and caves of wild beasts, neither fearing them nor receiving any harm. For just as that divine mark is darkened by sin, so when sin is purged and expiated, it shines forth again more and more.

## Various opinions on what happens to man after death.
### Chapter XLI.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'O' depicting the bust of a man with a beard wearing a headwrap or turban.</image-desc>
It is appointed for all men once to die; death is fatal to all. But one kind is natural, another violent, another voluntarily undertaken; another is imposed for a crime by human laws, or inflicted by God because of sin, so that they seem not to have paid a debt to nature, but to have rendered a penalty for their offenses—which (as the masters of the Hebrews say) God remits to no one. Whence the assembly of Hezekiah <note>referring to the Talmudic tradition of the 'Men of Hezekiah'</note> handed down that after the destruction of the sanctuary, although no order of judicial execution remained, nevertheless no one guilty of death escaped without retaliation through the fourfold types of punishment by which they used to be condemned. For he who had deserved death by stoning was, by God's providence, either cast down from a roof, trampled by wild beasts, or overwhelmed by a ruin or a fall. He who had deserved fire ended his life either consumed by a conflagration, or by a poisonous bite, the strike of a serpent, or by toxin. He who was to perish by the sword was slaughtered either by the violence of the government, by a popular tumult, by faction, or by the snares of robbers. He who was to be hanged by a noose was either suffocated in a whirlpool of water or extinguished by some other strangling plague. And by this reasoning of doctrine, even the great Origen <note>an early Christian theologian</note> thought that Gospel of Christ should be explained: *He who strikes with the sword, perishes by the sword.*
<margin>Adrastia.</margin>
Furthermore, even the ethnic <note>pagan</note> philosophers pronounce that this order of retaliation is Adrastia <note>the Greek goddess of inescapable destiny</note>—namely, the inevitable power of divine laws, by which in future circuits <note>cycles of rebirth</note> it is repaid to each according to the reason and merits of his prior life. Thus, he who ruled unjustly in a prior life might fall back into a servile state in another life; he who polluted his hands with blood is forced to undergo retaliation; he who lived a beastly life is cast down, rolled back into a brutal body.
<margin>Plotinus.</margin>
Plotinus writes about these things in his book *On One's Own Daemon*: "Whosoever among men have preserved their human property are born again as men; but whosoever have used only their senses return as brute animals," yet in such a way that those who lived chiefly by sense joined with anger become animals...

### THIRD BOOK.

...wild beasts arise; however, those who use their senses only for lust and pleasure return as deceitful and gluttonous animals. But if they have lived not so much by the senses as by the degeneration of the senses, they sprout again as plants; for in these, only the vital force flourished, and their only care was to be changed into plants. Truly, those who lived too much charmed by musical melodies, but were not depraved in other matters, are reborn as musical animals. And those who ruled without reason become eagles, unless they are infected by some wickedness. But he who has attained civic virtue returns as a human. And Solomon himself in the Proverbs calls man now a lion, a tiger, a bear, or a boar; now a hare, a greyhound, or a rabbit; now an ant, a hedgehog, a serpent, or a spider; now he names him an eagle, a lizard, a rooster, or another bird, and many things of this sort. However, the Hebrew Cabalists <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah)</note> do not allow that souls are cast down into brute beasts; yet they do not deny that those who have utterly cast off reason are left to brutal affection and imagination in another life.

<margin>Souls return to this life three times.</margin>
They also assert that souls are revolved back here three times, and no more; since this number seems abundantly sufficient for the purging of sins, according to that passage in Job: *He has delivered his soul from going into destruction, but living he might see the light.* <note>original: "Liberauit animam suā..."</note> Behold, God works all these things three times for each person, so that he may recall their souls from corruption and illuminate them with the light of the living. But now at last, let us see what the ancients felt concerning the dead. When a man dies, the body returns to the earth from which it was taken; the mind returns to the heavens from whence it descended, just as Ecclesiastes says: *The dust returns to its earth where it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it,* which Lucretius expressed in these little verses:
> That which was of the earth before, yields back
> Into the lands; and what was sent from the borders of the ether,
> The shining temples of heaven receive that back again.

->But Ovid says it better in these verses:<-

> Man has twice two parts: the spirits of the dead, the flesh, the soul, and the shade;
> Twice two places receive these four.
> The earth covers the flesh, the shade flits around the tomb,
> The Underworld <note>original: "Orcus"</note> holds the spirits of the dead, the soul seeks the stars.

<margin>The Flesh.</margin>
Therefore, the abandoned flesh and the body finished with life is called a corpse; which, as the Hebrew theologians say, is left in the power of the demon Zazel <note>Likely referring to Azazel, a wilderness demon</note>, of whom it is said in scripture: *You shall eat the earth all the days [of your life]*; and elsewhere: *The dust of the earth is his bread.* For man was created from the dust of the earth, whence that demon is called the lord of flesh and blood as long as the body has not been expiated and sanctified by righteous funeral rites. Hence, not without cause, the ancient fathers ordained the expiations of the corpse: so that what is exceedingly unclean may be sprinkled with holy water, perfumed with incense, exorcised with sacred prayers, and honored with lights as long as it is above the ground, and finally buried in a sacred place. Hence in Homer, Elpenor says: *I ask you, Ulysses, be mindful of me—*

# 296.
## ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

<margin>The fate of the mind and soul after death</margin>
...nor, departing from there, leave me unburied, lest being unsepulchred I become the cause of the gods' wrath. <note>A reference to the ancient belief that an unburied corpse brought divine displeasure and prevented the soul's rest.</note> The human mind, however, whose nature is sacred and of a divine race, because it is always innocent of fault, also escapes all punishment. But the soul, if it has acted well, rejoices together with the mind; and departing with its ethereal vehicle <term>ethereal vehicle: the "astral body" or subtle spirit that carries the soul</term>, it transcends freely to the choirs of heroes, or seeks the celestial beings. There, blessed with perpetual happiness in all its senses and powers, it enjoys a perfect knowledge of all things, and moreover, the divine vision and possession of the kingdom of heaven. Becoming a participant in divine power, it bestows various gifts and benefits upon these lower realms, like an immortal god. 

If the soul has acted wickedly, the mind judges it and leaves it to the will of a demon. Then the mournful soul, without the mind, wanders among the inhabitants of the underworld as an "idol," which they call an image <note>original: "imaginem," referring to the Greek 'eidolon' or phantom</note>, just as Dido laments in Virgil:

->And now my great image shall go beneath the earth.<-

Therefore, this soul, then deprived of its intelligible essence and left to the rule of a raging fantasy, is even subjected to the torment of corporeal qualities. It recognizes itself, by the just judgment of God and because of its own fault, to be perpetually deprived of the divine vision for which it was created. This divine vision, as Scripture testifies, is the absence of all evils; its loss is the most bitter punishment of all, which the sacred writings call the "outpouring of the wrath of God." Thus, this image of the soul sometimes enters an aerial body—a shadow—wrapped in which it now counsels friends and now haunts enemies, just as in Virgil, Dido threatens Aeneas, saying:

->I shall be present as a shadow in all places; you, wicked man, shall pay the penalty.<-

For since disturbances, memories, and senses remain in the soul when separated from the body, the Platonists say that the souls—especially of those who were murdered—haunt their enemies. This is effected not so much by human indignation as by divine Nemesis <note>The goddess of retribution</note> and a presiding demon providing and permitting it. Thus the spirit of Naboth (as the masters of the Hebrews interpret it) because he departed at the end of his life with a desire for vengeance, became (to fulfill that vengeance) a lying spirit. By God's permission, he went forth as a lying spirit in the mouths of all the prophets, until he caused Ahab to go up to Ramoth-Gilead. <note>Refers to 1 Kings 22, where Naboth's wrongful death is avenged through a deceiving spirit.</note> And Virgil himself, along with the Pythagoreans and Platonists—whom our own Augustine also follows—confesses that separated souls retain the memory and will of those things they did in this life, where he sings:

->The same grace for chariots<-
->And arms they had when living, the same care to feed<-
->Shining horses, follows them when laid beneath the earth.<-

And Algazel <note>Al-Ghazali, the Persian philosopher</note> in his book on divine science, and other Arabs and Mohammedan philosophers, feel that the operations of the soul common to the joined body imprint a character of use and exercise upon the soul. Once strongly imprinted, the separated soul will use these for similar operations and passions which were not erased in life. Therefore, although the body and its organs are destroyed, the operation will not cease for that reason, but the affections and similar dispositions will remain.

### BOOK THREE.

<margin>The Manes <note>original: "Manes." In Roman mythology, these were the souls of deceased loved ones, often treated as minor deities.</note></margin>
And these souls the ancients call by the common name of *Manes*: those among them who in this life were innocent, or purified by moral virtues, and—as Virgil sings:
> Those who suffered wounds fighting for their fatherland,
> And those who were chaste priests while life remained,
> And pious bards who spoke things worthy of Apollo,
> Or those who refined life through the discovered arts,
> And those who made others remember them through their merit,
<note>Quoting Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VI, describing the inhabitants of the Elysian Fields.</note>
Although they may have departed without grace and the justice of faith, many theologians believe they are carried away, free from suffering, into certain fortunate fields; and, as Virgil says:
> To reach the joyful places and the lovely green glades,
> The dwellings of the fortunate groves and the blessed seats,
Where they may enjoy certain wondrous pleasures; and they even rejoice in knowledge, both sensory and intellectual as well as revealed. Perhaps they are even instructed in faith and justice, no less than those spirits to whom Christ once preached the Gospel in prison <note>A reference to 1 Peter 3:19 regarding the "Harrowing of Hell."</note>. For as it is certain that no one can be saved without the faith of Christ, so it is probable that this faith is still preached to many pagans and Saracens <note>A medieval term for Muslims.</note> after this life in those receptacles of souls for their salvation, and that they are held in those places as if in a common custody until the time arrives when the Greatest Judge shall make an examination of merits. From this opinion even Lactantius, Irenaeus, Clement, Tertullian, Augustine, Ambrose, and many other Christian writers do not shrink. 

But those souls that migrate while impure, incontinent, and unjust with sins are not moved by such happy dreams, but wander through horrible phantasms and inferior places, relying on no free knowledge except that which is abstracted through concession or manifestation. Then, due to a continuous longing for flesh and blood, and because of the "rust" of their bodily stain, they are even subjected to the sense of pain, and they fear gladii and swords. Homer undoubtedly seems to have sensed this when, in the eleventh book of the *Odyssey*, he introduces the deceased mother of Ulysses standing near him as he offers sacrifice, but she neither recognized nor spoke to him as long as he himself, with drawn sword, kept the shadows away from the blood of the sacrifice. But after the mother, at the persuasion of the prophet Tiresias, had tasted of that sacrifice and the "cloud-dweller" drank the black blood, she immediately recognized her son and spoke to him weeping. Truly, the soul of the prophet Tiresias—despite the prohibition of the drawn sword—both recognized Ulysses and spoke to him even before tasting the blood, and pointed out that his mother's shadow was standing by. 

Therefore, those souls who did not atone in this life for the vices of crimes contracted in the body, carrying those habits with them, are compelled to wash them away among those below, and to pay the penalties for their commissions, which the poet explained in these verses:
> Nay, even when life has left them with the final light,
> Yet not all evil, nor all the plagues of the body,
> Entirely depart from the wretched ones; it is necessary that
> Many things, long hardened, should grow deep into their nature in strange ways.
<note>Continuing the quotation from Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VI, describing the purification of souls.</note>

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

> Therefore they are exercised by punishments, and for their ancient sins
> They pay the penalties. <note>A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI, describing the purification of souls in the underworld.</note>

For just as the habits and character of men are in this life, such affections generally follow the soul after death; the soul still revolves these things within its remembering mind, reflecting on what it once did in life. These memories occur then all the more intensely and sharply, because the various duties of life—of nourishing, growing, and procreating—have ceased, as have the various occupations and comforts of the senses and human business, and the obstacles of the thick, heavy body. Furthermore, those appearances occur to the phantastic reason <note>The "phantastic reason" refers to the faculty of the soul that deals with imagination and sensory images.</note> all the more turbulently and furiously, depending on whether the intellectual spark lies more or less dormant, or is entirely extinguished within such a soul. To these souls, the evil demons then thrust in appearances that are either utterly false or terrifying. 

Hence, in the faculty of desire, the soul is tortured by the longing for an imaginary good and for those things which it once craved in life, now being deprived of the power to obtain them. Although it sometimes seems to itself to almost reach its delights, it is kept away from them by demons for more bitter punishment—just as, among the poets, Tantalus is kept from the banquet, Sardanapalus from the embrace, Midas from his gold, and Sisyphus from power. These souls they have called <margin>Lemures. Lar.</margin> **Lemures** <note>Restless or malevolent spirits of the dead.</note>. If any such soul, caring for domestic matters, dwells quietly in a home, it is called a **household Lar** <note>A protective domestic spirit or tutelary deity of the home.</note>.

However, they are most sharply tortured in the faculty of anger by the hatred of an imaginary evil. At that time, the most false disturbances, suspicions, and horrible phantasms fall upon them. They dwell upon sad images: now the sky seems to fall upon their heads, now they are consumed by the rush of flames, now submerged under a vast whirlpool of waters, now swallowed by the gaping of the earth. Now they see themselves transformed into various beasts, now torn apart or devoured by deformed monsters; now they are driven everywhere through forests, through seas, through fires, through the air, and through the foulest places of the underworld. Now they perceive themselves being seized and tortured by demons. 

We believe that all these things happen to them after death no differently than they do in this life to those who rave with frenzy, mania, or melancholic humor, or those who are tortured in dreams, terrified by horrible visions, as if these things were truly happening to them. Yet, these things are not truly present with them, but are only the appearances of them apprehended in the imagination. So too, these souls after death are terrified by the horrible images of their sins as if dreaming, and the conscience of their wickedness drives them headlong through various places. For this reason, Orpheus calls them the "people of dreams," saying: *The gates of Pluto cannot be unlocked; within are the people of dreams.* 

Therefore, such wicked souls, relying on no good resting place, are called <margin>Larvae or terrors.</margin> **Larvae** or **terrors** when, wandering in an aerial body, they present any form to our sight. They are empty to the good, but harmful to the wicked. Appearing sometimes in thinner, sometimes in thicker remains, they take the form of various animals and monsters whose habits they once mirrored in life, just as the poet sings:

> Then various forms and faces of wild beasts mock them.

> For he will suddenly become a bristling sow, and a dark tigress,

For the impure soul of man, which in this life has contracted an excessive habit toward bodies, weaves for itself another body from the vapors of the elements by a certain intimate affection for the elemental body. It creates this from a pliable matter, constantly refreshing that ever-vanishing body as if by a certain draught. To this body, as if to a prison and a sensible instrument, the soul is enslaved by a certain divine law; in it, the soul suffers cold and fire, and whatever things offend the body, spirit, and sense: stenches, wailing, lamentation, gnashing of teeth, lashings, tearings, and chains, just as Virgil sang:

> Therefore they are exercised by punishments, and for ancient evils
> They pay the penalties: some are stretched out empty,
> Suspended to the winds; for others, the infected guilt
> Is washed away under a vast whirlpool, or burnt out by fire.
<note>original: "Ergo exercentur pœnis..." From Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VI, describing the purification of souls in the underworld.</note>

And in Homer, in his *Necyomantia* <note>The "Book of the Dead" or the descent into the underworld in the *Odyssey*.</note>, Alcinous relates to Ulysses:

> We also saw Tityos, the famous nursling of the earth,
> His body spread across nine acres, whose entrails
> A vulture, sitting on either side, beats and tears.

<margin>Depraved souls are cast down into brutes</margin>
Sometimes those souls do not only inhabit these figurative bodies, but through an excessive affection for flesh and blood, they even cast themselves headlong into animals; entering the bodies of reptiles and brutes of whatever species, they seize and possess them like demons. Pythagoras supports these views, and before him Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the *Hermetica*.</note>, asserting that depraved souls are often cast down into reptiles and brutes. Yet they do not animate and give form to those bodies as essential forms <term>essential forms: the internal principle that gives a thing its specific nature and life</term>, but rather inhabit them in the manner of a tenant as if in a prison, or they stand by them through local inseparability, like an internal mover to the thing it moves. Or they are tortured while bound around them, like Ixion to the wheels of serpents, or Sisyphus to the stone. Nor do they seize only brutes, but sometimes even men, just as we said of the soul of Naboth, who went out as a lying spirit in the mouth of the prophets. Hence some have asserted that the lives or spirits of wicked men, entering into the bodies of certain people, keep them in a bad state for a long time and sometimes kill them. This is perhaps granted much more favorably even to blessed souls, so that like good angels they can inhabit and enlighten us, just as we read of Elijah: that when he was taken away from men, his spirit settled upon Elisha. And elsewhere we read that God took from the spirit that was in Moses and gave it to the seventy men. A great mystery lies hidden here, but it is not to be revealed rashly. Sometimes also (which is nevertheless very rare) souls are driven by such great madness...

<margin>Danish History, Book 5</margin>
in the writings of Saxo Grammaticus <note>A 12th-century Danish historian.</note> regarding a certain Asuitus and Asmundus, who had sworn a mutual oath to one another: that whichever of them lived longer would be buried together with the one who died.
