> A spirit sent from the underworld in the form of Asuitus
> Devoured his horse with savage teeth
> And offered his dog to his unspeakable mouth.
> Not content with eating the horse or the dog,
> He soon turned his swift claws upon me,
> And tearing my cheek, he took my ear.
> Hence the image of my mangled face is a horror,
> And blood flashes in the fierce wound.
> Yet the monster-bearer did not act with impunity:
> For with my sword I soon cut off his head,
> And pierced his guilty body with a stake.

Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer.</note> relates something not unlike this, received from the interpreters of Delphi: namely, that there is a certain infernal demon whom they called Eurynomus, who consumes and devours the flesh of the dead, so that the bones are left barely bare. We also read in the annals of the Cretans that the spirits of the dead, whom they call *Catechanas* <note>original: "Catechanas"; likely a reference to the Greek 'katakhanas', a type of vampire or revenant.</note>, are accustomed to return into their bodies, go in to their widowed wives, and fulfill their lust. To avoid this, and so that they might no longer infest their wives, it is provided by local laws to pierce the heart of the rising corpse with a nail and burn the entire body. These things are undoubtedly marvelous, and might perhaps seem hostile to common opinion, were it not for the evidence of both established laws and the trusted histories of antiquity. Nor, finally, is it foreign to the Christian religion that many souls can be restored to their bodies before the universal resurrection of the flesh; indeed, we believe many have been taken up into glory with their bodies by the singular benefit of God, and many have even descended alive into hell. And we have heard not infrequently of the bodies of the dead being taken from their graves by demons, undoubtedly for no other purpose...

Aristotle relates that among the Aeolian Islands near Italy, there was a certain mound on Lipara which could not be safely approached at night. The inhabitants constantly asserted that the clashing of cymbals and the rattling of castanets <term>crotalorum: ancient percussion instruments similar to clappers</term> were heard there, along with certain rude laughter, tumult, and empty sounds. A certain drunken youth once approached that place and fell asleep near the cave of the mound toward nightfall; he was finally found there after the third day by those searching for him and was carried away as if dead. When the funeral was being led out with the rites prepared, he suddenly woke up and narrated in order, to the great admiration of all, the many things he had seen and endured. There is also in Norway a certain mountain, the most formidable of all, surrounded by the sea, which the common people call Hechelberg <note>Mount Hekla, though located in Iceland, was often associated with Norway or the general North in early modern texts and was famously considered a gate to Hell</note>, bearing the appearance of the infernal regions. From there, such mournful voices of wailing and cries are heard that those horrific noises spread for nearly a mile around; moreover, huge vultures and blackest ravens fly around it with terrifying cries, frightening...

There are similar miracles in various regions and provinces; but I myself do not wish to report here those things which I have seen with my own eyes and touched with my hands, lest on account of the stupendous wonder of these things, I happen to be accused of lying by the incredulous.

Nor indeed do I think I should pass over here what many of our own people have felt regarding the receptacles of souls, <margin>Tertullian</margin> which do not differ greatly from these things we have already said. Among them, Tertullian, in the fourth book *Against the Heresies of Marcion*, says: "It appears to any wise man who has ever heard of the Elysian Fields <note>The blessed afterlife in Greek mythology</note> that there is some kind of local determination, which is called the Bosom of Abraham, for receiving the souls of his children; and that region is not celestial, yet higher than the underworld, where the souls of the righteous may rest until the consummation of things restores the resurrection of all in the fullness of reward."

<margin>Peter the Apostle</margin> Moreover, the Apostle Peter, to Clement <note>Clement of Rome, an early Christian father</note> asking about these matters, said: "You compel me, O Clement, to publish some of the ineffable things; nevertheless, as far as it is permitted to bring them forth, I shall not be loath. Christ, who was from the beginning and always, was always present through individual generations of the pious, though hiddenly, especially to those by whom he was expected and to whom he frequently appeared. But it was not yet the time that the resurrection should occur for those with dissolved bodies; rather, this seemed a greater reward from God: that he who was found righteous should remain longer in the body, or certainly (as is clearly reported in the scriptures concerning a certain righteous man <note>Likely referring to Enoch or Elijah</note>) that the Lord translated him." By a similar example, it was done with the others who pleased His will, so that being translated to paradise, they are preserved for the Kingdom. But of those who could not fully complete the rule of justice, but had some remnants of malice in their flesh, their bodies are indeed dissolved, but their souls are preserved in good and joyful regions, so that in the resurrection of the dead, when they have received their bodies—now purified by that very dissolution—they may possess the eternal inheritance for the things they had done well.

<margin>Irenaeus</margin> Irenaeus himself also, at the end of the book which he wrote *Against the Heresies of the Valentinians*, says: "Since the Lord went away into the midst of the shadow of death, where the souls of the dead were, and afterward rose again bodily, and after the resurrection was taken up, it is manifest that the souls of his disciples (for whose sake the Lord performed these things) will go away into an invisible place defined for them by God, and will stay there until the resurrection, awaiting the resurrection; afterward receiving their bodies and rising perfectly, that is bodily, just as the Lord rose again, so they shall come into the sight of God. For no disciple is above the master."

### PAGE 303.
#### BOOK THE THIRD.

"But everyone will be perfect, just as his master." <note>original: "perfectus autem erit omnis sicut magister eius." A reference to Luke 6:40.</note> Therefore, just as our Master did not immediately fly away and depart, but waited for the time of His resurrection defined by the Father—which was also made manifest through Jonah—and rising after three days was taken up: so we also ought to await the time of our resurrection defined by God and foretold by the prophets, and thus rising be taken up, as many of us as the Lord shall have deemed worthy of this honor. Lactantius Firmianus also joins these thinkers in that book of his *Divine Institutes* entitled *On the Divine Reward*, saying: "And let no one think that souls are judged immediately after death: for all are detained in one common custody until the time arrives when the Supreme Judge performs the examination of merits. Then, those whose justice has been approved shall receive the reward of immortality; but those whose sins and crimes are uncovered shall not rise, but shall be hidden away with the ungodly in the same darkness, destined for certain punishments." <margin>Lactantius.</margin> Augustine and Ambrose are of the same opinion; the former says in his *Enchiridion*: "The time which is interposed between a man's death and the final resurrection holds the souls in hidden receptacles, according as each is worthy of rest or of hardship, based on what it earned in the flesh while it lived." <margin>Augustine.</margin> Ambrose, indeed, in his book *On the Good of Death*, says: "The Scripture of Esdras <note>Referring to the apocryphal book 4 Esdras (or 2 Esdras), which discusses the 'storehouses' of souls.</note> called the dwellings of souls 'storehouses' <term>promptuaria: storehouses or chambers where souls are kept</term>; which, meeting the human complaint (because the righteous who have gone before seem to be cheated of their due reward for a very long time until the day of judgment), says that the day of judgment is like a crown. For the day of the crown is expected by all, so that within it the conquered may blush and the victors may obtain the palm of victory. Therefore, while the fullness of time is awaited, souls await their due reward; for some, punishment remains, for others, glory." <margin>Ambrose.</margin> And in the same chapter, he calls the underworld a "place which is not seen," which souls seek when freed from their bodies. And in the second book *On Cain and Abel*, he says: "The soul is released from the body, and after the end of this life, it is still held in suspense, uncertain of the future judgment." This is supported by that Gospel passage concerning the Last Judgment, where Christ says in Matthew: "Many will say to me on that day, 'Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and perform many miracles in your name?' And then I will declare to them, 'I never knew you.'" From this speech, it seems clear that they were uncertain of their sentence until that day, and through confidence in the miracles they had performed in Jesus' name while they still lived, they were meanwhile held in suspense by a certain hope of salvation. Because, therefore, the judgment of souls is delayed until the last day, many theologians think that before the preordained day of judgment, intercessory prayers <term>piacularia suffragia: prayers or acts of atonement offered for the dead</term> can be of help not only to those to be justified, but even to the damned. Thus, they say the Emperor Trajan was freed from the underworld by Saint Gregory and justified unto salvation; although some think he was not freed from the guilt of his penalty, but that the justice of his punishment was merely deferred until the day of judgment. However, Thomas Aquinas says it seems more probable that Trajan returned to life through the prayers of Saint Gregory, and obtained a gift of grace by which he was freed from punishment and the bond of his crimes.

And there are some among the theologians who believe that by the offerings for the dead, neither is the punishment removed nor the fine diminished, but rather that only certain comforts and soothings for the pains are brought—likening it to a sweating porter who, by the sprinkling of water, seems to be relieved of the pressure of his burden, or helped to bear it more easily, even though nothing has been taken away from the weight itself. But leaving these things aside now, and hastening to further matters, we shall discuss the restorations of souls.

### By what reasons Mages and Necromancers thought they were able to evoke the souls of the dead. Chapter XLII.

From these things which have already been said, it is clear that those souls which after death still love their abandoned bodies—such as the souls of those lacking a proper burial, or those who left their bodies by a violent death, and still wander in that turbid and moist spirit around their corpses as if around something kindred attracting them—can be easily evoked and enticed. This is done by knowing the means through which they were once joined to their bodies: through similar vapors, liquids, and scents, and also by employing certain artificial lights, songs, sounds, and the like, which move the imaginative and spiritual harmony of the soul itself. Sacred invocations and such things as pertain to religion are not neglected, on account of the rational portion of the soul which is superior by nature. Thus the Pythoness <note>The Witch of Endor.</note> is read to have evoked Samuel; thus the Thessalian prophetess in the works of Lucan raised a corpse. Hence we read among the poets and narrators of such things that the souls of the dead are not evoked without blood and a corpse; but that shadows are easily enticed by their fumigations, with the addition of eggs, milk, honey, oil, wine, water, and flour, as if providing a fit medium for the souls to take up bodies, just as Circe teaches Ulysses with long instruction in Homer. Moreover, they judge that these things can only be done in those places where such souls are known to frequent most, either because of something kindred, like the abandoned body attracting them, or because of some affection impressed during life drawing the soul to certain places, or because of the nature of the place, which is suited to a Tartarean <note>Infernal or hellish.</note> nature for the purging or punishing of souls. Such places are mostly recognized by the experience of visions, nocturnal incursions, and the occurrence of similar phantasms.

<margin>Two species of necromancy.</margin>
species of necromancy: one is *necyomancy* <note>original: "necyomantia"; from Greek *nekys* (corpse). Finally, it performs all its experiments through the corpses, bones, and limbs of the slaughtered, and those things which come from them: because a demonic power friendly to them is present there. Therefore, they easily entice the flow of wicked demons because of a very familiar likeness and property. Since these demons have great power in earthly and human affairs, the necromancers, relying on their work, kindle illicit loves, send dreams, diseases, hatreds, and similar passions, to which they can then also contribute the powers of those souls which, still wrapped in a moist and turbulent spirit, wander around their remains, committing the same acts as the wicked demons. Since, therefore, they have learned by experience that the depraved and impure souls violently torn from their bodies—and those of men not purified and lacking burial—linger around the bodies and are drawn to what is kindred to them, sorcerers easily abuse them to effect their wicked deeds, luring the unhappy souls by the placement of the body or the taking up of a part of it, then compelling them with Stygian invocations, by beseeching them by the shapeless corpses scattered across wide fields, and the wandering shadows of those lacking burial, and the spirits sent back from Acheron <note>One of the rivers of the underworld in Greek mythology.</note>, and the guests of the infernal regions whom premature death dragged down into Tartarus, and by the horrendous desires of the damned, and the proud demons, the avengers of crimes. [...continued from previous page] finally, by what influences the body is joined together: for the <term>art of raising the dead</term><note>original: "ars suscitationis mortuorum"</note> requires all these things. This art belongs not to men, but to God alone, and to those with whom He wishes to share it, such as Elisha, who caused the dead son of the Shunammite woman to live again. So also Alcestis is said to have been raised by Hercules and to have lived a long time afterward; and <term>Apollonius of Tyana</term><note>A 1st-century Greek philosopher and reputed miracle-worker often compared to Jesus in antiquity.</note> restored a dead girl to life. And here it must be noted that it sometimes happens to men that the life-giving spirit is withdrawn within them, and they appear dead and without feeling, even though the intellectual nature remains united to the body and keeps the same form. The body remains the same, even if the power of giving life does not actively extend into it but remains withdrawn in union with the intellectual nature; nevertheless, it does not cease to be. And although that man may now truly be called dead, insofar as death is the absence of life-giving power, yet that body would not be truly separated [from the soul], and it can be awakened and live again. Thus many miracles appear in these cases, of the kind seen in previous ages among the Pagans and Jews. Among their number is what <term>Plato</term> recites in the tenth book of the *Republic*: namely, that a certain Er the Pamphylian <note>original: "Phereū quēdam Pamphilium"; Agrippa likely refers to Er, son of Armenius, whose story concludes Plato's Republic.</note> lay for ten days among those who had fallen in battle, and two days after he had been taken from there and placed upon the funeral pyre, he revived and narrated certain wonders which he had seen during the time of his death. We have spoken of these partly in the first book, and we shall speak even more extensively below, where we shall discuss the oracles that occur during the rapture, ecstasy, and the death-struggle of the dying.

->On the power of the human soul, in the mind, the reason, and the idol.<-

## Chapter XLIV.

<margin>Of what the human soul consists.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' containing a woodcut illustration of a scholar or cleric sitting at a desk with an open book, gesturing towards the text.</image-desc>The human soul consists of the <term>mind</term><note>Latin: "mens"; the highest, most divine part of the soul.</note>, the <term>reason</term><note>Latin: "ratio"; the logical, discursive faculty.</note>, and the <term>idol</term><note>Latin: "idolum"; the "image" or "shadow" of the soul, often associated with the astral body or the faculty of imagination.</note>. The mind illuminates the reason, the reason flows into the idol, and all is one soul. Unless the reason is illuminated by the mind, it is not immune from error; however, the mind does not provide light to the reason unless God shines—the first light, that is. For the first light in God is transcendent above all intellect; for which reason it cannot be called "intelligible" light. But when that light is poured into the mind, it becomes intellectual and can be understood. Then, when it is poured through the mind into the reason, it becomes rational, and can not only be understood but also thought about. Then, when it is poured through the reason into the idol of the soul, it becomes not only thinkable but also imaginable, though not yet corporeal. But when it migrates from there into the <term>ethereal vehicle of the soul</term><note>The "spirit-body" that carries the soul between the physical and divine realms.</note>, it first becomes corporeal, though not clearly perceptible to the senses, until it passes into the elemental body—whether simple and airy, or composite—in which it becomes light clearly visible to the eye. Considering this progression of light, the <term>Chaldean philosophers</term><note>Refers to the practitioners of ancient Near Eastern magic and astrology, highly respected in Renaissance occultism.</note> tell of a certain stupendous power of our mind: namely, that it is possible for the mind itself, with its whole focus fixed upon God, to be filled with the divine power. Thus filled with light, it pours out rays through every medium, down to this thick, dark, heavy, mortal body, surrounding the body itself with abundant light, rendering it like the stars and equally glittering; then also by the abundance of its rays...

and by its lightness lifts it on high, just as flax is raised by a flame of fire; sometimes it may transport the standing body like a spirit to distant parts: just as we read of Philip in the Acts of the Apostles, when, after baptizing the Eunuch in India <note>original: "India" - likely a reference to Ethiopia/the East in general</note>, he was immediately found in Azotus; and similar things are read of Habakkuk in the book of Daniel. So others, penetrating closed doors, have escaped guards and chains, as is read of Peter the Apostle and of Peter the Exorcist. One should marvel at this less if he has seen those famous melancholics who walk in their dreams, traveling through pathless places and climbing through inaccessible heights, performing the works of those who are awake—things which those awake could not do at all. There is no other reason for this in nature than a strong and unrestrained imagination. Indeed, this power exists in every human being and is present in the human soul from the root of its creation, but it varies in different men in strength and weakness; it is increased and diminished according to exercise and use, through which it is drawn out from potential into action. He who rightly knows this can ascend in his knowledge until his imaginative power transcends and is anointed with the universal power, which Al-Kindi, Roger Bacon, and William of Auvergne <note>original: "Gulielmus Parisiensis"</note> call the "sense of nature," Virgil calls the "ethereal sense," and Plato calls the "sense of the vehicle" <note>original: "sensum vehiculi" - referring to the subtle body or astral carriage of the soul</note>.
<margin>The sense of nature, the ethereal sense, and the vehicle.</margin>
And let his thought be made most strong when that ethereal and celestial power is poured over it, by whose splendor it is strengthened until it grasps the species, notions, and knowledge of true things; so much so that what he has thought in his mind comes to pass just as he thought it. He acquires such power that he can immerse himself, join, and insinuate himself into the souls of men, making them certain of his thoughts, his will, and his desire, even across great and remote distances, as if they perceived those things with their senses from a present object. He can do many things in a short time, as if they were done without time at all. These gifts are not given to everyone, but to those whose imaginative and cognitive power is strongest and has reached the height of speculation. Such a person is fit to perceive and announce all things through the splendor of the universal power, or the spiritual intelligence and apprehension that is over him; and this is the necessary power which must be followed, and which everyone who follows the truth must obey. If, therefore, the power of the imagination is now so great that it can insinuate itself into whomever it wishes, hindered by no interval of place or time, and sometimes draws a heavy body along with it to wherever it dreams and imagines, it is not to be doubted that the power of the mind <term>Mind (Mens): the highest, most divine part of the human soul</term> is even greater when it has attained its own nature, not weighed down by the allurements of the senses, and has remained incorrupt and true to itself. But now, according to the pattern, the souls abound with the copious light of the celestial stars, and a huge abundance of light overflows from there into their bodies. Thus the face of Moses shone so much that the children of Israel could not look upon him because of the splendor of his countenance. Thus Socrates is read to have been transfigured, surpassing the light of the sun's light-bearing wheels; thus Zoroaster was transfigured and lifted up bodily; thus Enoch and Elijah ascended to the heavens in a certain fiery chariot; thus Paul was caught up to the third heaven; thus

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

### Page 308

We can say that our bodies, after the judgment of the world—which shall then be called "glorified"—will similarly be snatched up and shine like the sun and moon. That this is indeed possible, and has occurred, is admitted and demonstrated by Avicebron the Moor <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol, an 11th-century Jewish philosopher</note> as well as the Arab Avicenna, Hippocrates of Cos, and the entire school of the Chaldeans. Furthermore, it is handed down in the monuments of history that Alexander the Great, when surrounded in India at great peril, was so inflamed in spirit that he appeared to the barbarians to pour forth light. The father of Theodoric <note>Theodoric the Great, King of the Ostrogoths</note> is also said to have poured forth sparks from his whole body. A certain wise man reported the same of himself, such that sparkling flames leaped out from here and there, even with a sound. Nor is this power of the spirit found only in humans, but it is also sometimes discovered in brute animals, as in the horse of Tiberius, which appeared to breathe flames from its mouth.

The Mind <term>Mens: the highest, divine part of the soul</term>, however, is above fate in the realm of providence; therefore, it is affected neither by the influences of the celestial bodies nor by the qualities of natural things. Religion alone, therefore, provides its remedy. But the "Idol" <term>Idolum: the "image" or "shadow" of the soul; the lower vital spirit</term> of the soul is within fate, above nature (which is in a way the knot of the body and soul), yet below fate and above the body. Therefore, it is changed by the influences of celestial bodies and affected by the qualities of natural and corporeal things. 

<margin>What the Idol of the soul is.</margin> I call the "Idol of the soul" that vivifying and governing power of the body, the origin of the senses, through which the soul itself unfolds its powers of perceiving in this body. It perceives corporeal things through the body, moves the body through space, governs it in its place, and nourishes the body in its sluggishness. 

<margin>Two virtues in the Idol.</margin> In this Idol, two most powerful virtues dominate: one, namely, which is called the *phantasy* <note>The faculty of imagination</note>, or the imaginative or cogitative virtue, concerning whose power we have already spoken, and also where we treated the passions of the soul. The other virtue is that which is called the "sense of nature," of which we also spoke when we made mention of soothsaying <note>original: *aruspicina*, the art of divining from entrails</note>. 

Thus, man is under fate by the nature of his body; the soul of man moves nature through the Idol within fate; but through the Mind, he is above fate, in the order of providence. Reason, however, is free and of its own right. The soul, therefore, ascends through Reason into the Mind, where it is filled with divine light; at other times it descends into the Idol, where it is affected by the influences of celestial bodies and the qualities of natural things, and is distracted by the passions and encounters of sensible things. Sometimes the soul folds itself entirely back into Reason, either investigating other things by arguing or by contemplating itself. For it is possible that the rational part of the soul—which the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> call the "possible intellect"—may reach the point where it discourses and operates freely without turning toward mental images <note>original: *phantasmata*</note>. 

Finally, the command of Reason itself is so great that whenever anything occurs either in the Mind, or in the Idol, or in nature, or in the body, it cannot pass into the soul unless Reason applies itself to it. In this way, in the exterior senses, the soul perceives itself neither to see, nor hear, nor feel, nor suffer anything, until the cogitative Reason first comprehends it. It comprehends, however, when it is at leisure, not when it gapes at something else—as we clearly see in those who do not notice people they meet while they are thinking more intently on something else. Know, therefore, that neither heavenly influences, nor natural affections, nor sensations, nor those of the body...

<margin>The constancy of Anaxarchus.</margin>

Thus Anaxarchus of Abdera, the philosopher <note>A Greek philosopher of the 4th century BCE, known for his endurance</note>, having been cast into a hollow stone by order of Nicocreon, the tyrant of Cyprus, while he was being beaten with iron hammers, disregarded the punishment of his body and is said to have cried out: "Pound, pound the vessel of Anaxarchus; you do not terrify Anaxarchus himself." <note>original: "Tunde tunde Anaxarchi vasculum, Anaxarchum ipsum nihil terres."</note> Then the tyrant ordered his tongue to be cut out; but he bit off his own tongue with his teeth and spat it into the tyrant's face.

### On the levels of souls, and their destruction or immortality. Chapter 44.

<margin>Not all men attain the Mind.</margin>
Because the Mind <term>Mens: the highest, divine part of the soul</term> is from God, or from the intelligible world, it is therefore immortal and eternal. However, celestial reason, by virtue of its origin from the heavens, is long-lived; but the "image" <term>idolum: the lower, shadow-soul or astral body</term>, because it depends on the womb of matter and sublunary nature, is subject to destruction and corruption. Thus the soul is immortal through its Mind, and long-lived through its reason in its ethereal vehicle, yet it is dissolvable unless it is restored in the circuit of a new body. It is therefore not immortal unless it is united to the immortal Mind. Likewise, the "image" of the soul, or the sensible and animal soul itself, because it was drawn out from the womb of corporeal matter, perishes along with the body when it is dissolved; or, it does not survive long as a shadow in the vapors of its dissolved body, participating in nothing of immortality unless it too is united to a higher power. Therefore, that soul which is united to the Mind is called a "standing and not falling" soul. Truly, not all men have attained the Mind, because (as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism</note> says) God the Father wished to propose it as a contest and a prize for souls. Those who neglect this, being devoid of Mind and enslaved to the corporeal senses, are made like irrational animals and share the same destruction with them, just as Ecclesiastes says:

> There is one end for man and for beasts, and the condition of both is equal: as man dies, so they die. All things breathe alike, and man has nothing more than the beast. <note>original: "Unus interitus est hominis & iumentorum..." quoting Ecclesiastes 3:19</note>

So he says. From this, many theologians believe that no immortality remains for such souls after this body is cast off, except for the sole hope of resurrection, when all men are to be restored. Augustine reports that such was the heresy of the Arabs, who said that souls perish together with the body and will rise again with it at the judgment. But whoever, supported by divine grace, has attained the Mind, these become immortal according to the comparison of their works, as Hermes says, embracing in their intelligence all things that are on the earth, in the sea, and in the heavens—and if there is anything beyond them above the heaven—so that they may behold the Good itself. However, those who happen to live a middle life, although they have not attained divine intelligence but only a certain rational image of it, when their souls have departed from the body, they are relegated to certain secret receptacles. There, affected by their sensible powers and engaged in a certain kind of activity, from opi—

### Page 310.

Through the imagination, and the powers of anger and desire, they either rejoice excessively or grieve deeply; Saint Augustine was also of this opinion in the book he wrote, *On the Spirit and the Soul* <note>original: "De spiritu & anima"</note>. The wise men of the Indians, Persians, Egyptians, and Chaldeans handed down the tradition that this soul survives its body for a long time, yet does not immediately become immortal except through transcorporation <note>The migration of the soul into a new body; reincarnation</note>. However, our own theologians philosophize far differently about these matters. For they say that although the origin and birth of all souls are common, they are nevertheless distinguished from one another by the Creator in various degrees—not only by accidental qualities, but by certain intrinsic degrees rooted in their very essence. By these, each soul differs from another through that which is its own. John Scotus <note>Likely Duns Scotus, a major medieval philosopher</note> holds this view, and the Parisian theologians decreed in their articles that this is how it must be understood. Hence the Wise Man says: "I was a witty child, and received a good soul," <note>Wisdom of Solomon 8:19</note> namely, a better one than many others. And according to this inequality of souls in their degrees, each is capable of its own office, which it receives from God as a free gift, just as we read in the Gospels: "Because to one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his own particular virtue." And the Apostle says: "He gave some to be apostles, others prophets, others evangelists and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ." For there are (as Origen says) certain invisible powers to whom the administration of things on earth is entrusted; among them there is no small difference, just as is required among men. Wherefore one reaches the highest degree of wisdom or dignity, while another is little distant from the beasts, and by feeding beasts becomes a half-beast. One is abundant in virtues and rich in fortune, while another has either nothing or very little; often even that little which he has is taken from him and given to the one who has. And such is divine justice in the distribution of gifts, that they correspond to the virtue of each recipient; to these also rewards are rendered according to their works, so that whatever the proportion of gifts to gifts and merits to merits, the same is the proportion of rewards to rewards.

<margin>The fourfold operation of the noble soul.</margin>
Finally, it must be known that every noble soul has a fourfold operation: one divine, through the image of the divine property; the second intellectual, through the formality of participation with the Intelligences <note>Angelic or celestial minds</note>; the third rational, through the perfection of its own essentiality; the fourth animal or natural, through communion with the body and with these lower things. Thus, there is no work in the entire series of the world so admirable, so excellent, or so miraculous that the human soul—having embraced its image of divinity, which the Magi call the "standing and not falling soul"—cannot effect by its own power without any external aid. Therefore, the form of all magical power is from the standing and not falling soul of man.

# THIRD BOOK. 311.

Prophecy <note>original: "Vaticinium"</note> is that state by which priests or others are moved, and they both discern the causes of things and foresee future events, specifically when oracles descend into them from the gods or from spirits <note>original: "dæmonibus," referring here to intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses rather than "demons" in the modern sense</note>, and breaths of spirit are handed down by them. The Platonists call these descents the "glidings" <note>original: "illapsiones"</note> of higher souls into our own souls; and Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> calls them the senses of spirits and the souls of spirits. The ancients called such spirits "Eurydices" and "Pythons," and antiquity constantly believed that they were accustomed to enter the bodies of men and use their voices and tongues for the prediction of future things; Plutarch also mentions these in his *Dialogue on the Obsolescence of Oracles*.

<margin>Foreknowledge of the future belongs to the gods alone.</margin>
But Cicero, following the Stoics, affirms that the foreknowledge of future things belongs just as much to the gods; and Ptolemy the astrologer says: "Only those inspired by a divine power predict particulars." Peter the Apostle agrees with these, saying: "For prophecy was not brought at any time by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit." <note>2 Peter 1:21</note> Moreover, Isaiah affirms that prophecies of the future are the proper domain of divine glidings, saying: "Tell us the things that are to come, and we shall say that you are gods." <note>Isaiah 41:23</note> However, glidings or perceptions of this kind do not transfer into our soul when it is occupied, gazing too intently upon something else; rather, they pass through when the soul is at leisure. Of such leisure <note>original: "uacatiōis," a state of being empty or receptive</note>

<margin>Three kinds of leisure</margin>
there are three kinds: namely, frenzy <note>original: "furor," or divine madness</note>, rapture, and dreaming, about each of which we shall now speak in order.

### Concerning the first species of frenzy, from the Muses. Chapter XLVI.

Frenzy is an illumination of the soul proceeding from the gods or from spirits, whence comes this poem by Ovid <note>original: "Nasonis"</note>:
> ->There is a god within us, and we have dealings with heaven,<-
> ->That spirit comes from the ethereal seats.<-

Plato defines this through alienation and connection: for it withdraws from those things by which the bodily senses are excited, and being alienated from the animal man, it adheres to the divine power, from which it receives what it cannot investigate by its own strengths. For when the soul is free and loosed, the reins of the body having been relaxed—as if having exited a prison left unguarded—it steps across the chains of the limbs more freely, with nothing restraining it; driven by its own impulses and stirred by the divine spirit, it comprehends all things and foresees the future.

<margin>Four species of divine frenzy.</margin>
There are, moreover, four species of divine frenzy proceeding from individual deities: namely, from the Muses, from Dionysus, from Apollo, and from Venus. Thus the first frenzy, proceeding from the Muses, stirs up and tempers the soul, and renders it divine, by

<margin>Frenzy from the Muses.</margin>
drawing higher things to lower things through natural objects. Furthermore, the Muses are the souls of the celestial spheres, according to which individual steps are found by which the attraction of higher things to lower things occurs. The lowest of these, reflecting the sphere of the moon, holds those things which are of the vegetable kingdom, such as plants, the fruits of trees, roots, and those things which are of harder materials, such as stones and metals, and their bindings and suspensions. Thus it is said that the moonstone <note>original: "selenites"</note> and the "hyena-stone" <note>a mythical stone supposedly found in the eye of a hyena</note> provide divination; similarly, vervain and the herb *theangelida* <note>an ancient Persian herb mentioned by Pliny for its prophetic powers</note> provide prophecy.

Whence **Hermes**, **Pythagoras**, and **Plato** command that a discordant mind be composed and uplifted by song and harmony. Thus **Timothy** is said to have incited King **Alexander** into a frenzy by sounds: thus the priest of **Calamus** (according to the testimony of **Aurelius Augustine**) used to evoke himself from his body into rapture and ecstasy at his own will by a certain plaintive harmony. Concerning these things, discourse has also been held above. 

The fifth degree agrees with **Mars**: this governs vehement imaginations and affections of the mind, concepts, and motions, all of which are evident from what was said above. 

The sixth degree responds to **Jupiter**: this governs the discourses of reason, deliberations, consultations, and moral purifications: of these, mention was partly made above, and partly will be said below. It has, moreover, under itself wonders and venerations, by the stupor of which the phantasy and reason are sometimes so bridled that they suddenly omit all their own acts: whence then the mind itself, being free and exposed to the divine power alone—whether to some god or a demon—conceives supernal and divine influxes, namely those about which it had previously deliberated. Thus we read that the **Sibyls** and the priests of the **Pythia** were accustomed to receive oracles in the caves of **Jupiter** and **Apollo**. 

<margin>Contemplation</margin> The seventh degree reflects **Saturn**: this governs the more secret intelligences and the tranquil contemplations of the mind: I call contemplation here the free perspicacity of the mind, suspended in admiration at the spectacles of wisdom. For that thinking which occurs through enigmas or images is "speculation," which is a certain discourse pertaining to **Jupiter**, not "contemplation." 

The eighth degree, reflecting the **Starry Heaven**: this observes the position, motion, rays, and light of the celestial bodies: it also governs images, rings, and similar things which are fabricated according to the celestial pattern, of which we have spoken above. 

The ninth degree corresponds to the **First Mover** <note>term: "primum mobile"; in the Ptolemaic system, the outermost moving sphere that carries all others</note>, namely the ninth sphere or the universe itself: this governs more formal things, such as numbers, figures, characters, and occult properties in...

### Concerning the third species of frenzy, from Apollo. Chapter XLVIII.

<margin>A marvelous art.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring a human face within the letter's ornate scrollwork.</image-desc>
The third frenzy proceeds from Apollo, that is, from the Mind of the World. This frenzy—through certain sacred mysteries, vows, sacrifices, adorations, invocations, and certain sacred techniques, or secret preparations into which the gods have infused the power of their spirit—causes the soul to rise above the mind, joining it with divinities and spirits. We read of this regarding the Ephod <note>A ceremonial garment worn by High Priests in the Old Testament, used for divination.</note>, which, when applied, caused men to prophesy immediately. So we read in the *Book of the Senators*, in the chapters of Eleazar, that Rabbi Ishmael prepared certain small cakes inscribed with specific divine and angelic names and thus consecrated them; whoever ate these with faith, hope, and charity was immediately radiant with the prophetic spirit of wisdom. We read in the same place that Rabbi Johanan, son of Jochahidis, so illuminated a certain unrefined farmer named Eleazar—who was unskilled in all literature—that, surrounded by a sudden brightness, he unexpectedly preached such deep mysteries of the Law in the assembly of the wise that it was a wonder to all standing by. And it is recorded in memory concerning a certain Egyptian named Heraiscus that he was endowed with a certain divine nature, such that by the mere sight of statues which held some divinity within them, he was immediately stirred by a divine frenzy. We also read in the sacred scriptures that when Saul was among the prophets, the spirit of the Lord leaped upon him and he prophesied; and when he departed from the company of the prophets, he ceased to prophesy. A similar thing happened to those lictors <note>officers or guards</note> whom Saul sent to capture David: when they saw the company of prophets and Samuel standing over them, the spirit of the Lord came upon them also, and they themselves prophesied. So great is the exuberance of divine light in prophets seized by divine frenzy that it often seizes those near them and compels them to rave with a similar spirit. Therefore, it is not incredible that someone can suddenly become wise from being ignorant, and again ignorant from being wise. For there is a certain art (but known to very few) of so informing, adorning, and illustrating the faithful and pure soul of a man, that he is suddenly raised from the darkness of ignorance to the lights of wisdom and learning. Conversely, there is a faculty to strip the impure and unbelieving of that same gift of wisdom and learning through certain hidden secrets, and restore them to their former ignorance. The human soul can also (according to Apuleius) especially if it is simple and pure, be lulled to sleep by the distraction and charm of certain sacred rites and be carried out of itself into a forgetfulness of present things, so that with the body's memory removed...

### BOOK THREE. 315.

<margin>Prophets inspired by the divine fear no one</margin> [the soul] may be restored to its divine nature, and thus, illuminated by divine light and inspired by divine fury, it may foretell the future of things, and also undertake the power of certain wonderful effects. Whence Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on theurgy and mysteries.</note> says: When prophets are inspired by the power of a god, they fear nothing and respect no [earthly] danger; for they walk through pathless places, and are carried unharmed into fire, and cross rivers. Thus we read that certain caves, such as those of Apollo and Trophonius, and tripods, and caverns, and springs, and lakes, and such things were consecrated to the gods in this way, or constructed with that mystery, so that from them the priests might draw the spirit of prophesying. As Iamblichus says to Porphyry <note>Referring to the work "On the Mysteries," a response to Porphyry's doubts about Egyptian and Chaldean magic.</note>: The Sibyl at Delphi was accustomed to receive the god in a twofold manner: either through a thin spirit and fire, which broke out somewhere from the mouth of the cave; or while she herself sat in the inner sanctuary upon a bronze three-legged seat <term>tripod</term> dedicated to the deity. In both cases, driven by this divine spirit, she poured forth prophecies. Then, a great amount of fire flying out of the cave surrounds the prophetess on all sides, and agitates her as she is filled with his power; or, clinging to the sacred seat through which she is inspired by the god, she immediately breaks out into prophecies. But also the fate-telling prophetess among the Branchidae <note>An ancient line of priests who served the temple of Apollo at Didyma.</note>, who sits upon an axle, or carries a wand in her hand granted to her by some deity, or sometimes washes her feet and the hem of her garment in the waters, or draws the vapor of fire from the waters. By all these means she is filled with divine splendor, and having been uttered, she reveals full oracles of things. We also read that in the region of Thrace there was a sanctuary sacred to Bacchus <note>original: "Libero," an Italian deity identified with the Greek Dionysus/Bacchus.</note>, from which prophecies and oracles were accustomed to be given; the priests of this temple performed their duties after drinking wine in abundance. Among the Clarians also, where the temple of Clarian Apollo was, those to whom it was permitted to speak divine things performed their duties after first taking in water. There was also a fate-telling spring of Achaia at Patras, situated before the temple of Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture, identified with the Greek Demeter.</note>, where those consulting about the outcomes for the sick would lower a mirror tied with a thin cord until it reached the surface of the spring's waters; and after certain supplications and incense-burnings were performed, the event of the matter itself would present itself in the mirror. There was also, not far from Epidaurus, a city of Laconia, a deep pool which was called the water of Juno; into which, when grain cakes were thrown, answers were given: prosperous, if the waves had calmly retained those thrown in; but adverse, if they had rejected them as if in scorn. It is recorded that the craters of Etna <note>The active volcano in Sicily.</note> did something similar, into which coins or victims being thrown, showed the same omen of joy or sorrow by the retention or rejection of the things thrown in. Dion <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian.</note> relates similar things in Roman history concerning a place which he says was called the Nympheum: where, when incense was thrown into the flames in this manner, oracles were received concerning everything which anyone desired to know, except concerning death and matters pertaining to marriages. It is also a wonder what Aristotle related concerning the spring of the Palici in Sicily, to which those about to swear an oath approached; whatever they wished to affirm, they threw into the spring written and sealed on tablets. If these were true, they were seen to float upon the waters; but if they were false and perjured with evil intent, they were immediately submerged along with the petitioners; then, fire suddenly leaping out, seized the one guilty of perjury...

### Concerning the fourth kind of frenzy, from Venus. Chapter 49.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial Q featuring a seated figure, possibly a philosopher or Hermes, holding a celestial sphere.</image-desc>

<margin>Why Love is blind.</margin>
The fourth frenzy, proceeding from Venus, turns and transforms the soul into God through fervent love, and makes it entirely like God, as if it were God’s own image. Regarding this, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with magic and alchemy</note> says: "O Asclepius, man is a great miracle, a living being to be honored and adored: for he passes into the nature of God, as if he himself were God; he knows the race of demons, as he recognizes that he originated from the same source; he despises the part of human nature within himself, trusting in the divinity of his other part." Therefore, the soul having been transformed and made similar to God, is so shaped by God that—beyond all intellect—it knows all things by a certain essential contact with divinity. For this reason, Orpheus describes Love as being without eyes, because it is above the intellect. And now, the soul having been so turned toward God by love, and raised above the intellectual sphere, besides the fact that it has attained the spirit of prophecy and prediction by its full power, it sometimes works even greater and more wonderful things than the nature of the world itself, which work is indeed called a miracle. For just as 
<margin>Miracle.</margin>
the heavens—by their own image, light, and heat—perform those things which the force of fire does not achieve by its natural quality (which is very well known in Alchemy even by experience), so also God, through His own image and light, perfects those things which the world cannot do by its own innate power. Now, the image of God is man—at least the man who, having been made like God by the frenzy of Venus, lives by the mind alone and receives Jupiter <note>Here used to mean the supreme Divine spirit</note> with his whole heart. Nevertheless, the soul of man, according to the teachers of the Hebrews and the 
<term>Cabalists<gloss>Jewish mystics who study the hidden meanings of scripture</gloss></term>, is defined as being the light of God, created after the image of the Word, the cause of causes and the first pattern; it is a substance of God, shaped by a seal whose character is the eternal Word. Beholding this, Hermes Trismegistus says that such a man is either superior to the inhabitants of heaven, or at least possesses an equal lot.

### Concerning rapture and ecstasy, and the prophecies that happen to those seized by the falling sickness and fainting, and those which happen to the dying. Chapter 50.

Rapture is an abstraction, an alienation, and an illumination of the soul proceeding from God, through which God draws the soul—which had fallen from the heights to the depths—back again from the depths to the heights. The cause of this in us is the continuous contemplation of higher things, which, insofar as it joins the soul to incorporeal wisdom by the deepest intention of the mind, so much more vehemently...

By its more intense agitations, the soul calls itself away from sensible and bodily things, and (as **Plato** says) it does so in such a way at times that the body itself may even fail and seem almost to dissolve. This is much like what **Aurelius Augustine** relates concerning the priest of Calama (whom we mentioned above): "He lay there," he says, "exactly like a dead man, without breath; and even when he was burned and cut, he felt nothing." <note>Augustine, *City of God*, 14.24, describing a priest named Restitutus who could withdraw his senses at will.</note> So great, therefore, is the command of the soul—specifically when it has attained its own true nature and is no longer weighed down by the allurements of the senses—that by its own virtue it may suddenly ascend. It does this not only while remaining in the body, but sometimes, having been freed from its shackles, it flies outside the body to a super-celestial dwelling place. There, being now most proximate and most similar to God, having been made a receptacle for divine things, it is filled with divine light and oracles. Hence **Zoroaster** says: "You must ascend to the light itself, and to the rays of the Father, from whence the soul was sent to you, clothed in much mind." <note>A reference to the Chaldean Oracles.</note> And **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic wisdom.</note> says: "It will behoove you to ascend above the heavens, and to be far distant from the choirs of demons." And **Pythagoras** says: "If you, leaving the body behind, pass into the free ether, you shall be an immortal god." Thus we read that **Hermes**, **Socrates**, **Xenocrates**, **Plato**, **Plotinus**, **Heraclitus**, **Pythagoras**, and **Zoroaster** were accustomed to be called away by ecstasy, and thus to learn the wisdom of many things. We also read in **Herodotus** that there was in Proconnesus a philosopher of wondrous knowledge named **Aristeas**, whose soul would sometimes exit his body, and after seeing distant spaces in its travels, would return to the body more learned. **Pliny** relates the same of the soul of **Hermotimus of Clazomenae**, which was accustomed to wander after leaving the body and would report many true things from afar. And there are even to this day among the **Norwegians** and **Lapps** <note>original: "Nouergios & Pilappios"</note> many who call themselves away from the body for a full three days; upon returning, they report many things from distant places. Meanwhile, it is necessary to guard them, lest any living animal should happen to step over them; otherwise, they say the soul does not return into its body.

<margin>The soul, freed from the body, encompasses all place and time.</margin>
It should be known, therefore, that (according to the doctrine of the **Egyptians**) since the soul is a certain spiritual light, when it is released from the body, it encompasses all place and all time. This is not unlike a light enclosed in a lantern, which, when opened, is diffused everywhere and does not fail; for it is everywhere and always. And **Cicero**, in his book *On Divination*, says: "The mind of man never divines, except when it is so released that it has absolutely nothing or very little to do with the body." When, therefore, it has reached that state which is the highest degree of contemplative perfection, it is then snatched away from all created forms, and it understands not through acquired forms, but by gazing upon the **Ideas** <note>The Platonic archetypes or universal forms.</note>, and it knows all things in the light of the Ideas. **Plato** says that very few men become participants in this light in this life, but almost all the gods do. Fainting spells and the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy; original: "morbiq; comitiales"</note> also imitate this ecstasy in a way, and in these states, just as in ecstasy, prophecies very often occur; we read that **Hercules** and many **Arabs** excelled in this kind of prophesying. And there are certain prophecies which are midway between the boundaries of natural divinations and supernatural oracles—namely, those which arise from an excess of some passion, such as excessive love, or sadness, or amidst frequent sighing, or in the agony of death...

For there is within our souls a certain power, clear and capable of all things, but it is obstructed and hindered by the gloom of the body and mortality; however, after death, having attained immortality and being released from the body, it possesses full and perfect knowledge. We know, however, that it survives the body, and that—having now cast off the barriers of its own senses—it discerns with a free gaze those things which it did not see before while situated in the body; we can estimate this by the example of those sleeping, whose souls, while the body is buried in rest, raise themselves to higher things and report back to the body visions of absent or even celestial things.

### On the prophetic dream. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter 51.

<margin>Whence it happens that one sees dreams and understands them.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting two figures: one standing figure holding a staff and one seated figure, possibly representing a visionary or a traveler in a landscape.</image-desc>By "dream" I mean here that which proceeds from the phantastic spirit <term>spiritus phantasticus</term> <note>The "imagination" or the faculty that processes mental images.</note> and the intellect united with one another—either through the illumination of the active intellect <term>intellectus agens</term> acting upon our soul, or through the wondrous revelation of some divinity—with a purified and tranquil mind. For from this, our soul receives true oracles and provides us with prophecies in abundance: for in dreams we seem to ask questions, to learn, to read, and to find. Many doubts, many counsels, many unknown and unexpected things never before attempted by our minds are opened to us in dreams; images of unknown places appear, as well as likenesses of men both living and dead. Future things which have not yet occurred are portended, and things are revealed to have happened elsewhere which have not yet been made known by any report of knowledge. These dreams require no other art of interpretation, unlike those of which we spoke in the first book, which belong to divination rather than foreknowledge. It happens that those who have seen them most often do not understand them: because (as Abdala the Arab <note>Likely referring to a medieval Arabic source or commentator, possibly Al-Kindi or a similar figure.</note> says) just as seeing dreams comes from the strength of the imagination, so understanding them comes from the strength of the intellect. Therefore, he whose intellect is put to sleep by being submerged in too much commerce with the flesh, or whose imaginative or phantastic spirit is so dull and unpolished that it cannot receive the forms and flowing images of the higher intellect, nor retain them once received—such a person is plainly useless for the prophecies of dreams. It is necessary, therefore, for one who wishes to receive true dreams to keep the phantastic spirit pure, unshaken, and undisturbed, and to compose it in such a way that it is made worthy for the mind and intellect to preside over it and become known to it. For such a spirit is most fit for prophecies, receiving all the "idols" <note>In the sense of "images" or "emanations" from the Greek *eidolon*.</note> flowing from things on all sides (as he says)...

# BOOK THREE.

<note>original: "LIBER TERTIVS"</note>

Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher-bishop who wrote extensively on dreams as a gateway to the divine.</note> is a most clear mirror of this truth. When, therefore, we are healthy in body, undisturbed in mind, not weighed down by food, nor grieving in poverty, and with no vices of lust or anger clamoring within us, we go to bed chastely and sleep. Then our soul—pure and divine, released from every harmful thought and now free through sleep—relies upon this divine spirit as its instrument. It receives into itself the radiating and shining beams and images from divine minds. As if in a certain god-like mirror, the soul beholds these things far more certainly, clearly, and effectively than through any common investigation of the intellect or wandering of reason. The divine powers invite the soul to their assembly, taking advantage of the opportunity provided by the stillness of the night. Even then, the favorable divinity will not be absent from the waking person to moderate their actions.

Whoever, therefore, keeps their spirit pure through tranquil and religious meditation, and through a temperate diet moderated according to nature, uses a spirit that is perfectly prepared. In this way, they become divine and knowing. On the other hand, whoever suffers from a sluggish <margin>*A comparison.*</margin> imaginative spirit does not receive clear and distinct visions. Just as a one-eyed man <note>original: "luscus oculus"</note> judges confusedly and indistinctly because of weakness, so too when we are filled with gluttony and wine, our spirit is oppressed by harmful vapors. (Just as turbid water is affected differently even under the same form). The spirit is deceived and grows dull. For this reason, the prophet Amphiaraus <note>A legendary Greek hero and seer.</note> (as we read in Philostratus) <margin>*Philostratus book 2, chapter 14.*</margin> ordered anyone wishing to receive oracles to abstain from food for an entire day and from wine for three days. He maintained that the soul could not prophesy correctly unless it were freed from wine and food; for the gods are accustomed to grant oracles to sober and religious souls who are devoted to divine worship. Whence Orpheus exclaims:

> *Greatest prophet and messenger of things to come,*
> *You approach souls soothed by the quiet of sleep.*
> *Addressing them, you rouse the mind,*
> *You suggest the decrees of the blessed deities to them through sleep,*
> *Silent, you announce the future to silent souls—*
> *To those souls, I say, whose minds are most rightly employed in divine worship.*

Hence it was the custom among the ancients that those about to receive responses would first celebrate certain sacred purifications and sacrifices. Having performed the divine worship, they would lie down religiously in a consecrated chamber, or at least upon the fleeces of their own sacrifices. Virgil mentions this rite in these verses:

> *In times of doubt they seek responses; here the priest*
> *Brought gifts, and under the silent night, upon the skins*
> *Of slaughtered sheep he lay and sought sleep.*

->*And a little later he sings:*<-

> *Here also then, father Latinus himself, seeking responses,*
> *Duly sacrificed a hundred wool-bearing sheep,*
> *And lay supported upon their backs and spread-out*
> *Fleeces.*

<margin>
The time for dreams is night.
</margin>
And those who ruled over the Spartans (as Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, Roman statesman and philosopher</note> says) were accustomed to lie down in the temple of Pasiphaë <note>A Greek goddess associated with oracles</note> for the sake of dreaming; the same was done in the temple of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine</note>, by whom true dreams were thought to be sent. And the Calabrians, wishing to consult Podalirius, the son of Aesculapius, would fall asleep near his tomb upon the skins of lambs; for in this way, one would be warned in dreams about whatever they desired to know. However, the most familiar time for dreams is the night, when the senses are freed from wandering objects, midday errors, and vain affections; when fear does not strike the soul, nor thought waver, and the mind is most peaceful, it may perseveringly cling to the divine. Moreover (as Rabbi Johanan <note>original: "Rabi Iohenan"; likely referring to a figure from the Talmudic "Book of Senators" or Sanhedrin</note> says in the *Book of the Senators*), there are four kinds of true dreams: 

<margin>
Four kinds of true dreams.
</margin>
The first is the morning dream, which occurs between sleep and waking; the second is what one sees concerning another person; the third is that whose interpretation is shown to the dreamer himself by a nocturnal vision; the fourth is that which is repeated to the same dreamer, according to what Joseph said to Pharaoh, saying: "As for the dream having been seen by you a second time pertaining to the same matter, it is a sign of its firmness" <note>Genesis 41:32</note>. Furthermore, the firmest dream is that which concerns those things which a person revolves within themselves and agitates in the mind when going to sleep, just as it is written: "O King, thoughts began to come into your mind upon your bed as to what should come to pass hereafter" <note>Daniel 2:29</note>. It is necessary, however, for an interpreter of others' dreams to possess the knowledge by which he can distinguish and discern the similarities of all things, and to know the customs of all nations, according to the laws they have received concerning God and the angels. 

<margin>
Vain things mixed with dreams.
</margin>
Besides this, it should be known that there is scarcely any dream, or none at all, without some vain thing mixed in, just as there is no grain of wheat without chaff; which even the dream of the patriarch Joseph himself testifies, which his father Jacob interpreted, saying: "What does this dream mean that you have seen? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow down to you on the earth?" <note>Genesis 37:10</note>—which indeed was not fulfilled regarding his mother, who had died shortly after. These things Rabbi Johanan also says in the aforementioned book; to which Rabbi Levi adds, saying that every prophetic dream can be delayed in its effect for as long as twenty-two years: thus Joseph dreamed in the seventeenth year of his age what afterwards came into action in the thirty-ninth year of his age. 

<margin>
What things are required for receiving divine dreams.
</margin>
Therefore, one wishing now to receive divine dreams should be well-disposed in body, the brain free from vapors, and the mind free from disturbances; on that day let him abstain from supper, nor drink anything that can intoxicate. Let him have a bedroom that is clean and bright, even exorcised and consecrated, in which, having performed a fumigation <note>The burning of incense or herbs for ritual purification</note>, with the temples <insert>of the head</insert> joined, the fingers bound with rings of dreams, a celestial image and a sacred parchment placed under the head, and the deity invoked with sacred prayers, let him seek his bed with his thought intent upon the matter he desires to know. For thus he shall see most true and indubitable dreams, with a true illumination of the intellect. Whoever, therefore, knows how to join together those things which we have said dispersedly in these books concerning this matter, shall easily obtain the gift of oracles and dreams.

# BOOK THREE
### D iii

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' at the beginning of the text, featuring a woodcut illustration of two men in a scholarly or clerical setting, engaged in conversation or study.</image-desc>

There are also certain kinds of lots <note>Latin: *sortes*</note> possessing a divine power of oracles, acting as indicators of divine judgment. These are sought after with much prayer and supplication by those who inquire, and sometimes they are even commanded by God himself to be performed. We read of this in Leviticus regarding the goat to be offered to the Lord and the scapegoat; and in the book of Numbers, regarding the rods of the tribes of Israel. Furthermore, Moses and Joshua, having cast lots in the sight of the Lord, divided the lands and inheritances among the tribes of Israel according to the command of God. The Apostles of Christ, after offering prayers, chose Matthias by lot to take the place of the traitor Judas. When the prophet Jonah was sailing to Tarshish while fleeing from the face of the Lord, and a storm arose, the sailors found him by lot to be the cause of the danger; once he was cast into the sea, the storm ceased. Caesar relates that when Marcus Valerius Procillus was captured by enemies, the lots were consulted three times to determine whether he should be killed by fire immediately or reserved for another time; by the favor of the lots, he escaped unharmed. There was formerly at Bura, a town in Achaia <note>A region in Greece</note>, an oracle of Hercules consisting of dice <note>Latin: *talis*, specifically knucklebone dice</note> and a counting board <note>Latin: *abaco*</note>. There, one wishing to consult on any matter would, after prayers to the god, throw four dice; the priest, observing their positions and figures, would find what was to come written upon the board. All these dice were made from the bones of sacrificial animals. Truly, it must be known

<margin>The ancient fathers did not cast lots rashly</margin>
that the ancient fathers were not accustomed to cast lots for any trivial reason, but only when urged by necessity or great utility, and never without great religion, reverence, expiations, fasts, cleanliness, prayers, invocations, vows, sacrifices, consecrations, and other sacred mysteries of religion. For these sacred rites, when duly performed before our works, are most effective in provoking the divine will and benevolence, and the presence of divine spirits. By their dispensation, the lot is directed, and we receive a true judgment on the matter sought.

<margin>The disposition of one who wishes to work through lots.</margin>
Therefore, whoever works through lots must approach with a well-disposed mind—not troubled, not distracted—and with a strong desire, firm deliberation, and a constant intention of knowing that which is asked. Furthermore, one should be flourishing in purity, chastity, and holiness toward God and the celestial powers, with undoubting hope and firm faith, invoking them with sacred prayers so that he may be made worthy for the divine spirits to join him and for the divine will to become known. For if you are so disposed, the greatest secrets will be opened to you by the power of the lots, and you will be a truth-telling prophet of the past, present, and future things about which you are asked. What we have said here concerning lots must also be observed in the auguries of omens and signs <note>Latin: *notaminum*</note>; namely, when with awe, yet with firm expectation, we set before ourselves certain signs for the sake of prophesying, or demand a sign, as we read that Eleazar, the servant of Abraham, and Gideon, a judge in Israel, did. There was formerly in Pharae, a city of Achaia, a statue of Mercury in the middle of the marketplace. ### How one wishing to receive oracles ought to dispose himself. Chapter LIII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a figure seated at a desk or table, seemingly engaged in study or writing.</image-desc>Whoever, desiring to approach the supreme state of the soul, sets out to seek oracles, it is necessary that he approach disposed chastely and holily, pure and clean, so that his soul is defiled by the infection of no filth, and bears no scars of sins impressed upon his breast. It will be necessary to thoroughly segregate and purge the soul—as far as the necessity of nature permits—from every disease, dullness, malice, and passions of that kind, and from every irrational condition which follows the soul like rust follows iron, by rightly composing and arranging those things which pertain to the tranquility of the mind: for thus he will receive truer and more effective responses. By what means the soul may be purged and restored to its divine purity, we must learn thoroughly from religion and wisdom; for wisdom is not without religion, nor is religion to be approved without wisdom. For wisdom (says Solomon) is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her: and Lucretius says that it is a discovery of God, or a breath of God, where he sings:

> He was a god, that famous Memmius,
> Who first discovered that reasoned way of life which
> Is now called wisdom, and who through his art
> Rescued life from such great waves and such great darkness
> And placed it in such a tranquil and such a clear light.

Indeed, to achieve such things in a moment is certainly not of the human mind, but of the divinely inspired mind, namely one in which God is present, working all things: for God himself, transferring himself into holy souls, establishes prophets and workers of wonders, powerful in deed and word, just as Plato and Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius," referring to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> assert, and <margin>Man is the temple of God.</margin> even Xystus the Pythagorean himself, asserting that a man of this kind is the temple of God, and God...

# BOOK THREE.

Even Aristotle confesses this in his *Meteorology* and *Ethics*, stating that there is no virtue, whether natural or moral, except through God. In his *Secrets* <note>referring to the "Secretum Secretorum," a text attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages</note> he adds that a good and healthy intellect can penetrate the secrets of nature, provided that the influence of divine power is present; otherwise, it is impossible. We receive this influence only when we release ourselves from the weighing-down impediments, from carnal and earthly preoccupations, and from all external agitation. For a blurry and unclean eye cannot gaze upon objects that are too bright, nor can one who is ignorant of the soul's purification grasp divine matters.

<margin>One must arrive at purity of soul step by step.</margin>
It is necessary, however, to arrive at this purity of soul gradually and, as it were, through certain steps. For not everyone newly initiated into these mysteries immediately comprehends all things clearly; rather, the mind must be accustomed little by little, until the intellect stands out within us and, applying itself to the divine light, becomes mingled with it. Therefore, when the human soul has been rightly purified and expiated, and then released from all variety <note>distractions of the material world</note>, it flashes forth with free movement, ascends upward, grasps divine things, and even instructs itself, even when it seems to be instructed from elsewhere. In that state, it needs neither reminder nor demonstration because of its natural skill; then, through its own mind—which is the head and charioteer of the soul—it imitates the angels by its very nature, attaining what it desires not through succession or time, but in a sudden moment.

<margin>David, Solomon, and the other prophets and apostles were taught suddenly.</margin>
For David did not learn letters, yet from a shepherd he was made a prophet and most learned in divine matters. Solomon, in the dream of a single night, was filled with the wisdom of all things above and below. Thus were Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the rest of the prophets and apostles educated. For the soul (which is the common opinion of the Pythagoreans and Platonists) can—through the purgative way without other study or investigation, but through only a brief and easy dwelling upon the intelligible things already held from above—acquire a perfect knowledge of all things knowable. It can also reach this through external expiation, so that it understands all things indivisibly through its own substantial form.

<margin>How the mind is to be expiated.</margin>
The mind is purified and expiated through cleanliness, through abstinence, through penance, and through almsgiving. Certain sacred institutions also contribute to the same end, as will be shown below; for the soul must be cared for through religious studies—which are indeed hidden from the common people—so that, restored to health, strengthened by truth, and fortified by divine protections, it does not fear the shocks that arise.

> *The gods are angry at this, and bestow sorrows thereafter.*

> *In a living stream.*

> *Aeneas reaches the entrance, and sprinkles his body*
> *With fresh water.*

Also, where he tells of the burial of Misenus, he sings:

> *Three times he carried pure water around his companions,*
> *Sprinkling them with a light dew and a branch of a fruitful olive tree.*

For when cleanliness is achieved, man becomes celestial and spiritual, and is thus prepared for the intuition and union of God, provided that he serves God with a clean body and a pure mind, and embraces cleanliness in all things: in the internal organs, in the skin, in garments, in utensils, in dwellings, in gifts, in offerings, and in sacrifices. ## On abstinence and fasts, and chastity, solitude, and 
## tranquility of the soul and its ascent.
### Chapter LV.

Abstinence also familiarly fortifies and protects its observers everywhere against vices and evil demons, and renders the soul like an uncontaminated temple of God, joining the mind to God. Furthermore, nothing is better for the health and the balance of one's temperament <term>complexionis: the physical and mental makeup of a person based on the four humors</term> than to gather as little superfluity as possible, and not to exceed the measure of necessary food. For nourishment should not be taken that is stronger than nature, but rather that by which nature is made stronger; just as some assert regarding Christ, that he took food in such a measure that he generated no superfluity of the "fourth digestion" <note>In medieval physiology, the fourth digestion was the final stage where nutrients became part of the living tissue; the author suggests Christ's body was so efficient it left no waste.</note>. Many others also rejoiced in the sparingness of food along with health and agility of the body, such as Moses and Elijah, who extended their fasting until the fortieth day. Hence, the former shone in his face, and the latter, being lifted up, led his body as easily as a spirit at his command. For the magi and philosophers assert that our spirit is not nourished like an earthly thing, or like a body through the digestion of food or drink received through specific organs, but rather, in the manner of sponges, it draws its nourishment from all sides through the whole body—namely, from the thinnest vapors penetrating the body everywhere. Therefore, those who desire to have this spirit pure and powerful use drier foods, and they thin out this thick body with fasts, rendering it easily permeable, lest by its weight the spirit either becomes thickened or suffocated. Then, by washings and rubbings, and exercises, and clothing, they keep the body itself clean, and they strengthen the spirit with purifications and incense, leading it to a pure and thin sincerity. We ought, therefore, to be pure and abstinent in taking food, just as the Pythagorean philosophers, keeping a sacred and sober table, prolonged their lives in all temperance. For temperance of life and temperament—
<margin>The effects of temperance.</margin>
because such a state brings us no tumult of any dominating humor <note>The four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> which might stir the imagination toward any [false] image—ensures that our soul, very often while dreaming and sometimes even while awake, is always subjected to celestial influences. Moreover, the Pythagoreans promise perpetual health of both and even a long life, if one prudently moderates every motion of both soul and body through abstinence. Thus the Brahmans <note>original: "Bragmani"</note> admitted no one to their college unless they abstained from wine, meat, and vices, saying that no one can understand God except he who emulates Him through divine conversation; Phraotes also taught this to the lower Indians in the works of Philostratus.
