...he wrote and performed many things concerning the art of divination and prophecy <note>original: "diuinandi ac uaticinandi"</note>. The writings of Orpheus to Musaeus declare that he performed similar works in the deserts of Thrace. So we read that Epimenides the Cretan was instructed by a very long sleep, for they say he slept for fifty years: by this they understand that he remained in hiding. Pythagoras is likewise said to have remained hidden for ten years, and Heraclitus and Democritus delighted in solitude for the same reason. For the more we leave behind the animal and human life, the more we live as angels and God; joined to them and restored to a better lot, we are capable of all things, dominating all things. How our soul is to be separated from the animal life and from all multitude, and how it is to be raised until it ascends to the One itself—the Good, the True, the Beautiful—through each individual step of both the knowable things and the acts of cognition, Proclus teaches in his commentaries on the *Alcibiades* <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher; the *Alcibiades* is a dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of the self.</note>. <margin>What things a human must especially flee.</margin>

first of all, sensible things <note>Physical things perceived by the five senses.</note> must be fled, so that we may transfer ourselves to the incorporeal essence. There, one must overcome the order of souls—which is nevertheless multiplied through many reasons, various habits and proportions, many bonds, and a multiform variety of powers—and strive toward the intellect and the intelligible realms. One must contemplate by how great a distance these are better than souls. Furthermore, it is permitted to leave behind even that intellectual multitude, though it be united and indivisible, and to reach the super-intellectual and essential Unity, which is absolute and free from all multitude, the very fountain of the Good and the True. By a similar reasoning, we must flee all knowledge that distracts and deceives in manifold ways, so that we may attain the simplest truth. Therefore, the multitude of affections, senses, imaginations, and opinions must be left behind, which are so diverse in themselves that some are contrary to others in any respect. We must ascend to the sciences, in which, although there is a varied multitude, there is nevertheless no contrariety; for all are connected to one another, and one serves and ministers to the other in turn, up to the one science presupposed by all, which presupposes nothing further, to which all others must be referred. Yet even there is not the highest peak of cognitions, but above it is pure intellect. Thus, having laid aside all composition, division, and multiform discourse, ascending to the intellectual life and simple intuition, beholding the intelligible essence with indivisible and simple perceptions, we may attain the very highest existence of the soul, through which we are one, and under which our multitude is united. And thus we may touch the First One, from whom union is in all things, through that "one" which is, as it were, the flower of our essence. This we finally achieve only when, fleeing all multitude, we rise up into our own unity, and are made one, and act with uniformity.

<margin>What repentance is.</margin>
...a familiar path leading back to the heavens. Repentance <note>Latin: *pœnitentia*</note> is therefore not only the mortification of vices, but also a spiritual martyrdom of the soul, which is pierced on every side by the sword of the spirit; and the sword of the spirit is the word of God. Hence says the prophet Jeremiah, and also Paul writing to the Ephesians: "Cursed is he who keeps back his sword from blood" <note>Jeremiah 48:10</note>; and the Psalmist sings: "A sword is in their lips." Therefore, thoughts and affections of the mind, and all evils which come out of our heart and mouth, must be exposed to the priest in confession, so that he may judge them according to the word of God, and according to the power granted to him by God, cleanse and purge them by enjoined penance, and direct them toward the good. Indeed, no sacrament is found in religion more powerful for abolishing sins than repentance; hence the gods themselves (as Ovid witnesses in *Letters from the Black Sea*)

->Often lighten punishments, and restore sight that was taken away,<-
->When they see that one has truly repented for the sin.<-

<margin>Praise of almsgiving.</margin>
There is yet another sacrament of expiation, namely almsgiving <note>Latin: *eleemosyna*</note> itself, about which I remember reading little or nothing among the philosophers; but the Supreme Truth <note>referring to Christ</note> taught it to us, saying: "Give alms, and all things are clean unto you." And in Ecclesiasticus it is read: "As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin." And Daniel taught the King of Babylon to redeem his sins with alms, and the angel Raphael testifies to Tobias: "Because alms delivers from death, and it is that which purges sins and makes one find eternal life." Hence Christ commanded us to pray to the Father, "forgive as we forgive, and give as we give"; concerning which he said elsewhere: "You shall receive a hundredfold, and possess eternal life." The same one, when about to judge the living and the dead, will reproach the damned above all others for neglected alms and works of mercy, saying: "I was hungry and thirsty and you gave me nothing to eat or drink." And yet in another place, speaking of the poor, he says: "What you did for one of these, you did for me." Homer also seems to me to have felt this, where he introduces a youth speaking to the suitor Antinous in these words: "Antinous, you did not strike the wretched beggar well; if there is a god in heaven, he will destroy you, for even the gods, taking the likeness of foreign guests and going out into the world, overturn the cities of men, looking upon both injuries and wickedness."

Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on magic and theurgy.</note> also writes that priests were accustomed to using sulfur and asphalt in purifications, or the washing of sea water: for sulfur purifies because of the sharpness of its odor, while sea water purifies because of its fiery portion. In a similar way, the herb <term>pentaphyllon</term> <note>Cinquefoil or five-leaved grass.</note> purifies, which is why the ancient priests used it in their cleansings on account of its purity. Likewise with the branches of olives: for this tree is said to be of such great purity that they say an olive tree planted by a prostitute will either remain perpetually fruitless or wither away entirely. In a similar manner, frankincense, myrrh, vervain, and Valerian—which is also called the herb of light <note>original: "herba lucia"</note> and is called *Fu* in Arabic—contribute to expiation. Likewise, the fumes of the gall of a black dog are said to be most excellent in these matters, both for driving out evil demons and for undoing sorcery wherever it may be. Similarly, the smoked feathers of a hoopoe <note>original: "upupæ"</note> drive away phantasms.

<margin>Wonders concerning the Baaras root.</margin>
However, a thing marvelous and scarcely credible—unless it were told by that grave and not-to-be-despised author Josephus in his *History of Jerusalem*—is told concerning the **Baaras root**, named after a place near Machaerus, a town of Judea. He says this root is flame-colored and emits a glow at night, yet it is very difficult to capture, as it deceives the hand of the one trying to take it and flees from the eyes; nor does it stand still until it has been sprinkled with the urine of a menstruating woman. Yet even when held in this way, it is not pulled up without danger, for instant death follows the one who extracts it unless they are protected by an amulet made of the same root. Those lacking this, having scarred the earth all around it, tie the root with a tethered dog and then quickly depart; finally, the dog, following with too much effort, pulls out the root and, as if paying the price for its master, dies on the spot. Afterward, that root can be handled by anyone without danger. Its power in expiations is most excellent, so that it has been found to immediately liberate even those who are vexed by unclean spirits. 

They believe that materials of this kind act upon spiritual substances—by putting them to flight, or alluring them, or mitigating them, or inciting them—no differently than the 
<margin>Fire in Sicily.</margin>
**fire in Sicily** acts upon souls. This fire (according to the testimony of William of Paris <note>William of Auvergne, a 13th-century theologian who wrote on the soul and the universe.</note>), while not harming bodies, intolerably torments the souls of those who approach it. However, these matters have been partly treated above.

### On Adorations and Vows. Chapter 58.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut drop-cap 'A'. The interior of the letter depicts a figure seated in a landscape with architectural ruins or a large pedestal, with trees and hills in the background.</image-desc>

**A**dorations and vows, sacrifices and offerings, are indeed steps in the sacred rites for seeking out God. They are the primary things that provoke the divine will and forge a sacred and indissoluble communion between souls and the gods. For from the prayers which we utter with true and sacred words, in sense and mind, we acquire great power; when we apply them to some divinity, they move that divinity to direct its word and response toward us through a divine ray. By this ray (as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> says), God speaks with men, but so secretly that scarcely a few perceive it. However, that king and prophet David perceived it very often. "When," he said, "shall I hear what the Lord God speaks in me?" Therefore, a very long adoration...

<margin>How man returns to God.</margin> Man returns to God through prayers: reaching which place (says Plato in the *Phaedrus*) he stops his horses and enters the banquet chamber, where he feeds on ambrosia and drinks nectar. Therefore, those who desire to possess any virtue must pray and supplicate frequently to Him who contains all virtue within Himself. However, the better and best prayer is not that which is uttered by the mouth, but that which is offered to God in holy silence and with an untainted mind, and which, crying out with the voice of the mind, worships the presiding gods of the intellectual world with words. <margin>What a vow is.</margin> A vow is an ardent affection of a chaste soul dedicated to God, which by vowing desires that which appears good: this affection (as Iamblichus and Proclus <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who emphasized theurgy and the soul's connection to the divine.</note> testify) so joins souls to God that at times a single operation of God and the soul occurs: namely, of God as the craftsman, and of the soul as the divine instrument. Hence, all antiquity testifies that through vows miracles are sometimes performed, diseases cured, storms turned away, and similar things. Thus we read that the most excellent and wisest men among all nations—the Brahmans of the Indians, the Magi of the Persians, the Gymnosophists <note>term: Gymnosophists; "naked philosophers," a Greek term for Indian ascetics.</note> of the Egyptians, the theologians of the Greeks and Chaldeans, who established the festivals of the gods and hidden mysteries—chiefly devoted themselves to divine vows and prayers, and accomplished many wonderful things. <margin>Two things required for the perfection of a vow.</margin> For the perfection of a vow and adoration (for there is no vow without adoration, nor is adoration in any way perfect without a vow), two things are chiefly required: first, the knowledge of that which is to be adored and to whom the vow is to be made, and by what reason, in what order, and by what means it should be worshipped. For there are many coworkers and instruments of God, namely the heavens, the stars, administrative spirits, celestial souls, and heroes, whom one who proceeds toward the Archetypal God <note>The original, supreme divine pattern or Creator.</note>—who alone is the ultimate end of adoration—must first implore as gatekeepers, interpreters, administrators, and mediators. The other deities are like entrances to God Himself. Know therefore that prayers and vows must be made principally with a pure and pious mind to the one God alone, the supreme Father, King and Lord of all gods; but when they proceed to the lower gods, it should only be with the intention of an administration delegated by the supreme Father. Thus, when adorations and vows are directed to lower deities, Zoroaster and Orpheus thought it permissible to use fumigations, characters <note>term: characters; magical signs or symbols believed to hold spiritual power.</note>, and the like; but when they are raised to the majesty of the supreme Jupiter <note>Used here as a name for the supreme God.</note>, they should not be done at all—which Hermes and Plato also forbid. Whence Hermes says to Tatius: "This is like sacrilege, when you pray to God, to wish to burn incense and such things; for these are foreign (as Porphyry says) to all piety; for nothing material can be found which is not [unfitting] to the immaterial God..."

### Concerning sacrifices and offerings, and their kinds and modes.
### Chapter LIX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting two figures in a landscape setting with trees.</image-desc>
A sacrifice, moreover, is an offering which both becomes sacred by the act of offering, and sacrates or sanctifies the one offering it, unless irreverence or some other sin should hinder him. Therefore, these sacrifices and offerings provide us with much confidence, and make us of the household of God, and repel many evils threatening us: which indeed the teachers of the Hebrews <note>The "Hebræorum doctores" likely refers to Kabbalistic or Rabbinic sources.</note> confirm above others, saying: through this, that we slay our animals and dissipate our possessions in sacrifice, imminent evils are deflected from us to things of that kind; then, just as this mortal priest in this lower world sacrifices to God the souls of irrational animals through the destruction of the body from the soul, so Michael the Archangel, the priest of the higher world, sacrifices the souls of men, and that through the separation of the soul from the body—not of the body from the soul, except by accident, as happens in fury, rapture, ecstasy, and sleep, and similar vacations of the soul, which the Hebrews call the "death of the kiss." <note>term: "death of the kiss" (mors osculi). A mystical concept in Kabbalah where the soul departs the body in a state of divine union or ecstasy.</note> Truly, sacrifices and offerings are to be made first and principally to the supreme God: but when they are directed to the secondary powers <note>original: "secunda numina," referring to angels or celestial intelligences.</note>, understand this to be done just as was said concerning prayer and vows: then, whatever things were said there, we shall also understand here by way of similarity. 
<margin>Many kinds of sacrifices.</margin>
There are indeed many kinds of sacrifices: for a certain kind is called a "holocaust," when the victim is consumed by fire; another is an "immolation" on account of the shedding of blood. Furthermore, certain ones are called "salutary sacrifices," which are made for the obtaining of health; some "pacific," for the obtaining of peace; some "praises," for liberation from evils or the bestowing of goods; some "gratulatory," for divine veneration and the giving of thanks; some are made neither for the honor of God nor out of good will, such as was among the Hebrews the "sacrifice of jealousy," which was only done for the sake of detecting hidden adultery. 
<margin>Sacrifice of expiation.</margin>
And there was formerly among the nations a "sacrifice of expiation," by which cities were purged of hunger or pestilence, or other...

->### BOOK THREE.<-

<margin>666 types of sacrifices among the Egyptians.</margin>
...in bread and wine alone, as if in the primary substance of human food, we no longer require the sacrifice of animals or other things, or the shedding of blood for our cleansing, as we have already been perfectly cleansed in His blood <note>The author contrasts Christian Communion with ancient blood sacrifices</note>. There were also among the Egyptians six hundred and sixty-six types of sacrifices; they established divine honors and sacred sacrifices to individual stars and planets, because they believed them to be divine living beings, participating in an intellectual soul and a divine mind. <margin>The stars hear prayers and bestow celestial gifts.</margin> Hence they say that the stars themselves, when humbly entreated, hear our prayers and bestow celestial gifts, not so much by a natural law as by their own free will. And this is what Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on theurgy and mysteries</note> says: that the celestial bodies and worldly divinities possess certain divine and superior powers within themselves, and others that are natural and inferior. Orpheus calls these "keys" for opening and closing; through the latter they bind us to the influences of fate, but through the former they release us from fate. Therefore, if some misfortune threatens someone from Saturn or Mars, the Magi <note>Wise men or practitioners of high magic</note> command that one should not flee immediately to Jupiter or Venus, but rather to that very Saturn or Mars. Thus, the famous Psyche of Apuleius <note>Referring to the story of Cupid and Psyche in 'The Golden Ass'</note>, persecuted by Venus because of her equal beauty, was forced to earn favor not from Ceres or Juno, but from Venus herself. <margin>How the ancients sacrificed to the stars.</margin> Moreover, they used to sacrifice to individual stars with things pertaining to them: to the Sun, with solar things and its own animals, such as the laurel, the rooster, the swan, or the bull; to Venus through her own animals, such as the dove or the turtledove, and through her plants, such as vervain, just as Virgil sings:

> Bring water, and encircle these altars with a soft fillet,
> and burn fatty vervain and masculine frankincense. <note>Quoting Virgil's Eclogues 8.64-65</note>

Furthermore, whenever the Magi had completed some preparation, whether natural or artificial, pertaining to a certain star, they afterwards religiously consecrated and offered this to that same star. They did this not only to obtain natural power from its timely influence, but also to receive that same thing strengthened and made more powerful by divine confirmation through the religious offering itself. For the offering of any thing, when it is rightly offered to a god in some way, is sanctified by the offering itself no differently than a sacrifice, and it becomes a part of that god. <margin>Which victims were usually slaughtered for which gods.</margin> Furthermore, white victims were slaughtered for the celestial and ethereal gods; but for the earthly and infernal gods, black ones. For the earthly gods, they were sacrificed upon altars, but for the infernal ones in pits; for the gods of the air and water, birds were used—white for the former, black for the latter. Finally, birds were sacrificed to all gods and demons except for the earthly and infernal ones, for whom only four-footed animals were sacrificed, for "like rejoices in like." Finally, of those things sacrificed to the celestial and ethereal gods, it was permitted only to eat the meat once the extremities were reserved for the deity, but of the others, not at all. The oracle of Apollo expressed all these things in these verses:

> A threefold victim indeed for the celestial gods, and it
> must be slaughtered white; and threefold for the earthly,
> and they rejoice in the same being black. Furthermore, the
> celestials are received at open altars, while the [infernal] deities, conversely, in pits.

And these are what Orpheus calls the keys <note>original: "claues"</note> which open the gates of the elements and the heavens, so that through them man may penetrate to the super-celestial realms, and the intelligences of the heavens and the spirits of the elements may descend to him. However, perfect and truly religious men do not need these things, but only those who (as Trismegistus says) having "fallen into harmony," <note>A reference to the Hermetic concept of the soul falling into the material world and becoming subject to the influence of the stars.</note> have become servants of the heavens and of creatures. Because they are subject to the heavens, they think they must be strengthened by the favor of celestial virtue, until, flying higher, they are released from that presidency and emerge more sublime than they.

### How these things are to be exhibited both to God and to the lower powers. Chapter 61.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'O' depicting a seated figure in an armchair or throne, possibly a scholar or biblical figure, within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>
Every adoration, offering or sacrifice, prayer, and invocation is centered on this distinction: namely, that it is made either to God alone, or to the lower powers <note>original: "numina," referring to spiritual beings or divinities</note>, such as angels, stars, and heroes. In these matters, you must observe such rules as these: whenever a prayer is to be offered to God alone to obtain some effect, this should be done with the commemoration of some work, miracle, sacrament, or promise drawn from the Holy Scriptures. For example, if a prayer is made for the destruction of enemies, let it be commemorated how God destroyed the giants in the flood of waters, and the attempt at Babel in the confusion of tongues, Sodom and Gomorrah in the rain of fire, the army of Pharaoh in the Red Sea, and the like: adding to these whatever curses can be gathered from the Psalms and here and there from the Holy Scriptures. By a similar reasoning, when about to pray against the dangers of waters, let us commemorate the salvation of Noah in the flood, the passage of the children of Israel through the midst of the Red Sea, and Christ walking with dry feet upon the waters, and the same one having saved the boat in peril, having commanded the winds and the waves, and having led the sinking Peter out of the waters of the sea, and such things. But if a prayer is necessary for seeking oracles or dreams, whether to God or to angels and heroes, there now offer themselves innumerable places from the Old Testament where God is read to have spoken with men, with many verses promising omens and revelations, then various prophetic dreams—of Jacob, Joseph, Pharaoh, Daniel, Nebuchadnezzar—then whatever revelations are found in the New Testament and in all religion: of John, Paul, the Holy Magi, then of Helena, Constantine, and Charlemagne: then things...

Furthermore, we also invoke the sacred names of God, but especially those which are expressive of the desired outcome, or are in some way suited to it: for instance, for the destruction of enemies we invoke the names of God's wrath, God's vengeance, God's fear, God's justice, and God's strength; but to avoid some danger, we invoke the names of mercy, defense, salvation, goodness, and the like. Moreover, we ask for the fulfillment of our desire from some angel, or star, or one of the heroes <note>In this context, "heroes" refers to divinized human souls or semi-divine beings in the Neoplatonic tradition</note> to whom that office belongs, to whom a similar invocation is directed. This invocation itself must be constructed with due number, weight, and measure, according to the rules handed down where we treated 

<margin>The difference between incantations and prayers.</margin>
the composition of incantations. For there is no difference, except that they are incantations insofar as they affect our mind and dispose its passions to be conformable to certain divine powers; but they are prayers insofar as they are offered to some divine power for the sake of worship and veneration. From this same root, the method of consecration can also be derived, of which we shall now speak consequently.

### On consecrations and their method. Chapter LXII.

<margin>The efficacy of consecrations is perfected by two things.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring a human figure within a framework of vine-like foliage.</image-desc>
Consecration is the sublimation of experiments, through which a spiritual soul—drawn by proportion and conformity—is infused into the matter of our works, which has been duly and lawfully prepared according to the tradition of the magical art; thus our work is quickened by the spirit of the intellect. The efficacy of consecrations is perfected chiefly by two things: namely, by the virtue of the person consecrating, and by the virtue of the prayer itself. Regarding the rites by which consecration is administered, there is required in the person a holiness of life and a power of sanctifying. Nature and merit provide the first; the second is acquired through initiation and "dignification" <note>term: Dignification; the process of making oneself worthy or spiritually 'heavy' enough to command spiritual forces</note>, which we have discussed elsewhere. Furthermore, it is necessary that the consecrator himself recognizes this virtue and power within himself with a firm and 

<margin>Prayer and its power.</margin>
undoubting faith. Now, our intention is to speak of what is required in the prayer. It is a certain power of sanctifying inherent in it by divine gift, as if it were ordained by God for this very purpose—such as many we read in the holy utterances of the Bible. Or, it may be instituted for this purpose by the ordinance of the Church through the power of the Holy Spirit; many of this kind also exist everywhere. Or, this holiness is in the prayer itself, not by virtue of institution, but by the commemoration of holy things: such as holy scripture, histories, miracles, works, effects, graces, promises, sacraments, and sacramentals, which seem to belong to the thing to be consecrated either properly, improperly, or by some similarity. We shall now give some examples of this, through which the way to this entire 

<margin>The consecration of water.</margin>
consideration will easily lie open. Thus, in the consecration of water, a commemoration is made: how God placed the firmament in the midst of the waters; how He established a sacred fountain in the earthly paradise, from which the entire world is irrigated by four sacred rivers; how He made waters the instrument of His justice <note>original: "aquas iustitiæ suæ"; likely referring to the Great Flood</note>...

<margin>Another rite of consecration and purification.</margin> You will find many more things of this kind in the prophets and the Book of Revelation <note>original: "Apocalypsi"</note>, such as the sacred names: the sword of God, the rod of God, the staff of God, the vengeance of God, and the like. Furthermore, it should be known that a vow, an offering, or a sacrifice possesses a certain power of both real and personal consecration, insofar as things or persons are devoted and offered to specific divine powers.

### Which things are called sacred, which are consecrated: and how these relate to us and the gods, and concerning sacred times. Chapter LXIII.

<margin>Sacred things.</margin> Those things are called sacred which have been hallowed by the gods themselves or by their attending spirits <note>original: "daemonibus"</note>, as if—so to speak—dedicated to us by the gods themselves. In this way, we call spirits sacred because God dwells in them, and they are often said to bear His name. Whence we read in Exodus: *I will send my angel who shall go before thee; observe him, and do not think him to be despised, for my name is in him.* In this same way, mysteries are called sacred.

<margin>Mystery.</margin> For a mystery is that which possesses a hallowed and hidden virtue and grace bestowed by the gods or spirits, or dispensed by the Supreme God himself—just as are the sacred names and characters <note>talismanic symbols</note> mentioned above. Thus the Cross itself is sacred and mysterious, hallowed by the passion of Jesus Christ. Hence also certain prayers and petitions are called sacred and mystical, which were instituted not by human devotion but by divine revelation—just as we read in the Gospels that Christ instituted the Lord's Prayer. In a similar way, certain preparations are called sacred, into which God has infused a singular ray of His power, as we read in Exodus concerning the incense and the oil of unction; and as among us, the sacred font, the holy chrism, the oil of catechumens, and the like. There is also another kind of sacred thing, by which we call "sacred" those things dedicated and consecrated to God by men, such as vows and sacrifices, which were mentioned above. Whence Virgil writes:

> But Caesar, entering the Roman walls in triple triumph,
> Consecrated an immortal vow to the Italian gods.

And Ovid sings in the books of the *Metamorphoses*:

> The feast day had arrived, on which Achilles, the conqueror of Cycnus,
> Was appeasing Pallas with the blood of a slaughtered cow.
> When he placed the gift upon the warm altars,
> And the smoke, accepted by the gods, rose into the air:
> They performed the sacred rites; a portion was given, the rest to the tables.

In a similar way, we speak of sacred likenesses, shrines, idols, statues, images, and paintings made in the likeness of the gods, or dedicated to the gods themselves, just as Orpheus sings in his hymn to the Lycian Venus:

->For our leaders, looking upon the divine things of the fatherland,<-

->And Virgil:<-

<note>original: "Tu genitor cape ſacra manu patriosq; penates." From the Aeneid, Book 2.</note>

<margin>Interpretation of the statue of Jupiter.</margin>
Hence the divine Plato, in the eleventh book of *The Laws*, commanded that the sacred statues and images of the gods ought to be honored—not for their own sake, but because they represent the gods to us. This is how the ancients venerated that famous statue of Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, king of the gods.</note>, interpreting it thus: because it bears the likeness of a man, it signifies that he is Mind, which produces all things through seminal reason. He is depicted sitting so that his stable and unchangeable power may be expressed. His upper parts are naked and open because he is visible to the Intelligences and superior beings; however, his lower parts are covered because he is hidden from the inferior creatures. He holds a scepter in his left hand because the most spiritual dwelling-place of life is found in those parts of the body. Indeed, the creator is the Intellect, the king and life-giving spirit of the world. In his right hand, he extends both an eagle and a Victory: the one because he is the lord of the other gods, just as the eagle is of other birds; the other because all things are subject to him. In a similar way, we also venerate the figure of a lamb because it represents Christ; and the figure of a dove because it denotes the Holy Spirit; and the figures of the lion, the ox, the eagle, and the man, signifying the Evangelists <note>The traditional symbols for Matthew (man), Mark (lion), Luke (ox), and John (eagle).</note>, and other similar figures which we find expressed in the revelations of the prophets and in various places in the Holy Scriptures. Indeed, these very things contribute to similar revelations and dreams, and for that reason, they are called sacred paintings. There are also sacred rites and observations performed for the veneration of the gods and religion, such as devout gestures, genuflections, the uncovering of the head, washings, the sprinkling of holy water, fumigations <note>The burning of incense or herbs for purification.</note>, external expiations, and likewise processions of supplications. There is also the external adornment of divine praises, such as musical resonance, the lighting of candles and lamps, the ringing of signals and bells, and the decoration of temples, altars, and statues. In all of these, the highest and most beautiful worship and decorum are required; therefore, whatever is most beautiful, fair, and precious—gold, silver, precious stones, and the like—is employed for these purposes. These acts of veneration and external sacred things are, as it were, instructions and invitations to spiritual sacred things, intended to obtain benefits from the gods, as Proserpina <note>Queen of the Underworld; the author attributes these verses to her oracular voice.</note> testified in these verses:

->Who among men would ever neglect forms of bronze,<-
->Or the yellow gifts of gold, or the white gifts of silver?<-
->Who would not marvel? Who would not say these very things<-
->Belong to the gods?<-

They are also called sacred priests, the ministers of the spirits <note>original: "numinum"</note> and the gods, and those who administer the sacred titles and any sacred rites to them, and who consecrate things. Hence Lucan says:

Indeed, sacred things of this kind are like certain pacts between the gods and us, offered under praise, or veneration, or obedience, through the mediation of which we often obtain some wonderful power from that spirit to whom such veneration is paid: such are sacred hymns, and speeches, and exorcisms, and incantations, and voices, which are composed and dedicated to the praises and venerations of the gods. And the primitive church used certain sacred incantations against diseases and storms, all of which we often obtain some power from such a spirit—which men greatly admire—either by praying and pronouncing them under the veneration of some divinity, or even sometimes by carrying them written down, hung, or bound [to the body]. In this way there are also sacred names, figures, characters, and seals, which contemplative men have vowed, dedicated, and consecrated with a pure mind for the veneration of God according to their secret vows. Indeed, if anyone should later pronounce these with the same purity of mind with which they were first instituted, he will likewise effect wonders, provided also that the manner and rule handed down by the first institutor be observed: for those who are ignorant of these things lose their labor and work in vain. In this way, we sometimes effect wonders not only with foreign <note>original: "barbaris," referring to non-Latin/Greek "barbarous" words of power</note> words, but also with Hebrew, Egyptian, Greek, Latin, and names of any other language, devoted to God and attributed and dedicated to His essence, or power, or operation.

<margin>There is sometimes a wonderful power in names.</margin>

Thus, according to Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note>, there are names such as Osiris, Icto, Emeph, Ptha, Epies, Amun: so according to Plato and the Greeks, *the Being* <note>original: "ὤν"</note>, *of all things* <note>original: "τῶν παντῶν"</note>; so the Greeks call Jupiter *Zena* <note>original: "ζῆνα"</note>, from *to live* <note>original: "δι' ὃν ζῆν"</note>, because he provides life to individuals: similarly *Dia* <note>original: "Δια"</note>, which signifies *through*, because through him all things are made: so *athanaton* <note>original: "ἀθάνατον"</note>, which signifies *immortal*. So among the Latins he is called *Jupiter*, as if a *helping father* <note>original: "iuuans pater"</note>, and things similar to these, just as certain proper names are also given to men according to a wish, such as Eutychides <note>meaning "fortunate"</note>, Sosias <note>meaning "savior"</note>, and Theophilus, which is "prosperous," "servant," and "dear to God." Similarly, certain material things conceive no small amount of sanctity and power from consecration, especially priestly consecration, just as we see those waxen seals <note>The "Agnus Dei" wax discs</note> on which the figure of lambs is inscribed, receive power through the blessing of the Roman Pontiff against lightning and storms so that they do not harm those carrying them: for divine power is breathed into sacred images of this kind, and is contained in them as if in a certain sacred letter which holds the image of God. ### BOOK THREE

Through their consecration and blessing, they receive power to ward off and restrain lightning and storms, so that they do not cause harm in places where their sound is heard at that time. In a similar way, salt and water receive, through their blessings and exorcisms, the power of purifying and driving away evil demons, and so <margin>Sacred times.</margin> it is with similar things. There are also sacred times, always observed with the highest veneration among the peoples of every religion, which were either commanded to us to be sanctified by the gods themselves, or dedicated to them by our fathers and ancestors in perpetual commemoration of a benefit received from the gods and in continual thanksgiving. Thus the Hebrews have their Sabbaths, thus the heathens their festivals, and thus we have received our solemn days of sacred rites to be venerated always with the greatest celebrity. There are also times contrary to these, which <margin>Expiatory times.</margin> we call expiatory, and those which we call "black days" <note>Latin: *dies atri*, days considered unlucky or cursed in the Roman calendar.</note>, because on those days the state suffered some notable slaughter or calamity. Of such a kind among the Romans was the fourth day before the Nones of August <note>August 2nd; the text refers to the "Sextilis," the old Roman name for the sixth month.</note>, because on that day they suffered that most vast slaughter of the <margin>Black days.</margin> Battle of Cannae. For a similar reason, all days following a festival were called "black," because on those days they very often fought unsuccessfully. Thus among the Jews there are black days, such as the seventeenth of the month of June <note>Tammuz in the Hebrew calendar; the text uses Roman month names for clarity.</note>, because they hold it as certain that on that day Moses broke the tablets, Manasseh erected an idol in the Holy of Holies, and the walls of Jerusalem were destroyed by enemies. Similarly, the ninth of July <note>Tisha B'Av</note> is a black day for them, because on that day both destructions of the Temple were carried out. By this reasoning, they are called <margin>Egyptian days.</margin> "Egyptian Days," formerly observed by the Egyptians; and any nation can easily fashion for itself a similar calculation of favorable and unfavorable days by this reasoning. The Magi command that these sacred and religious days be observed no differently than planetary days and celestial arrangements; indeed, they maintain that these are much more effective, especially for attaining spiritual and divine powers. This is because their power and influence descend not so much from the elements and celestial bodies, but from the intelligible and super-celestial world; aided by the common prayers of the saints, it cannot be broken by any opposing arrangement of the celestial bodies, nor frustrated by the corruptible contagion of the elements—provided there is no lack of firm belief and religious veneration. This veneration is joined with fear and awe, for that is what "religion" properly signifies. Hence those days are called "religious" which it is a sin to violate, and which we observe anxiously, fearing some great evil if anything should be done on them otherwise than it ought to be.

For taxes, and for the purification of colonies or armies, the **Censors** <note>original: "CENSS." - Roman officials responsible for the census and public morality</note> used to choose men with auspicious names. Furthermore, by changing unlucky names into fortunate ones, they believed the very fortune of affairs could be changed for the better. Thus, they established that *Epidamnum* should be called *Dyrrachium*, lest those sailing there should encounter "damage" <note>original: "damnum"; the Romans renamed the city to avoid the linguistic omen of the word "loss" or "harm"</note>. By the same reasoning, they called *Maleoton* by the name *Beneventum* <note>original: "Beneventum" means "well-come" or "good event," replacing "Maleventum" which sounded like "bad event"</note>, lest it bring anything of "evil" <note>original: "mali"</note>. Indeed, they considered Lake *Lucrinus* the most fortunate of all because of the prosperity implied by its name <note>The name Lucrinus was associated with "lucrum" or profit, due to its productive oyster beds</note>. Choose also the hours and days for your own works, for the Savior did not speak without cause: *Are there not twelve hours in the day?* and what follows. For the **Astrologers** have taught, and the **Magi** have observed, that specific times can provide a certain fortune to our affairs.

<margin>Times can provide fortune.</margin>

Finally, all the wisest ancients agree on this: that it is of the greatest importance at what moment of time, or by what disposition of the heavenly bodies, anything in this world receives its existence—not only natural things, but even artificial ones. For they have handed down that this moment of beginning has such great power that the entire course of fortune depends upon it and can be predicted from it. By the same reasoning, they firmly believed and asserted, with experience itself as a witness, that the beginning of a thing can be traced backward from the successes of its fortune. Just as **Sulla** the Astrologer, when consulted by **Caligula** <note>The Roman Emperor</note> about his nature, predicted that a most certain death was approaching. **Metheon** the astrologer, when the Athenians were planning an expedition against the Syracusans, foresaw the future calamity of the war; and when the same people were about to sail to Sicily, **Meson** the astrologer predicted a storm. **Anaxagoras**, through this science of times, warned on which days a stone would fall from the sun, just as later happened at the river of **Aegospotami** in Thrace. Conversely, **L. Tarnucius Firmianus**, from the deeds and fortune of **Romulus**, discovered both his conception and his birth. He likewise discovered the birthday of the city of Rome from the recorded successes of its fortune. So also the beginning or "nativity" of the world was found from the outcomes of events, as **Maternus** reports.

That times have great power in natural things can be shown by many examples. For there are trees that turn their leaves after the solstice, such as the poplar, the elm, the olive, the lime, and the white willow. And shellfish, crabs, and oysters grow larger with the waxing moon and grow lean with the waning moon; and the seas, by their ebb and flow, observe the motions and times of the moon. And does not the **Euripus** in Euboea flow down and back seven times with marvelous speed? The same remains motionless for three days in every month, namely on the seventh, eighth, and ninth moon. And among the **Troglodytes** <note>A legendary group of cave-dwellers</note> there is a lake that becomes bitter and salty three times a day, and then sweet again. Indeed, on a winter day when all things wither, dried pennyroyal flourishes. On the same day, they say that inflated bladders burst, and the leaves of willows and the seeds of apples turn and rotate. And it is manifest—something I have seen in both Italy and France, and I know the planting of it—namely a nut tree which, though dry throughout the whole year, produces leaves, flowers, and mature fruit on the very Vigil of Saint John. This entire miracle consists solely in the observation of the time of its planting. That times can provide certain marvelous virtues to artificial things, the Astrologers themselves constantly affirm in their books of *Elections* and *Images* <note>Technical manuals for choosing auspicious times and creating talismans</note>. And for this reason, we read in **Plutarch** that a statue was fashioned among the **Pellenians** with such art...

At Troy, around the statue of Minerva, abandoned sacrifices did not rot. In the sanctuary of Venus at Paphos, it did not rain in the courtyard. If anything was dug up from the tomb of Antaeus, showers would scatter from the sky until that which had been excavated was restored. On the tomb of King Bibria of Pontus, a laurel tree stood out; if anyone plucked a branch from it and brought it onto a ship, quarrels would not cease there as long as it had not been cast away. In the temple of Achilles on the island of Borysthenes, no bird would intrude. At Rome, in the temple of Hercules in the Forum Boarium, neither a fly nor a dog would enter. In Olynthus in Thrace, there was a place where, if a beetle fell into it, it could not leave, but twisting itself about, it would die. I could bring forward almost innumerable examples, and many more wonderful than these, which antiquity relates were made by the art of images and the observation of [astrological] times. 

But lest anyone believe these things to be long since obsolete and consider them trifles, I shall add certain more recent, skillfully made miracles still existing in some places in these times. For it is said to be effected by the art of images that at Byzantium <note>modern-day Istanbul</note> serpents harm no one, and jackdaws do not fly within the walls. That Crete does not bear owls; that in the territory of Naples cicadas are not heard; that the public barbershops of Venus are entered by no kind of flies; and that at Toledo, in the public meat market, throughout the whole year, no more than one fly is seen, and that one indeed of a notable whiteness. And we have already narrated in the preceding book both the methods and the times by the observation of which these and similar things can be done. 

Furthermore, the power of speech and words is especially to be observed by you: for through these the soul is expanded into inferior substances—into stones, metals, plants, animals, and all natural things—impressing upon them various forms and passions, exerting force over all creatures, or leading and drawing them by a certain love. Thus Cato <note>Cato the Elder, in his work on agriculture</note> testifies that weary oxen are restored by words. Then, that it can be obtained from the Earth <note>original: "Tellure"</note> by words and prayers that she nourish unusual trees; and that the trees themselves can be similarly entreated to migrate and grow in foreign soil. Also, that turnips become larger if, while they are being sown, they are beseeched to contribute generously to oneself, the family, and the neighbors. The peacock also, when praised, soon spreads its feathers; on the other hand, it is found that the herb basil <note>original: "ocymum"</note>, when planted with great curses and reproaches, brings forth more joyful fruit. Even the *garus* <note>a type of fish sauce or the fish itself</note> heals burns and inflammations if, meanwhile, the *garus* is not named. Then also, those who use the "evil eye" <note>original: "fascino"</note> kill trees by praising them, and harm crops and children. 

Furthermore, they say the power of human imprecations is so great that they even drive away and exterminate evil demons. For this reason, Eusebius relates that Serapis among the Egyptians produced cymbals by which demons were expelled; he also taught how demons, having assumed the shapes of brute animals, lie in wait for men. Finally, in all things, keep God before your eyes, for it is written in Deuteronomy: *When you seek the Lord your God, you will find him, if however you seek him with all your heart and with all the tribulation of your soul.* <note>Deuteronomy 4:29</note> Moreover, through a truthful and constant faith, one can appease God and all demons,

### The conclusion of the entire work.
->Chapter 65.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'H' featuring a scholar or clerical figure seated in a chair, possibly reading or teaching, within an ornate rectangular frame.</image-desc>
These are the things which we have gathered into this book concerning the introduction to magic <term>magia: the art of understanding and directing natural and divine forces</term> from the tradition of the ancients and various compilations, in a brief discourse indeed, but sufficient for those who are meant to understand. Some of these things are written in order, some without order; some are handed down in fragments, and some even hidden and left to the investigation of the intelligent, who, by looking more sharply and searching through what is written, are able to attain the complete teachings of the magical art as well as infallible experiments. For we have handed down this art in such a way that it might not happen to be hidden from the prudent and intelligent, but it does not admit the wicked and the faithless to the secrets of those mysteries <note>original: "secretorū illorum arcana"</note>; rather, it leaves them abandoned in a stupor, under the shadow of ignorance and desperation. You, therefore, sons of learning and wisdom, search through this book by gathering our scattered intention, which we have set forth in various places; and what was hidden by us in one place, we have made manifest in another, so that it may be open to you who are wise. For we have written for you alone, whose minds are incorrupt and established in the right order of living, whose chaste and modest minds and untainted faith fear and revere God, whose hands are separated from every wickedness and crime, and whose manners are modest, sober, and temperate. For you alone will find the doctrine preserved for you, and the secrets hidden by many riddles, which are not drawn out except by hidden intelligence. When you have attained this, the complete and invincible science of the magical discipline will instill itself into you, and those virtues will appear to you, such as formerly Hermes, Zoroaster, Apollonius, and the other workers of wonders attained. But you, malevolent slanderers, sons of wicked ignorance and foolish malice, flee from these our writings, for they are hostile to you and placed on a precipice, so that you may wander and fall into misery. If anyone, therefore, because of his own faithlessness and sluggishness of intellect, does not obtain his desire, let him not impute the fault of his ignorance to me, nor say that I have erred, or written false things on purpose, or lied, but let him accuse himself...

# TO THE VENERABLE FATHER,

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'E' within a square frame, depicting two figures in a room with architectural details; one figure is seated at a table, appearing to be engaged in writing or study.</image-desc>
From the letters which you sent to me on the second of this month, I perceived the sincerity of your mind toward me, Reverend Father; and I recognized you as a man of universal learning <note>original: "cyclice doctum," referring to the circle of liberal arts</note>, and a curious explorer of those things which still lie hidden in darkness. I rejoiced immediately, and I congratulate myself that I have obtained the friendship of such a man, with whom I might one day cultivate both my spirit and my intellect: and I now receive you (witnessed by this handwriting) among my closest friends. But hark! Who are your leaders whom you follow, you who dare to enter the inescapable house of Daedalus <note>The Labyrinth</note> and of the terrible Minos, to pass through the sentries, and to commit yourself to the Fates <note>original: "Parcis"</note>? Who are your masters, you who occupy yourself with immense things, daring to attempt to make the wandering stable, the treacherous constant, and the most fleeting of all gods more steadfast than Adrastia <note>A goddess of inevitable fate or retribution</note> herself? Beware lest you be deceived by those who were themselves deceived. For no amount of reading books will be able to direct you here, since they sound of nothing but mere enigmas. Oh, how many writings are read concerning the invincible power of the magical art, concerning the prodigious images of the astrologers, concerning the monstrous metamorphosis of the alchemists, and concerning that blessed stone, by which—like Midas—all things touched are soon changed into gold or silver; all of which are found to be vain, fictitious, and false whenever they are practiced according to the letter. And yet these things are handed down and written by great and most grave philosophers and holy men, whose traditions who would dare to call false? Indeed, it would be impious to believe that they wrote lies on purpose: there is, therefore, another sense than what is handed down in the letters, and that sense is covered with various mysteries, but so far explained openly by none of the masters; I know not if anyone could attain it by the reading of books alone without a skilled and faithful master, unless he be enlightened by a divine power, which is granted to very few. Therefore, many run in vain who pursue these most secret mysteries of nature, applying their minds only to the bare sequence of the reading. For having fallen away from the true understanding by an unpromising intellect, into...

# BOOK THREE.

...ensnared by the vessels of external spirits, through false imaginations, they have become dangerous servants to those whom they were meant to rule. Ignorant of their own selves, they wander backward following the tracks of their own flocks, seeking outside of themselves that which they possess within. And this is what I wish you to know now: that within us ourselves dwells the operator of all wonderful effects. He knows how to discern and accomplish whatever the portentous mathematicians, the prodigious magi, the envious alchemists <note>original: "alchymiſtæ"; those who seek to transform base metals into gold or find the elixir of life</note> who persecute nature, and the wicked necromancers <note>original: "necromantes"; those who communicate with the dead</note>—who are worse than demons—dare to promise. And he does so without any crime, without offense to God, and without injury to religion. Within us, I say, is that worker of wonders:

> He dwells in us, not in the underworld, nor in the stars of heaven;
> The Spirit that flourishes within us performs those deeds.

Truly, we should confer with you as extensively as possible regarding these matters, but in person. For these things are not committed to letters, nor written with a pen; rather, they are infused from spirit to spirit with a few sacred words, and that shall happen if ever I chance to come to you. As for the books you request, some of them were once in my possession, but they are no longer. Regarding the books of my youth titled *Of Occult Philosophy* <note>original: "De Occulta Philosophia"; Agrippa's famous work on magic</note> which are circulated among you: the first two are deficient in many ways, and the third is entirely mutilated, containing nothing but a certain epitome of my writings. But, the Lord favoring me, I shall one day publish the entire work, integrated and revised—though the key to the work shall be reserved for only my closest friends, of whom you should not doubt you are one. Farewell most happily. From Lyon <note>original: "Lugduno"</note>. September 24, Year 1527.

->TO THE SAME.<-

From your most kind letters (venerable father), I have looked into your whole soul as if into a mirror, and I embrace it entirely. I wish you to be persuaded that you are more welcome to me than can be shown in writing, and you reside most deeply in my soul. I am one who writes this from the abundance of the heart, and who is never accustomed to desert those who have committed themselves to my friendship, no matter the storm. Therefore, so that you may attain your wishes—which are no less than mine—I shall come to you shortly. When it is granted to hear and return voices in person, I know our friendship will be indissoluble and endure forever. 

Now, regarding the Philosophy you requested, I want you to know that to know God himself, the maker of all things, and to pass into him with the entire image of likeness (as if by a certain essential contact or bond), by which you yourself may be transformed and made a god—just as the Lord said of Moses, saying: *Behold, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh* <note>A reference to Exodus 7:1</note>. This is that true and supreme, most hidden philosophy of wonderful works. Its key is the intellect <note>original: "intellectus"; here meaning the higher spiritual understanding</note>. For the higher the things we understand, the more sublime the virtues we put on, and the greater the works we perform, both more easily and more effectively. is entirely ineffective for perceiving those most hidden secrets of God and nature; and "this is the task, this is the toil: to emerge into the upper air" <note>original: "hoc opus, hic labor est, superas euadere ad auras" — a famous quote from Virgil's Aeneid regarding the difficulty of returning from the underworld.</note>. For how shall he who has lost himself in ash and mortal dust find God himself? How shall he, immersed in flesh and blood, apprehend spiritual things? Shall a man see the Lord and live? Not that the body is separated from the soul, but that the soul leaves the body; concerning which death Paul writes to the Colossians: "You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ." And elsewhere he says more clearly of himself: "I know a man, whether in the body or out of the body I know not, God knows, caught up even to the third heaven," and what follows. In this death, I say, "precious in the sight of the Lord," it is necessary to die. This happens to very few, and perhaps not always. For "the few whom impartial Jupiter has loved, or whom glowing virtue has lifted to the heavens, born of the gods, were able to do it" <note>Another Virgilian reference (Aeneid VI) regarding the rare few who achieve divine heights.</note>. First, those who are born not of flesh and blood, but of God; next, those who, by the benefit of nature and the gift of their birth-horoscope <term>genethliaco dono: a gift determined by the stars at the moment of birth</term>, have been made worthy of it. The rest strive by merits and by art, concerning which a living voice shall make you more certain.

But I wish you to be warned of this: do not be deceived regarding me, as if I, having at some time experienced divine things, preach these things to you, or wish to claim such a thing for myself, or hope it could be granted to me. For I, who have until now been a soldier consecrated in human blood, almost always a courtier, bound by the bond of the flesh to a most dear wife, and exposed to all the blasts of unstable fortune, driven sideways entirely by the flesh, by the world, and by domestic cares, have not attained such sublime gifts of the immortal gods. But I wish to be accepted as a signpost <note>original: "indicem" — a pointer or guide</note> who, always remaining before the gates himself, shows to others which path must be entered. Furthermore, concerning my love for you, you are indeed not at all deceived; what you owe to my favors I do not see, since I have contributed nothing to you, except that I am ready, when the opportunity is given, to contribute everything. Now, most happily, Farewell. From Lyon, November 19, in the year 1527.

# CCCXLI
## LETTER.

I shall explain its argument to you. Hear now, therefore, a matter both foolish and impious:
A certain man of demons—that is, a <term>cacomagus</term> <note>original: "cacomagus"; a Greek-derived term for an evil sorcerer or black magician</note>—has been summoned from Germany at no small expense. He is one in whom the power of demons dwells, so that just as Jannes and Mambres <note>The traditional names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses in Exodus</note> resisted Moses, so this man might resist Caesar. For they have been persuaded by the father of lies that he has foreknowledge of all future events, is privy to any secret counsels whatsoever, and is an interpreter of deliberate thoughts. Furthermore, he is said to be endowed with such great power that he can transport the royal children through the air, just as it is read that Habakkuk was carried with his pottage to the lions' den. He is supposedly able, like Elisha when besieged in Dothan, to show mountains full of horses and chariots of fire and a vast army. Moreover, he can reveal and transfer the treasures of the earth, compel or dissolve marriages and loves as he wishes, and cure every desperate disease with Stygian medicine—such as deep-rooted consumption, established dropsy, or bone-deep elephantiasis, and that which:
> Medicine knows not how to untie, the knotty gout,
> And many things besides which obscure rumor hides.

You see where their faith is placed, where their hope is stored—they who attempt to subject the elements, heaven, the fates, nature, providence, God, and all things to the command of a single magician. They seek the safety of the kingdom from the demons, the enemies of public safety, saying in their hearts with Ahaziah: "Is there no God in Israel, that we go to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron?" And just as Saul spoke to the medium <note>original: "Pythonem"; referring to the Witch of Endor</note>, saying: "The Philistines fight against me, and the Lord has departed from me and would not hear me; therefore I have called you." Has hope in God been so despaired of among these men that they have judged it necessary to seek the aid of demons? Is this not, according to the word of Jude and Peter, to deny our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior and Him who redeemed us, and to bring upon themselves swift destruction? Do they not store up for themselves the wrath of the Lord's indignation, which sends among them infestations by evil angels? Have they not been given over to a reprobate mind, they who seek the truth of a secret counsel from the devil, the father of lies, and demand victory from elsewhere than from the Lord of Hosts? And yet, for such a nefarious practitioner of idolatry and sacrilege, boldness is provided by that "orthodox mother" <note>Likely a sarcastic reference to the Queen Mother or the Church institution supporting the court</note> who so dearly favors these things; the authority of the "Most Christian sons" is granted to him, and gifts are bestowed from sacred funds. Even the pillars of the Church—the bishops and cardinals—wink at and hire such wicked labor, and the impious nobles applaud the minister of impiety, just as crows congratulate the works of the wolf. What greater sin did Pharaoh, Balak, Saul, Ahab with his Jezebel, Ahaziah, Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Sennacherib, and the other worshippers of Baal commit? Pharaoh called his magicians against Moses, and they, defeated at the third plague, confessed the finger of God; but the king, being obstinate through ten plagues, perished in the Red Sea. Balak the Moabite called Balaam the soothsayer to curse Israel, and God himself turned the curse into a blessing, while Balak himself was cursed. What did the answers of his Samuel or the medium profit Saul? Was he not pierced through on Mount Gilboa? Ahab and Jezebel, joined in nefarious marriage, trusted in the prophets...

# EPISTLE

Baal, and according to the word of God, a lying spirit went forth into the mouths of all the prophets <note>referring to 1 Kings 22:22</note> who promised success to Ahab as he was about to go up into Ramoth-Gilead; and so Ahab fell, and Jezebel was cast down, and the dogs devoured them. Asa, King of Judah, was rebuked by the prophet of the Lord because in his sickness he did not seek the Lord, but trusted in the skill of physicians. Will not those be held in greater sin who, abandoning God the Savior and the healthy forces of nature, seek health from Satan? Ahaziah once did so, and for that reason he heard from the prophet of the Lord: "From the bed which you have climbed, you shall not descend, but you shall die the death."

Let the series of other unfaithful kings be run through, even the histories of the pagans: Zoroaster, Deiotarus, Croesus, Pompey, Pyrrhus, Crassus, Nero, Julian—what did they gain from their mages and diviners who lied to them of happy outcomes? Were they not all reduced to nothing and perished miserably in their sins? Thus those impious trifles are always accustomed to bring ruin to those who cultivate them; indeed, those who trust in them most are rendered the most unhappy of all.

I do not deny that there are natural sciences, there are metaphysical arts, and there are hidden talents by which—without offending God and without injury to faith and religion—kingdoms can be protected, plans explored, enemies conquered, captives rescued, riches increased, the goodwill of men won over, sicknesses driven away, health preserved, life prolonged, and the strength of youth restored. There are, moreover, the intercessions of holy religion, public supplications, and the private prayers of good men, by which we are able not only to turn away the wrath of God but also to obtain His favor for ourselves.

But if, besides these, there is a certain art of foreknowledge and of wonderful works, which the ancients call <term>Calomagia</term> <note>Beautiful or Good Magic</note> or <term>Theurgy</term> <note>Divine-working or high white magic</note>, certainly this is unknown to those triflers and slaves of demons. For to investigate the truth regarding the future or imminent events or other hidden things—those things portended to men by divine will—and to perform works of power exceeding the common custom of nature, belongs only to those of profound and perfect learning and of the most upright life and faith, not to men who are most frivolous and unlearned.

To men who are innocent and learned in the law of the Lord, every creature serves according to the devotion of their faith, and they are heard in whatever they ask. Thus the raven fed Elijah, and at his prayers the earth withheld its fruit, the heaven denied rain, and vomited its fires upon the impious. Thus bears served Elisha, angels fought for him, and rivers were crossed with dry feet. To Daniel, the lions—their ferocity set aside and their hunger ignored—acted with fawning affection; and the fire kindled in the furnace did not burn the boys. Works of this kind belong not to <term>Cacomagi</term> <note>Evil magicians</note>, nor to <term>Geotici</term> <note>Practitioners of 'goetia' or low, earthy sorcery</note>, nor to demons, but to faithful and divine men; for it is not demons, but the Spirit of God that serves them.

I confess there are some, even to this day (and perhaps many), men grave in wisdom, distinguished in knowledge, powerful in virtues and abilities, upright in life and character, unconquered in prudence, and even fit in age and strength, so that they might be of great benefit to the commonwealth by their counsel and labor. But your courtiers despise these men as being far different from their own purpose, for whom malice stands in place of wisdom, and fraud and de—

# THE JUDGMENT OR RETRACTION OF
## HENRY CORNELIUS
### AGRIPPA
### Concerning Magic, from his declamation on the Vanity of the Sciences and the Excellence of the Word of God.

### ON MAGIC IN GENERAL.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a seated figure in academic or clerical robes, possibly a scholar or teacher, within an architectural frame.</image-desc> This place also demands that we speak of Magic, for it is so joined and related to astrology that he who professes magic without astrology achieves nothing, but wanders entirely from the path. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> thinks that magic derived both its name and origin from the Maguseans. The common opinion is that the name is Persian, which Porphyry and Apuleius support, and that in their language it signifies the same as a priest, a wise man, or a philosopher. Magic, therefore, having embraced all philosophy, Physics, and Mathematics, also joins the powers of religions to them. Hence it also contains within itself both <term>Goetia</term> <note>Low magic or sorcery involving the invocation of spirits</note> and <term>Theurgy</term> <note>High magic or "divine work" aimed at union with the divine</note>. For this reason, most people divide magic into two parts: namely, the natural and the ceremonial.

### ON NATURAL MAGIC.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring a seated figure, possibly a youth or an angel, resting against the letter within a square frame.</image-desc> They consider Natural Magic to be nothing other than the highest power of the natural sciences, which they therefore call the highest peak of natural philosophy and its most absolute consummation; it is the active portion of natural philosophy, which [harnesses] the [virtues] of natural things...

# ON NATURAL MAGIC. 355.

With the assistance of virtues, and from their mutual and timely application, it produces works that are beyond all grasp of admiration. This was the magic used most extensively by the Ethiopians and Indians, where there was an abundance of herbs, stones, and other things pertaining to that faculty. They wish to recall that Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin.</note> in his letter to Paulinus says that Apollonius of Tyana <note>A Greek Neopythagorean philosopher often compared to Jesus in antiquity.</note> was a mage, or a philosopher, as the Pythagoreans were. Of this kind also were the Magi who visited and adored the newborn Christ with gifts, whom the interpreters of the Gospels explain were the philosophers of the Chaldeans. Such were Hiarchas among the Brahmans, Tespion among the Gymnosophists <note>term: Gymnosophists (Ancient Greek "naked philosophers"), a sect of Indian philosophers who practiced asceticism.</note>, Buddha among the Babylonians, Numa Pompilius among the Romans, Zamolxides among the Thracians, Abbaris among the Hyperboreans, Hermes among the Egyptians, and Zoroaster the son of Oromasus among the Persians. For the Indians, Ethiopians, Chaldeans, and Persians especially excelled in this magic. Because of this (as Plato narrates in the *Alcibiades*), the sons of the Persian kings are imbued with it, so that they might learn to administer and distribute their own republic according to the image of the world’s republic. And Cicero, in his books *On Divination*, says that no one among the Persians obtains the kingdom who has not first learned magic.

Natural magic, therefore, is that which, having contemplated the powers of all natural and celestial things and having scrutinized their sympathy <note>The "sympathy of all things" is the occult belief that all parts of the universe are interconnected.</note> with curious investigation, brings forth into the open the hidden and latent powers in nature. It joins lower things to the endowments of higher things as if they were certain allurements, through the mutual application of their properties to one another, so that from there, stupendous miracles often arise—not so much by art as by nature, to which this art shows itself as a servant while nature works. For the Magi, as the most accurate explorers of nature, by bringing together those things which have been prepared by nature and by applying active things to passive ones, very often produce effects before the time ordained by nature. The common people think these are miracles, when they are nevertheless natural works, occurring only through the intervention of the prevention of time <note>i.e., accelerating natural processes.</note>. For example, if someone should produce roses in the month of March, or ripe grapes, or make sown beans or parsley grow into a perfect plant within a few hours; and greater things than these, such as clouds, rains, thunder, and various kinds of animals, and many transmutations of things, many of which Roger Bacon boasts he performed by pure and natural magic.

Zoroaster, Hermes, Euanthes the King of the Arabs, Zacharias the Babylonian, Joseph the Hebrew, Bocus, Aaron, Zenotenus, Kiranides, Almadal, Thetel, Alchindus, Abel, Ptolemy, Geber, Zahel, Nazabarub, Tebith, Berith, Solomon, Astaphon, Hipparchus, Alcmeon, Apollonius, Triphon, and many others wrote about its works. Some of their works are still intact, and many fragments still exist, and have sometimes come into my hands. Among the more recent authors, however, few have written on natural magic, and those few have written little, such as Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, the medieval polymath.</note>, Arnold of Villanova, Raymond Lull, Bacon, and Abano, and the author of the book to Alfonso published under the name of *Picatrix* <note>A famous medieval grimoire of astrological magic.</note>, who nevertheless mixes much superstition in with natural magic, which indeed others have also done.

...[they] promise that by adopting the influences of the heavens, they can produce works similar to those of nature, such as bodies that walk or speak, which nevertheless do not possess animal souls. Such was the wooden dove of Archytas <note>Archytas of Tarentum (4th century BCE), a Greek philosopher and mathematician credited with inventing the first self-propelled flying machine.</note> which flew, and the statues of Mercury which spoke, and the bronze head fabricated by Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century scholar and bishop; legend claims he built a mechanical brass head that could answer questions.</note> which they say talked. Boethius excelled in these matters, a man of the greatest genius and manifold erudition; Cassiodorus, writing to him about such things, said: "It is your purpose to know difficult things and to show miracles; by the genius of your art, metals low, Diomedes sounds a trumpet more gravely in brass, a bronze snake hisses, imitation birds—which do not know how to have their own voice—are proven to emit the sweetness of song; we report small things of him for whom it is lawful to imitate the heavens." I think it was said of these crafts what we read in Plato in the eleventh book of the *Laws*: "Art was given to mortals so they might generate certain later things, not indeed participants in truth and divinity, but they might lead down certain likenesses related to themselves." And the most audacious magi have progressed so far as to perpetrate all things, favored especially by that ancient and powerful serpent, the promiser of knowledge, so that like apes, they might attempt to emulate God and nature.

### ON VENOMOUS MAGIC.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' featuring a seated scholar or cleric working at a desk or lectern with books and instruments.</image-desc>

There is, furthermore, a species of natural magic which they call venomous, or pharmacy <note>original: "veneficam, siue pharmaciā"; in this context, it refers to the use of drugs, potions, and herbs rather than just poisons.</note>, which is accomplished by cups, philters, and various medicaments of sorcery. We read that Democritus composed such a thing by which good, happy, and fortunate sons might be begotten; and another by which we might rightly understand the voices of birds, as Philostratus and Porphyry relate concerning Apollonius. Virgil also, speaking of certain Pontic herbs, said:

> By these I have often seen Moeris become a wolf and hide in the woods,
> often seen souls come out from the depths of the tombs,
> and seen crops translated to another place.

And Pliny relates that a certain Demarchus of Parrhasia, in a sacrifice which the Arcadians made to Lycaean Jove with a human victim, tasted the entrails of an immolated boy and turned himself into a wolf. Because of this change of men into wolves, Augustine thinks the name was given to Lycaean Pan and Lycaean Jove <note>The term "Lycaean" relates to the Greek 'lykos' for wolf; this refers to the origins of lycanthropy myths.</note>. The same Augustine relates that while he was in Italy, certain female magi, like Circe, having given a sorcery in cheese to travelers, turned them into beasts of burden; and when they had carried whatever loads pleased the women, they restored them back into men, and that this happened to a certain father, Praestantius, at that time. But lest anyone think these things are entirely ravings and impossibilities, let him remember how the Sacred Scriptures relate that King Nebuchadnezzar was changed into an ox and lived on hay for seven years, and finally by the mercy of God returned to being a man; whose body after death his son Evil-Merodach gave as food to vultures, lest he should ever rise from the dead, because he had already returned from a beast into a man. Exodus relates many such things concerning the magi of Pharaoh. Truly, the Wise Man speaks of these, whether magi or sorcerers, when he says: "You abhorred them, O God, because they did horrible works to you through medicaments."
